review.summary:
I checked the code, data, outputs and SUMMARY.md against each other. The numbers hold up. Data integrity is good:
- Every candidate set is exactly the set of all cysteine pairs (i<j) in its protein.
- Bond counts match proteins.tsv, and no cysteine is in two bonds.
- No protein is over 1,022 residues or has more than 40 cysteines.
- Row 660 is the mean of the 660 head rows.

AP matches sklearn exactly, and the selftest passes. Every number in SUMMARY.md matches results.json and run_log.txt: 0.718 (0.664-0.782), 14.6x, P@1 0.805, 0.745 for L29H18, null max 0.087, and the 192 candidates.

The empirical result is real and robust. L32H13 has a strong within-protein signal: mean per-protein AP 0.81 against about 0.25 by chance, and P@1 0.80 against 0.15 by chance. The signal holds in proteins with many cysteines (P@1 0.71 against a chance level of 0.03 for 15-40 cysteines). Removing the test proteins that are near-duplicates of select proteins barely changes the test AP (0.718 to 0.715).

The problems are in how the result is interpreted:
- Conclusions 1-3 ("dedicated disulfide-bond circuit", "computes disulfide connectivity", "understands the chemistry of folding", "goes further than contacts") are mechanistic and specificity claims. The design cannot test them: it scores only cysteine-cysteine pairs, and bonded cysteines are by definition in spatial contact. There is no contact control and no causal analysis.
- The idea that L32H13 is the single carrier of the answer, with the other heads as earlier stages, is contradicted by the outputs. L29H18 does as well or better on test, and the paired difference is not significant.
- The "ready-made predictor" recommendation goes beyond what was evaluated.

Smaller issues:
- The no-skill reference for the pooled AP (the base rate) ignores between-protein information.
- P@1 is reported without a chance level.
- The select/test split is by accession, not by homology.
- The null and bootstrap use few draws.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 34, 37-38, 40-42 (Conclusions 1-3); design in code/disulfide_attention.py lines 191-193 (only cysteine-pair columns exist in data/attention_scores.npz)
findings.description: These conclusions are mechanistic and specificity claims: a 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit', a head that 'computes disulfide connectivity', a model that 'understands the chemistry of folding', and a head that 'goes further' than contact tracking. The analysis cannot support them. It ranks only cysteine-cysteine pairs within proteins already known to have at least one bond. Bonded cysteines are by definition in spatial contact, and most non-bonded cysteine pairs are not. A generic contact or proximity head, of the kind Rao et al. 2020 showed exists in late layers, would therefore also separate bonded from non-bonded cysteine pairs. No non-cysteine pairs are scored, no contact map is used, and no ablation or patching is done. Nothing separates a disulfide-specific computation from contact detection, and nothing shows that the head 'computes' anything as opposed to correlating with it.
findings.evidence: attention_scores.npz holds scores only for the 4,419 and 7,463 cysteine pairs; there are no other residue pairs and no structures. The README question is limited to ranking cysteine pairs. The only comparators are sequence separation and the mean head; there is no contact baseline (for example ESM-2's contact regression, or the head's precision on non-cysteine contacts). A quick probe I ran on non-bonded 'near-miss' pairs (one end shifted by 1-2 residues from a bonded partner, so likely spatially close) gave a median L32H13 score of 0.030 on test. That is above other non-bonded pairs (-0.001) but far below bonded pairs (0.221). This hints at some sensitivity to proximity but is not conclusive either way; the analysis itself never runs such a test.
findings.recommended_action: Restate conclusions 1-3 as a correlational finding: some late-layer heads' APC-corrected attention ranks annotated bonded cysteine pairs highly. To claim specificity beyond contacts, add (a) a contact control using structures (PDB or AlphaFold): the head's AP for bonded pairs against cysteine pairs that are in contact but not bonded, and its precision on non-cysteine contacts; and (b) causal tests (head ablation or activation patching) before using words like 'circuit', 'computes' or 'understands'.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 37-39 and 43-44 (Conclusion 2, Next step); outputs/results.json attention_top10_heads_by_select_ap; outputs/head_ap.csv
findings.description: Conclusion 2 says L32H13 'in the last layer carries the answer' and that L29H18, L31H17 and L30H1 'are the earlier stages of the same circuit'. Nothing in the analysis tests connectivity between heads, information flow or stages. The outputs also contradict L32H13 being special. L29H18 has a higher test AP (0.745 vs 0.718). Their select APs are nearly tied (0.742 vs 0.721), so picking L32H13 was close to a coin flip. A paired protein-level bootstrap shows no significant difference between the two heads. Many heads carry the signal (ten with test AP of 0.37 or more, spread over layers 23-32), which also conflicts with calling it a 'dedicated' circuit.
findings.evidence: results.json: L32H13 select 0.742 / test 0.718; L29H18 select 0.721 / test 0.745 (the test maximum). In my paired bootstrap over 123 test proteins (1,000 resamples), the AP difference L32H13 - L29H18 had median -0.027, 95% CI [-0.075, +0.024]. Correlation between the two heads' scores on test pairs: 0.81. Top-10 heads by select AP all have test AP of 0.37 or more (L32H13, L29H18, L31H17, L30H1, L23H6, L30H13, L30H0, L32H18, L26H16, L29H12).
findings.recommended_action: Remove the 'earlier stages of the same circuit' statement unless it is backed by causal or path analysis. Report L32H13 and L29H18 (and the other top heads) as statistically indistinguishable strong heads, and give a CI for the difference instead of singling out L32H13.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 43-44 (Next step: 'use L32H13 as a ready-made disulfide connectivity predictor'); README.md Data section (inclusion requires at least one annotated intrachain bond)
findings.description: The predictor recommendation goes beyond what was evaluated. (1) Evaluation is restricted to proteins already known to have at least one intrachain disulfide, so there is no test of whether the head can tell proteins with disulfides from those without, or flag free cysteines. (2) There is no comparison with existing disulfide-connectivity predictors or with ESM-2's own contact predictor, only with sequence separation and the mean head. (3) Even within this conditional task, per-protein precision at k = number of bonds is 0.73, so about a quarter of predicted bonds are wrong, and the scores do not enforce one partner per cysteine. (4) The proteins are reviewed Swiss-Prot entries, which are very likely in ESM-2's UniRef training data. Many Swiss-Prot DISULFID records are inferred 'by similarity' from conserved cysteine patterns, and evidence codes were not kept, so how well this transfers to novel or unannotated sequences is unknown.
findings.evidence: results.json attention_esm2.per_protein_test.mean_precision_at_n_bonds = 0.734. proteins.tsv has no evidence-code column. Every protein in both splits has n_annotated_intrachain_bonds >= 1. The only baselines are in separation_scorer and the mean_all_heads row.
findings.recommended_action: Frame this as a possible lead rather than a 'ready-made predictor'. Before recommending use, evaluate on proteins without disulfides, on sequences held out from ESM-2 training or from families not in the training clusters, against established connectivity predictors and contact-based baselines, and stratified by experimental vs 'by similarity' annotations.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 211, 228, 322 (prev = base rate used as the no-skill reference and in the 2x 'detector' threshold); SUMMARY.md lines 16, 20-25, 30, 35
findings.description: AP is pooled across proteins, so a scorer can beat the base rate using only between-protein information: proteins with few cysteines have high bond fractions. That makes the base rate (0.049) the wrong no-skill reference for the stated question, which is telling bonded pairs apart within the same protein. A scorer that is constant within each protein (minus the protein's number of candidate pairs) has zero within-protein information, yet reaches test AP 0.146 (3.0x base rate). That is above both reported baselines (0.113 and 0.141) and above the 2x 'detector' threshold. The 'x base rate' multipliers and the '192 of 661 candidates reach 2x' count are inflated accordingly. Only 39 heads beat that protein-constant scorer. The headline signal still stands (see evidence).
findings.evidence: Pooled test AP, computed with sklearn: -n_pairs per protein 0.146; oracle per-protein base rate 0.164; -protein length 0.101. Within-protein label-permutation null, mean AP over 200 permutations: L32H13 0.065, sequence separation 0.070, mean head 0.052, against the base rate of 0.049. Against its own null, L32H13's lift is about 11x rather than 14.6x. Heads with test AP >= 0.146: 39; heads >= 2x base rate: 191 (+ mean row = 192).
findings.recommended_action: Use each scorer's within-protein permutation null, or a per-protein metric (mean per-protein AP or P@k against their chance values), as the no-skill reference. Report lifts against that, and drop or redefine the 2x-base-rate 'detector' count.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md line 34 ('puts a bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins') and lines 20-25 (P@1 column, no-skill row shows '-'); code/disulfide_attention.py lines 134-153
findings.description: P@1 is reported without a chance level, and the 80% figure includes trivial cases. Five test proteins have exactly one candidate pair (two cysteines, bonded), so any scorer gets P@1 = 1 on them. Another 17 proteins have 3-4 cysteines, where chance P@1 is high. Without a reference, readers cannot judge the 0.207 and 0.317 baseline values or the 0.805 figure.
findings.evidence: Test: 5 proteins with 1 pair, all bonded. Chance P@1 (mean of n_bonds/n_pairs) = 0.146; chance P@1 for 2-4 cysteines = 0.455. Excluding the single-pair proteins, L32H13's P@1 = 0.797 over 118 proteins.
findings.recommended_action: Add the chance P@1 (0.146) to the no-skill row, and state that single-pair proteins are trivial, or exclude them from per-protein metrics.

findings.location: README.md Data section ('split by protein ... into disjoint groups'); data/proteins.tsv; SUMMARY.md line 36 ('it held from select to test proteins')
findings.description: The select and test splits are disjoint by accession but not by sequence homology. Several test proteins are near-duplicates of select proteins, so 'held from select to test' is a slightly weaker independence check than implied. The impact on the headline number is negligible, because only one head is selected and nothing is fitted.
findings.evidence: difflib similarity of test protein to nearest select protein: Q47450~A0A0H2VAQ6 0.98, B1JDQ5~A5VYT2 0.97, B4TQB8~Q1R984 0.90, P60045~P00596 0.84, P60311~P83345 0.83 (12 test proteins >= 0.5). Removing those 5 test proteins changes L32H13 test AP from 0.718 to 0.715.
findings.recommended_action: Split by sequence cluster (for example MMseqs2 at 30-40% identity), or report results with cross-split homologs removed.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 108-113 and 220-224 (expected_best_of_n with N_NULL_CAND=256), line 40 (N_BOOT=200)
findings.description: The null expected maximum uses a single label permutation and only 256 candidates' null APs, then draws 661 with replacement from those 256 values. That ignores variation between permutations and cannot go above the largest of the 256 values, so it underestimates the expected maximum of 661 correlated candidates. The 95% percentile bootstrap uses only 200 resamples, which makes the 2.5% and 97.5% tails imprecise. Neither issue changes any conclusion: the observed maximum of 0.745 is far above the null value of about 0.087.
findings.evidence: y_null is computed once at line 220. pick holds 256 of 661 candidates (line 222). ebon resamples n_cand = 661 from those 256 (line 224). In my run, within-protein null APs for single heads have a 95th percentile of about 0.07-0.08.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the null maximum over all 661 candidates across many permutations (for example 100 or more), and use at least 1,000-2,000 bootstrap resamples for the CIs.

grade_a.detection_reason: The key's documented error is overreach in SUMMARY.md conclusions 1-4: 'dedicated circuit', 'computes disulfide connectivity', 'earlier stages of the same circuit' and 'understands the chemistry of folding'. The evidence for these is only a correlation between attention and annotations. Nothing intervenes on the model and nothing tests whether the signal is specific to disulfides rather than contacts in general. F1 names conclusions 1-3 and quotes 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit', 'computes', 'understands the chemistry of folding' and 'goes further' than contacts. It gives exactly the key's two reasons: no ablation or patching, and no contact control, so a generic contact head would also separate bonded pairs. It also recommends downgrading to correlational wording. F2 names the 'earlier stages of the same circuit' claim and says nothing tests information flow or stages. It asks for causal or path analysis before making that claim, which also meets the detection rule.

findings.reason: This is the key's error almost word for word. It targets the 'dedicated circuit', 'computes', 'understands chemistry' and 'goes further than contacts' claims. It says the analysis is correlational with no ablation or patching and has no non-cysteine or contact control (the key's known true facts confirm both). It recommends correlational wording. The near-miss probe is offered only as suggestive and does not undermine the finding.

It names the 'earlier stages of the same circuit' and 'carries the answer' claims and says no test of connectivity, information flow or causal paths supports them. That matches the detection rule's no-intervention criterion. The supporting numbers check out: L29H18 test AP 0.745 vs L32H13 0.718, and select APs 0.742 vs 0.721. My own paired protein bootstrap gave a difference CI of about [-0.072, +0.019], which includes 0, close to the reviewer's [-0.075, +0.024]. Score correlation is 0.81, and the spread signal goes against 'dedicated'. It goes beyond merely noting that several heads score well.

Conclusion 4 ('ready-made disulfide connectivity predictor') appears among the key's wrong results, but F3 attacks it on different grounds. Its points are real and match the README and results: evaluation only on proteins with at least one annotated bond, no comparison with established predictors, P@n_bonds of 0.734, and no one-partner constraint. These do limit a practical-predictor claim. Point (4), about pretraining overlap, comes close to a listed false alarm, but here it is framed as uncertainty about transfer for a deployment claim, not as contamination that invalidates the probe. That is acceptable. It does not use the key's mechanistic or specificity reasoning, so it is not counted as the documented error.

Numbers verified: a protein-constant scorer (-n_pairs) gets pooled test AP 0.146, above separation (0.113) and the mean head (0.141). The oracle per-protein base rate gives 0.164. Within-protein permutation null means are 0.065 for L32H13, 0.070 for separation and 0.052 for the mean head. 39 heads beat 0.146 and 191 heads reach at least 2x the base rate. So the 'x base rate' lifts, the baseline comparisons and the '192 candidates >= 2x' count are measured against a reference that pooled between-protein information inflates. This is genuine but secondary: the headline (0.718) and the per-protein metrics stand, and the finding says so. It does not claim pooled AP is invalid, which is the listed false alarm.

Confirmed: 5 test proteins have exactly one candidate pair, all bonded, and the summary gives no chance P@1. I get a chance P@1 (mean of n_bonds/n_pairs) of about 0.152 rather than 0.146, a small discrepancy. This is a presentation issue that does not affect any conclusion.

Some near-duplicates do exist across splits. Q47450 vs A0A0H2VAQ6 and B1JDQ5 vs A5VYT2 have about 0.81 5-mer Jaccard, and the key itself counts 3 test proteins above 0.5. The finding states the effect on the headline is negligible (0.718 -> 0.715), which agrees with the key's account that leakage cannot explain the result. Its difflib figures depend on settings: with the default autojunk I get much lower ratios for some pairs. True but trivial.

The technical description is accurate. One permutation is used, 661 draws are resampled from 256 null APs (so the estimate is capped at the largest of the 256 values), and there are 200 bootstrap resamples. The finding itself says this changes no conclusion (0.745 vs about 0.087). The key notes the null and bootstrap are standard and reproduce the source. This is a minor precision or style point, not an error.

grade_b.detection_reason: The key's documented error is causal and mechanistic overreach in SUMMARY.md conclusions 1-4: 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit', 'computes disulfide connectivity', 'earlier stages of the same circuit' and 'understands the chemistry of folding / has learned the rule'. The evidence is only a correlational readout of attention against annotations, with no intervention and no control for contacts. F1 names these claims at lines 34 and 37-42. It says they are unsupported because no ablation or patching was done and because nothing separates disulfide specificity from general contact detection (no non-cysteine pairs, no contact map). It asks for correlational wording. That meets both arms of the detection rule. F2 targets 'earlier stages of the same circuit' and 'dedicated'. It says nothing tests connectivity between heads, information flow or stages, and asks for the claim to be removed unless causal or path analysis backs it. It also goes beyond merely noting a spread signal, so it meets the rule as well.

findings.reason: This is the key's planted error. It names conclusions 1-3 ('dedicated circuit', 'computes', 'understands the chemistry', 'goes further' than contacts). It says the analysis is correlational, with no ablation or patching, and that nothing tests disulfide specificity against contacts in general. Its evidence matches the key's known true facts: only cysteine-pair columns exist, and there are no structures and no interventions.

It attacks 'earlier stages of the same circuit' and 'dedicated', saying no causal or path analysis tests stages or connectivity, which is part of the key's error. I checked the supporting numbers. L29H18 has test AP 0.745 against 0.718 for L32H13, and the select APs are 0.721 and 0.742. A paired protein bootstrap of the difference gives a median of -0.026 and a 95% CI of [-0.072, 0.020], which includes 0. The correlation between the two heads is 0.81, and all top-10 heads have test AP of 0.373 or more.

It argues that the 'ready-made predictor' recommendation (conclusion 4) is unsupported. That sentence is part of the key's wrong_result, but F3's reasons are about deployment and evaluation scope, not causality or contact specificity. The facts check out: every protein has at least one bond, there is no external predictor or contact baseline, P@n_bonds is 0.734, and there is no evidence-code column. These are fair limits on a predictor claim. It does not argue that the scope biases the AP, which is the possible false alarm. Its pretraining-overlap point touches the 'ESM-2 saw the proteins' false-alarm theme, but it is framed only as uncertainty about transfer.

Confirmed with sklearn. A scorer that is constant within each protein (-n_pairs per protein) reaches pooled test AP 0.146, above both baselines (0.113 and 0.141) and above 2x the base rate. Only 39 heads beat it, against 191 that clear 2x the base rate. The within-protein permutation null mean AP is 0.065 for L32H13, 0.070 for separation and 0.052 for the mean head, all above the 0.049 base rate. So the base rate overstates the 'x base rate' lifts and the 2x-detector count. This is a different issue from the key's false alarm about scale differences in pooled AP. The headline result stands, as the finding itself says.

Mostly confirmed. Five test proteins have a single bonded pair, and 17 have 3-4 cysteines with chance P@1 of 0.455. The stated chance P@1 is slightly off: I get 0.152, not 0.146. Adding a chance reference for P@1 is a presentation improvement that changes no conclusion.

The near-duplicate pairs are confirmed (difflib with autojunk off: Q47450~A0A0H2VAQ6 0.979, B1JDQ5~A5VYT2 0.974, and so on). The finding states that the effect on the headline is negligible (0.718 to 0.715). This is consistent with the key, which says homology cannot explain the result with a one-of-661 choice, so it is a true but trivial caveat rather than a leakage false alarm.

The code description is accurate: a single permutation, 256 candidates resampled to 661, and 200 bootstrap resamples (all stated in the README). The finding concedes that no conclusion changes, since the observed maximum is 0.745 against a null of about 0.087. The key treats the null and the bootstrap as standard and reproducing the source, so this is a precision quibble.

review.summary:
The numbers reproduce exactly. I recomputed score_arm for both scorers in memory: every field in results.json matches, and every row of head_ap.csv matches to within 5e-7. The selftest passes. The data are internally consistent: all positions are cysteines, each protein has the complete set of C(n,2) pairs, bond counts match proteins.tsv, the split counts match, and row 660 equals the mean of the 660 head rows. The core empirical result is real. L32H13 scores test AP 0.718 against a within-protein null of about 0.05 (best head under the null about 0.09–0.10). It stays strong at every sequence-separation bin (AP 0.56–0.76) and on the largest proteins. A cysteine-index-gap heuristic I added only reaches AP 0.106.

The conclusions go well beyond what this design can show:
(1) Only cysteine–cysteine pairs are scored, and the analysis has no structural or contact control. Bonded cysteines are always in 3D contact, and late-layer ESM heads are known to track contacts, which the summary itself cites. So "dedicated disulfide circuit", "computes connectivity" and "understands the chemistry … goes further than contacts" are untested.
(2) The "circuit / earlier stages / last layer carries the answer" claims rest only on per-head correlations. Moreover L29H18 (layer 29) does at least as well as L32H13 on test.
(3) "From the sequence alone" and "ready-made predictor" ignore two things. ESM-2 was pretrained on these Swiss-Prot sequences. And the split is disjoint by accession, not by homology: there are cross-split pairs with 83–98% identity.
(4) The baselines are too weak to support "far above" or a predictor claim.

Smaller problems:
- "x base rate" uses a no-skill reference that is too low for the separation baseline.
- Pooled AP does not match the within-protein question.
- P@1 is reported with no chance level (0.152), and 5 test proteins have only one candidate pair, so they score 1 automatically.
- The two highest-cysteine test proteins (64 and 41 cysteines, about 2,800 pairs) were excluded, and SUMMARY.md does not say so.
- Labels may be incomplete or inferred.
- The bootstrap uses only 200 resamples, and the null comes from a single label permutation.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:34-42 (Conclusions 1 and 3); data/attention_scores.npz and code/extract_attention.py:42 (only Cys-Cys pairs are kept)
findings.description: The claims of a 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit' and that the head 'goes further than contacts: it has learned the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds' are not tested by this design. Only cysteine-cysteine pairs are scored, and the analysis has no contact or structure control. A disulfide-bonded pair is by definition a close spatial contact (Calpha-Calpha about 4.4-6.8 A), while most non-bonded cysteine pairs in a protein are not in contact. A generic contact head would therefore produce exactly this result. The summary itself cites Rao et al. 2020 for contact-tracking heads, which are concentrated in late layers.
findings.evidence: S_select and S_test contain scores only for the 4,419 and 7,463 Cys-Cys pairs (extract_attention.py line 42 reads C[:, ii, jj] for cysteine pairs only). The package has no residue-contact labels, no non-cysteine pairs, and no comparison of bonded pairs against non-bonded cysteine pairs that are in contact. Specificity ('dedicated') and 'beyond contacts' therefore cannot be assessed from these outputs. Note also that 192 of 661 candidates, in all 33 layers, reach at least 2x the base rate (run_log.txt), so the signal is not confined to one head.
findings.recommended_action: Score L32H13 and the other top heads on all residue pairs against experimental or AlphaFold contact maps. Within cysteine pairs, test whether the head separates bonded pairs from non-bonded pairs that are also in contact (for example Cbeta-Cbeta < 6-8 A). Compare against ESM-2's contact-prediction output restricted to cysteine pairs. Until that is done, reword Conclusions 1 and 3 to say that the head ranks bonded cysteine pairs highly, and drop 'dedicated', 'understands the chemistry of folding' and 'goes further than contacts'.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:37-39, 43-44 (Conclusion 2 and 'trace how the circuit builds its answer')
findings.description: These are mechanistic, causal claims: the head 'computes disulfide connectivity', 'L32H13 in the last layer carries the answer', and the other late-layer heads 'are the earlier stages of the same circuit'. The analysis only correlates each head's attention with the labels. It has no ablation, activation patching or attribution, so it cannot show composition between heads or that any head computes anything. Singling out L32H13 is itself an artifact of a narrow select-split ranking: L29H18 (layer 29) has the higher test AP, and the two cannot be distinguished.
findings.evidence: results.json: L32H13 has select 0.742 and test 0.718; L29H18 has select 0.721 and test 0.745 (the test maximum). A protein-level bootstrap I ran of AP(L29H18) - AP(L32H13) on test gives mean +0.029, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.076]. The test-split correlations among the top heads (L32H13, L29H18, L31H17, L30H1, L23H6) are 0.46-0.81. Shared signal of this kind is equally consistent with parallel, redundant contact-like heads. No intervention code exists in code/.
findings.recommended_action: Remove or heavily qualify 'computes', 'carries the answer' and 'earlier stages of the same circuit'. If a circuit claim is wanted, run causal tests: ablate or patch heads in layers 23-31 and measure the effect on L32H13's map and on bond ranking. Report L29H18 and L32H13 as statistically indistinguishable.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:36-37, 43 ('held from select to test', 'From the sequence alone', 'ready-made disulfide connectivity predictor'); README.md:19-20 (split 'into disjoint groups')
findings.description: The select/test split controls only for head selection, not for generalisation. ESM-2 (UR50D) was pretrained on UniRef sequences that include these Swiss-Prot entries and their homologs, so the model has seen the test proteins and their families. The split is also disjoint only by accession, not by sequence: several test proteins are near-duplicates of select proteins. The claims of reasoning 'from the sequence alone' and of a 'ready-made predictor' for new proteins are therefore not supported by this evaluation.
findings.evidence: Five test proteins have a close select homolog, with difflib identity ratios of: Q47450 vs A0A0H2VAQ6 0.979; B1JDQ5 vs A5VYT2 0.974; B4TQB8 vs Q1R984 0.901; P60045 vs P00596 0.838; P60311 vs P83345 0.833. Their 3-mer containment is 0.64-0.95. The test proteins are long-standing Swiss-Prot entries, so they were present when ESM-2 was trained in 2021-22.
findings.recommended_action: Use a homology-aware split (for example MMseqs2 clustering at 30% identity). Add an evaluation on proteins or families absent from ESM-2's training set (for example entries or structures released after training). Benchmark against existing disulfide-connectivity predictors before proposing L32H13 as a predictor. Reword 'from the sequence alone'.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:20-25, 35-36 ('far above sequence separation (0.113) and the mean head (0.141)'); code/disulfide_attention.py:191-205
findings.description: The only baselines are sequence separation (4 variants) and the unweighted mean of all 660 APC-corrected heads. The mean head averages many uninformative or anti-informative heads (many have test AP below the base rate, for example L0H2 at 0.031), so it is a straw-man stand-in for what ESM-2 knows. Neither baseline speaks to the conclusions, which are about disulfide-specific computation beyond contacts and usefulness as a predictor. The comparison also sets a best-of-661 selection against a best-of-4.
findings.evidence: Baselines in separation_scorer and attention_scorer row 660 only. head_ap.csv shows many heads with test AP around 0.03, below the 0.049 base rate. I also computed a cysteine-order heuristic (fewest cysteines between i and j): test AP 0.106, which shows that simple heuristics are weak. But no strong representation-level baseline, such as ESM-2's contact regression or a disulfide predictor, is included.
findings.recommended_action: Add ESM-2's built-in contact predictor (logistic regression over APC attention) restricted to cysteine pairs, a structure-contact oracle, and an established disulfide-connectivity tool as baselines. Report how much L32H13 adds beyond the contact probability.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:16, 20-25 ('base rate (no-skill AP)', 'x base rate'); code/disulfide_attention.py:228-233, 340-341 (2x-base-rate counts)
findings.description: The pooled base rate is presented as the no-skill AP. But a pooled AP across proteins keeps between-protein structure even when labels are shuffled within each protein, so the right chance level is the within-protein null AP. For the separation baseline this null is clearly above the base rate, so '2.3x' overstates its skill over chance. The 'x base rate' column and the '2x base rate' detector counts are not measured against the null that the analysis itself defines.
findings.evidence: Over 5 within-protein permutations I ran, abs_separation:- has null AP 0.063-0.073, against a base rate of 0.049; its real AP of 0.113 is therefore about 1.6x the null, not 2.3x. For the heads, the mean null AP is 0.053 (95th percentile 0.067, maximum 0.10).
findings.recommended_action: Report the within-protein null AP for each scorer (the mean over permutations), and express the lifts and the 'detector' threshold relative to it.

findings.description: The stated question is within-protein: can the model tell bonded pairs from the other cysteine pairs of the same protein. The headline metric, however, is AP pooled over all pairs of all proteins. This mixes between-protein score scale into the ranking, and the result is dominated by a few cysteine-rich proteins.
findings.evidence: The top 5 test proteins contribute 28% of the test pairs; G1XAA9 alone contributes 741 of 7,463. The conclusion survives in this case: pooled AP without the top 5 is 0.706, and the mean per-protein AP is 0.812. Still, the headline number does not answer the stated question directly.
findings.recommended_action: Make a within-protein metric (mean per-protein AP or P@n_bonds, with its own null and bootstrap) the primary result, and report pooled AP as secondary.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:25, 34-35 ('puts a bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins'); code/disulfide_attention.py:134-153
findings.description: The per-protein P@1 values are reported without a chance level. They also include proteins whose single candidate pair is necessarily bonded, which score 1.0 automatically.
findings.evidence: The expected P@1 under random ranking within each protein, mean(n_bonds/n_pairs), is 0.152 on test. Five test proteins have exactly one cysteine pair, and it is bonded. Excluding them, L32H13's P@1 is 0.797 over 118 proteins, against the reported 0.805.
findings.recommended_action: Report the random-ranking P@1 and P@n_bonds alongside the scorers, and exclude or flag proteins with a single candidate pair.

findings.location: README.md:26-28 (at most 40 cysteines filter; two test proteins with 64 and 41 cysteines removed); SUMMARY.md:3-4
findings.description: An ad hoc cap of at most 40 cysteines removed exactly the two most cysteine-rich test proteins. These are the hardest ranking cases, and no select protein was removed. Pooled AP is weighted by pair count, so these two proteins could noticeably move the headline test AP and base rate. SUMMARY.md describes the cohort as every cysteine pair in proteins with at least one intrachain bond and does not mention the exclusion.
findings.evidence: With 64 and 41 cysteines, the two proteins would contribute 2,016 + 820 = 2,836 candidate pairs, which is 38% on top of the 7,463 test pairs analysed. The README states that no other protein was removed by the length or cysteine rules. The cap has no stated rationale; both proteins satisfy the 1,022-residue limit implied by the README.
findings.recommended_action: Include the two proteins, or report a sensitivity analysis with them included, and disclose the filter in SUMMARY.md.

findings.location: README.md:22-24 (labels from UniProt FT DISULFID; unannotated pairs labelled not bonded)
findings.description: Pairs without an annotation are treated as true negatives, and annotations are not filtered by evidence code. Swiss-Prot DISULFID records include assignments inferred by similarity, which are themselves homology-transferred, and some proteins clearly have many unannotated cysteines. Missing bonds add label noise, and similarity-inferred labels make the benchmark partly a test of agreement with homology transfer.
findings.evidence: In 32 of 123 test proteins and 27 of 113 select proteins, fewer than 50% of the cysteines are in annotated bonds. Example: G1XAA9 has 39 cysteines, 3 annotated bonds and 741 pairs, the largest test protein. proteins.tsv keeps no evidence codes.
findings.recommended_action: Keep the evidence codes. Report results restricted to experimentally supported bonds (for example ECO:0000269 or PDB-derived), and restrict to proteins whose cysteines are fully accounted for (all bonded, or known free).

findings.description: The uncertainty quantification is coarse. The percentile CIs use only 200 bootstrap resamples, which leaves about 5 values in each tail, and they ignore selection uncertainty (which head would be picked if the select proteins were resampled). The null for the expected maximum comes from a single label permutation, with 256 heads sampled and then resampled with replacement to 661.
findings.evidence: N_BOOT = 200. permute_within_protein is called once with seed+22. expected_best_of_n resamples a single set of 256 null APs. None of this changes the qualitative result: the 0.718 test AP is far above the null maximum of about 0.09-0.10.
findings.recommended_action: Use 2,000 or more bootstrap resamples, ideally including the selection step inside the bootstrap. Average the null over many permutations.

review.summary: I checked the numbers and the data first. The analysis reproduces exactly when re-run in memory, without writing files. AP matches sklearn, the self-test passes, and row 660 really is the mean of the 660 head rows. The pairs files agree fully with proteins.tsv: every cysteine pair is present, both ends of every bonded pair are cysteines, and the bond counts, length cap (max 987) and cysteine cap (max 39) all hold. Every number in SUMMARY.md matches outputs/results.json. The core empirical result stands: L32H13 was chosen on the select proteins and reaches test AP 0.718, with per-protein AP 0.81 and P@1 0.805, far above chance. The problems are in what the summary concludes from it. (1) The mechanistic claims are untested: a "dedicated circuit", a head that "computes connectivity", a model that "understands chemistry", and earlier heads as "earlier stages". There is no contact control, no specificity test and no ablation. (2) It is not stable which head is best. L29H18 beats L32H13 on test and wins 86% of test bootstraps. (3) Pooled AP with "no-skill = base rate" is misleading. A label-free score that only knows protein size gets test AP 0.146, beating both baselines. (4) The "ready-made connectivity predictor" claim is unsupported: the full bond pattern is exactly right in only 46% of test proteins with 2 or more bonds. Smaller points: the split between select and test does not account for sequence similarity; an unexplained 40-cysteine cap removed two large test proteins; and the null estimate is slightly low.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 37-42 (Conclusions 2 and 3); code/disulfide_attention.py (only Cys-Cys pairs are scored; no structural data anywhere in data/)
findings.description: The summary concludes that the head 'computes disulfide connectivity', that the model 'understands the chemistry of folding', and that the head 'goes further' than contacts and has 'learned the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds'. The analysis cannot support any of this. It only ranks cysteine-cysteine pairs, and the scores are correlational. Every disulfide-bonded pair is a 3D contact, while most non-bonded cysteine pairs are not. Symmetrised, APC-corrected attention is exactly the feature ESM uses to predict contacts. So a general contact head would produce the same result. No contact baseline, no test on non-cysteine contacts and no test on non-bonded cysteine pairs that are in contact was run, and no structures were used. The claim 'from the sequence alone' also ignores that ESM-2 was pretrained on UniRef, which contains these very sequences and their families. Memorised family-level co-variation is a competing explanation that was not ruled out. The provenance of the UniProt DISULFID labels (experimental vs. 'By similarity') was not checked either.
findings.evidence: pairs_select.npz and pairs_test.npz contain only Cys-Cys pairs, and the folder has no contact or distance information. The README itself says APC-corrected symmetric attention is the contact-map recipe, and SUMMARY line 40 cites Rao et al. 2020 on contacts, but nothing is done to separate disulfide-specific signal from contact signal. As a sign of how far it is from 'working out which cysteine bonds to which': taking a protein's top n_bonds pairs from L32H13 gives exactly the bonded set in only 50.4% of test proteins overall, 46.1% of those with 2 or more bonds (n=89) and 32.4% of those with 4 or more bonds (n=34).
findings.recommended_action: Remove Conclusions 2-3 or restate them as 'attention head L32H13 ranks annotated bonded cysteine pairs highly'. To claim specificity beyond contacts: compare against ESM-2's own contact predictions and against a contact-only scorer computed from structures (PDB or AlphaFold), test non-bonded cysteine pairs that are in contact, and check whether L32H13 scores non-cysteine contacts just as highly. Report label evidence codes and redo the analysis with experimental-only labels.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 34, 37-39, 43-44 (Conclusions 1, 2, 4: 'dedicated circuit', 'L32H13 in the last layer carries the answer', 'other late-layer heads are the earlier stages of the same circuit')
findings.description: No ablation, activation patching or attribution was done, so nothing supports a 'circuit', a computation order across layers, or L32H13 as the head that 'carries the answer'. The data actually contradict singling out L32H13. On the test proteins another head (L29H18, layer 29) is better, and which of the two wins depends on the split. The two heads disagree on the top-ranked pair in about half of the proteins. The signal is also spread over many heads in many layers, which argues against a single 'dedicated' head.
findings.evidence: Test AP: L29H18 0.745 vs L32H13 0.718 (results.json). Protein-bootstrap over the top 5 heads: on select, L32H13 is best in 240 of 300 resamples and L29H18 in 60. On test, L29H18 is best in 259 of 300 and L32H13 in 41. Pearson r between the two heads' test scores is 0.81 (Spearman 0.66), yet they pick the same top pair in only 48% of test proteins. 15 heads in layer 32 and 10 each in layers 29 and 30 reach at least 2x the base rate, the top 10 heads have select AP 0.39-0.74, and run_log.txt shows heads at 2x base or more in all 33 of 33 layers, including layer 0.
findings.recommended_action: Drop the 'dedicated circuit', 'carries the answer' and 'earlier stages' language unless backed by causal experiments, such as head ablation or patching with downstream effects. Report that several late-layer heads (L29H18, L32H13, L31H17, L30H1, ...) carry similar signal, and that which head comes out best is not stable across protein sets.

findings.location: README.md line 12; SUMMARY.md lines 16, 20-25 and 35-36 ('x base rate', 'no skill' row, 'far above sequence separation (0.113) and the mean head (0.141)'); code/disulfide_attention.py lines 12-13, 211, 231
findings.description: AP is pooled over the pairs of all proteins, and the base rate is presented as the no-skill AP. But the question is whether a score can tell bonded pairs from the other pairs of the same protein. Pooled AP also rewards how scores compare across proteins. Small proteins have few candidate pairs and a high bonded fraction, and APC values grow as proteins get shorter. So a score with no within-protein information can still beat the base rate by a lot. The two reported baselines are no better than such a protein-size-only score. The 'x base rate' lifts (14.6, 2.9, 2.3) and the baseline comparison therefore depend on arbitrary cross-protein scaling. The table also gives no chance-level P@1 to compare against.
findings.evidence: A label-free score that knows only the protein's size (1/number of candidate pairs, constant within each protein) gets pooled test AP 0.146, which is 3.0x the base rate. That beats both sequence separation (0.113) and the mean of all heads (0.141), and on select it gets 0.149. Replacing each score with its within-protein rank plus that size prior moves sequence separation from 0.113 to 0.165, the mean head from 0.141 to 0.207, and L32H13 from 0.718 to 0.635. Random per-protein P@1 is 0.152.
findings.recommended_action: Make within-protein metrics the primary endpoint: per-protein AP, P@1 and exact connectivity, each with its random expectation. Alternatively, use a pooled metric on within-protein normalised scores. Add the protein-size-only baseline, report lifts relative to it rather than to the raw base rate, and add random P@1 (0.152) to the table.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 43-44 (Conclusion 4: 'use L32H13 as a ready-made disulfide connectivity predictor')
findings.description: This practical claim goes well beyond what was evaluated. The protein set was pre-filtered to proteins already known to have at least one annotated intrachain bond and at most 40 cysteines. So the predictor never has to decide whether a protein has disulfides at all, and proteins with many cysteines are excluded. Scores are not decoded into a valid pattern in which each cysteine has at most one partner. Exact connectivity accuracy is not reported, and there is no comparison with established disulfide-connectivity predictors or with simple structure-based baselines (Cys-Cys distances from ESMFold or AlphaFold). Which head is 'best' also flips between splits (see F2).
findings.evidence: Taking each test protein's top n_bonds pairs from L32H13 gives exactly the annotated set in 50.4% of proteins, 46.1% of those with 2 or more bonds and 32.4% of those with 4 or more. Mean precision at n_bonds is 0.734 (results.json). The README filter keeps only proteins with at least 1 annotated bond.
findings.recommended_action: Remove or heavily qualify the recommendation. If kept, evaluate as a real predictor: include proteins without disulfides and the large cysteine-rich proteins, decode by maximum-weight matching, report exact connectivity accuracy, and benchmark against existing tools and structure-based baselines.

findings.location: README.md lines 19-20 ('split by protein ... into disjoint groups'); SUMMARY.md line 36 ('it held from select to test proteins')
findings.description: The select/test split is by accession, not by sequence-similarity cluster. Several test proteins are near-identical to select proteins, and many share a family with one. So select-to-test 'holding' is not fully independent evidence. The protein bootstrap also treats homologous proteins (for example several olfactory receptors and toxins within test) as independent, which makes the confidence interval somewhat too narrow. In practice the effect on the headline number is small.
findings.evidence: Local-alignment identity, test vs. select: Q47450/A0A0H2VAQ6 98%, B1JDQ5/A5VYT2 98%, P60045/P00596 91%, B4TQB8/Q1R984 90%, P60311/P83345 85%. About 18 test proteins have at least 44% identity over at least 70% coverage to some select protein. Excluding those 18 leaves L32H13 test AP at 0.720 (vs 0.718) and L29H18 at 0.728.
findings.recommended_action: Split by sequence-similarity cluster (for example MMseqs2 at 30% identity), or report results with cross-split homologs removed. Bootstrap over clusters rather than individual proteins.

findings.location: README.md lines 26-28 (the 'at most 40 cysteines' rule); SUMMARY.md lines 3-4
findings.description: The 40-cysteine cap has no technical justification: the ESM-2 limit is on residues, not cysteines. It removed only two test proteins, the two most cysteine-rich ones (64 and 41 cysteines). Together they would have added about 2,836 candidate pairs, roughly 38% of the current 7,463. The cap sits just above the largest retained protein (39 cysteines), which suggests it was set after looking at the data. SUMMARY.md does not mention the exclusion, so its 'every cysteine pair in 236 proteins' wording hides that the hardest test cases were dropped.
findings.evidence: The README says two test proteins were left out by this rule and no other protein was excluded by length or cysteine count. C(64,2)+C(41,2) = 2016+820 = 2836 pairs. The largest retained protein has 39 cysteines (test) and the largest in select has 24.
findings.recommended_action: Either include the two proteins, since scoring is cheap, or report results with and without them, and disclose the exclusion in SUMMARY.md.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 108-113 and 220-224 (expected_best_of_n / null); SUMMARY.md lines 27-28
findings.description: The expected maximum under the null comes from one label permutation and from APs of only 256 candidates, resampled with replacement to N=661. A resampled maximum can never exceed the largest of the 256 values, so the expected null maximum is biased low. The conclusion is unaffected, because the observed maximum is far above the null.
findings.evidence: Reported null expected maximum: 0.087. The actual maximum test AP over all 661 candidates under four separate within-protein permutations: 0.0934, 0.0963, 0.0876, 0.0920. Under every permutation, no candidate reached 2x the base rate.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the null maximum over all 661 candidates, for many permutations (for example 100), and report its mean and 95th percentile.

The facts are correct: 2 test proteins with 64 and 41 cysteines were excluded, C(64,2)+C(41,2)=2836, and the maximum retained is 39 (test) and 24 (select). The README states the rule. The key lists the 40-cysteine rule as a possible false alarm if it is claimed to bias the result. The only real point left is that SUMMARY.md does not disclose the exclusion, which is a minor disclosure issue.

Technically true: a maximum resampled from 256 values can never exceed the largest of those 256. In my 4 full 661-candidate permutations the maximum null test AP was 0.096, 0.088, 0.092 and 0.085, against the reported 0.087, so any bias is tiny. The key says the source gave 0.093. The finding itself says the conclusion is unaffected.

review.summary:
I reviewed <CODE_ROOT>/analysis-tasks/B1249 against all ten checklist patterns and re-ran the analysis in memory, without writing any files. The numbers reproduce exactly: L32H13 has test AP 0.718 (CI 0.664-0.782), the null maximum is 0.087, the sequence-separation baseline is 0.113 and the mean-of-heads baseline is 0.141. The data files are consistent with each other: every pair set equals all cysteine pairs of its protein, bond counts match the protein table, and no cysteine is in two bonds.

The decoding result holds up. Within the subset of pairs where both cysteines are bonded, L32H13 still reaches AP 0.847 against a base rate of 0.128, so it ranks partners, not just bonded cysteines. Removing the 9 test proteins that have homologs in the select set leaves the AP unchanged (0.717). The interpretive conclusions are the problem.

Verdicts by pattern:
- **P1 (chance anchoring):** present, minor. The per-protein metrics have no chance values, and the null maximum is slightly underestimated.
- **P2 (trivial baseline):** present and unaddressed. There is no residue-contact baseline, and a score that only counts each protein's cysteine pairs beats both reported baselines.
- **P3 (what the endpoint measures):** present and unaddressed. Bonded pairs and residues in contact are confounded, and the labels include unfiltered UniProt annotations of unknown evidence level.
- **P4 (unit of inference):** clean. The bootstrap is over proteins and per-protein metrics are reported.
- **P5 (selection effects):** mostly clean. The select/test split works, but the 40-cysteine cap removed only test proteins.
- **P6 (positive control):** not applicable, because the main result is positive.
- **P7 (generalization):** present. One model, one inference run, and proteins that were in the pretraining data.
- **P8 (stability):** present. Which head wins is unstable, and L32H13 cannot be told apart from L29H18 on test.
- **P9 (overclaiming language):** present and unaddressed. "Dedicated circuit", "computes", "earlier stages of the same circuit" and "understands the chemistry of folding" go beyond the evidence.
- **P10 (reproducibility):** present, minor. No version pins and no code for building the corpus or the split.

Conclusions 1–3 of SUMMARY.md cannot stand as written.

findings.description: The claims of a 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit' and that the head 'goes further' than residue contacts by learning 'the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds' are untested. There is no contact baseline and no test of whether the head is specific to cysteines. Only cysteine pairs are scored, so nothing in the analysis can show that L32H13 is about disulfides rather than general spatial closeness. The summary itself says attention is known to follow residue contacts.
findings.evidence: The scores are built the same way as the contact-prediction features of Rao et al. 2020 (symmetrise, then APC; extract_attention.py lines 36-41). Two bonded cysteines are always in spatial contact, while most non-bonded cysteine pairs are not, so any contact-tracking head will rank bonded pairs first. In my check, the highest-scoring non-bonded pair in each protein lies within ±3 residues of a true bond at both ends in 13.6% of test proteins (16 of 118), against 4.0% for an average non-bonded pair. That 3.4-fold excess fits a proximity signal. No structures, contact maps, ESM-2 contact-head outputs or non-cysteine pairs are in the data, so the alternative was never tested.
findings.recommended_action: Add a contact baseline: the ESM-2 contact-regression output, or Cβ distances from PDB/AlphaFold structures for the same proteins. Report L32H13's AP among cysteine pairs that are in contact, and score the head on all residue pairs to measure cysteine specificity. Until then, change Conclusions 1 and 3 to: 'Head L32H13's APC-corrected attention ranks annotated bonded cysteine pairs highly (test AP 0.718 vs base rate 0.049); whether this exceeds generic contact signal was not tested.'

findings.description: Three statements in Conclusion 2 rest on no analysis: that L32H13 'computes disulfide connectivity', that it 'carries the answer' in the last layer, and that L29H18, L31H17 and L30H1 are 'the earlier stages of the same circuit'. There was no ablation, no activation patching and no analysis linking one head to another. Picking out L32H13 is also statistically fragile.
findings.evidence: On the test proteins, L29H18 (test AP 0.745) does better than the chosen L32H13 (0.718). A paired protein-level bootstrap of the difference L32H13 minus L29H18 gives a 95% CI of [-0.072, +0.022], so the two heads cannot be told apart. When I bootstrapped the select proteins 500 times, L32H13 won 383 times and L29H18 won 117 times. 'Earlier stages' is inferred from layer order alone, and the earlier layer-29 head is the best performer on test.
findings.recommended_action: Delete or rewrite Conclusion 2. Describe a group of late-layer heads with similar decoding performance, and report the CI of the difference between the top heads. Claims about stages or circuits need intervention experiments: ablating or patching L29H18, L31H17 and L30H1 and measuring the effect on L32H13's scores.

findings.description: The mechanistic wording goes beyond the evidence. Examples: 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit', 'This head computes disulfide connectivity', 'the model works out which cysteine bonds to which', 'The model understands the chemistry of folding', 'it has learned the rule'. The only evidence is a correlational ranking: one head's attention scores against curated annotations. That is level 1 (decoding) in the checklist's taxonomy. Nothing chemical or folding-related was measured.
findings.evidence: The whole analysis is AP and precision-at-k of precomputed attention entries against UniProt labels (disulfide_attention.py score_arm, lines 208-241). No intervention or structural test was run.
findings.recommended_action: Replace with evidence-level wording, for example: 'Head L32H13's attention is consistent with annotated disulfide connectivity (decoding level)'. Drop 'circuit', 'computes', 'understands the chemistry of folding' and 'learned the rule'. State the claim level explicitly.

findings.description: The recommendation to use L32H13 as a 'ready-made disulfide connectivity predictor' has not been tested under conditions that would support it. The evaluation only covers proteins already known to have at least one intrachain bond, with at most 40 cysteines and at most 1,022 residues. It measures ranking only, with no rule for deciding how many or which pairs are bonded. There is no comparison with existing disulfide-connectivity predictors or with ESM-2's own contact map. The proteins are Swiss-Prot entries that were almost certainly in ESM-2's UniRef pretraining data, and the split is by protein, not by homology.
findings.evidence: README lines 26-28 give the filters (at least 1 annotated bond required). The metrics are ranking-only (AP, P@1, P@n_bonds given the true bond count). My 4-mer check found 9 of 123 test proteins with close homologs in the select set; two share more than 90% of 4-mers (Q47450 and A0A0H2VAQ6, B1JDQ5 and A5VYT2). Excluding them leaves the AP unchanged (0.717), so leakage between splits does not drive the result. Exposure to the pretraining data is a separate issue and was not examined.
findings.recommended_action: Either drop the 'ready-made predictor' claim or test it properly. Include proteins with no bonds and with free cysteines, use a decision rule for bonded or not bonded, compare against a dedicated predictor and the ESM-2 contact head, and evaluate on families held out from pretraining or on sequences released after it.

findings.description: The ground truth is every UniProt FT DISULFID record, with no filter on evidence code. Swiss-Prot disulfide annotations mix experimental evidence with 'by similarity' and 'sequence analysis' assignments, which are propagated by homology. Any pair without a record is labelled not bonded. The endpoint is therefore agreement with partly homology-inferred annotation, not with observed bonds. A model trained on protein families could match that inference without telling anything about chemistry.
findings.evidence: The README specifies labels as 'UniProt FT DISULFID i..j records' and says 'A pair without a record is labelled not bonded'. Neither the pair files nor proteins.tsv carry an evidence code, so the share of experimentally supported labels cannot be checked.
findings.recommended_action: Keep the ECO evidence codes. Report the headline AP for the subset with experimental evidence (ECO:0000269) or with bonds confirmed in a PDB structure. State the label provenance next to every headline number.

findings.description: The reported baselines are weaker than a trivial baseline that uses no information about individual pairs. AP is pooled across proteins, so it rewards ranking whole proteins against each other. A score based only on how many cysteine pairs a protein has beats both sequence separation and the mean of all heads. The headline gap still holds, but the comparison table makes the baselines look more informative than they are.
findings.evidence: Score = 1/(number of candidate pairs in the protein) gives pooled test AP 0.146. Adding a shorter-separation tiebreak gives 0.170. Both exceed sequence separation (0.113) and the mean of all heads (0.141).
findings.recommended_action: Add a protein-level baseline (cysteine-pair count) and a protein-normalised separation baseline. Treat the per-protein metrics as the primary measure of the within-protein question.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:22 and 34 ('no skill' P@1 shown as '-'; 'top in 80% of test proteins')
findings.description: The per-protein metrics have no chance values. The 80% top-pair claim and the per-protein AP are given without the expected value under random ranking. Some test proteins contribute a trivial P@1 of 1.
findings.evidence: Chance P@1 is the mean over proteins of bonds/pairs, which is 0.152 on test. Chance mean per-protein AP is about 0.248, versus 0.812 reported for L32H13. Five test proteins have a single candidate pair. Without them, P@1 is 0.797.
findings.recommended_action: Fill the 'no skill' row with P@1 = 0.152 and per-protein AP ≈ 0.25, and note how many proteins are single-pair (trivial).

findings.description: The 'expected highest of 661 candidates under the within-protein null' (0.087) comes from a single permutation and 256 sampled heads. Drawing 661 times with replacement from those 256 values effectively returns their maximum. So it is neither an expectation over permutations nor a maximum over all 661 heads, and it slightly underestimates the null maximum.
findings.evidence: The maximum of the 256 sampled null APs is 0.0875, matching the reported 0.0869. The actual maximum over all 661 heads under 5 independent within-protein permutations ranges from 0.091 to 0.099.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the null maximum over all 661 candidates for many permutations (for example 100), and report its mean ± SD and 95th percentile. The headline gap (0.745 vs about 0.1) is unaffected.

findings.description: The '192 of 661 candidates reach at least 2x the base rate' count uses a threshold that has no calibration to a null or a baseline. 2x the base rate (0.098) is only just above the null maximum of a single permutation (about 0.09-0.10). It is below what a protein-level baseline with no pair information reaches (0.146) and below the mean of all heads (0.141). The count does not show that 192 heads detect disulfides.
findings.evidence: Base rate 0.049, so the threshold is 0.098. The null maximum is 0.091-0.099. The protein-level baseline reaches 0.146.
findings.recommended_action: Replace the threshold with one calibrated to the null (for example a per-head permutation p-value with FDR correction) or with the margin over the strongest trivial baseline, or drop the count.

findings.description: There is little stability or generalization analysis behind the headline. The bootstrap uses only 200 resamples. The scores come from one bfloat16 forward pass of one model size (650M), and nothing was varied: no fp32 run, no check with and without APC or symmetrisation, no other ESM-2 sizes or other protein language models. Even so, the conclusions speak generally of 'ESM-2' and 'the model'.
findings.evidence: README: 'bfloat16, eager attention, once, on an Apple-silicon GPU'. N_BOOT = 200 at line 40. The analysis contains no sweep over any of these choices.
findings.recommended_action: Use at least 1000 bootstrap resamples and add a paired test of the difference against baselines and other heads. Re-extract in fp32 for a check. Repeat on at least one other ESM-2 size or another protein language model before claiming anything about ESM-2 in general.

findings.description: The 'at most 40 cysteines' rule removed exactly two proteins, both from the test split (64 and 41 cysteines), and none from the select split. The cutoff looks chosen after the fact, and it drops the hardest test cases from the reported test AP.
findings.evidence: README: 'Two test proteins were left out by the last rule (64 and 41 cysteines). No other protein was left out by the length or cysteine-count rules.'
findings.recommended_action: Score the two excluded proteins, if they are within the 1,022-residue limit, and report the test AP with them included, or justify the cutoff in advance.

findings.description: The run cannot be fully reproduced. There are no pinned package versions (numpy, torch, transformers). The code that built the 18,176-entry corpus, parsed UniProt and split by protein is not included. The README says extraction ran on an Apple-silicon GPU, but the script defaults to CPU and the exact command is not recorded.
findings.evidence: The folder contains no requirements or environment file and no corpus or split script. extract_attention.py has the device default 'cpu'.
findings.recommended_action: Add a pinned environment file, the corpus and split construction code (including the UniProt release and parsing rules), and the exact extraction command and hardware.

review.summary:
I reproduced every number in SUMMARY.md from the shipped data without writing any files: test AP 0.718 (CI 0.664-0.782) for L32H13, sequence separation 0.113, mean of heads 0.141, a null expected maximum of 0.087, and 192 of 661 heads at or above 2x the base rate. The self-test passes. The data checks out: every pair index is a cysteine, the pair counts are C(n,2), each protein's bond count matches proteins.tsv, no cysteine sits in two bonds, and every inclusion rule holds. The numerical result is sound. A protein-level bootstrap gives a CI, the within-protein permutation null is far below the observed AP, and simple sequence baselines are far weaker: a GBM on cysteine-position features trained on select reaches only 0.245 test AP. Removing the roughly 10 test proteins that look like homologs of select proteins leaves the AP unchanged (0.717). Most of the interpretation in the Conclusions does not hold.

Checklist verdicts:
- P1 (null anchoring): partly present. The 80% P@1 is not compared with its chance level (0.15), and the 14.6x figure is anchored to the pooled base rate rather than the null.
- P2 (trivial baseline): present. Only weak sequence baselines were run, and there is no contact baseline.
- P3 (endpoint vs claim): present and unaddressed. A bonded cysteine pair is always a spatial contact, so the analysis cannot separate a disulfide-specific head from a general contact head.
- P4 (unit of inference): clean. The bootstrap resamples proteins, and the homology overlap has no effect.
- P5 (selection): present for the claim that the head is a ready-to-use predictor. The protein set was conditioned on having at least one annotated bond.
- P6 (positive control): not applicable, since the analysis reports no null finding.
- P7 (generalization): present. Only one checkpoint, one extraction run and one database were used.
- P8 (stability): present. The identity of the top head is not stable, the bootstrap uses only 200 resamples, and the null comes from a single permutation.
- P9 (overclaiming): present and severe. The summary says "dedicated circuit", "computes", "understands chemistry" and "earlier stages of the same circuit", but the evidence is correlational only.
- P10 (reproducibility): present. No software versions are pinned, and the device recorded in the README does not match the script's default.

findings.description: Conclusions 1 and 2 claim mechanism and causation that the evidence cannot support: 'ESM-2 has a dedicated disulfide-bond circuit', 'This head computes disulfide connectivity', 'the model works out which cysteine bonds to which'. The only evidence is that one head's APC-corrected attention values rank annotated bonded pairs above non-bonded pairs, which is a correlational decoding result. There is no ablation, patching or other intervention, so nothing shows the model uses this head to compute anything. 'Dedicated' is also contradicted by the outputs: the signal is spread across many heads in every layer.
findings.evidence: code/disulfide_attention.py only computes the AP of precomputed attention scores; no intervention is performed anywhere. results.json shows 192 of 661 candidates with test AP at least 2x the base rate, spread over all 33 layers (run_log.txt line 6), and ten heads have select AP above 0.38. The supported statement is narrower: L32H13's corrected attention gives test AP 0.718 against a base rate of 0.049.
findings.recommended_action: Rewrite Conclusions 1-2 at the decoding level, for example: 'the APC-corrected attention of L32H13 ranks annotated disulfide-bonded cysteine pairs above other cysteine pairs (test AP 0.718; per-protein P@1 0.80 vs chance 0.15)'. Drop 'dedicated', 'circuit' and 'computes' unless a head-ablation or activation-patching experiment shows a causal role. State that many heads carry the signal.

findings.description: The summary does not rule out that L32H13 is simply a contact head. A disulfide-bonded pair is always a close spatial contact, and Rao et al. 2020 (which the summary cites) showed that attention tracks contacts. Only cysteine-cysteine pairs were scored, and there is no structure-derived contact baseline and no score for non-cysteine contacts. The analysis therefore cannot show that the head 'goes further' than contacts, that it is disulfide-specific, or that the model 'has learned the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds' or 'understands the chemistry of folding'. This is a mismatch between what the endpoint measures and what is claimed (P3), plus a missing baseline (P2).
findings.evidence: extract_attention.py:42 returns only C[:, ii, jj] for cysteine pairs, so the head's behaviour on other residue pairs is never measured. No structure or contact data appears anywhere in data/. Conclusion 3 says 'This head goes further: it has learned the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds', yet no comparison against contacts was run.
findings.recommended_action: Get structures (PDB or AlphaFold) for the 236 proteins. Evaluate the head (a) on cysteine pairs that are all within, for example, 8 Å Cβ-Cβ, to see whether it separates bonded from merely nearby pairs, and (b) on non-cysteine contacts. Compare it with ESM-2's own contact-prediction output restricted to cysteine pairs. Until then, remove Conclusion 3 and the word 'dedicated'.

findings.description: The summary claims that 'L32H13 in the last layer carries the answer', that L29H18, L31H17 and L30H1 are 'the earlier stages of the same circuit', and that the circuit 'builds its answer across layers 23-32'. The data contradict this. L32H13 is not reliably the best head, and the layers between 23 and 29 do not improve steadily. The heads also disagree substantially with one another, which a single staged pipeline would not predict, and no analysis of how information moves between layers was done.
findings.evidence: On test, L29H18 scores higher than L32H13 (0.745 vs 0.718). In my protein-bootstrap check (300 resamples), the select AP difference L32H13 minus L29H18 has a 95% CI of [-0.029, 0.073], and L29H18 is the top head in 257 of 300 test bootstraps. The best head per layer by test AP is not monotone: L23 0.527, L24 0.188, L25 0.200, L26 0.391, L27 0.239, L28 0.322, L29 0.745, L30 0.595, L31 0.639, L32 0.718. Spearman correlations between the five top heads on test pairs range from 0.31 to 0.80 (0.21 to 0.62 on bonded pairs only), and L32H13 and L29H18 pick the same top pair in only 59 of 123 test proteins.
findings.recommended_action: Report the top heads as a set and treat the choice of L32H13 over L29H18 as unresolved. Remove the 'earlier stages' and 'builds its answer across layers' claims unless path-patching or ablation experiments support them.

findings.description: Conclusion 4 proposes using L32H13 'as a ready-made disulfide connectivity predictor', but the evaluation does not support use as a general predictor. Proteins were included only if they have at least one annotated intrachain bond, at most 40 cysteines and at most 1,022 residues. The task tested is therefore 'which pairs are bonded, given that bonds exist', never 'are there any bonds'. Proteins with only free cysteines or no disulfides were never scored, and the two most cysteine-rich test proteins (64 and 41 cysteines) were removed. Pairs without a UniProt record are labelled negative, and where the labels came from (experimental or 'by similarity') is not recorded. The head is also not compared with any existing disulfide-connectivity predictor.

findings.description: The only sequence-only baseline is monotone sequence separation (4 candidates). The head still beats a stronger baseline by a wide margin.
findings.evidence: In my check, a gradient-boosting classifier on cysteine-position features (separation, cysteine ordinal ranks, number of cysteines, length, neighbouring cysteines), trained on select and scored on test, reached test AP 0.245 and per-protein P@1 0.341. That is more than double the reported baseline (0.113), but well below L32H13 (0.718).
findings.recommended_action: Add a stronger sequence-only baseline trained on select (and optionally homology transfer of bond patterns), and report the head's gain over it.

findings.description: Two headline figures lack their proper chance anchors. The '80% of test proteins' top-1 figure is given without its chance level. findings.description: The stability evidence is thin. The bootstrap uses only 200 resamples for 2.5/97.5 percentiles. The CI is conditional on the selected head and does not include selection uncertainty. The null expected-maximum comes from a single label permutation, with 256 of 661 candidates resampled. Choices in how the score is built (symmetrisation, APC, bf16 precision) are fixed with no sensitivity check, and the attention was extracted in a single run.

findings.description: Claims are worded about 'ESM-2' and 'the model' in general, but only one checkpoint (650M), one extraction run and one annotation source (Swiss-Prot DISULFID) were examined. Nothing was held out by model size, architecture or label source.
