review.summary:
I reviewed B1249 (ESM-2 650M attention heads ranking disulfide-bonded cysteine pairs) against all ten checklist patterns. I re-ran the analysis in memory and the outputs reproduce exactly: L32H13 test AP 0.7179, CI [0.664, 0.782], null max 0.0869, P@1 0.805, and head_ap.csv matches to within 1e-6. The selftest passes, and the data check out (every pair is C-C, every protein's full set of pairs is present, bond counts match, no cysteine has two partners, and no accession or sequence appears in both splits).

The numbers are sound. Head L32H13 separates bonded from non-bonded cysteine pairs far better than chance and better than the baselines tested:
- per-protein mean AP 0.81 vs 0.25 for random scores;
- P@1 0.80 vs 0.15 for random scores;
- sequence separation 0.11 and simple cysteine-order heuristics 0.10-0.13, both well below the head.
Selection is clean (chosen on select, reported on test). A full within-protein null puts 0 or 1 of the 661 candidates at 2x the base rate, so the 192 heads reported above that line are not a null artefact.

The problems are in what the summary concludes from these numbers:
- **Critical (P2/P3):** the analysis only scores cysteine pairs and never compares against residue contacts. A general contact head of the kind the summary itself cites (Rao et al. 2020) would give the same result, so 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit' and 'goes further [than contacts]' are not tested.
- **Critical (P9):** the circuit and mechanism language ('computes connectivity', 'earlier stages of the same circuit', 'understands the chemistry of folding') has no intervention behind it.
- **Major:** the 'ready-made connectivity predictor' recommendation is not supported. The evaluation only included proteins already known to have bonds, never assigned a full bond pattern, and never compared against existing predictors.
- **Minor:**
  - The pooled AP mixes comparisons between proteins: normalising scores within each protein lowers it from 0.718 to 0.59-0.64.
  - P@1 is not compared with chance in the summary.
  - The best-of-661 null expectation is slightly underestimated (0.087 vs about 0.095).
  - The 40-cysteine cap removed two test proteins only (about 2,836 pairs, 38% of the test pairs kept), with no sensitivity check.
  - The split is by accession, not by sequence similarity, and the test proteins were probably in ESM-2's training data.
  - Which head comes out on top is only moderately stable (L32H13 in 155 of 200 bootstrap resamples of the select proteins).
  - Bond labels come from UniProt annotations, not structures.
  - Software versions are not pinned.

By pattern:
- P1: mostly anchored; minor issues.
- P2: present and unaddressed (contact baseline missing).
- P3: present and unaddressed.
- P4: mostly clean (the bootstrap resamples proteins and n=123 proteins is stated); minor homology leakage.
- P5: minor (test-only exclusion).
- P6: not applicable, since the headline finding is positive.
- P7: present (one model, one dataset).
- P8: minor.
- P9: present and unaddressed.
- P10: minor.

One side effect: my imports may have regenerated the existing code/__pycache__/disulfide_attention.cpython-312.pyc (timestamp 13:01), from unchanged source. outputs/ and data/ were not touched.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 34-35 and 40-42 (Conclusions 1 and 3); code/extract_attention.py line 42; code/disulfide_attention.py lines 191-205 and 316-326
findings.description: The summary concludes that ESM-2 has a 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit' and that the head 'goes further' than residue contacts by learning 'the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds'. The analysis cannot tell a disulfide-specific head from a general contact head. Bonded cysteines are always in close spatial contact, while most non-bonded cysteine pairs in a protein are not. A head that follows 3D contacts, which the summary itself says attention is known to do, would therefore rank bonded pairs first and give the same AP. There is no contact-matched comparison and no check of whether the head ranks non-cysteine contacts just as high.
findings.evidence: Scores are taken only at cysteine-cysteine pairs (extract_attention.py line 42 `return C[:, ii, jj]`, with ii and jj the cysteine pairs from pairs_*.npz), so nothing shows the head singles out cysteines. The only baselines are sequence separation (disulfide_attention.py lines 196-205) and the mean of all heads (lines 316-326); neither is a contact map. My extra baselines (cysteine-order distance, nested pairing) reach only AP 0.10-0.13, so the head clearly beats sequence heuristics, but no structure-based or contact-prediction comparator was computed. The data hold no contact or structure information.
findings.recommended_action: Get contact maps (PDB, or AlphaFold DB for these Swiss-Prot entries). Compare the head's score on bonded pairs with non-bonded cysteine pairs that are also in contact (e.g. Cbeta < 8 A). Score all residue pairs to see whether L32H13 ranks non-cysteine contacts as high as bonded cysteines. Report ESM-2's own contact-regression output, or the true contact map, as a baseline for the disulfide ranking. Until then, restate Conclusions 1 and 3 as: 'head L32H13's APC attention ranks annotated bonded cysteine pairs above other cysteine pairs (per-protein AP 0.81 vs 0.25 chance); whether this goes beyond general contact attention was not tested.'

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 34, 37-39, 40 (Conclusions 1-3: 'circuit', 'computes disulfide connectivity', 'works out which cysteine bonds to which', 'carries the answer', 'earlier stages of the same circuit', 'understands the chemistry of folding')
findings.description: The summary describes a circuit and a mechanism that the analysis never tested. All the evidence is correlational: one head's attention scores are compared with annotated labels. There is no ablation, activation patching or path analysis, so nothing shows that L32H13 'computes' connectivity, that later outputs depend on it, or that other heads feed into it. The claim that L29H18, L31H17 and L30H1 are 'earlier stages of the same circuit' has no evidence behind it, and the data partly contradict it.
findings.evidence: No intervention appears anywhere in the code (disulfide_attention.py only computes AP, bootstrap and per-protein metrics). L29H18, called an 'earlier stage', does better on test than L32H13 (0.745 vs 0.718; results.json lines 337-339). Spearman correlations between the top heads' test scores, which I computed, are only 0.48-0.80 (L32H13 vs L29H18 0.66, vs L30H1 0.62, vs L23H6 0.35). That fits separate parallel heads as well as a pipeline. 'Understands the chemistry of folding' rests on one ranking metric.
findings.recommended_action: Rephrase as a decoding-level result (level 1 of the claim taxonomy): 'the attention of head L32H13 is strongly aligned with annotated disulfide pairs'. Drop 'circuit', 'computes', 'understands' and 'earlier stages'. To claim a circuit, ablate or patch L32H13 and the upstream heads and measure the effect on downstream representations or on a disulfide probe.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md line 43 (Conclusion 4); README.md lines 26-28 (inclusion rules); code/disulfide_attention.py lines 134-153
findings.description: The recommendation to 'use L32H13 as a ready-made disulfide connectivity predictor' goes beyond what was evaluated. Only proteins already known to have at least one annotated intrachain bond, at most 40 cysteines and at most 1,022 residues were scored, so a user would need to know in advance that the protein has disulfides. The head produces a ranking of pairs, not a connectivity, because nothing enforces one partner per cysteine. Whole-pattern accuracy and bonded-vs-free-cysteine classification were never measured, and there is no comparison with existing disulfide-connectivity predictors or ESM contact predictions.
findings.evidence: README line 26: 'A protein is kept if it has ... at least 1 annotated intrachain bond'. Per-protein precision at k = number of bonds is 0.734 (results.json line 72), so about a quarter of the top-k pairs are wrong even in this pre-filtered set. No matching step or full-connectivity metric exists in the code.
findings.recommended_action: Remove the predictor recommendation, or support it with: (a) evaluation on unselected proteins, including ones with free cysteines and no disulfides; (b) a connectivity metric (fraction of proteins whose full bond pattern is exactly right after maximum-weight matching); (c) a comparison with established disulfide-connectivity tools and with ESM-2 contact predictions.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 72-75 and 212-217 (pooled AP); SUMMARY.md lines 16, 25, 35 ('AP 14.6 times the base rate')
findings.description: The question is within-protein: which pairs of the same protein are bonded. The headline metric, however, pools all pairs across proteins, so it also rewards differences in score scale between proteins. For example, short proteins have larger APC attention values and a higher fraction of bonded pairs. The 0.718 AP and the 14.6x lift over the pooled base rate are partly inflated by this.
findings.evidence: Recomputed with L32H13 scores normalised within each protein, the test AP falls from 0.718 to 0.591 (within-protein ranks) or 0.638 (within-protein z-scores); the select AP falls from 0.742 to 0.615 / 0.646. The within-protein metrics remain strong (per-protein AP 0.81 vs 0.25 for random scores).
findings.recommended_action: Make the per-protein metrics (mean per-protein AP and P@1, each with its per-protein chance value) the headline. Report the pooled AP only alongside a within-protein-normalised version, and state that the 14.6x factor depends on pooling.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 20-25 and 34 ('puts a bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins')
findings.description: The P@1 figures in the results table and in Conclusion 1 are not compared with chance. Random scoring already gives a mean P@1 of 0.15. Five test proteins have only one candidate pair (P@1 = 1 whatever the score), and 10 have three or fewer pairs.
findings.evidence: Recomputed: chance P@1 = 0.150 and chance per-protein AP = 0.250 on test. Excluding proteins with three or fewer pairs, L32H13 P@1 is 0.788 (113 proteins), against 0.805 overall.
findings.recommended_action: Add the chance values to the table, e.g. 'P@1 0.805 (chance 0.150)', and either drop single-pair proteins from the per-protein metrics or flag them.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 108-113 and 220-224; SUMMARY.md lines 27-28 ('expected highest of 661 candidates under the within-protein null is 0.087')
findings.description: The 'expected maximum of 661 candidates' under the null is underestimated. It uses a single label permutation and 256 sampled candidates, then resamples 661 values with replacement from those 256. That effectively gives the maximum of about 256 candidates under one permutation, not the maximum of 661.
findings.evidence: Scoring all 661 candidates under 5 independent within-protein permutations gives null maxima of 0.0914-0.0985 (mean 0.0946), against the reported 0.0869. This does not change any conclusion, since the observed maximum is 0.745.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the null maximum over all 661 candidates, averaged over at least 20 permutations, and report its mean and 95th percentile.

findings.description: The 'at most 40 cysteines' rule is not a model limit, yet it removed only test proteins. The two excluded test proteins (64 and 41 cysteines) would have added about 2,836 candidate pairs, about 38% of the 7,463 test pairs kept. Performance falls as cysteine count rises, so the pooled test AP could be materially lower with them included. The summary does not mention the exclusion.
findings.evidence: The largest select protein has 24 cysteines and the largest kept test protein 39, so the cap only applied to test. Pairs removed: 64*63/2 + 41*40/2 = 2,836. L32H13 per-protein AP by cysteine count: 0.861 (4-7 Cys), 0.774 (8-15), 0.708 (16-40).
findings.recommended_action: Score the two excluded proteins (both are within the 1,022-residue limit) and report the headline with and without them, or justify the cap before looking at the data. Mention the exclusion in SUMMARY.md.

findings.location: README.md lines 19-20 (split by protein); SUMMARY.md lines 37-38 ('From the sequence alone, the model works out ...')
findings.description: The select/test split is by accession, not by sequence similarity, so a few test proteins are near-copies of select proteins. More importantly, the Swiss-Prot test proteins were probably in ESM-2's pretraining data (UniRef). The analysis therefore cannot separate 'working out' connectivity from the sequence from recalling learned family patterns. All results come from one model size, one bf16 extraction and one dataset, yet the claims are made about 'ESM-2' and 'the model' in general.
findings.evidence: 5-mer containment against select: Q47450~A0A0H2VAQ6 0.89, B1JDQ5~A5VYT2 0.89, B4TQB8~Q1R984 0.71, P60045~P00596 0.62. No held-out-family test, no check of overlap with pretraining data, and no second model or model size.
findings.recommended_action: Re-split by sequence-similarity cluster (e.g. MMseqs2 at 30% identity), or report results without the near-duplicate test proteins. Test proteins or families not in UniRef50 for ESM-2. Repeat on at least one other ESM-2 size or another protein language model before claiming a general property.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 34 and 38 ('Head L32H13 ...', 'L32H13 in the last layer carries the answer'); code/disulfide_attention.py lines 216, 40
findings.description: The summary gives L32H13 a unique role, but which head wins is only moderately stable. L29H18 is almost tied on select and better on test. No sensitivity check was run on extraction choices (symmetrisation and APC, bf16 run once). The bootstrap uses only 200 resamples.
findings.evidence: In 200 protein-level bootstrap resamples of the select split, L32H13 was chosen 155 times and L29H18 45 times. Select AP 0.742 vs 0.721; test AP 0.718 vs 0.745. A 2,000-resample bootstrap gives a test-AP CI of [0.647, 0.787], close to the reported [0.664, 0.782].
findings.recommended_action: Report that the 'best head' is a set of nearly equivalent late-layer heads (L32H13 and L29H18), give the selection frequency, use at least 1,000 bootstrap resamples, and add a sensitivity check (raw vs APC, fp32 vs bf16).

findings.description: The bond labels are UniProt FT DISULFID annotations, which include 'by similarity' inferences, not bonds observed in structures. Every pair without an annotation is labelled non-bonded, and cysteines bonded to another chain stay in as negatives. The endpoint is agreement with curated annotation, which the summary presents as the model 'working out' true connectivity.
findings.evidence: README: 'A pair without a record is labelled not bonded'; 'Records with a single position (bonds to another chain) are not used' (those cysteines remain as candidates). No evidence codes are kept in proteins.tsv.
findings.recommended_action: Record the annotation evidence level, test a subset with experimental or structure-derived bonds, and state that the endpoint is agreement with curated UniProt annotation.

findings.description: There is no environment record: numpy, torch and transformers versions are not given, and there are no hardware or runtime figures for the extraction step. The extraction calls `from_pretrained(..., dtype=...)`; older transformers releases expect `torch_dtype`, so the attention scores, which were produced once on an Apple GPU in bf16, cannot be reliably regenerated or checked.
findings.evidence: README: 'Needs numpy.' No requirements or environment file exists anywhere in the folder. The scores cannot be checked here without the model weights.
findings.recommended_action: Add pinned versions (requirements.txt or environment.yml) for both scripts, and record hardware and runtime for the extraction. Optionally, ship a checksum or a small rebuilt subset to show the scores can be regenerated.

This is the intervention branch of the detection rule.

Attacks Conclusion 4 (use L32H13 as a ready-made connectivity predictor), which is part of the key's wrong result, but for a different reason than the key. Evaluation covered only proteins pre-filtered to have at least one bond. The head gives a ranking, not a one-partner-per-cysteine connectivity. There is no full-pattern metric and no comparison with existing tools. P@n_bonds 0.734 verified. This is a genuine point about the scope of the recommendation, not the bonded-only-scope-biases-AP false alarm. It does not give the key's causal or contact reasons, so it is not the documented error itself.

The numbers reproduce: within-protein rank and z-normalised test AP are 0.591 and 0.638, select 0.615 and 0.646. However, the key explicitly lists 'pooled AP is invalid because attention scores are on different scales in different proteins' as a possible false alarm: the per-protein view gives the same ordering (0.812 vs 0.383 vs 0.331). Pooled AP is the stated metric, and the scale-dependence of the 14.6x lift does not reflect an error in the analysis.

True: chance P@1 is about 0.15 (I get 0.152). Five test proteins have a single candidate pair and 10 have three or fewer. Excluding the latter gives P@1 0.788. Adding chance values is a reasonable presentation fix; it does not change any conclusion.

Technically correct. Resampling 661 values with replacement from 256 null APs under a single permutation biases the expected maximum low. Scoring all 661 candidates under 5 permutations gives 0.091-0.099 (mean 0.0946) vs the reported 0.0869. The key's source value is 0.093. The effect is trivial against an observed 0.745 and changes no conclusion.

The facts check out: the select maximum is 24 Cys and the test maximum 39, and the two dropped proteins hold 2,836 pairs. But the key lists 'the <=40-cysteine rule biases the result' as a possible false alarm: the rule is stated in the README and applies to every scorer. The claim that test AP 'could be materially lower' is speculative and was not tested.

The core claims are homology leakage between splits and pretraining contamination (Swiss-Prot sequences in UniRef). The key lists both as possible false alarms: no identical sequences, only 3 test proteins above 0.5 5-mer Jaccard, a single parameter chosen, and no labels used in pretraining. The single-model-size remark is a generic limitation.

Verified: in 200 protein-level bootstrap resamples of select, L32H13 was chosen 150 times and L29H18 50 times. L29H18 is near-tied on select and better on test. This fits the key's point that the signal is spread over several late-layer heads, but it is a modest robustness note. The bf16 and 200-resample concerns are minor: the key reports a CPU re-run correlation of 0.9996.

A fair limitation note. Labels are curated UniProt annotations, and unannotated or interchain-bonded cysteines count as negatives. The finding does not claim the result is invalid. The key notes that such label noise would lower AP for every scorer.

True that the package pins no numpy, torch or transformers versions and that the `dtype=` keyword depends on the transformers version. But the key says the shipped scores match the source cache and the code reproduces them on a CPU spot check (correlation 0.9996), so 'cannot be reliably regenerated or checked' overstates the issue. This is a reproducibility nit.

grade_b.detection_reason: The key's documented error is causal and mechanistic overreach in SUMMARY.md Conclusions 1-4. F2 quotes the 'circuit', 'computes disulfide connectivity', 'works out which cysteine bonds to which', 'earlier stages of the same circuit' and 'understands the chemistry of folding' claims. It says they are unsupported because the evidence is only a correlation between attention and annotations, with no ablation, patching or path analysis, and it asks for decoding-level wording. That matches the first branch of the detection rule. F1 targets 'dedicated disulfide-bond circuit' and 'goes further ... learned the rule that pairs cysteines into bonds'. It says nothing separates a disulfide-specific head from a general contact head, because there is no contact-matched comparison and no check on non-cysteine contacts. That matches the second branch (specificity versus residue contacts).

findings.reason: This hits the key's specificity branch. It names Conclusions 1 and 3 ('dedicated circuit', 'goes further', 'learned the rule'). It notes that bonded cysteines are in contact and attention follows contacts, and that there is no contact-matched or non-cysteine comparison. The key's known facts confirm that nothing in the package compares against non-cysteine contacts or structures.

This hits the key's intervention branch. It names 'circuit', 'computes', 'works out', 'earlier stages' and 'understands the chemistry' and points out there is no ablation or patching, only correlation. The supporting numbers check out. L29H18 has test AP 0.745 vs 0.718 for L32H13 (results.json lines 337-339). The Spearman correlations I recomputed on the test scores were L32H13 vs L29H18 0.657, vs L30H1 0.617, vs L31H17 0.800 and vs L23H6 0.345.

Conclusion 4, which recommends L32H13 as a ready-made connectivity predictor, is in the key's wrong_result, but F3 argues against it for a different reason than the key. Its reasons: only proteins already known to have disulfides were evaluated, nothing enforces one partner per cysteine, whole-pattern accuracy was not measured, and there is no comparison with existing tools. These points are accurate (P@n_bonds is 0.734, results.json line 72, and the code has no matching step). They show the deployment recommendation goes beyond the evaluation. F3 does not say the scope biases the AP, so it is not the scope false alarm the key lists. It does not raise the causal or contact-specificity argument, so it does not count as detecting the error.

The numbers are confirmed. With L32H13 scores normalised within each protein, test AP falls from 0.718 to 0.591 (rank) or 0.638 (z-score), and select AP falls from 0.742 to 0.615 / 0.646. The finding does not say the pooled AP is invalid, and it accepts that the per-protein metrics are strong, which is the key's point. It sits close to the key's listed false alarm about score scales but is a true and non-load-bearing reporting refinement. The ordering against the baselines is unchanged: the rank-normalised mean head is 0.147 and separation 0.106.

True. I recomputed chance P@1 as 0.152, close to the finding's 0.150. Five test proteins have a single candidate pair and 10 have three or fewer. P@1 without those 10 proteins is 0.788 over 113 proteins. Adding a chance reference is a presentation improvement and changes no conclusion.

Confirmed. Scoring all 661 candidates under 5 within-protein permutations gives null maxima of 0.091-0.099 (mean 0.096), against the reported 0.087. Resampling 661 values with replacement from 256 sampled nulls slightly underestimates the maximum. The key notes the source run gave 0.093 under different draws. The gap is trivial next to the observed 0.745, so no conclusion changes.

The facts are correct: two test proteins (64 and 41 cysteines) were dropped, the select maximum is 24 Cys and the kept test maximum is 39, and 2,836 pairs were removed. But the key explicitly lists 'the <=40-cysteine rule ... biases the result' as a false alarm. The rule is stated in the README and applies to every scorer, and the claim that the AP 'could be materially lower' is speculation.

Its main arguments, homology leakage across the accession split and ESM-2 pretraining contamination, are both listed false alarms in the key. Only 3 test proteins have more than 0.5 5-mer Jaccard similarity to a select protein, only one parameter is chosen, and no labels entered training. The point about using a single model size is a generic limitation.

True. I reran a 200-resample protein bootstrap on the select split: L32H13 was chosen 148 times and L29H18 52 times, close to the finding's 155/45. The two heads are nearly tied, which matches the key's note that the signal is spread over several heads. This does not change the headline. Its request for a bf16/APC sensitivity check overlaps the key's false alarm (CPU re-run correlation is 0.9996).

This is a true labeling limitation: UniProt annotations, unannotated pairs counted as negatives, no evidence codes. The finding does not claim the result is invalid, which would be the key's false alarm. It only asks to state that the endpoint is agreement with annotation, a minor wording point. The key notes that missing labels would lower AP for every scorer.

There are indeed no pinned versions, and the dtype= keyword needs a recent transformers release. That is a minor reproducibility gap. The suggestion that the scores 'cannot be reliably regenerated or checked' overlaps the key's false alarm, because the shipped scores match the source cache and a CPU spot check reproduces them.

review.summary:
I re-ran the pipeline inline and got the same numbers as outputs/transfer_rpe1.json (model within 0.886 and transfer 0.789; expression within 0.913 and transfer 0.878; offsets 356.2 and 357.5 deg). Row alignment is correct (row_cell_ids are the identity in both datasets). There are no duplicate rows in either dataset and no activation rows shared between them. The phase orientation behaves as intended: per-bin S and G2M scores rise and fall in the expected order in both lines. The result is not sensitive to the ridge alpha (1e2 to 1e5) or to building the RPE1 label from K562's 87 markers instead of 93.

So the narrow claim stands: both frozen readouts do far better than chance on RPE1. The problems are with what the summary says that evidence shows.
(1) The chance floors and the pass/fail rule are far too weak. Three simple marker-based predictors that use no RPE1 labels match or beat the model readout:
- a 3-class G1/S/G2M call: R_diff 0.869;
- a 2-feature ridge on the S and G2M module scores: R_diff 0.961;
- a yes/no G2M-score threshold: R_diff 0.646, which still passes the rule.
(2) The summary says the rule checks the best rotation. It does not: both the score and the error it uses ignore rotation.
(3) The claim that the RPE1 label "behaves as a cell-cycle label" is circular, and the expression reference includes the marker genes that define the label.
(4) The matching S peak is forced by the method, not a finding.
(5) The source and target differ in batch, gene panel and normalisation, not only in cell line, which contradicts the Limits section.
(6) "Within about 20 deg" overstates the model's accuracy, especially in S phase.

findings.location: code/transfer_test.py lines 130-153 (chance floors and validity rule); SUMMARY.md lines 13-14, 21-25, 31-36
findings.description: The only comparisons are a constant predictor and a uniform random predictor, and the pass/fail rule is very lax (R_diff > max(0.15, 2 x constant) and median error < 86 deg). R_diff on these labels is driven mainly by coarse phase class, because about a quarter of RPE1 cells sit in one G1 cluster at 270-300 deg and the rest in S and G2/M arcs. A simple G1/S/G2M class call therefore scores as well as or better than the readouts. The summary reads 'Both transfer ... against 0.043 for a constant predictor' and 'recovers RPE1 phase' as evidence of a transferred phase readout, but these floors cannot tell a phase readout apart from a coarse marker-based classifier.
findings.evidence:
All computed inline with the package's own functions on RPE1, with no RPE1 labels used:
- Seurat-style 3-class call (G1/S/G2M from RPE1 module scores), each class mapped to its K562 class-mean angle: R_diff 0.869, median error 15.7 deg. That beats the model readout (0.789, 23 deg) and nearly ties the expression readout (0.878, 16 deg).
- Ridge fit on K562 using only the two module scores (S, G2M): transfer R_diff 0.961, median error 7 deg.
- 2-class predictor (G2M score > 0 -> 155 deg, else 285 deg): R_diff 0.646, 27 deg. It easily passes the rule (threshold 0.15 and 86 deg).
The model readout does carry some ordering within phase arcs (Spearman 0.70, 0.71 and 0.49 in three arcs), but the reported metric and floors do not show this.

findings.description: The summary says both readouts 'pass the validity rule' because the best rotation is small, so they 'land on the right part of the circle with no adjustment on RPE1'. The rule does not test this. It uses only R_diff, which ignores rotation, and the median error, which is measured after the best rotation. That rotation is fitted on the RPE1 labels. A readout whose predictions were rotated by any amount, for example because the phase conventions do not match, would get the same scores and the verdict 'VALID TRANSFER'. The reported median errors also use RPE1 labels (through the fitted rotation), which conflicts with 'no RPE1 labels used'. The headline zero-shot claim therefore depends on the offset being small, and the rule does not check that.
findings.evidence: valid = (transfer > thr) and (transfer_median_err_deg < const median); transfer_offset_deg is never used in the rule. med_err_rot fits off = angle(mean exp(i(true - pred))) on the target labels before taking the median. Rechecked here: the offsets happen to be small (356.2 and 357.5 deg). Mean cos(pred - true) without rotation is 0.788 for the model, and its median error without rotation is 24 deg. The conclusion survives in this run, but only because the offsets were checked separately.
findings.recommended_action: Make a measure that does not ignore rotation the primary transfer score: mean cos(pred - true), or median error with no rotation. Add a limit on the offset to the rule, or drop the rotation from it. Correct the summary text so it says the rotation was checked separately, not by the rule.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 33-34 (Interpretation 2) and 12, 23 (expression reference); code/cc_phase.py lines 54-69; code/transfer_test.py lines 118-128
findings.description: The label is the angle in the first two PCs of the standardised Tirosh marker genes, built the same way in each dataset. A readout fit on K562 that recovers a label built the same way from the same markers in RPE1 only shows that the two PCA planes agree. It does not show that the RPE1 label 'behaves as a cell-cycle label'. The expression 'point of reference' also includes the 87 marker genes that define the label (before atan2 the label is a linear function of them). It is therefore close to a ceiling built on the label's own genes, not a neutral reference. Its within score and retention (0.913 and 0.96) are inflated by this.
findings.evidence: Expression readout on the 87 shared marker genes only: within 0.975, transfer 0.918. Two module scores alone: transfer 0.961. Expression without the 94 markers (6,457 genes): within 0.863, transfer 0.839, retention 0.97.
findings.recommended_action: Remove or rephrase Interpretation 2, or support it with evidence that does not depend on the marker set (for example held-out marker sets, histone or DNA-content proxies). Report the expression reference with the label-defining marker genes excluded, alongside the full version.

findings.description: 'The phase convention is consistent. The S peak sits at 45 deg in both datasets' is presented as a finding, but phase_angle_oriented rotates each dataset so that the S peak is at exactly 45 deg. Only the S-to-G2/M gap says anything, and it differs by 12 deg between datasets (108.8 vs 97.1). That is a real mismatch in convention, not evidence of consistency.
findings.evidence: rot = deg2rad(s_at_deg) - mu_s; the log shows 'S peak 45.0deg' for both datasets by construction. The G2M peaks are at 153.8 and 142.1 deg.
findings.recommended_action: State that the S-peak position is fixed by construction. Report the G2/M offset (12 deg) as the remaining mismatch in convention and discuss how it affects the transfer offset and errors.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 40-41 and 35-36; README.md lines 36-38; data/k562/k562_controls.h5ad vs data/rpe1/rpe1_controls.h5ad
findings.description: The text says the test is 'a change of cell line, not of batch or platform'. In fact the K562 and RPE1 sets are separate experiments (a different batch) and differ in gene panel and normalisation. All of these are mixed up with cell line, so Interpretation 3's attribution to biology (karyotype, epithelial line) is not isolated. The model readout is not restricted to the shared gene space, unlike the expression readout. If the cell sentences were built from these panels, about 13% of an RPE1 cell's top 512 genes are genes K562 cells never had.
findings.evidence: K562: 6,546 genes; RPE1: 8,749 genes; 2,205 RPE1 genes are absent from K562. In RPE1, an average of 86.9% (minimum 74.0%) of each cell's top-512 genes are in the shared space. expm1 row sums are 7,447-9,573 in K562 (normalised before the genes were subset) but exactly 10,000 in RPE1 (normalised after). Both manifests are identical, so the panel difference is not recorded.
findings.recommended_action: Rewrite the Limits section to say that cell line is mixed up with batch, gene panel and normalisation. Normalise both datasets the same way on the shared genes. Build cell sentences for the model from the shared gene space, or report the effect of the panel difference.

findings.description: 'Recovers it to within about 20 deg' overstates how accurate the model readout is. Its median error is 23 deg after the fitted rotation and 24 deg without it. Its mean error is 31 deg, and in the S-phase arc errors are larger and biased. The predictions bunch up near the G1 and G2/M clusters.
findings.evidence: RPE1 model transfer, by true-phase bin: median errors 37, 28 and 41 deg for 0-30, 30-60 and 60-90 deg, with mean residuals of -39, +15 and +42 deg. The concentration of predicted phases is pred_R = 0.34, against 0.043 for the true phases. Mean absolute error is 31 deg.
findings.recommended_action: Report median and mean error per readout without rotation, plus errors by phase. Replace 'within about 20 deg' with the actual figures (model ~23-24 deg median, worse in S phase).

grade_a.detection_reason: The key marks B2101 as clean ("error": null), so there is no documented error to detect and error_detected is null. I ran checks on the package. None of the findings shows that a headline claim is wrong: the transfer scores beat chance by a wide margin, the offsets are small (356.2 and 357.5 deg), and the raw median error for the model is 24.0 deg. The load-bearing findings (F1, F3) match the key's listed possible false alarms (chance floor too lenient; marker-gene overlap with the label).

findings.reason: I reproduced the numbers. A 3-class module-score predictor mapped to the K562 class means gets R_diff 0.869 and 15.7 deg. A 2-class predictor gets 0.646 and 27 deg. 729 of the 3,000 RPE1 cells (24%) fall in the 270-300 deg bin. But the key lists 'chance floor too lenient' as a possible false alarm. A constant at the target mean is the right label-free chance level. The marker-class baseline is itself a K562-to-RPE1 transfer built from the same markers that define the label. So it does not show the activation readout failed to transfer, or that 'recovers RPE1 phase' is false. The summary never claims the readout resolves phase more finely than a coarse class call. This is a request for stronger baselines, not a confirmed error in the headline.

It is true that the validity rule ignores rotation (transfer_offset_deg is not used in it). But the finding itself admits the conclusion holds, and I confirmed it: offsets are 356.2 and 357.5 deg, the raw median error is 24 deg, and mean cos is 0.788. The key lists this exact point (rotation invariance hiding a failure) as a possible false alarm. The summary does report the small offset separately. What remains is a wording point: the bullet places the offset check under the rule, which does not test it.

The key says the overlap between label marker genes and readout features is a design property of a marker-defined label, and lists it as a possible false alarm. The key also says a ridge refit on RPE1 alone recovers the label (R_diff 0.909/0.952), so the RPE1 label is a valid cell-cycle phase. The finding's own numbers cut against its 'inflated' claim: with the markers removed, expression still transfers at 0.839 with retention 0.97.

I confirmed the normalisation mismatch. In K562 the expm1 row sums run from 7,447 to 9,573; in RPE1 they are exactly 10,000. The gene panels also differ (6,546 vs 8,749 genes). K562 and RPE1 come from separate Replogle experiments, so 'not of batch' in the Limits section is imprecise. This is a real caveat the key does not cover, but it does not overturn any result, since both readouts transfer well.

It is true that the S peak at 45 deg is set by construction (phase_angle_oriented rotates it there), so citing it as evidence of consistency is weak. The key treats the orientation as correct: the direction is consistent, with G2/M following S by 109 and 97 deg. Calling the 12 deg difference in G2/M separation a 'mismatch in convention' overstates a small difference. Not load-bearing.

I confirmed the figures: raw median error 24.0 deg, mean error 31 deg, and larger errors in the S arc (median 37-41 deg in some bins). But 'about 20 deg' is a loose average of the two readouts (23 and 16 deg), and 81.5% of cells fall within 45 deg. This is wording imprecision, not a wrong claim.

grade_b.detection_reason: The key marks B2101 as clean (error: null). So there is no documented error to detect, and error_detected is null. I checked the findings by running inline code on the package. Every number the review gives reproduced: 3-class call 0.869 / 15.7 deg, module-score ridge 0.961 / 7 deg, 2-class 0.646 / 27 deg, no-marker expression 0.839 transfer, markers-only 0.918, K562 expm1 row sums 7,447-9,573 vs 10,000 in RPE1, 86.8% of top-512 genes shared, raw model median 24 deg, mean 31 deg. None of these shows that a headline claim is wrong. The transfer stays far above the correct chance floors, the offsets are small, and the RPE1 label is valid (the key's RPE1 refit recovers it).

findings.reason: The numbers reproduce: 3-class call R_diff 0.869 / 15.7 deg, 2-class 0.646 / 27 deg, module-score ridge 0.961. But the finding mixes up chance floors with competing readouts. The summary claims transfer beyond chance, not that the model beats a marker classifier. The key lists 'chance floor is too lenient' as a possible false alarm: the constant at the target mean is the correct label-free floor. The finding's own within-arc Spearman values (0.49-0.71) show the readout carries phase within each arc, so 'recovers RPE1 phase' stands. The marker-based class call is itself a successful K562-to-RPE1 transfer on a marker-defined label.

It is true that the validity gate in code ignores transfer_offset_deg and uses the median error after rotation. However, the finding itself concedes the conclusion survives: offsets are 356.2 / 357.5 deg, raw median error is 24 deg, and mean cos is 0.788, all verified. The key lists rotation invariance hiding a failure as a false alarm. The summary reports the small rotation as a checked fact, and 'no RPE1 labels used' refers to fitting, not scoring. This is a gate-design nit, not an error in the results.

Marker overlap between the label and the features is explicitly a possible false alarm in the key, as a design property of a marker-defined label. The finding's own numbers, which I reproduced, undercut its 'inflated' claim. Without the 94 markers, expression transfer is 0.839 with retention 0.97, so retention is actually higher than 0.96. The key also confirms the RPE1 label is a valid cell-cycle phase: an RPE1 refit gives circ_corr 0.93 / 0.96. So Interpretation 2's conclusion holds.

It is true that the S peak at 45 deg is set by construction, but the README states this openly. Calling the 12 deg G2/M difference 'a real mismatch in convention' goes against the key, which says the orientation is consistent (S at 45, G2/M 109 / 97 deg after S). A difference in G2/M peak position can reflect biology. This is a wording point and does not affect any result.

I confirmed a preprocessing inconsistency the key does not mention. K562 expm1 row sums are 7,447-9,573, while RPE1 sums are exactly 10,000. Of RPE1's 8,749 genes, 2,205 are missing from K562, and only 86.8% (min 74%) of each RPE1 cell's top-512 genes are in the shared space. These differences make the transfer harder, not easier, so the positive conclusion stands. Attributing the transfer to cell line alone is slightly overstated, but this is a minor limitation, not a load-bearing error.

The figures are verified: model raw median 24 deg, mean 31 deg, per-bin medians 37 / 28 / 41 deg. 'About 20 deg' is a loose summary of 23 and 16 deg, and the exact numbers are in the table. The concentration of predictions is a possible false alarm in the key, since most cells are within 45 deg. This is a wording precision issue.

review.summary: I re-ran the pipeline inline without writing any files, and every number in outputs/transfer_rpe1.json and SUMMARY.md reproduces exactly: R_diff 0.886/0.789 for the model and 0.913/0.878 for expression, median errors 13/23 and 11/16 deg, offsets -3.8 and -2.5 deg, and chance floors 0.043/0.017. Row alignment between the activations and the h5ad files is the identity, and there are no duplicate cells. The PCA phase labels match marker-based G1/S/G2M groupings in both datasets, with circular means of about 286, 22-26 and 146-157 deg. The headline result is robust. A permutation null gives about 0.05 at the 99th percentile. The orientation flips do not change with marker-ranking depth (top = 50 to 1000) or with seed. Model transfer stays clearly above chance for ridge alpha from 1 to 1e5. Renormalising both datasets to a common scale leaves the expression transfer unchanged. I found no coding error that changes the results, so the main claim (both readouts transfer zero-shot, well above chance) stands. The problems are in how some claims are argued and how the validity rule is described. Interpretation 2 rests on circular evidence. The 'phase convention is consistent' bullet cites something that is true by construction. The validity rule cannot detect a wrongly placed (rotated) readout, although the summary presents it as if it could. The median-error summary hides errors that depend on phase. There are also smaller problems with the marker-scoring and marker lists, preprocessing that the README does not document, and the absence of any uncertainty or sensitivity reporting.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:33-34 (Interpretation 2); label built in code/cc_phase.py:54-69; expression readout in code/transfer_test.py:118-128
findings.description: The claim that 'the RPE1 phase label behaves as a cell-cycle label' rests on circular evidence. The label in both datasets is made the same way: the atan2 of PC1/PC2 of the same standardised Tirosh marker genes. The expression readout is a linear map over features that include those same markers. If a K562-trained readout recovers the RPE1 label, that shows the two datasets share a similar marker covariance structure. It does not show that the shared angle is cell cycle. Any axis common to both datasets that the markers load on, such as a library-size or technical component, would transfer just as well. The model readout's success also does not validate the label, for the same reason.
findings.evidence: An expression readout restricted to the 87 shared marker genes transfers better than the full readout: R_diff 0.918 and 12.7 deg, against 0.878 with all 6,544 genes. The transfer score therefore mostly measures how similar the marker loadings are. Both labels were built with the identical marker/PCA procedure (cc_phase.phase_angle). The only cell-cycle anchor is the S/G2M score orientation, which uses the same marker genes again.
findings.recommended_action: Remove the claim, or support it with evidence independent of the markers. Examples: agreement with a phase estimated from a separate gene set (histone genes, cyclins, a Whitfield/tricycle reference projection); the readout's performance when the marker genes are excluded (about 0.84 here); or DNA-content or FUCCI ground truth if available.

findings.description: The summary says the phase convention is consistent because 'the S peak sits at 45 deg in both datasets'. That holds by construction: phase_angle_oriented rotates each dataset so its S peak lands at s_at_deg = 45. Only the G2/M-S separation (109 vs 97 deg) and the transfer offset carry any information about consistency. The offset also depends on the choice of top.
findings.evidence: rot = deg2rad(s_at_deg) - mu_s forces s_peak_deg = 45.0 in every dataset. Changing top (the number of highest-scoring cells used for the peaks) shifts the model's best-rotation offset from about -4 deg (top = 200) to -10 deg (top = 500) and -18 deg (top = 1000). R_diff stays at 0.789 throughout.
findings.recommended_action: Remove the S-at-45 statement as evidence. Report the G2/M separation difference and the transfer offset as the consistency check, and give the sensitivity of the offset to the orientation hyperparameters.

findings.description: The validity rule cannot check the property the summary attaches to it. Both quantities it tests are rotation-invariant: R_diff, and the median error taken after the best rotation. A frozen readout that put every cell 90 or 180 deg away from the right place would still be labelled 'VALID TRANSFER'. The summary links passing the rule to 'land on the right part of the circle with no adjustment', but only the separately reported offset supports that statement. The rule's floor is also weak: the constant predictor's R_diff equals the target phase R (0.043), so the threshold is effectively a fixed 0.15, and the median-error condition only requires beating about 86 deg.
findings.evidence: thr = max(0.15, 2*0.043) = 0.15. valid() checks r['transfer'] > thr and r['transfer_median_err_deg'] < 86.0, and both inputs are computed after the optimal rotation (med_err_rot, circ_R_diff). transfer_offset_deg is computed but never used in the rule. The unrotated median errors are 24.0 and 16.0 deg.
findings.recommended_action: Add an offset bound (for example |offset| < 30 deg) or an unrotated error criterion to the rule, report the unrotated median error, and use a permutation null as the chance floor. In the summary, keep 'passes the rule' separate from 'small rotation'.

findings.description: The single median error hides large distortion that depends on phase. The frozen model readout compresses and shifts phases, so the 'within about 20 deg' description does not hold for S-phase cells or for a substantial fraction of cells.
findings.evidence: Model on RPE1, by marker-score phase class: S-phase median error 34 deg (R_diff 0.62); G2M cells biased +27 deg; G1 cells -14 deg. 19% of cells are more than 45 deg off. The predicted angles are concentrated (pred_R = 0.34) while the true RPE1 phase is nearly uniform (R = 0.043): about 500 predictions fall in 180-225 deg, where only 103 true cells lie.
findings.recommended_action: Report errors broken down by phase (or by true-phase bin) and the fraction of cells with error above 45 deg, and state that the readout distorts phase as well as rotating it.

findings.description: The module score is described as 'Scanpy-style' but differs from Scanpy. The control pool for each bin includes the marker genes themselves. The function draws n_markers_in_bin × 50 controls, so any bin with 6 or more markers uses the entire bin, markers included, as its control set. Scanpy samples ctrl_size genes per bin and excludes the gene list. As a result, S and G2M scores partly subtract each other's genes, and these scores set the flip and the S-at-45 rotation.
findings.evidence: pool = np.where(bins == b)[0] does not exclude idx. k = (bins[idx]==b).sum()*n_ctrl, and with about 262 genes per bin, min(k, len(pool)) takes the whole bin once a bin holds 6 or more markers. corr(S, G2M) is -0.006 in K562 and 0.29 in RPE1. The orientation is currently robust to this: the flip decisions are unchanged for top = 50-1000.
findings.recommended_action: Exclude the marker genes from the control pool and sample a fixed control count per bin, or call scanpy.tl.score_genes directly. Then re-check the orientation outputs.

findings.description: The marker lists are presented as the Tirosh/Scanpy sets but are a trimmed 94-gene version. MLF1IP, FAM64A and HN1 are left out entirely, although their current symbols CENPU and JPT1 are present in both panels and PIMREG is in RPE1. In addition, the two labels are built from different gene sets: 87 markers in K562 (UBE2C, CCNE2, MSH2, EXO1, WDR76, GAS2L3 and E2F8 are missing) against 93 in RPE1. The README's '93 of the 94' figure is relative to this trimmed list.
findings.evidence: The script prints 87 cc genes for SOURCE and 93 for TARGET. CENPU and JPT1 are found in both var_names, PIMREG in RPE1 only.
findings.recommended_action: Map the outdated symbols to current names and use the full 97-gene list. Build both labels from the marker set shared by the two datasets, or show that the result does not depend on the difference in marker sets.

findings.description: The K562 input has undocumented preprocessing. Its gene panel looks pre-restricted to genes that exist in the RPE1 panel: 6,544 of its 6,546 genes are shared, and dominant K562 genes such as HBG1, HBG2, GATA1 and TAL1 are absent. It was also normalised before subsetting, so rows do not sum to 1e4, unlike RPE1, even though the README calls it 'same format'. If the C2S cell sentences were built from these files, the K562 inputs to the model were harmonised towards the target gene space while the RPE1 sentences were not. That bears on the 'not specific to K562' interpretation and on reproducibility.
findings.evidence: The expm1 row sums for K562 range from 7,447 to 9,573; for RPE1 every row sums to exactly 10,000. The only K562-only genes are HSPA14 and HSPA14-1. Renormalising both datasets to a common scale leaves the expression transfer unchanged (0.878), so the effect on the numbers is negligible.
findings.recommended_action: Document how the K562 panel was chosen and how both datasets were normalised, and record in the manifests which gene panel was used to build the cell sentences. Ideally, extract K562 activations from the unrestricted K562 transcriptome.

findings.description: The scores and retention values are reported without uncertainty, and the analysis sensitivity is not shown. Ridge alpha is fixed at 1000 without tuning on the source data, and the model's transfer depends noticeably on it. Retention compares a 5-fold CV score (trained on 2,400 cells) with a transfer score (trained on 3,000 cells, evaluated on a label of different quality, PC1-2 variance 0.31 vs 0.35). This slightly biases retention and makes the 0.89 vs 0.96 contrast hard to interpret.
findings.evidence: Model transfer R_diff by alpha: 0.591 (alpha = 1), 0.661 (10), 0.708 (100), 0.789 (1e3), 0.821 (1e4), 0.795 (1e5). There are no bootstrap CIs, and only one CV seed is used.
findings.recommended_action: Choose alpha by nested CV on K562 only. Report bootstrap CIs for the within, transfer and retention scores, and note how retention depends on the training-set size and on label quality.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 33-34 (Interpretation 2) and 19-23; code/cc_phase.py lines 57-65 (label = PCA projection of z-scored marker genes); code/transfer_test.py lines 118-128 (expression features include those same markers)
findings.description: The evidence is circular. In each dataset the 'ground-truth' phase is a fixed linear projection of the same Tirosh marker genes, and that projection is almost identical in K562 and RPE1. A K562-trained readout recovering the RPE1 label therefore only shows that the marker-PCA plane is shared. It does not show that the RPE1 label tracks the cell cycle. The expression 'point of reference' is close to a reconstruction of the label formula, not a plain baseline: its features contain the very genes that define the label.
findings.evidence: I took K562's marker-PCA loadings (Vt[:2] over the 87 markers) together with K562's flip and rotation, with no fitting, and applied them to RPE1's z-scored markers. This reproduces the RPE1 label with R_diff 0.992 and a median error of 2.4 deg (offset -2 deg). An expression readout on the 87 marker genes alone gets within 0.975 and transfer 0.918, both above the reported full-expression values (0.913 / 0.878). Without the markers, the expression readout gets within 0.863 and transfer 0.839.
findings.recommended_action: Remove or reword Interpretation 2. Check the label against a cell-cycle measure that does not depend on it (e.g. FUCCI or DNA-content data, or gene programs that are not markers). Build labels from genes that are excluded from the readout features. Report the no-marker expression readout and the label-projection ceiling (0.992) as references, instead of presenting the all-gene expression readout as an independent baseline.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 16-17, 24-25 and 34; code/transfer_test.py lines 41-55 and 149-153
findings.description: The summary says the frozen readouts 'pass the validity rule' because the best rotation is small, so they 'land on the right part of the circle with no adjustment'. The rule in the code never checks the rotation. It only needs R_diff > max(0.15, 2x the constant predictor's R_diff) and a median error below the constant predictor's. Both R_diff and the reported median errors are rotation-invariant: the median error is taken after a best rotation that is fitted on RPE1 labels. That conflicts with 'no RPE1 labels used'. The gate is also very lax: thr = 0.15 against trivial chance floors only.
findings.evidence: thr = max(0.15, 0.085) = 0.15. transfer_offset_deg is computed but no rule uses it. Median errors without the rotation are 24.0 and 16.0 deg, against the reported 23 and 16, so the numbers barely move. A 2-feature readout (log library size and number of detected genes) already reaches a transfer R_diff of 0.124, close to the 0.15 threshold.
findings.recommended_action: Either add the offset (or an unrotated error) to the validity rule, or describe the rule accurately in the summary. Report unrotated errors as the main frozen-transfer metric. Compare against meaningful baselines, not only constant and random predictors.

findings.description: 'The phase convention is consistent. The S peak sits at 45 deg in both datasets' is presented as a finding, but phase_angle_oriented forces the S peak to 45 deg by construction. The one quantity not fixed by construction, the S-to-G2/M separation, differs between datasets (109 vs 97 deg). So the two label scales do not match beyond the anchor point, and this mismatch adds to the transfer error.
findings.evidence: rot = deg2rad(45) - mu_s gives s_peak_deg = 45.0 by definition (run_log: K562 S 45.0 / G2M 153.8; RPE1 S 45.0 / G2M 142.1).
findings.recommended_action: Present the 45-deg S peak as a convention, not as evidence. If the convention needs validating, use something not fixed by construction, e.g. the separation or the positions of G1 cells. Discuss the 12-deg difference in the G2/M position.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 24-25; outputs/transfer_rpe1.json model.pred_R; code/transfer_test.py lines 77-80
findings.description: Using the K562-fitted StandardScaler on RPE1 introduces a domain offset. It distorts the frozen model readout's predicted phases in a way that the small global rotation does not show. Many RPE1 cells are moved away from the S/G1-S part of the circle, so 'land on the right part of the circle' is overstated. The summary does not mention the large pred_R.
findings.evidence: pred_R is 0.341 for the model (0.215 for expression) against 0.043 for the true RPE1 phases. The mean predicted (cos, sin) vector is (-0.31, -0.26). In the 0-90 deg range there are 677 true cells but only 256 predictions. In 150-210 deg there are 375 true cells but 942 predictions. Per-bin median errors are 28-41 deg for true phases 0-120 deg and 11 deg for the G1 cluster. Standardising RPE1 features with RPE1's own (unlabelled) statistics raises the model transfer from 0.789 to 0.892.
findings.recommended_action: Report per-phase errors or a confusion of predicted against true phase bins, plus the predicted-phase distribution. Describe the bias that the source scaler introduces, and qualify the 'right part of the circle' claim.

findings.description: Retention = transfer / within compares scores against two different labels. The K562 label is built from 87 markers and the RPE1 label from 93 (UBE2C and others are missing in K562), and the label geometry differs. 'Within' also uses fits on 2,400 cells while transfer uses 3,000. So retention mixes how well the readout transfers with how easy each dataset's label is.
findings.evidence: A model readout cross-validated within RPE1 reaches 0.909, above K562's 0.886. Measured against the target's own ceiling, the model's transfer ratio is 0.789/0.909 = 0.87, not 0.89. Marker coverage is 87/94 in K562 and 93/94 in RPE1. PC1-PC2 variance ratio is 0.31 in K562 and 0.35 in RPE1.
findings.recommended_action: Also report transfer relative to the target-within ceiling, and build both labels from the same intersected marker set.

findings.location: data/k562/k562_controls.h5ad vs data/rpe1/rpe1_controls.h5ad; README.md lines 43-46; code/transfer_test.py lines 123-128
findings.description: The two datasets are normalised differently, although the README calls them 'same format' log-normalised data. K562 looks normalised to 10,000 before the gene subset was taken. RPE1 is normalised to 10,000 over its own 8,749-gene panel. The frozen expression readout (and the gene panels the cell sentences may be drawn from) therefore see a systematic shift between source and target that has nothing to do with biology.
findings.evidence: Row sums of expm1(X): K562 ranges from 7,447 to 9,573 (median 9,137); RPE1 is exactly 10,000 in every cell. Panels are 6,546 genes (K562) and 8,749 genes (RPE1).
findings.recommended_action: Re-normalise both datasets the same way on the shared gene set, and state which gene panel was used to build the cell sentences for each line.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 40-41; README.md lines 36-38; code/transfer_test.py lines 12-13
findings.description: The claim that this tests 'a change of cell line, not of batch or platform' is not supported. The K562 and RPE1 controls come from separate screens and runs, with different gene panels and different preprocessing. Batch and processing are therefore fully confounded with cell line.
findings.evidence: Gene panels differ (6,546 vs 8,749 genes), normalisation differs (see F6), and the obs naming schemes differ (integer row indices in K562, gem-group barcodes in RPE1). Nothing in the data lets batch be separated from cell line.
findings.recommended_action: Say that cell line, batch and preprocessing are changed together, and do not describe the result as a pure biology shift.

findings.description: The size of the model's transfer depends strongly on the ridge penalty, which is fixed at 1000 with no justification and no tuning on the source. Only one seed and one fit are reported, with no uncertainty.
findings.evidence: Model transfer R_diff is 0.661 at alpha 10, 0.708 at 100, 0.789 at 1000 and 0.821 at 1e4 (within: 0.822 / 0.868 / 0.886 / 0.893). Bootstrap 95% CIs at alpha 1000: model [0.774, 0.801], expression [0.869, 0.888].
findings.recommended_action: Choose alpha by inner cross-validation on K562 only. Report bootstrap CIs and sensitivity to alpha alongside the retention figures.

review.summary: I reproduced every reported number exactly from the code and data: model within 0.886, transfer 0.789 (23 deg), retention 0.89; expression 0.913, 0.878 (16 deg); offsets -4 and -2 deg; G2/M separation 109 and 97 deg. The code has no indexing or alignment bugs: row_cell_ids are the identity, activations are aligned with the h5ad rows, and the metrics are computed correctly. The main problem is circularity in interpretation (major). The RPE1 'ground-truth' phase is the same linear projection of marker genes as in K562. K562's marker-PCA loadings applied directly to RPE1, with no fitting, reproduce the RPE1 label at R_diff 0.992. So 'the RPE1 label behaves as a cell-cycle label' is not shown, and the all-gene expression 'reference' largely rebuilds the label formula. A marker-only readout gets 0.975 within and 0.918 transfer; a readout without markers gets 0.839 transfer. The remaining problems are minor and do not overturn the finding that the model readout transfers. (1) The summary's description of the validity rule is wrong (the rule has no rotation check), the metrics are rotation-invariant, and the gate is lax. (2) The '45-deg S peak' consistency holds by construction. (3) The source-fitted scaler distorts the frozen model predictions (pred_R 0.34; the S region is under-predicted; 0.892 with target standardisation). (4) Retention compares scores on labels that differ between datasets. (5) The two datasets are normalised differently and use different gene panels. (6) 'Not a batch change' is not supported, since batch is confounded with cell line. (7) Results are sensitive to the fixed ridge alpha (transfer 0.66-0.82) and no CIs are reported.
