review.summary:
I re-ran all the geometry statistics from the shipped embeddings and the numbers in SUMMARY.md match outputs/run_log.txt exactly. All three files have the same cells in the same order: cell_idx, pseudotime and cell types agree, the STATE category codes map to the alphabetical names, and there are no NaN, zero or duplicate rows. The width caveat also holds: randomly projecting STATE down to 512 dimensions still gives PR 51.7.

The interpretation of the headline numbers does not hold.
(1) Geneformer's dominant direction, the '58% of variance' behind its PR of 2.7, is a sequencing-depth / gene-detection axis. Its PC1 correlates r=0.95 with log(number of detected genes) in the 200 cells that have raw counts, and r=0.94-0.98 within single cell types. Regressing out depth removes 58% of Geneformer's variance and changes PR from 2.7 to 6.7 and d90 from 16 to 53, while scGPT's d90 stays at 18. Cell type explains only 4.4% of Geneformer's variance. STATE's PC1 is also mostly depth (r=0.96-0.98).
(2) The Geneformer inputs were tokenized wrongly. log1p is applied before dividing by the gene medians, and sequences are cut to 2048 tokens even though V2 accepts 4096. So the 'Geneformer V2-316M' geometry is not that model's representation of these cells.
(3) STATE's d90 of 775 is not a stable property. It rises with the number of cells (288 at n=500, 459 at 1000, 645 at 2134, 775 at 4269) and halves when the embedding is projected to 512 dimensions. The full-data value even falls outside its own random-half range of 644-650; the summary leaves that range out and says the halves 'agree closely' and the result is 'not a sampling effect'.
(4) The d90 tie between scGPT and Geneformer ('just as low-dimensional') only holds at exactly 90%. At 80% the order reverses (5 vs 11 PCs); at 95% and 99% the gap is large (31 vs 81, 99 vs 476). PR (8.1 vs 2.7) also contradicts the claim.
(5) Norm CV is not a compactness measure. It mostly reflects how far the cloud sits from the origin compared with its spread (scGPT: mean norm 20.8 vs spread 2.75). Mean-pooling random gene vectors gives a CV of 0.0001. Also, the code does not compute norm CV on the random halves.

Other problems:
- The models see different gene windows: scGPT keeps the top 1200 genes (98% of cells are cut, losing a median 64% of their expressed genes), Geneformer about 2046, STATE 2047. scGPT's top-by-expression cut also differs from how it was trained (random gene sampling).
- There is no reference or null baseline.
- Layer 11 is the last layer of one model but a middle layer of the other two (stated as a caveat, but the conclusions are not hedged).
- The stability check only resamples cells, not donors.
- Model weights are loaded without checking for missing keys, and there is little reproducibility support (no environment file, no pinned versions, the full count matrix is not included).

The one claim that survives is the ranking: STATE is the least compact on every measure and in every random half, and Geneformer has a lower PR than scGPT even after removing depth (6.7 vs 10.6 on 200 cells). The magnitudes and the 'cell manifold' reading are not supported.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 25-29 (Conclusions 1-2); code/geometry.py lines 32-50 (no covariate adjustment)
findings.description: Confound carried through (P5). The 'most compact cell manifold' result for Geneformer, with one direction holding 58% of the variance and PR 2.7, comes from a technical axis: per-cell gene detection / sequencing depth. It is not cell-state structure. STATE's PC1 is the same depth axis. No measure was residualized against depth.
findings.evidence:
Checks on the 200 cells with raw counts (data/raw, rows 0-199 of the npz files; all three models' PCs computed on all 4269 cells):
- Correlation of PC1 with log(number of detected genes): Geneformer 0.946, STATE 0.958, scGPT 0.595.
- Correlation of PC1 with log(total UMI): Geneformer 0.914, STATE 0.977, scGPT 0.722.
- Within single cell types, Geneformer PC1 vs log(detected genes): 0.979 (enteroendocrine, n=49) and 0.938 (progenitor, n=120). STATE: 0.86 and 0.99.
- Regressing log(detected genes) and log(UMI) out of the 200-cell embeddings removes 58.4% of Geneformer's variance (scGPT 21%, STATE 12%).
- After residualization, Geneformer goes from PR 2.71 / PC1 0.578 / d90 16 to PR 6.73 / PC1 0.340 / d90 53. scGPT goes from 8.75 / 0.250 / 17 to 10.59 / 0.198 / 18. The d90 'parity' in Conclusion 2 therefore disappears (53 vs 18).
- Cell type explains only 4.4% of Geneformer's total variance (STATE 6.6%, scGPT 19.7%). Cell-type R2 of Geneformer's PC1 is 0.056.
findings.recommended_action: Compute detected genes and UMI per cell from the full count matrix. Report PR, PC1 share and d90 after regressing out log(detected genes) and log(UMI), next to the raw values, and report how much variance cell type explains. Say explicitly that Geneformer's 58% PC1 is a depth axis. Restate Conclusions 1-2 using the residualized numbers.

findings.description: Geneformer's input is not built the way the model expects. (a) Expression is log1p-transformed (line 129) before being divided by the Geneformer gene medians (line 56). Geneformer's rank-value encoding ranks counts/total*1e4/median with no log, and the medians are on that unlogged scale. Taking the log first squashes the cell's own expression, so the ranking is driven mostly by each gene's median, i.e. by gene identity. (b) Sequences are cut at MAX_SEQ_LEN=2048, but V2-316M has a 4096-token context, and most cells have more detected genes than that (median 3476 in the 200-cell sample). So every Geneformer number in the summary, including the headline 'most compact', describes the model on inputs it was never trained on.
findings.evidence: Line 129: tokenize(np.log1p(expr / rs * 1e4), ...). Line 56: norm = e_nz / m_nz, i.e. log1p(x)/median. Example of an order flip: x=100, median=5 gives x/m=20 but log1p(x)/m=0.92; x=2, median=0.5 gives x/m=4 but log1p(x)/m=2.2. The two genes swap rank. config.json has max_position_embeddings 4096; the script sets MAX_SEQ_LEN=2048. The size of the effect on the geometry cannot be measured here because the median dictionary and weights are not shipped. The strong depth axis in F1 fits rankings driven by gene identity.
findings.recommended_action: Re-extract the Geneformer embeddings using the official TranscriptomeTokenizer (no log; divide normalized counts by the median; 4096-token input for V2) and rerun geometry.py. Until then, do not attribute the Geneformer results to Geneformer V2-316M.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 18, 20-21, 30-33; outputs/run_log.txt line 5; code/geometry.py lines 63-74
findings.description: STATE's d90 of 775 depends on the number of cells and on the width, so it is not a property of the model. The summary leaves out STATE's own d90 range across the random halves (644-650), which does not contain the full-data value. It still says the halves 'agree closely' and that the result 'is not a sampling effect'. Ten overlapping 50% subsamples cannot show stability for a statistic that changes with n.
findings.evidence: STATE d90 by number of cells (mean of 3 subsamples): 288 at n=500, 459 at 1000, 645 at 2134, 715 at 3000, 775 at 4269. It never levels off, which points to a noise-like tail in the spectrum. A bootstrap with replacement at n=4269 gives about 662-668. A random orthonormal projection of STATE to 512 dimensions gives d90 328 (579 at 1152). By contrast, scGPT and Geneformer d90 stay within 17-20 for n from 500 to 4269.
findings.recommended_action: Report d90 (and PR) as a function of n, or at a fixed common n, with the halves range included. Remove '775 PCs' as a model property, or flag it as dependent on n and width. Remove 'It is not a sampling effect', or limit it to the rank order.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 27-29 (Conclusion 2), line 16 (bold d90); code/geometry.py line 47
findings.description: The claim that scGPT is 'just as low-dimensional' as Geneformer, needing 'the same' number of PCs, only holds at exactly 90%. It also conflicts with PR (8.1 vs 2.7). No threshold sweep was done (P8). The bolding of scGPT's d90 as 'more compact' (19 vs 20) treats a one-PC difference, with overlapping halves, as a ranking.
findings.evidence:
Recomputed from the shipped embeddings:
- PCs needed for 80%: scGPT 11, Geneformer 5 (order reversed).
- 90%: 19 vs 20.
- 95%: 31 vs 81.
- 99%: 99 vs 476.
- With z-scored features, d90 is 21 vs 68.
- After depth residualization (F1, 200 cells), d90 is 18 vs 53.
findings.recommended_action: Report the dimension needed at several variance thresholds (80/90/95/99%). Limit the comparison claim to thresholds where it holds, and drop 'just as low-dimensional' / 'the same as Geneformer'.

findings.location: README.md table (norm CV row); SUMMARY.md lines 16-18, 29, 32-33; code/geometry.py lines 43, 49, 71
findings.description: Norm CV is not a valid compactness measure. It changes when the cloud is shifted, and it is set mainly by how far the cloud's centre sits from the origin relative to its spread; that offset largely reflects LayerNorm gain/bias. 'Per-cell norms are almost constant (CV 0.3%)' therefore says nothing about how compact the cloud is. Separately, geometry.py does not compute norm CV on the random halves (line 71 loops only over PR, PC1 share and d90). So the claim that STATE is last 'on every measure and in every random half' is not supported by the outputs for this measure (my own check confirms the order does hold).
findings.evidence: Distance of the cloud's centre from the origin vs RMS spread around the centre: scGPT 20.8 vs 2.75, Geneformer 6.52 vs 1.75, STATE 11.64 vs 10.34. The norm-CV order matches the order of spread/offset. Mean-pooling random gene vectors with a shared offset over each cell's genes gives norm CV 0.0000-0.0001, lower than scGPT's 0.0029. Norm CV on the halves (my run): 0.0028-0.0029, 0.0179-0.0190, 0.0276-0.0288.
findings.recommended_action: Drop norm CV as a compactness measure, or replace it with a statistic that does not change when the cloud is shifted, such as the spread of distances to the centroid relative to typical distances between cells. If it is kept, compute it on the halves in geometry.py and do not use it as independent support in Conclusion 4.

findings.location: code/extraction/extract_scgpt.py lines 33, 76-79; extract_geneformer.py line 58; extract_state.py lines 69-74, 116-121; README.md lines 31-32; SUMMARY.md lines 6-7
findings.description: The three models are pooled over different, truncated subsets of genes, so the comparison is affected by the tokenization windows (P5). scGPT keeps only the top 1200 genes by expression and assigns expression bins after the cut. scGPT whole-human was trained with trunc_by_sample=true (random gene sampling), so this is a shift in input distribution. Geneformer keeps about 2046 genes (and in the wrong order, F2); STATE keeps a 2047-gene sentence. The README and SUMMARY say embeddings are 'mean-pooled over the cell's expressed genes', which is wrong for most cells. Averaging over different numbers of tokens changes how spread out the pooled vectors are. extract_state.py also sets no random seed, and only one extraction run was done.
findings.evidence: In the 200-cell sample, scGPT has 768-8310 expressed in-vocab genes per cell (median 3378). 98% of cells are cut to 1200, losing a median 64% of their expressed genes. args.json has max_seq_len 1200 and trunc_by_sample true. The STATE config has pad_length 2048.
findings.recommended_action: Document the window and how genes are chosen for each model. Use each model's native truncation (random sampling for scGPT, 4096 for Geneformer V2). Rerun with a common, fixed gene window as a sensitivity check, and with ≥3 extraction seeds where tokenization is stochastic.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 25-33 (Conclusions) vs caveats lines 37-42; code/geometry.py (no reference distributions)
findings.description: There is no reference or null baseline (P1/P2). Nothing shows what PR, PC1 share, d90 or norm CV would be from mean-pooling alone, from the input-layer or random-weight embeddings, or from the expression data. Without that, differences cannot be credited to what the models learned rather than to pooling, tokenization or depth.
findings.evidence: Mean-pooling random Gaussian gene vectors over each cell's genes (200 cells) gives a PC1 that correlates 0.56-0.92 with log(detected genes) and a norm CV of about 0.0001. Both effects that drive the reported results appear with no model at all. Log-normalized expression (top 2000 variable genes, 200 cells) gives PR 70.8 and d90 131.
findings.recommended_action: For each model, add at least: (i) the layer-0 / input-embedding mean-pool, (ii) a random-weight version of the same architecture, and (iii) PCA of the expression data on the same cells. Report each statistic against these references.

findings.description: The comparison mixes layer depths and is limited to one condition (P7). Layer 11 is the final layer of scGPT but a middle layer of Geneformer (11/18) and STATE (11/16). The summary admits this, yet the conclusions are still worded as properties of each model ('STATE is by far the most diffuse', 'Geneformer has the most compact cell manifold'). Only one tissue, one layer and one extraction run were analysed.
findings.evidence: Caveat at lines 37-38 and 'Not tested: other tissues, other layers' at line 41, while Conclusions 1-4 carry no qualification. No result at matched relative depth (for example the last layer of each model, or layers at the same fraction of depth) is reported.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the statistics at matched relative depth (for example the last layer, or 0.66 of depth) and for each model's own cell embedding (CLS). Limit the conclusions to 'layer 11 of each model in fetal gut epithelium' unless the ranking holds across depths.

findings.description: The endpoint does not match the object and the language goes too far (P3/P9). PR, PC1 share and d90 are linear statistics of the global covariance spectrum, not measures of a 'cell manifold' or its intrinsic dimension. Most of the variance is not cell-state structure (F1). Calling the result the compactness of each model's 'cell manifold' overstates what was measured.
findings.evidence: Cell type explains 4.4% (Geneformer), 6.6% (STATE) and 19.7% (scGPT) of total embedding variance. The leading PCs of Geneformer and STATE are depth axes.
findings.recommended_action: Rephrase as 'global covariance spectrum of mean-pooled layer-11 gene-token activations'. Say what each measure literally computes before interpreting it, and report how much of the variance is biological and how much technical.

findings.location: code/geometry.py lines 63-75; SUMMARY.md lines 20-21, 33; README.md lines 21-23
findings.description: The stability check uses the wrong unit (P4/P8). It takes 10 random halves of the same 4,269 cells; any two halves share about 50% of their cells, and only the min-max range is reported, with no confidence interval. Cells are treated as interchangeable, although they come from several embryos/donors (6-11 PCW) and the cell-type mix is fixed by an 800-per-type cap. findings.recommended_action: Bootstrap by donor/sample if that metadata exists, report 95% intervals, and test how the statistics change with cell-type composition (for example natural proportions vs the 800 cap).

findings.location: code/extraction/extract_scgpt.py line 98; code/extraction/state_loader.py line 62; code/extraction/extract_state.py lines 37-39; README.md lines 55-73
findings.description: Reproducibility and weight loading cannot be checked (P10). Confirmed in the code: line 129 applies log1p(CP10k) before the division by the median at line 56, and MAX_SEQ_LEN is 2048 (lines 27 and 58) while config.json has max_position_embeddings 4096. The key lists exactly these deviations under other_real_issues ('A finding that reports it is CORRECT ... but does not count as detecting the documented error'). The finding presents it as invalidating the headline Geneformer result, but the key's 120-cell re-run with Geneformer's own convention makes Geneformer slightly MORE compact (PR 2.32, PC1 0.648, d90 14), and no conclusion changes. The claim that the ranking is 'driven mostly by each gene's median' also overstates it (median Spearman 0.82 between the two orders).

The n-dependence is real. STATE d90 is about 287 at n=500, about 456 at 1000, about 718 at 3000 and 775 at 4269, and the summary leaves out STATE's 644-650 d90 range for the halves. The key states this is a sample-size effect on a long-tailed spectrum and changes no ranking. It lists claiming instability or a bug from it as a false alarm. The finding itself only asks to narrow the wording to the rank order. This is a reporting nuance, not a wrong conclusion.

The threshold sweep is correct (recomputed): scGPT/Geneformer need 11/5 PCs at 80%, 19/20 at 90%, 31/81 at 95% and 99/476 at 99%. Conclusion 2 explicitly says '90% of the variance', Conclusion 1 already notes Geneformer's long tail, and Conclusion 4 says the winner depends on the measure. The key treats Conclusion 2 as a near tie that roughly holds. Only the phrase 'just as low-dimensional' overgeneralizes, so this is a wording issue.

The offset vs spread numbers are correct: scGPT 20.83 vs 2.75, Geneformer 6.52 vs 1.75, STATE 11.64 vs 10.34. geometry.py does not compute norm CV on the halves (line 71 loops only over PR, PC1 share and d90). The critique of norm CV as a compactness measure is a fair methodological point, but the formula is coded correctly. The finding itself confirms the STATE-last order holds for norm CV on the halves, so no conclusion changes.

The truncation exists (scGPT keeps the top 1,200 genes by count; args.json has trunc_by_sample true), and the README's 'mean-pooled over the cell's expressed genes' is imprecise. But the key lists top-1,200 truncation and binning after the cut as possible false alarms. scGPT's own pipeline (random sampling of 1,200 genes after binning all genes) gives nearly the same geometry (PR 7.73 vs 7.20, cosine 0.97), so the tokenization windows do not change the comparison. The Geneformer window part repeats F2. Net effect: a documentation imprecision.

This is a suggestion for extra reference baselines (input layer, random weights, expression PCA). The summary describes the geometry of each model's layer-11 embeddings and does not claim the differences come from learned structure. Baselines would help interpretation, but their absence does not make any reported statistic or ranking wrong.

The layer-11 depth mismatch and the single tissue/layer scope are stated as caveats in SUMMARY lines 37-42. The key lists claiming the relative-depth difference as the load-bearing error as a possible false alarm. The finding only complains that the conclusions are not qualified enough, which is a scope and wording point.

The cell-type R2 values are correct (recomputed: scGPT 0.197, Geneformer 0.044, STATE 0.066). Calling global covariance-spectrum statistics a 'cell manifold' is loose terminology, but README line 15 defines exactly what is computed. This is a wording issue.

True that the random halves share about 50% of their cells, that only min-max ranges are reported, and that there is no donor information in the package. The key says the half-sample ranges are tight and the rankings are stable. This is a limit on how the stability check can be read, not an error in a result.

Confirmed: extract_scgpt.py line 98 calls load_state_dict(strict=False) and ignores the return value. extract_state.py never prints the missing/unexpected keys (only state_loader's __main__ block does). Nothing is pinned. But the key reports that re-running the shipped extractors with the real weights reproduces the stored embeddings (scGPT max diff 1.9e-6, Geneformer exact), and lists 'results cannot be trusted because extraction cannot be re-run' as a false alarm. This is reproducibility housekeeping only.

review.summary:
I reproduced every number in SUMMARY.md from data/embeddings with code/geometry.py, and the cell rows line up across the three models. The arithmetic is correct, but the interpretation does not hold up. The main problem: the dominant direction that makes Geneformer look "most compact" is a technical axis, the number of genes detected (library complexity), not cell-state structure. In the 200 cells where raw counts are available, Geneformer's PC1 has Spearman rho = 0.99 with log(genes detected). STATE's PC1 has rho = 0.97. Cell type explains only 4.4% of Geneformer's total variance and 5.6% of its PC1. After regressing out depth covariates, Geneformer's PR goes from 2.7 to 15.3 and its PC1 share from 0.58 to 0.20, which reverses its ranking against scGPT (PR 10.1, PC1 0.22). Other problems:
- STATE's d90 of 775 depends on how many cells are used: 289 / 457 / 645 / 775 at n = 500 / 1000 / 2134 / 4269. The random halves (644-650) do not contain the full-sample value, and the summary leaves this out.
- "scGPT is just as low-dimensional as Geneformer" depends on the 90% cut-off. At 80% the counts are 11 vs 5 PCs, at 95% they are 31 vs 81. It also contradicts the analysis's own PR definition of dimensionality (8.1 vs 2.7).
- Norm CV is computed on un-centred vectors. That contradicts the README, and it does not measure how compact the cloud is.
- The layers are at different depths (last layer for scGPT, middle for the other two), and the inputs are tokenized and pooled differently and non-standardly for each model. So the conclusions describe this extraction setup, not the models.
- There is no baseline or null to anchor what "compact" means.
- "Not a sampling effect" claims more than the halves test shows.
- Reproducibility support is thin.
Checks that came out clean: the d90, PR and PC1 code is correct; STATE's labels decode correctly; and the width caveat holds (randomly projecting STATE down to 512 dimensions still gives PR 49.9).

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 25-26 (Conclusion 1), 1 and 23-33 ('cell manifold' framing); code/geometry.py lines 40-50 (shape_stats has no covariate adjustment)
findings.description: The headline 'Geneformer has the most compact cell manifold by PR and PC1 share; one direction holds 58% of the variance' is driven by a technical covariate: the number of genes detected / sequencing depth per cell. The four measures are applied to the raw cloud of embeddings with no adjustment for depth. The dominant PC of both Geneformer and STATE is essentially a library-complexity axis, not cell-state structure. Once depth is removed, Geneformer is no longer more compact than scGPT. (P5 confound carry-through; P9 'cell manifold' overreach)
findings.evidence: I used data/raw/gut_epithelium_first200.h5ad, whose rows 0-199 match the .npz rows (labels and pseudotime agree). Spearman rho between full-data PC1 scores and log(genes detected): Geneformer 0.99 (0.99 within progenitor cells only), STATE 0.97 (0.98 within progenitors), scGPT 0.65. Cell type explains 4.4% of Geneformer's total variance and 5.6% of its PC1 (scGPT 19.7% / 30.7%; STATE 6.6% / 5.8%). I regressed the embeddings on cubic log(genes detected) plus quadratic log(total counts). Depth covariates explain 72.8% of Geneformer's embedding variance (scGPT 28.6%, STATE 15.7%). Before vs after the adjustment: Geneformer PR 2.71 -> 15.30, PC1 0.578 -> 0.202, d90 16 -> 75. scGPT PR 8.75 -> 10.11, PC1 0.250 -> 0.216, d90 17 -> 19. So after adjustment scGPT is more compact than Geneformer on PR, PC1 share and d90. A linear log(genes detected) term alone already cuts Geneformer's PC1 share from 0.578 to 0.392 and doubles its PR from 2.71 to 5.44.
findings.recommended_action: Record genes-detected and total counts for all 4,269 cells (they come from the full count matrix) and report each measure before and after regressing them out (or within depth strata). Report how much of each model's PC1 correlates with depth and with cell type. Restate Conclusion 1 as 'the dominant axis of Geneformer layer-11 mean-pooled embeddings tracks genes detected', and stop calling it a property of the cell manifold unless it survives the adjustment.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 18, 20-21, 30-33; outputs/run_log.txt line 5; code/geometry.py line 47
findings.description: STATE's d90 = 775 is not a stable property of the embedding: it keeps rising with the number of cells and has not converged at n=4,269. The stability check actually contradicts it, because the random-half d90 values (644-650) do not include the full-sample 775. The summary reports the random-half ranges only for PR and PC1 share, says the halves 'agree closely', and Conclusion 3 cites '775 PCs for 90% of the variance' as a fact.
findings.evidence: run_log.txt: STATE d90 = 775 vs d90 halves 644-650. My subsample check (seed 1): STATE d90 = 289 / 457 / 645 / 716 / 775 at n = 500 / 1000 / 2134 / 3000 / 4269. scGPT (18-19) and Geneformer (18-20) are flat over the same range. The 90% point lies deep in the near-isotropic tail of STATE's spectrum (d80 = 502, d85 = 619, d95 = 1015 out of 2048 dimensions). With n=2134 and p=2048, the half-sample covariance is close to rank-deficient.
findings.recommended_action: Report d90 for STATE together with its dependence on sample size, or drop it as a headline number. Report the d90 random-half ranges for all models in the Results. Consider a noise-floor-corrected dimension estimate (for example, the number of eigenvalues above the Marchenko-Pastur edge or a shuffle-null spectrum) instead of a raw 90% cut-off.

findings.description: 'scGPT ... is just as low-dimensional [as Geneformer]' rests on one cut-off (90%), and that happens to be where the two cumulative-variance curves cross. At nearby cut-offs the two models are clearly apart, in opposite directions. The sentence also contradicts the analysis's own definition of PR as 'an effective number of dimensions', on which scGPT (8.1) is about 3 times higher-dimensional than Geneformer (2.7). (P8 threshold sensitivity)
findings.evidence: From the full-data spectra: PCs needed for 80/85/90/95% of the variance are scGPT 11/14/19/31 and Geneformer 5/9/20/81. The d90 random-half ranges (18-19 vs 19-20) only show that both values are stable at 90%, not that the two models are equivalent.
findings.recommended_action: Report d at several cut-offs (for example 80/90/95%) or the whole cumulative-variance curve, and restrict the 'same dimensionality' statement to the 90% cut-off or remove it. Remove 'just as low-dimensional' or reconcile it with PR.

findings.location: README.md lines 13 and 15; code/geometry.py lines 43 and 49; SUMMARY.md lines 29 and 32-33
findings.description: Norm CV is computed on un-centred embeddings. The README says 'All four use the full covariance spectrum of the mean-centred embeddings', which is false for this measure. Norm CV measures radial spread relative to the distance of the cloud from the origin, not how compact the cloud is. A cloud that is widely spread over a spherical shell has CV close to 0, and the value is largely set by where each architecture places its LayerNorm. Treating 'lower norm CV = more compact' and including it in 'STATE is last on every measure' is not valid. The code also never computes norm CV on the random halves, yet Conclusion 4 says STATE is last 'in every random half' across all measures.
findings.evidence: scGPT: norm CV = 0.0029 while the centred cloud's RMS spread is 2.76 against a mean-vector norm of 20.8, i.e. a 13% spread sitting on an almost constant-norm shell. STATE: mean norm 11.6, spread 10.3. geometry.py line 71 loops only over participation_ratio, pc1_share and d90 for the halves. I computed the half ranges myself (scGPT 0.0028-0.0029, Geneformer 0.0179-0.0190, STATE 0.0276-0.0288). The ordering does hold, but the outputs do not show it.
findings.recommended_action: Correct the README text. Either drop norm CV as a 'compactness' measure or report it separately as a radial or normalization property, with a note on where each architecture places its LayerNorm. If the claim is kept, add norm CV to the random-half output.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 23-33 (Conclusions phrased as model properties) vs lines 37-38 (caveat); README.md line 31
findings.description: The models are compared at different relative depths: layer 11 is the final layer of scGPT (12 layers), 61% depth of Geneformer (18) and 69% of STATE (16). Yet the conclusions are written as properties of each model ('Geneformer has the most compact cell manifold', 'STATE is by far the most diffuse'). The caveat admits that compactness can change with depth, but the headline wording does not reflect it. (P3/P7, present but acknowledged)
findings.evidence: README line 31 and the extraction scripts confirm a fixed LAYER = 11 for all three models (extract_scgpt.py line 33, extract_geneformer.py line 27, extract_state.py line 30). No other layer was analysed.
findings.recommended_action: Either compare at matched relative depth (for example the final layer, or the same depth fraction) with a short layer sweep, or reword every conclusion as 'the layer-11 mean-pooled embedding of model X ...'.

findings.location: README.md lines 31-32; code/extraction/extract_scgpt.py lines 33, 77-79; code/extraction/extract_geneformer.py lines 27, 56-58, 129; code/extraction/extract_state.py lines 69-74, 116-121
findings.description:
The 'mean over the cell's expressed genes' is a different, truncated and non-standard gene set for each model, so the three clouds are not comparable objects:
- scGPT keeps the top 1,200 genes by raw count and computes its quantile bins on those 1,200 values only. The pretraining config instead uses trunc_by_sample and bins all genes.
- Geneformer ranks genes by log1p(normalised counts) divided by the gene median, whereas Geneformer's own tokenizer ranks by normalised counts divided by the median with no log. This reorders genes with different medians. It also truncates to 2,046 genes even though the model's context is 4,096 (config.json max_position_embeddings).
- STATE's gene set is chosen by the arc-state collator (pad_length 2048) with no documentation and no seed.
Because the dominant axis of variation is genes detected (F1), how much each model's input is truncated directly affects the measured geometry.
findings.evidence: In the 200 provided cells, genes detected per cell range from 788 to 8,557 (median 3,476). 98.5% of cells exceed 1,200 genes and 92.5% exceed 2,046, so nearly every cell is truncated, and by a different amount for each model. models/geneformer_v2_316m/config.json has max_position_embeddings 4096 while the extraction uses MAX_SEQ_LEN = 2048. models/scgpt_whole_human/args.json has trunc_by_sample: true.
findings.recommended_action: Use each model's reference tokenizer: Geneformer's rank by normalised counts divided by the median with the 4,096 context, and scGPT's binning before sampling. Document exactly which genes each model pools. Test sensitivity by pooling over a common gene set or a common token count.

findings.description: There is no reference point for the PR, PC1 share and d90 values (P1/P2). The analysis has no raw-expression PCA baseline, no input-layer (static token embedding) mean-pool baseline, no random-weight or shuffled-token null, and no noise-floor correction. Without these, one cannot tell whether a 'compact' or 'diffuse' manifold is learned by the transformer or inherited from the input embeddings (for example STATE's ESM2 protein embeddings), from mean pooling over about 1-2k tokens, or from depth effects.
findings.evidence: Only the three model embeddings are analysed. For context, on the 200 provided cells the log-normalised expression gives PR 110.6, PC1 share 0.041 and d90 144 (top-2,000 variable genes: PR 70.8), compared with model PR on the same cells of scGPT 8.75, Geneformer 2.71 and STATE 47.5. Whether the models' compactness exceeds what their input layer already gives is untested.
findings.recommended_action: Add at least an expression-PCA baseline and an input-embedding (layer-0) mean-pool baseline for each model, ideally also a random-initialisation model of the same architecture. Report each measure relative to these baselines.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 16-21 and 32-33 ('It is not a sampling effect'); code/geometry.py lines 63-64
findings.description: The random halves only re-split one fixed set of 4,269 cells from one extraction run, and each pair of halves overlaps by about 50%. They do not test donor-level variation (the inference unit and the number of donors are never reported), the choice of cells (seed-0 subsample capped at 800 per type), or randomness in extraction (STATE collator sampling, scGPT random tie-breaking in binning, MPS non-determinism). Saying the result is 'not a sampling effect' overstates what was tested, and the headline numbers come with no confidence intervals. (P4/P8)
findings.evidence: The halves are drawn by rng.choice over row indices with no grouping. The README never mentions donors. extract_state.py sets no random seed.
findings.recommended_action: Rephrase as 'stable to cell subsampling'. If donor IDs exist, resample by donor; re-extract STATE with at least 2-3 seeds; report bootstrap CIs.

findings.description: All conclusions rest on one tissue, one layer, one pooling scheme and one extraction seed (P7). The caveats acknowledge this, but the conclusions are worded generally.
findings.evidence: TISSUE = 'gut' only (geometry.py line 27). The caveats list other tissues, other layers and CLS pooling as untested.
findings.recommended_action: Add at least one held-out tissue or dataset and the CLS / cell-token embedding, or narrow the conclusions to this setting.

findings.location: code/extraction/extract_scgpt.py line 98; code/extraction/state_loader.py line 62 / extract_state.py line 37; code/extraction/extract_geneformer.py line 93; README.md lines 68-85
findings.description:
Reproducibility gaps (P10):
- The scGPT and STATE weights are loaded with strict=False and the missing or unexpected keys are never checked or logged, so a partly randomly initialised model would go unnoticed.
- The Geneformer hub weights have no pinned revision.
- There is no environment or requirements file and no package versions, except arc-state 0.11.1.
- The STATE collator is unseeded and the extraction runs on MPS.
- The extraction cannot be run from the package (no full count matrix, weights or dictionaries).
findings.evidence: build_model() calls m.load_state_dict(sd, strict=False) and discards the return value. extract_state.py never prints info['missing'] or info['unexpected']. BertForMaskedLM.from_pretrained is called without a revision argument.
findings.recommended_action: Assert or log zero missing encoder keys. Pin the hub revision and package versions in an environment file. Set seeds. Record the extraction logs (kept/total cells, key-mismatch counts) in outputs/.

review.summary:
I reproduced every number in SUMMARY.md exactly from the shipped embeddings with code/geometry.py, and the cells line up across the three files (same cell_idx, pseudotime and cell-type labels; STATE's codes map to names alphabetically). The arithmetic is right. The problem is what the numbers measure.

The headline conclusion, that Geneformer has the most compact cell manifold and scGPT is "just as low-dimensional", does not hold. Geneformer's PC1 (58% of variance) and PC2 (18%) are a technical sequencing-depth / sequence-length axis, not cell biology. On the 200 cells with counts available, depth covariates explain R2 = 0.98 and 0.90 of those two PCs and 77% of Geneformer's total variance. Cell type explains only 5.6% of PC1 (eta2, all 4,269 cells). After removing depth, Geneformer becomes less compact than scGPT on PR, PC1 share and d90.

Three further major problems:
- **norm CV:** it is computed on uncentred embeddings, although the README says all four measures use mean-centred data. Computed on centred data, the ranking reverses and STATE comes out most compact.
- **STATE d90 = 775:** this is not a stable property of the model. It keeps rising with the number of cells, and the random halves (644-650) do not bracket it. The summary leaves this out.
- **Geneformer input:** extraction does not follow Geneformer's standard input. It applies log1p before dividing by gene medians and truncates at 2,046 genes although the model accepts 4,096.

- The conclusions rank the models from one fixed absolute layer, with no layer sweep.
- The stability claims rest on overlapping cell-level random halves, and norm CV was never computed on the halves.
- No baseline anchors what the compactness values mean.
- Pooling and tokenisation differ between models, including deviations from how scGPT was pretrained.
- Reproducibility is limited: no pinned versions, weights loaded with strict=False without checking for missing keys, and no per-cell depth stored.

Verdicts for the ten checklist patterns:
- P1 (null too weak / no chance anchor): present and unaddressed.
- P2 (trivial baseline absent): present and unaddressed.
- P3 (endpoint–object mismatch): present. Compactness is read as a cell-manifold property but is depth-driven.
- P4 (pseudoreplication / unit of inference): present. Stability rests on cell-level halves; donors are ignored.
- P5 (selection / confound carry-through): present and unaddressed. This is the depth confound, and it is critical.
- P6 (positive control): not applicable, since no null finding is claimed.
- P7 (single-condition generalisation): present but acknowledged.
- P8 (stability of headline numbers): present. STATE's d90 depends on sample size, and there is no layer or pooling sweep.
- P9 (language overreach): present. "Cell manifold" wording and "not a sampling effect".
- P10 (reproducibility): partly present.

review.summary: I re-ran the label build with the package code. The npz and concept_summary.json reproduce exactly, and every count in SUMMARY.md matches the outputs. Accession parsing is sound: all 5,000 corpus accessions are primary accessions in the flat file, sequence lengths match the ID lines, order is the same, and 4,124 proteins carry at least one concept key. The problems are in what the labels mean, not in the bookkeeping. (1) DISULFID and CROSSLNK use 'x..y' to mean a bonded pair of residues, but the code fills every residue between the two. As a result 93% of the 33,467 DISULFID positives are not the bonded cysteines. The true count is 2,154 residues (prevalence 1.3e-3), not 2.1% and fifth overall, so the DISULFID claims in the PTM section and Conclusion 2 do not hold. (2) The variation 'negative control' clears the 1e-3 floor only because of a few long deletion or replacement ranges. 61% of VARIANT positives come from 5 proteins. Point variants alone give 3.7e-4, and CONFLICT without its 5 long ranges falls below the floor. (3) Missing annotation is treated as a negative. Only 307 of 5,000 proteins carry any HELIX/STRAND/TURN annotation, so 93% of residues count as 'not helix' simply because no structure was solved. (4) The floor is set on residue prevalence, which does not measure how many independent positives a concept has. TRANSIT (74 features) is scored while ACT_SITE (1,537 sites in 928 proteins) is not. (5) Minor: fuzzy ends are handled inconsistently, and the three empty legacy keys are framed loosely. The count of 21 scored concepts survives even after DISULFID is fixed.

findings.location: code/dataset.py lines 157-176 (every unannotated residue is False); SUMMARY.md lines 49, 61-62
findings.description: Every residue without an annotation is treated as a negative. For HELIX, STRAND and TURN, Swiss-Prot annotation exists only for proteins with a solved 3D structure, so almost all 'negatives' are unlabelled rather than non-helical. A feature that faithfully tracks helices will look low-precision just because 93% of residues come from proteins with no structural annotation. The same problem, less severely, affects TOPO_DOM (258 proteins) and other sparsely curated keys. The claim that the label set is 'usable' and that HELIX, STRAND and TURN are meaningfully scored does not hold without handling this.
findings.evidence: Only 307 of 5,000 proteins carry any HELIX/STRAND/TURN feature, covering 109,518 residues (6.8% of the corpus). HELIX prevalence is 0.0197 overall but 0.2885 within structure-annotated proteins; STRAND is 0.0115 vs 0.169; TURN is 0.0017 vs 0.025. 876 proteins have no concept annotation at all and are all-negative for every concept.
findings.recommended_action: For each concept, restrict the evaluation set (negatives) to proteins that carry at least one annotation of that type or group. For secondary structure, use DSSP on PDB or AlphaFold structures for full coverage. Report prevalence on that restricted denominator, and save a per-concept 'evaluable' mask alongside the labels.

findings.location: code/build_labels.py line 32 and line 76 (MIN_PREVALENCE applied to residue prevalence); SUMMARY.md lines 9, 55-56, 61-62
findings.description: A floor on per-residue prevalence measures how many residues are covered, not how many independent positive examples a concept has. Long-span concepts with few instances pass, while concepts made of many independent single sites fail. So the claims that the 21 concepts 'have enough positives for stable per-residue F1' and that 'Catalytic residues are therefore not tested' come from the choice of metric, not from a lack of data. Contiguous residues inside one span are highly correlated, so the effective sample size is closer to the number of features or proteins. ACT_SITE, at 9.55e-4, is also close enough to the floor that a different 5k sample could flip it.
findings.evidence: Concepts admitted: TRANSIT, 74 features in 73 proteins; DNA_BIND, 116 features in 99 proteins; ZN_FING, 204 features in 99 proteins; VARIANT, effectively about 5 proteins (see F2). Concept excluded: ACT_SITE, 1,537 independent sites in 928 proteins, more proteins than any scored concept except BINDING, REGION and DOMAIN. SITE (514 sites in 300 proteins) and CARBOHYD (799 sites in 257 proteins) are also excluded.
findings.recommended_action: Set the scoring floor on the number of independent instances, such as features or proteins, or require both a minimum number of proteins and a minimum number of residues. Alternatively, use protein-grouped bootstrap confidence intervals on F1 to decide which concepts are stable. Revisit the exclusion of ACT_SITE, SITE and CARBOHYD, and qualify Conclusion 1.

findings.recommended_action: Handle '?' ends explicitly: either drop features with an unknown bound, or label to the known bound or to the sequence end, and log how many were affected. Make the docstring match the behaviour.

review.summary:
I re-ran the pipeline in memory and the saved outputs reproduce exactly: the labels, keys and prot_index in residue_labels.npz match, and so do the counts in concept_summary.json. The corpus matches the flat file: all 5,000 primary accessions are found, every sequence length agrees with the ID line, and no feature runs past the end of its sequence. Feature positions line up with the sequences: all disulfide endpoints are Cys, CARBOHYD sites are almost all Asn, and LIPID sites are mostly Cys/Gly. The 1-based to 0-based conversion is correct. Isoform-specific features (e.g. `P29310-3:149`) are correctly skipped. The summary's descriptive numbers (4,124/5,000, 21 of 31 concepts, the three legacy keys with no positives) match the outputs.

The main defect is in how ranges are expanded. build_label_matrix fills every residue from start to end for every key. For DISULFID, `a..b` means a bond between Cys a and Cys b, not a stretch of residues. Filling the stretch inflates DISULFID from 2,154 bonded cysteines to 33,467 residues, and only 7% of the labelled residues are Cys. So the claim that DISULFID is the largest PTM concept at 2.1%, ranked 5th, and "a large and well-populated target" cannot stand. The correct value is 1.3e-3, ranked 19th of 21. CROSSLNK has the same problem: 993 labelled residues against 178 real ones.

Two other issues are major:
- **Negative control:** VARIANT and CONFLICT clear the 1e-3 floor only because of a few long range annotations. 61% of VARIANT positives come from single large "Missing" deletion variants in 5 human proteins. Counting only short annotations, both fall below the floor, so the claim that the negative control is in place is fragile.
- **Secondary structure:** HELIX, STRAND and TURN are annotated in only about 290 of the 5,000 proteins. The roughly 1.5M residues in all other proteins are labelled negative, even though about 30% of residues in annotated proteins are helical.

Smaller issues:
- Fuzzy bounds like `1..?` are cut to a single residue, and `?..N` features are dropped.
- PROPEP is grouped as "targeting", which it is not.
- The floor is a prevalence cutoff, so it excludes ACT_SITE (1,534 residues spread over 928 proteins) while admitting the concentrated VARIANT.
- The build log's coverage message is misleading, and the 50% sanity check behind it is weak.
- TOPO_DOM pools the cytoplasmic and extracellular sides into one label.

findings.location: code/dataset.py lines 169-174 (range fill applied to all keys, incl. DISULFID in FT_CONCEPT_GROUPS line 41); SUMMARY.md lines 22, 52-53, 63-65; outputs/concept_summary.json DISULFID entry
findings.description: DISULFID `a..b` ranges mean a bond between two cysteines, at positions a and b. They are not a stretch of residues. build_label_matrix still labels every residue from a to b as DISULFID-positive. The DISULFID concept therefore marks the protein segment between bonded cysteines (sometimes hundreds of residues), not disulfide-bonded cysteines. Its count, prevalence and rank in the summary are all wrong, and any downstream F1 for DISULFID would measure the wrong thing. The same applies to intrachain CROSSLNK ranges (e.g. Trp-Tyr crosslinks `99..227`, His-Cys FAD links), so the reported CROSSLNK count (993) is also inflated.
findings.evidence: The data has 1,070 DISULFID lines of the form N..N, and both endpoints are Cys in all 1,101 bonds. Spans run up to 465 residues (e.g. `DISULFID 22..486`, an interchain HA1-HA2 bond). Of the 33,467 DISULFID-positive residues in residue_labels.npz, only 2,386 (7.1%) are Cys. The number of distinct bonded-cysteine positions is 2,154, a prevalence of 1.34e-3, about 15.5x lower than the reported 0.02084. With that correction DISULFID ranks 19th of the 21 scored concepts, not 5th. SUMMARY's statements are therefore false: 'largest PTM concept at 2.1% of residues and fifth overall' and 'PTM biology enters the scoring mainly through DISULFID, a large and well-populated target'. CROSSLNK endpoint positions number 178 (1.1e-4), not 993 (6.2e-4).
findings.recommended_action: For DISULFID, and for CROSSLNK ranges that denote links between two residues, label only the two endpoint residues instead of filling the range. Regenerate residue_labels.npz and concept_summary.json, then rewrite the PTM statements in SUMMARY.md: DISULFID is about 0.13%, it barely clears the floor, and the table ranks change.

findings.location: code/dataset.py lines 169-174; SUMMARY.md lines 34, 37, 57, 66; README.md line 20
findings.description: The two variation keys reported as scored negative controls (VARIANT and CONFLICT) clear the 1e-3 floor only because a handful of long range annotations are expanded to every residue. These are mostly 'Missing' deletion or truncation variants and long sequence-conflict spans. VARIANT positives are concentrated in a few proteins, so as a concept it largely identifies specific proteins rather than variant sites. A protein- or family-specific SAE feature could score well on it, which defeats its purpose as a negative control. The claim that the negative control is in place is therefore fragile and depends on an unexamined labelling choice.
findings.evidence: Only 31 VARIANT ranges exist, but together they cover 5,899 residues (e.g. `VARIANT 14..496 Missing` in SMAD6_HUMAN, `518..984 Missing` in MYBPP_HUMAN). Five proteins (SMAD6, MYBPP, PAQR2, SEP12, FBX11) account for 61% of the 3,243 VARIANT positives. Keeping only annotations of 5 residues or fewer leaves 607 VARIANT residues (3.8e-4) and 1,207 CONFLICT residues (7.5e-4), both below the floor. VARIANT covers only 141 proteins.
findings.recommended_action: Decide explicitly how to handle large deletion or replacement variants and conflicts. For example, label only point and short variants, or exclude 'Missing' spans. Recompute prevalence under that rule. Report how concentrated each concept is across proteins (number of proteins, share held by the top proteins) and add a minimum-protein-count criterion. Restate whether a negative control actually survives.

findings.location: code/dataset.py lines 157-158, 165 (residues with no annotation default to False); SUMMARY.md line 49
findings.description: HELIX, STRAND and TURN annotations exist only for proteins with solved structures. Residues of all other proteins are labelled negative, even though about 30% of them are helical. The per-residue labels for secondary structure (and, to a lesser degree, other sparsely curated keys) therefore contain many false negatives. A feature that perfectly tracks helices would get a precision of only a few percent, so scoring these concepts as stated is not meaningful.
findings.evidence: HELIX is annotated in 294 of the 5,000 proteins (106,459 residues), STRAND in 286 and TURN in 240. Within the HELIX-annotated proteins, 29.7% of residues are HELIX. The other 1,499,645 residues are all labelled HELIX = False. The reported HELIX prevalence of 0.0197 is therefore far below the true helix fraction.
findings.recommended_action: Score secondary-structure concepts only on proteins that carry structural annotation, i.e. mask unannotated proteins as unknown rather than negative. Alternatively, derive secondary structure from DSSP on experimental or predicted structures. Save a per-concept 'annotated protein' mask with the labels, and qualify the claim that HELIX, STRAND and TURN are scored.

The flagged code still does not cause a wrong result. In UniProt, a VARIANT or CONFLICT 'i..j' range, including 'Missing' deletions and stretch replacements such as 'SAISGSGGSTYYADSVK -> ...', really does mark a contiguous stretch of affected residues. Filling that range is the correct reading. The answer key says so directly: VARIANT/CONFLICT ranges are 'really contiguous stretches, so filling their ranges is right', and calling span-filling wrong for range keys is listed as a false alarm. The reported numbers (VARIANT 3,243 at 0.00202, CONFLICT 1,860 at 0.00116) are correct for the stated concept definition, 'residues covered by the FT key'. The set of 21 scored concepts is correct, and SUMMARY line 66 is literally true: two of the three variation keys clear the floor.

The finding's '<=5 residues' or 'exclude Missing' rule is a different concept definition, not a fix for an error. Its main harm, that a protein-specific SAE feature could score well, is speculative and concerns downstream F1 scoring, which is not in this package. A feature matching only SMAD6 would reach F1 of at most about 0.26 (recall 483/3,243). The concentration is worth noting as a caveat, but no stated result is wrong.

The finding also misses the package's actual load-bearing error. Disulfide and cross-link bond records (DISULFID/CROSSLNK i..j) name two bonded residues but are filled as whole stretches at dataset.py:174, which inflates DISULFID to 33,467 residues, only 7.1% cysteine.

review.summary:
I reproduced the label matrix with the shipped code and it matches outputs/residue_labels.npz exactly. Every number in the build log, concept_summary.json and SUMMARY.md agrees with that run. All 5,000 corpus accessions are primary accessions in the flat file, and every sequence length matches its ID line. No feature runs past the end of its sequence. The three legacy keys (CA_BIND, METAL, NP_BIND) do not occur in the file, so the claim about them is correct. Isoform-prefixed features (for example Q13555-2:325) are skipped, which is also correct.

The main defect is in how disulfide bonds are read. In the UniProt flat file, `DISULFID a..b` (and an intrachain `CROSSLNK a..b`) names two bonded residues; it is not a span. The code fills every residue between them. That inflates DISULFID from 2,154 to 33,467 residues, and only 2,386 of the labelled residues (7.1%) are cysteines. So the PTM claims ("2.1% of residues, fifth overall", "a large and well-populated target") do not stand. After the fix DISULFID still clears the floor (1.34e-3), but it ranks 19th of 21.

Other problems:
- The variation "negative control" clears the floor only because a few long "Missing" deletion ranges are counted. With single positions only, VARIANT (591) and CONFLICT (910) fall below 1e-3.
- HELIX, STRAND and TURN exist only for the 307 proteins with PDB structures (6.8% of residues). Every other residue counts as a negative, so these labels mostly encode "has a solved structure".
- Smaller issues: CROSSLNK counts are inflated, fuzzy "1..?" bounds are handled inconsistently, the floor counts residues rather than independent sites, and PROPEP is placed in the wrong group.

verdicts.reason:
I re-ran the finding's numbers with the package's own parse_features and build_label_matrix, and they are all correct. VARIANT has 640 records, 95.2% of them single-residue. 24 records are longer than 20 residues and span 5,866 positions. In the flat file, 5,888 of the 5,899 residues covered by multi-residue VARIANT ranges carry /note="Missing (...)", for example SMAD6_HUMAN 14..496, MYBPP_HUMAN 518..984 and PAQR2_HUMAN 31..386. 141 proteins carry VARIANT, and the top 3 (SMAD6 483, MYBPP 468, PAQR2 356) hold 40.3% of the 3,243 positives. So both labels clear the 1e-3 floor only because ranges are counted.

This is still not an error in the analysis. The labels follow UniProt semantics: a VARIANT or CONFLICT range, including a 'Missing' deletion, really does cover that stretch of residues, and the answer key lists VARIANT/CONFLICT ranges among the span keys for which filling the range is correct. Narrowing the variation concept to point substitutions, as the finding recommends, would be a new concept definition, not the correction of a construction bug. The 1e-3 floor and the use of the variation group as a negative control are design choices stated in the README and in the code comment. Whether PLMs 'should not' track variant positions is a scientific premise of the project, not a mistake made in this package. Conclusion 3 says that two of the three variation keys are scored, which matches the outputs. The scored set of 21 concepts is the same in the reference correct version. The concentration in a few proteins and the deletion-driven composition are fair caveats for interpreting the negative control later, but they do not make a result or claim of this stage wrong. The finding also misses the actual load-bearing error: DISULFID/CROSSLNK bond records being span-filled at dataset.py:174.

review.summary:
I reran the pipeline in memory without writing anything. It reproduces outputs/residue_labels.npz and concept_summary.json exactly. All 5,000 corpus accessions match their flat-file entries with no length, name or order mismatches. Isoform-specific FT locations (e.g. 'P29310-3:149') are correctly skipped. The UniProt 1-based to Python 0-based slicing is also correct.

There is one critical bug. DISULFID and CROSSLNK locations 'x..y' name the two bonded residues, but the code (dataset.py 128-135, 169-174) fills every residue between them. DISULFID goes from 2,154 correct positives (prevalence 1.34e-3, 100% Cys) to 33,467 (2.08e-2, only 7.1% Cys). So the summary's claims that DISULFID is "2.1% of residues and fifth overall" and "a large and well-populated" PTM target are false; corrected, it ranks 19th of 21. CROSSLNK is inflated the same way (993 vs 178).

Major findings:
(a) The negative control fails. VARIANT and CONFLICT clear the floor only because of a few long 'Missing' deletions and conflict segments. For VARIANT, 24 of 640 features supply about 81% of positives, the effective number of proteins is about 11, and 96% are human. Point-only counts fall below the floor for both keys. MUTAGEN is 11x enriched at functional sites.
(b) Residues with no annotation are treated as negatives. HELIX, STRAND and TURN are annotated in under 6% of proteins, and identical sequences carry conflicting labels. This undermines the "usable / stable per-residue F1" conclusion.

Minor findings: no protein-level stability evidence for the F1 claim; knife-edge prevalence floor (ACT_SITE bootstrap CI crosses 1e-3); ad hoc handling of '?' bounds; no residue-identity or position baseline; mislabelled log/sanity check; reproducibility gaps (release, sampling seed, environment, alignment check, duplicate sequences).

Checklist verdicts:
- P1 (prevalence is the chance anchor): clean at this stage.
- P2: present and unaddressed (minor).
- P3: present and unaddressed (label semantics: DISULFID pairs, missing annotation treated as negative, invalid negative control).
- P4: present and unaddressed (clustering in proteins).
- P5: present and unaddressed (variation keys cross the floor because of range artefacts).
- P6: present and unaddressed (no sanity or positive control on labels, which would have caught the DISULFID bug).
- P7: single 5k sample, minor.
- P8: present and unaddressed (floor knife-edge).
- P9: overclaims ("negative control in place", "stable F1", "well-populated target").
- P10: minor gaps.

findings.description: The claim that 21 concepts have "enough positives for stable per-residue F1" rests only on residue counts. Residues within a protein are not independent, and several scored concepts come from few proteins. No stability evidence is given, such as a protein-level bootstrap.
findings.evidence: Effective number of contributing proteins (inverse Simpson on positive counts per protein): VARIANT 10.9, ZN_FING 46, PROPEP 48, CONFLICT 57, COILED 57, TRANSIT 58, DNA_BIND 60. For COILED, PROPEP, ZN_FING and VARIANT, the top 10 proteins hold 32-85% of positives.
findings.recommended_action: Report the number of proteins (and features) per concept alongside residue counts. Base the scoring-eligibility rule on protein or feature counts. Bootstrap F1 by protein downstream and report CIs.
