review.summary: I reran the pipeline (PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE, no outputs written) and it reproduces results.json and run_log.txt exactly. The data match the README: 2,000 controls, 105 singles with 113–400 cells, 131 doubles, and 115 doubles kept. The arithmetic in SUMMARY.md also matches the outputs (0.370/0.406 = 91%, +0.007, +0.029, 49/50/54%). The headline conclusions do not hold up, for four reasons. (1) The features dA and dB are the same noisy single-perturbation and control means that are subtracted inside the target I. That alone produces a negative dA+dB vs I relationship (regression to the mean). With features and target built from independent cell halves, sum-only drops from about 0.43 to about 0.21. On data that are additive by construction (true I = 0), sum-only still scores 0.25–0.33. An analytic estimate puts about 0.14 of the 0.37 down to shared noise. (2) The gain from the per-gene offset (+0.029, which gives the best model 0.406 / 54%) is leakage through the control mean, which appears in every pair's I. When training and test pairs use independent control halves, the gain falls to between 0 and 0.002. (3) The ceiling is not an upper bound when the features share noise with the target. Also, '46% unexplained' treats a ratio of correlations as a share of signal; on a variance scale about 71% is unexplained. (4) Even taking the numbers at face value, they contradict 'mostly shrinkage / most of the interaction is not pair-specific': sum-only explains 18% of I's variance against a reliability of 0.57 (about a third). Smaller issues: the claim of independence from the perturbed genes was never tested, because 99% of test pairs share a single with training pairs. The bootstrap intervals ignore dependence between pairs. The ceiling is aggregated before the non-linear transforms (Jensen bias). The 'variance explained' is uncentred, and the 'exactly 0' additive baseline has an undefined correlation.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 53-56, 61, 86-87 (I built from DA[x]+DA[y] and cmean) and 119-120 (the same DA used as features); SUMMARY.md claims 1-2 and the title
findings.description: The features (dA, dB, dA+dB) are the same noisy estimates that are subtracted inside the target I = dAB - dA - dB, and the control mean enters both: +c in I, -2c in dA+dB. So sampling error in the single and control means makes dA+dB and I negatively correlated even when the true interaction is zero (errors-in-variables / regression to the mean). The 'sum-only' result (+0.370) and the conclusion that 'the interaction term is mostly shrinkage... a ceiling/floor effect' are therefore substantially an artifact. Because the per-pair correlation of a one-feature model depends only on the sign of beta (fitted beta = -0.22), 'a trained model works' only shows that this correlation is negative.
findings.evidence: Independent re-analysis on the same data, 3 random splits each. Features built from half 1 of the single and control cells: if the target I uses the same half, sum-only CV corr is 0.431–0.435; if I uses the independent half 2 (all double cells), it is 0.200–0.217, and saturation adds nothing (0.195–0.216). A null that is additive by construction (pseudo-double = half-2 singles summed, so the true I is exactly 0) still gives sum-only 0.247–0.332 and saturation 0.257–0.361. An analytic estimate of the noise covariance -(Var(mA)+Var(mB)+2Var(c)) gives an expected shared-noise correlation of -0.136 against the observed mean corr(s, I) of -0.370 at full data.
findings.recommended_action: Estimate features and target from disjoint cells: split the single and control cells, build the features from one part and I from the other, and cross-fit. Alternatively, explicitly correct for the noise covariance. Report a null calibration (additive-by-construction or permuted data). Restate the sum-only and saturation results, and the 'shrinkage / ceiling-floor' interpretation, from noise-independent estimates.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 121-125 (goff = I[tr].mean(0)) together with line 53 (one control mean shared by every pair's I); SUMMARY.md table row 'saturation + per-gene offset', claim 1 ('best model +0.406, 54% of the ceiling'), claim 2 ('per-gene offsets add another +0.029')
findings.description: Every pair's I contains the same control-mean sampling error (+cmean noise), and test pairs share singles with training pairs. The per-gene mean of I over training pairs therefore carries noise that also sits in the held-out pairs' I. Holding out pairs does not stop this leakage. The +0.029 gain from per-gene offsets, and the best-model figures of 0.406 and 54% of the ceiling, are produced by this leakage, not by gene-level structure.
findings.evidence: Rerun with the control cells split in two: training pairs' features and I use control half 1, test pairs' use half 2. saturation+gene minus saturation = +0.0001, +0.0022, +0.0007 (3 seeds). With a shared control, the same comparison gives +0.030, +0.029, +0.028, matching the reported +0.029. In the additive-by-construction null, saturation+gene reaches 0.54–0.58. The variance of the control-mean noise is about 18% of the across-gene variance of the per-gene offset.
findings.recommended_action: Use independent control cells (or a control mean estimated without the cells used in the test I) for the training and test folds, and hold out singles as well as pairs (see F5). Re-estimate the per-gene-offset model and drop or revise the 0.406 / 54% headline and the +0.029 claim.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md claim 2 ('The interaction term is mostly shrinkage') and claim 3 ('Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity'); title
findings.description: Even at face value, the reported numbers do not support 'mostly'. So the generic shrinkage term accounts for roughly a third of the reliable interaction signal; on a correlation basis it is (0.370/0.752)^2 = 24%. Most of the reliable signal is left unexplained, i.e. it is pair-specific or at least not generic. Claim 3 also contradicts claim 4, which says real headroom remains. findings.evidence: results.json: sum-only var_explained 0.184, saturation 0.197, _ceiling.full 0.566 -> 0.184/0.566 = 0.33. (corr/ceiling)^2 = (0.370/0.752)^2 = 0.24. In noise-independent analyses (F1) sum-only correlation roughly halves.
findings.recommended_action: Remove the 'mostly shrinkage' and 'most of the interaction is not pair-specific' claims, or restate them quantitatively (e.g. 'a generic shrinkage term explains about X% of the reliable variance') using noise-corrected estimates.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 93-95, 137 (frac_of_ceiling = corr/ceiling); SUMMARY.md ceiling line, table 'share of ceiling' column, claim 4 ('46% unexplained')
findings.description: (a) sqrt(reliability) bounds the correlation only for predictors that are independent of the measurement noise in I. These predictors share noise with I (F1, F2), so they can and do correlate with the noise component, and 'share of ceiling' is not a share of the achievable signal. (b) Claim 4 reads 1 - corr/ceiling = 46% as 'just under half of the reliable interaction signal is unexplained'. findings.recommended_action: Compute the ceiling comparison only for predictions built from cells independent of those in the evaluated I. Express explained and unexplained shares in variance units (corr^2/reliability), and correct the '46% unexplained' statement.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py line 108 (folds over pairs only; the docstring at line 11 concedes singles recur); SUMMARY.md claim 2 ('does not depend on which genes were perturbed') and claim 3
findings.description: Cross-validation holds out pairs but not singles. 99% of test pairs share at least one single perturbation with training pairs, and singles are reused up to 12 times (66 distinct singles across 115 pairs). The shared singles also carry shared single-mean noise into the per-gene offset (F2).

findings.recommended_action: Add a leave-singles-out (or both-singles-unseen) CV split and report it separately. Otherwise drop the claim of independence from the perturbed genes.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 132-134 (bootstrap over per-pair correlations); SUMMARY.md CIs, 'tight interval', and the +0.007 / +0.029 increments

Pairs share singles (up to 12 times) and all share one control mean, and the bootstrap ignores the variability of the CV fold assignment. The intervals are likely too narrow. findings.description: The ceiling is computed by averaging per-pair split-half correlations first and then applying Spearman-Brown and the square root, both concave. By Jensen's inequality this overstates the average per-pair ceiling that the mean per-pair correlation is compared against, so 'share of ceiling' is biased downward. Some pairs have split-half r near 0 (min -0.018; 8 pairs below 0.1).

review.summary:
I reviewed B3100: README.md, SUMMARY.md, code/learn_interaction.py, data/norman2019_subset.npz and the outputs. I reproduced results.json exactly by running the code in memory without writing any files, then ran my own checks.

The arithmetic in the summary matches the code. The headline numbers and their interpretation do not hold up, for four reasons:
1. The sum-only "trained model works" score of +0.370 is inflated by sampling noise that the features and the target share. Both are built from the same single-perturbation means and the same control mean. About 0.14 of the 0.370 is expected from that shared noise alone. On independent halves of the data the correlation roughly halves.
2. The +0.029 gain from per-gene offsets disappears when training and test pairs use separate control cells. The best model's +0.406 and "54% of ceiling" therefore rest on leaked control noise.
3. The saturation / ceiling-floor reading is contradicted by the data. The non-linear features add nothing. Genes pushed in opposite directions by the two singles, and genes moved by only one of them, are damped about as much as genes pushed the same way.
4. The claims that the interaction is "mostly shrinkage", "not pair-specific" and does "not depend on which genes were perturbed" go against the analysis's own numbers. The best model explains only about 29% of the reliable signal variance. Per-pair shrinkage slopes are highly reproducible across independent halves (r = 0.92), and 27 to 30 of the 115 pairs show reproducible synergy instead of shrinkage.

Further problems: "46% unexplained" confuses a ratio of correlations with a share of variance (the true figure is about 71%). The ceiling is not an upper bound for predictors that share noise with the target. The bootstrap treats pairs as independent although the 115 pairs reuse only 66 singles.

Verdicts against the ten checklist patterns:
- P1 (weak null): present and unaddressed. There is no noise-only null; the additive baseline of 0 is used as chance.
- P2 (trivial baseline): mostly clean. The sum-only baseline is reported, but it is itself inflated.
- P3 (endpoint vs claim): present. A regression coefficient is read as a ceiling/floor mechanism.
- P4 (unit of inference / leaky CV): present. Pairs share singles; the bootstrap and folds are by pair only.
- P5 (selection / double-dipping): present. The same single and control means are reused in features and target; genes are the top 1,000 by expression; low-cell doubles are dropped.
- P6 (positive control): not applicable; there is no load-bearing null finding.
- P7 (single condition): present, minor. One cell line, one subset, one seed.
- P8 (stability): present. There are no confidence intervals on the model differences or on the share of ceiling.
- P9 (overreach): present. "what it learns is saturation", "needs no regulatory network".
- P10 (reproducibility): minor. The script that built the subset is missing and versions are not pinned.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py:86-87,119-120 (features dA,dB and target I built from the same DA[x], DA[y], cmean); SUMMARY.md:12,16-17
findings.description: The target I = dAB - dA - dB contains -(noise of single A + noise of single B) + control noise. The feature dA+dB contains +(noise of A + noise of B) - 2 x control noise. Any predictor linear in dA+dB therefore gets a negative covariance with I from sampling noise alone, even with no true interaction (errors-in-variables / regression to the mean). The +0.370 sum-only correlation, its 49% of ceiling, and the claim that 'a trained model works' with a tight interval are all inflated. No noise-only null is computed; 'additive = 0' is used as the chance level.
findings.evidence: I reproduced results.json exactly. Covariance decomposition, using each gene's sampling variance of the means (Var/n for single A, single B and control), gives an expected shared-noise covariance of -(VA+VB+2Vc). This accounts for about 0.136 of the mean per-pair r of 0.370, leaving about 0.234 (about 31% of the 0.752 ceiling). The direct empirical check agrees. With half-size data, features and target from the same half give mean per-pair r = -0.40 to -0.44 over 3 seeds. Features from one half and target from the independent other half give r = -0.19 to -0.23. The pooled slope is -0.22 on the full data and -0.18 cross-fitted.
findings.recommended_action: Cross-fit: estimate dA, dB (features) from cells and controls disjoint from those used to build the target I, or simulate a noise-only null with no interaction. Report the sum-only score against that null and restate the headline (roughly 0.2 instead of 0.37). State that part of the apparent 'shrinkage' is regression to the mean.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py:53 (single control mean cmean shared by every pair), 123-125 (goff = I[tr].mean(0)); SUMMARY.md:14,17,21,28
findings.description: Every pair's I contains the same +control-mean noise for each gene. The per-gene offset, the mean of I over training pairs, keeps that noise in full (averaging over pairs does not remove it) and uses it to predict the test pair's I, which carries the same noise. The +0.029 gain from per-gene offsets, the best-model +0.406, and '54% of the ceiling' are therefore leakage, not a real per-gene effect. Singles are also shared between training and test pairs (pair-level CV), which adds more leakage that was not quantified.
findings.evidence: Control cells were split into two halves of 1,000. When training-pair I/features use control half 1 and test-pair I/features use the same half 1: saturation 0.393, saturation+gene 0.421 (gain +0.028), matching the reported +0.029. When test pairs use the independent control half 2: saturation 0.384, saturation+gene 0.381 (gain -0.003). Across 5 fold seeds the gain is -0.006 to -0.011 with independent controls versus +0.020 to +0.028 with shared controls.
findings.recommended_action: Compute training-pair and test-pair I with disjoint control cells, and ideally disjoint single-perturbation cells or GroupKFold by single. Re-estimate the per-gene offset model. If the gain stays near zero, drop the 'per-gene offsets add +0.029' and '54% of ceiling' claims and report the best model as the sum-only/saturation level.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:1 (title 'what it learns is saturation'), 19-23 ('This is a ceiling/floor effect. It needs no regulatory network'), 25-26 ('a generic non-linearity'); code/learn_interaction.py:13-17
findings.description: The mechanistic reading is not supported, and the data contradict it. The model that carries the result is linear in dA+dB, which means a linear damping of the double response, not a non-linearity. The features that would capture saturation (product, min, max, sign agreement) add only +0.007. Saturation predicts damping only when both singles push a gene the same way, but opposite-sign and one-sided responses are damped just as much. Shared-noise regression to the mean (F1) also produces exactly this linear pattern. The 1,000 most highly expressed genes (MALAT1, MT-CO*, RPS/RPL...) are also the genes least likely to hit a floor.
findings.evidence: Cross-fitted data (features from half 1, I from independent half 2), genes with |dA| and |dB| > 0.1: same-sign responses (n = 9,225) have slope of I on dA+dB = -0.16. Opposite-sign responses (n = 2,069) have slope -0.19 (coefficients on dA and dB of -0.23 and -0.18). Genes where only A responds (n = 3,992) have slope -0.13. The saturation model reaches 0.3767 versus 0.3700 for sum-only.
findings.recommended_action: Replace 'saturation / ceiling-floor effect' with 'linear sub-additivity (a damped double response)', and say it is consistent with several mechanisms (dominance/epistasis, perturbation efficiency in doubles, regression to the mean). Remove 'needs no regulatory network' unless a test that targets saturation directly is run, e.g. dependence on baseline expression or sign agreement on cross-fitted data.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:20-26 ('The interaction term is mostly shrinkage', 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed', 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific')
findings.description: These claims contradict the analysis's own numbers and pair-level checks. Generic features explain a minority of the reliable interaction signal. How much a pair is damped, and even whether it is damped or amplified, is a reproducible property of each pair. The claim that the effect does not depend on which genes were perturbed was never tested.
findings.evidence: From the analysis's own numbers: the best model explains (0.406/0.752)^2 ≈ 29% of the reliable per-pair signal variance; pooled, 0.211/0.566 ≈ 37%; sum-only, 0.184/0.566 ≈ 33%. Each of these is less than half, before the F1/F2 corrections. My check: per-pair cross-fitted slopes of I on dA+dB, computed on fully independent halves (double, singles, control), correlate r = 0.92 across pairs (mean -0.10, SD 0.23). Per-pair r correlates 0.93 across halves. 27 to 30 of the 115 pairs show positive (synergistic) r in both independent halves over 3 seeds.
findings.recommended_action: Withdraw 'mostly shrinkage' and 'not pair-specific', or restate them as 'a damping term common to many pairs explains about a third of the reliable signal; the rest, including reproducible synergy in about a quarter of pairs, is pair-specific'. Test pair-specificity explicitly, e.g. with split-half reliability of per-pair slopes.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:28-31 ('just under half of the reliable interaction signal (46%) is unexplained'); code/learn_interaction.py:137
findings.description: The share of ceiling is a ratio of correlations (0.406/0.752 = 0.54). Subtracting it from 1 does not give the share of the signal left unexplained; the explained share of the reliable signal is the squared ratio. Combined with F1/F2, the true headroom is much larger than stated.
findings.evidence: 0.539^2 = 0.29, so about 71% of the reliable per-pair variance is unexplained (63% using pooled variance explained 0.211 divided by reliability 0.566), not 46%.
findings.recommended_action: Report the share of reliable variance explained as (r/ceiling)^2 or as pooled R^2/reliability, and correct the 46% statement after fixing F1/F2.

findings.description: The ceiling, sqrt of the Spearman-Brown-corrected split-half reliability, bounds only predictors whose errors are independent of the noise in the measured I. Every model here uses dA and dB, which share noise with I (F1), so the 'share of ceiling' is not interpretable and a model can exceed the ceiling. The ceiling also comes from one random split, has no uncertainty attached, and is aggregated as sqrt(SB(mean r)) instead of per pair.
findings.evidence: Per-pair split-half r of the I profile ranges down to -0.10 (2 pairs below 0, 9 below 0.1). sqrt(SB(mean r)) = 0.748 versus the mean of per-pair sqrt(SB(r_i)) = 0.703. 22 of 115 pairs have a sum-only r above their own (noisy) per-pair ceiling estimate.
findings.recommended_action: Compute model scores and the ceiling on cross-fitted data where predictors and target do not share cells. Aggregate the ceiling the same way as the metric (per pair). Bootstrap the ceiling and the share of ceiling together.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py:132-133 (bootstrap resamples pairs as independent); SUMMARY.md:12-14,16 ('with a tight interval')
findings.description: The 115 pairs are not independent. They use only 66 distinct singles, so a single's response vector and its noise recur in many pairs. The bootstrap resamples pairs and is conditional on one fold assignment and one cell split. The 95% intervals are therefore too narrow. There are also no paired intervals for the differences the summary relies on (+0.007, +0.029) or for the share of ceiling.
findings.evidence: Single reuse across kept pairs: PTPN12 in 12, KLF1 in 11, CEBPE in 10, UBASH3B in 10, ETS2 in 9. For the sum-only mean per-pair r, the naive SE is 0.036; the delete-one-single jackknife SE is 0.087 (even halving its variance for overlapping clusters gives about 0.06, 1.7x naive).
findings.recommended_action: Use a cluster bootstrap over singles (or a two-way pair/single bootstrap), report paired CIs for model differences, and repeat over several fold and split seeds.

findings.description: Cross-validation holds out whole pairs but not singles. A test pair's dA/dB vectors, with their noise, also appear in training pairs' features and targets, and fold sizes are random and unbalanced. The summary's 'the double of an evaluation pair is never seen in training' is true but suggests more independence than there is.
findings.evidence: fold = rng.integers(0, 5, 115) gives fold sizes of 22/23/21/23/26 at the seed used and 15 to 33 for other seeds. Singles are reused across up to 12 pairs.
findings.recommended_action: Add GroupKFold by single (hold out every pair that contains a held-out single) as a sensitivity analysis, and use balanced folds.

findings.description: The conclusions rest on one cell line and modality (K562 CRISPRa) and one subset: the 1,000 most highly expressed genes, capped cell numbers, and doubles with at least 120 cells. That filter drops 16 doubles such as CEBPB_CEBPA, JUN_CEBPA and CEBPE_CEBPB, which may be pairs with strong fitness or interaction effects. Results also come from one seed and one ridge alpha. Yet the summary states general rules ('Any method that claims to predict interactions must report the sum-only baseline').
findings.evidence: 16 of 131 doubles were dropped for having fewer than 120 cells (54 to 114 cells). The genes are dominated by MALAT1, mitochondrial and ribosomal transcripts. Fold-seed sensitivity is small (saturation+gene 0.412 to 0.421).
findings.recommended_action: State the scope (K562 CRISPRa, highly expressed genes, doubles with at least 120 cells). Add a sensitivity check with a different gene set (e.g. highly variable genes) and with the min-double threshold relaxed.

findings.description: The correlation of the additive model is undefined for a constant prediction. The code reports it as 0.000 with n = 0 and a [0, 0] interval, and the summary presents this as 'an additive baseline of exactly 0'. That is not a chance level for a correlation metric (see F1).
findings.evidence: results.json lists additive with corr 0.0, lo 0.0, hi 0.0, n 0.
findings.recommended_action: Mark the additive correlation as undefined. Use a noise-only or permutation null as the reference for the correlation metric.

findings.description: Reproducibility gaps. The script that drew the subset from the scPerturb h5ad (gene ranking, per-group caps, seed) is not included. No package versions are pinned; the README only says numpy and scikit-learn.
findings.evidence: The folder contains only code/learn_interaction.py, the npz, and the outputs; there is no subset-building code or requirements/environment file.
findings.recommended_action: Add the subset-extraction script with its seed and a requirements file with pinned versions.

grade_a.detection_reason: The key B3100 is the 'clean' version (error: null), so there is no documented error to detect and error_detected is null. No finding claims that the ceiling halves are not independent. The ceiling in code/learn_interaction.py:72-97 splits the double, both singles and the controls, so it is correct. The ceiling-related points in F6 are the coupling issue and the per-pair aggregation issue, and the key lists both as valid other_real_issues. I re-ran the analysis inline and reproduced sum-only 0.370, saturation 0.377 and saturation+gene 0.405. I checked F1 through F4 with cross-fitted splits.

findings.reason: This is the feature-target noise coupling issue that the key lists as valid in other_real_issues. I confirmed it with disjoint halves of every group. Within a half (features and target from the same cells), the mean per-pair r of I with dA+dB is -0.39 to -0.40 and the pooled slope is about -0.25. Cross-fitted (features from half 1, target from half 2), r is -0.20 to -0.21 and the slope is about -0.17. So the sum-only score and the 'shrinkage' reading are partly regression to the mean. The finding challenges the headline +0.370.

This is not the key's false alarm. It does not say test targets enter the offset; it says that the shared control mean (and shared singles) put a common noise component into every pair's I, and the training-pair mean keeps it. I confirmed this. With 1,000-cell control halves, the saturation+gene gain is +0.026 to +0.039 when train and test pairs use the same control half, and only +0.004 to +0.009 when test pairs use the independent half (3 seeds). Most of the reported +0.029 gain, and so the '54% of ceiling', comes from shared control noise. The reviewer's 'about 0 or negative' is slightly too strong, but the main claim holds.

The 'saturation / ceiling-floor' title claim does not survive cross-fitting. I computed slopes of I on dA+dB for genes with |dA| and |dB| above 0.1 (3 seeds). Same-sign responses give about -0.19, opposite-sign responses -0.15 to -0.22, and genes where only A responds -0.14 to -0.17. Damping is about as strong when the two singles push in opposite directions, which saturation does not predict. The saturation features add only +0.007 over sum-only (results.json). The 'needs no regulatory network' reading is unsupported.

I confirmed it with fully independent quarter splits of every group. Per-pair cross-fitted slopes from two independent replicates correlate 0.83 to 0.87, and 25 to 31 pairs have positive (synergistic) r in both replicates over 3 seeds. Attenuation cannot produce reproducible positive slopes. In variance terms, the analysis's own numbers (0.370 to 0.406 of 0.752) leave most of the reliable signal unexplained. 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific' and 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed' are therefore not supported.

The point is correct: a ratio of correlations, 0.54, is not a share of signal. In variance terms (0.54)^2 = 0.29, so about 71% of the reliable signal is unexplained, not 46%. It corrects a number in the summary, but the summary's conclusion that headroom remains holds, and becomes stronger.

It does not say the halves are dependent, and the ceiling itself is computed correctly. Its valid content is: (a) coupled predictors can exceed a noise-independent ceiling, which is F1's coupling issue again; (b) Spearman-Brown and the square root are applied to the mean r instead of per pair, which the key lists as a minor valid issue (0.752 vs about 0.71). The 'single split, no uncertainty' point is minor because the key reports the ceiling as stable at 0.740-0.752 across split seeds. Its numbers (0.748 vs 0.703) differ slightly from the run but are in the same direction.

The key lists this as a minor valid issue: the bootstrap over pairs ignores that pairs share singles. I confirmed the reuse counts: 66 distinct singles across 115 pairs, PTPN12 in 12, KLF1 in 11, CEBPE and UBASH3B in 10. The intervals are too narrow, but the main estimates do not change.

This is the key's listed false alarm: pair-level CV with recurring singles is what the held-out-pair claim requires, the docstring discloses it, and GroupKFold is a stricter variant, not a correction. Its evidence is also wrong. With the code's seed the fold sizes are 25/20/31/22/17, not 22/23/21/23/26.

Asking for the scope (K562 CRISPRa, top-1,000 genes, doubles with at least 120 cells) to be stated is fair. I confirmed that 16 doubles with 54 to 114 cells are dropped, including JUN_CEBPA, CEBPB_CEBPA and CEBPE_CEBPB. The README documents the subset, the finding does not show that it changes the results, and the key says subsampling is not an error.

The key says corr 0 with n 0 for the constant additive prediction is by design. The finding objects only to the summary calling it 'an additive baseline of exactly 0'. The useful content, that a noise-only null would not be 0, is F1's point.
True: the package has no subset-extraction script and no pinned versions. It is a reproducibility nicety and does not affect any result.

grade_b.detection_reason: Key B3100 has status 'clean' and error null, so there is no documented error to detect. None of the findings claims that the split-half ceiling's halves share cells, or that the ceiling construction (code/learn_interaction.py:72-97) has a load-bearing error. The main findings (F1, F2, F3, F4) are about feature-target noise coupling and how the results are interpreted. F1 matches the key's first other_real_issue. I re-checked F2, F3 and F4 independently on the data and they hold.

findings.reason: Matches the key's other_real_issue on feature-target noise coupling: dA and dB enter the features with a + sign and the target I with a - sign. I confirmed it. With fully disjoint halves (double, singles, controls), the mean per-pair r is about 0.39-0.40 when features and target come from the same half and about 0.19-0.21 when they come from different halves. The pooled slope is -0.25 same-half and -0.17 cross-fitted. This agrees with the key's build check (0.425 vs 0.227). The finding attacks the headline 0.370 and the 'trained model works' claim.

This is not the key's false alarm. The finding states correctly that the offset uses training pairs only. Its mechanism is that the single control mean enters every pair's I, so goff and the test I share the control noise. I confirmed this with 5 control-half splits and fold seeds. When training and test use the same control half, saturation+gene beats saturation by +0.021 to +0.034. When test pairs use the independent control half, the gain is -0.011 to +0.004. So the +0.029 per-gene-offset gain, and therefore the 54%-of-ceiling best model, comes from shared control noise. The ceiling uses disjoint cm1/cm2 and does not count that noise as signal. The side remark that shared singles add more leakage is the key's possible false alarm, but it is not central: the gain disappears even though singles are still shared.

Not in the key, but I confirmed it. On cross-fitted data (features from half 1, I from the independent half 2), the slope of I on dA+dB is -0.19 for same-sign responses, -0.15 to -0.22 for opposite-sign responses and -0.14 to -0.17 when only A responds. Damping does not depend on sign agreement, which a ceiling/floor (saturation) account predicts it should. Saturation features add only +0.007, and the model that carries the result is linear. The title claim ('what it learns is saturation', 'ceiling/floor effect') is therefore not supported.

Confirmed. Per-pair cross-fitted slopes of I on dA+dB, computed on fully independent halves, correlate about 0.89-0.92 across halves (mean -0.10, SD 0.23). Per-pair r correlates 0.89-0.93. 25-31 pairs show synergy (positive I vs dA+dB) in both halves. (0.406/0.752)^2 ≈ 0.29 and 0.211/0.566 ≈ 0.37 of the reliable variance are explained. This contradicts SUMMARY claims 2-3 ('mostly shrinkage', 'not pair-specific', 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed').

Correct statistically. A ratio of correlations, 0.54, is not a variance share. The share of reliable variance explained is about 0.29 ((r/ceiling)^2), or 0.37 pooled, so 46% unexplained understates the headroom. The summary's direction ('real headroom remains') still holds, so this corrects a number, not a headline conclusion.

Does not claim the halves are dependent. Its main point is that models whose features share noise with I are not bounded by the ceiling, which follows from the key's coupling issue (F1) and inflates the share-of-ceiling headline. The per-pair aggregation point is the key's valid minor issue: I get 0.752 vs mean per-pair 0.710, 3 pairs below 0. The reviewer's 0.748/0.703, '2 below 0' and min -0.10 do not match the code's own split (min -0.037), but they are close. The point about a single split is minor; per the key the ceiling is stable at 0.740-0.752 across seeds. Valid, mostly a restatement of F1 plus minor points.

Matches the key's valid minor issue (bootstrap over pairs that share singles). Confirmed: 66 distinct singles; PTPN12 in 12 pairs, KLF1 in 11, and so on. Naive SE is 0.036 vs a delete-one-single jackknife SE of 0.087 (which overstates, as the reviewer acknowledges). The intervals are too narrow, but they still exclude 0, so no headline changes.

The key's possible false alarms include this: pair-level CV matches the claim about held-out pairs, the docstring says singles recur, and GroupKFold is a stricter variant, not a correction. The finding admits the summary statement is true. My check suggests that sharing singles adds no meaningful leakage (the offset gain is about 0 when only singles are shared). Unbalanced fold sizes are trivial.

The facts are correct: 16 of 131 doubles have fewer than 120 cells (54-114), and the data are K562 CRISPRa and the 1,000 most highly expressed genes. But this is a scope and generalisation caveat. The subsetting is documented in the README and, per the key, does not invalidate the logic.

The key says corr 0 / n 0 for the constant additive prediction is by design. The finding's narrower point, that the summary presents an undefined correlation as a baseline 'of exactly 0', is a fair wording nit. Its link to a noise-only null overlaps with F1.

True: the package contains only learn_interaction.py, the npz and the outputs, with no subset-extraction script and no pinned versions. It is a reproducibility nit that does not affect results; the main script reproduces results.json.

review.summary:
I reran code/learn_interaction.py inline, without writing any files. It reproduces outputs/results.json exactly: sum-only 0.3700, saturation 0.3767, saturation+gene 0.4056, ceiling 0.752 (it runs in about 5 s). The arithmetic in SUMMARY.md is correct (91%, +0.007, +0.029, 54%). The main conclusions are not.

(1) The target is I = dAB − dA − dB, and the features are dA and dB, so they share sampling noise from the single-perturbation means and the control mean. That shared noise mechanically creates a positive correlation between I and −(dA+dB), which is the "shrinkage" the summary reports. If the double were exactly additive and only sampling noise were present, the sum-only metric would already be about 0.18. When the features and the target are built from independent cell halves, it falls from 0.43 to 0.22. An analytic noise correction on the full data gives about 0.24, against the reported 0.370.

(2) The +0.029 "per-gene offset" gain comes from training pairs that share a single perturbation with the test pair. When the cross-validation leaves those pairs out of training, the gain disappears (+0.002, CI −0.010 to 0.013).

(3) The claims that the interaction is "mostly shrinkage", "not pair-specific" and "does not depend on which genes were perturbed" contradict the summary's own numbers. Sum-only explains 18.4% of the variance against a reliability of 0.566. Pairs that share a single perturbation have correlated interaction profiles (0.27 vs 0.10 when built from independent halves).

(4) The ceiling and headroom figures compare correlations, not variance. They also assume the predictor's noise is independent of the target's, which is not the case here.

Other findings: the mechanism ("ceiling/floor effect") is asserted without a test, and a direct floor check argues against it. The bootstrap over pairs ignores that pairs share single perturbations. The increments between models have no paired tests. Everything comes from one dataset and one setting. Reproducibility scaffolding is incomplete.

Verdict for each checklist pattern:
- P1 (null not anchored to chance): present and unaddressed.
- P2 (trivial baseline): mostly clean, since sum-only is a trivial baseline, but that baseline is itself inflated by noise.
- P3 (endpoint–object mismatch): present. The metric contains −(dA+dB) by construction, and the per-pair correlation is dominated by noise.
- P4 (unit of inference / leaky CV): present. The pair-level CV and bootstrap ignore shared single perturbations.
- P5 (selection / confound carry-through): present. Shared noise is carried into the target, and the gene set is restricted to the 1,000 most-expressed genes.
- P6 (positive control): not directly applicable, because there is no null finding. However, nothing checks what the pipeline gives on exactly additive data.
- P7 (single condition): present (one dataset, one seed, one alpha).
- P8 (stability): partly present. There are no paired tests for the increments. The ceiling is stable across seeds (0.747 ± 0.002).
- P9 (language overreach): present.
- P10 (reproducibility): present but minor.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 86-87 (I = dAB - (DA[x]+DA[y]) using the same DA and cmean as features) and 119-128; SUMMARY.md lines 12, 16-17, 21-22
findings.description: The target I = dAB − dA − dB and the features dA, dB share the same single-perturbation means and the same control mean. The sampling noise in those means therefore enters the target and the features with opposite signs. This mechanically produces a positive correlation between I and −(dA+dB), a regression-to-the-mean / errors-in-variables artefact. The 'additive baseline of exactly 0' is not the right chance anchor. For a one-feature linear model, the per-pair Pearson correlation also does not depend on the fitted coefficient (only its sign matters), so 'a trained model works on held-out pairs' amounts to mean per-pair corr(−(dA+dB), I). Much of the headline 0.370 'shrinkage' signal is shared measurement noise rather than biological sub-additivity.
findings.evidence: (a) Parametric null with an exactly additive double (true I = 0) and only sampling noise, using per-gene cell variances and the observed cell counts (20 repeats): mean per-pair corr = 0.177 ± 0.006, p95 0.186, against the reported 0.370. (b) Split-half check over 5 seeds. With features from single/control half 1 and target I from half 2, mean per-pair corr = 0.220. With features and target from the same half 2, at the same noise level, it is 0.433. (c) Analytic removal of the shared noise covariance at full data gives a noise-corrected per-pair corr of about 0.24, against the observed 0.370. Pooled variance explained is much less affected: the null gives an R² of about 0.022 against the reported 0.184.
findings.recommended_action: Build the features and the target from disjoint cells: cross-fit the single and control means (features from one half, I from the other), or use an errors-in-variables correction. Report the sum-only metric against the additive-plus-noise null (about 0.18 ± 0.006), not against 0. Re-state claims 1–2 using the noise-corrected value (about 0.22–0.24) and drop the 'trained model works' framing for the sum-only model.

findings.description: The claims that 'the interaction term is mostly shrinkage', 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity' and that it 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed' are contradicted by the analysis's own numbers and by a direct check. Sum-only explains 18.4% of the pooled variance of I, and the best model explains 21.1%. The reliability of I is 0.566, so generic shrinkage accounts for at most about a third of the reliable variance, and less once the shared noise in F1 is removed. There is also clear structure specific to the perturbations involved.
findings.evidence: results.json: var_explained 0.184 (sum-only) and 0.211 (best); _ceiling.full = 0.566. Correlation of a test pair's I with the mean I of other pairs that share one of its single perturbations: 0.560. With pairs sharing none: 0.181. Built from independent cell halves, which removes shared noise: 0.272 vs 0.098. 27 of 115 pairs have a negative per-pair corr(−(dA+dB), I), so the 'generic' shrinkage does not hold for every pair.
findings.recommended_action: Withdraw 'mostly shrinkage', 'not pair-specific' and 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed'. Report the share of reliable variance explained (roughly var_explained / reliability, after the noise correction from F1). Test perturbation-specific structure explicitly, for example with a random effect per single perturbation, and state that a substantial perturbation-specific component exists.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 108, 114, 121-125 (folds over pairs; goff = I[tr].mean(0)); SUMMARY.md lines 14, 17, 20-21, 28
findings.description: The 'saturation + per-gene offset' model (0.406, '54% of ceiling', '+0.029 from per-gene offsets') depends on training pairs that share a single perturbation with the test pair. Those pairs carry both the shared single's estimation noise (−e_A appears in the I of every pair containing A) and real interaction structure specific to that single perturbation. The 'per-gene offset' therefore does not capture genes that are 'simply always non-additive'. Its gain vanishes when the cross-validation groups by single perturbation.
findings.evidence: Leave-one-pair-out, excluding every training pair that shares a single perturbation with the test pair (at least 94 training pairs, comparable to the original 5-fold): sum-only 0.3699, saturation 0.3662, saturation+gene 0.3683. The +gene gain is +0.002 (paired bootstrap CI −0.010 to +0.013). Plain leave-one-pair-out without the exclusion reproduces the gain: 0.4000, +0.024 (CI 0.013 to 0.036). 66 distinct single perturbations underlie the 115 pairs, with up to 12 pairs per perturbation (PTPN12).
findings.recommended_action: Use cross-validation grouped by single perturbation (train and test pairs share no single perturbation), or report the worst case across grouping schemes. Re-state the best-model number (about 0.37) and drop the '+0.029 per-gene offset' and '54% of ceiling' headlines, or relabel the gain as perturbation-specific leakage.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 93-95, 137; SUMMARY.md lines 7, 9-14 (share of ceiling column), 17, 28-31
findings.description: There are two problems with the ceiling comparison. First, sqrt(reliability) is the maximum correlation only for a predictor whose noise is independent of the target's noise. The models here use features that share noise with I (F1), so 'share of ceiling' mixes signal recovered with noise fitted. Second, claim 4 reads a ratio of correlations (0.406/0.752 = 54%) as a share of reliable signal ('just under half … (46%) is unexplained'). In variance terms the explained share of reliable signal is about (0.539)² ≈ 29%, so about 71% is unexplained. With the corrections in F1 and F3, the explained share is lower still (about 0.24/0.752 ≈ 32% in correlation, about 10% in variance). A minor additional point: the ceiling averages per-pair split-half r and then applies Spearman–Brown and a square root, which is not the same as averaging per-pair ceilings. 11 pairs have a split-half r below 0.1.
findings.evidence: results.json: corr 0.4056 and ceiling 0.7522 give 0.539; squared, 0.29. The noise-corrected sum-only value is about 0.24 (F1), and the grouped-CV best model is about 0.37 (F3). Over 10 split seeds the ceiling is stable (0.747 ± 0.002), so the problem is interpretation, not instability.
findings.recommended_action: Report headroom in variance units of reliable signal. Compute model performance with features independent of the target's noise before comparing it to the ceiling. Consider ceilings per pair, or a ceiling weighted by reliability.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 1, 21-23 ('This is a ceiling/floor effect', 'what it learns is saturation'); code docstring lines 13-17
findings.description: The mechanism is asserted without any test. The summary attributes the sub-additivity to expression being unable to fall below zero or rise without limit, but no analysis checks it. A direct floor check argues against it. Sampling-noise attenuation (F1) is an untested alternative explanation for part of the effect, and other biological explanations are not considered.
findings.evidence: Only 8 of 115,000 (pair, gene) entries have dA+dB below the log-expression floor (−control mean). Yet shrinkage is strongest among down-regulated entries: the pooled slope of dAB on dA+dB is 0.62 for s < −0.2 (n = 17,601) and 0.86 for s > 0.2 (n = 4,035). The analysis keeps only the 1,000 most-expressed genes, which are the genes least likely to hit a floor.
findings.recommended_action: Replace 'is a ceiling/floor effect' and 'what it learns is saturation' with 'is consistent with sub-additive combination'. If the mechanism is to be claimed, test it: relate the shrinkage to distance from the floor or ceiling after correcting for noise, and include lower-expression genes.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 132-134 (bootstrap over pairs); SUMMARY.md lines 4, 16-17 ('tight interval', '115,000 training examples')
findings.description: The pairs are not independent units. 115 pairs are built from 66 single perturbations; the singles' dA/dB features and their noise recur across pairs, and the control mean is shared by all pairs. The bootstrap resamples pairs as if they were exchangeable, so the 'tight interval' is too narrow. Counting 115,000 (pair, gene) examples also overstates the effective sample size.
findings.evidence: Naive bootstrap over pairs: [0.303, 0.438]. A bootstrap that resamples the 66 single perturbations (each pair weighted by the product of its singles' resample counts) gives [0.190, 0.529]: about 2.5 times wider and much closer to the noise null of 0.18.
findings.recommended_action: Use a bootstrap that resamples perturbations (or a two-way cluster bootstrap) and state the inference unit as 'n = 115 pairs over 66 single perturbations'. Drop the 'tight interval' wording.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 13, 20 ('add +0.007'), line 19 ('91% of the best model'); code lines 128-137
findings.description: The increments between models are stated without paired uncertainty. The +0.007 from saturation features cannot be distinguished from zero and turns negative under grouped CV. Each model's CI is computed separately, so overlapping CIs say nothing about the differences.
findings.evidence: Paired bootstrap of per-pair differences (leave-one-pair-out): saturation − sum-only = +0.0057, CI [−0.0012, 0.0122]. Under CV that excludes shared single perturbations: −0.0037, CI [−0.013, 0.005].
findings.recommended_action: Report paired bootstrap CIs, resampled at the perturbation level, for every model-to-model increment, and state that the saturation features add nothing detectable.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 25-26 ('Any method that claims to predict interactions must report the sum-only baseline'); code lines 34, 108, 126
findings.description: A general methodological prescription is drawn from one dataset (Norman 2019, K562, CRISPRa), one gene set (the 1,000 most-expressed genes), one ridge alpha, one fold seed and one minimum-cell threshold. No held-out dataset or sensitivity sweep is reported.
findings.evidence: SEED is fixed and there is a single random fold assignment; alpha = 1.0, min-double = 120 and top-genes = 1000 are not varied. The ceiling is stable across split seeds (0.747 ± 0.002), and the sum-only metric does not depend on the fold seed, but the +gene model does.
findings.recommended_action: Limit the claim to this dataset, or add a held-out perturbation screen (for example another combinatorial Perturb-seq dataset). Run small sweeps over alpha, the gene set size and the minimum-cell thresholds, plus several fold seeds.

findings.description: Reproducibility gaps. The script that builds data/norman2019_subset.npz from the scPerturb h5ad (gene ranking over 111,445 cells, the per-group caps and the seed) is not included, and package versions are not pinned. The subset-construction claims cannot be checked from the materials provided.
findings.evidence: The folder contains only code/learn_interaction.py, the npz file and the outputs. There is no subsetting script and no requirements or environment file. The README's statement about gene selection over the full file cannot be verified from the npz.
findings.recommended_action: Add the subset-building script with its seed, a requirements file with pinned numpy and scikit-learn versions, and a checksum of the source h5ad.

grade_a.detection_reason: The key (B3100) marks this version as clean ("error": null), so there is no documented error to detect. Under the key's rule, a finding would be a false alarm if it claimed the split-half halves are not independent or claimed some other load-bearing error in the ceiling. No finding does this. F4 explicitly says the ceiling is stable and that its problem is interpretation. F1 (feature-target noise coupling), F6 (pair bootstrap with shared singles) and the Spearman-Brown aggregation point inside F4 match the key's other_real_issues. I re-ran checks on the package data. There are 115 pairs built from 66 distinct singles, with PTPN12 in 12 of them. Only 8 of 115,000 entries fall below the floor. The slopes with intercept are 0.62 for down-regulated entries and 0.85 for up-regulated ones. With leave-one-pair-out, the per-gene offset adds +0.031, CI [0.018, 0.045]. When training pairs that share a single with the test pair are excluded, the gain drops to +0.005, CI [-0.008, 0.019]. When features and offsets come from one half of the single and control cells and the target from the other half, the gain is about +0.01 without the exclusion and about 0 with it. Residual I, after removing the generic sum-only shrinkage, correlates more with pairs that share a single than with pairs that share none (about 0.10 vs 0.04-0.05, using independent cell halves). So there is structure specific to the perturbed genes.

findings.reason: This is the key's first other_real_issue. dA and dB enter the features with a + sign and the target I with a - sign, so ridge fits a negative slope that looks like shrinkage. The key's build check gives 0.425 when features and target use the same single cells and 0.227 when they use different halves. The review's 0.433 vs 0.220 matches. It is a valid concern, not the documented error (none exists) and not a false alarm. It says the headline 0.370 and the shrinkage reading are largely noise, so it is load-bearing.

SUMMARY claims 2-3 say the interaction is 'mostly shrinkage', is 'not pair-specific' and 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed'. These do not fit the analysis's own numbers. Sum-only explains 18.4% of the variance of I against a reliability of 0.566, and claim 4 itself says 46% is unexplained. My cross-half check found residual structure tied to the perturbed genes: after generic shrinkage is removed, pairs sharing a single correlate at about 0.10 vs about 0.04-0.05 for pairs sharing none. The same pattern shows in the offset gain disappearing when shared singles are excluded. The key does not list this overclaim, and the data support it. It attacks the headline claims 2-3.

I reproduced the main numbers. The +gene gain is +0.031 with leave-one-pair-out, and +0.005 (CI includes 0) once training pairs sharing a single with the test pair are excluded. With independent cell halves the plain gain falls to about +0.01, so roughly two-thirds of it is shared estimation noise from the singles reaching the test pair through goff. The remainder depends on perturbation-specific structure. That undercuts the 'genes simply always non-additive' reading and the +0.029 / 54% headline. One caveat: the key lists 'should be grouped by perturbed gene' as a possible false alarm, calling a grouped split a stricter variant. But this finding's main argument is the noise-coupling mechanism plus the interpretation of the gain, and the data confirm it, so I grade it as a real problem rather than a false alarm.

It does not claim the halves are dependent or that the ceiling value is wrong. It says the ceiling is stable and the problem is interpretation. Two of its points are valid. Claim 4 reads a correlation ratio (0.539) as a share of reliable signal, while in variance terms only about 29% is explained, so about 71% is unexplained, not 46%. And model scores inflated by noise coupling distort the 'share of ceiling'. Its Spearman-Brown-on-mean-r point is the key's third other_real_issue. It attacks headline claim 4.

The title and claim 2 state a ceiling/floor mechanism ('what it learns is saturation', 'This is a ceiling/floor effect') that is never tested. Noise coupling, which the key accepts as a real issue, is an untested alternative that also produces apparent shrinkage. The cited numbers check out: 8 entries below the floor, and slopes of 0.62 vs 0.85 with intercept. However, the claim that the floor check 'argues against' saturation is weak. Log-scale saturation does not require crossing the floor, and stronger shrinkage for down-regulated entries is compatible with a floor effect. Still, the core point that the mechanism is asserted without a test is valid.

This is the key's second other_real_issue, described there as minor but valid. The 115 pairs come from 66 distinct singles (I confirmed this), so a bootstrap over pairs treats non-independent units as independent and gives intervals that are too narrow. It does not overturn a headline point estimate.

It is true that model-to-model increments have no paired CIs. But the summary already presents the +0.007 from saturation features as negligible ('one feature does most of the work'), so the conclusion does not change. This is a reporting improvement.

This is a generalisability and sensitivity caveat: one dataset and fixed hyperparameters. The key says alpha = 1.0 is not load-bearing. The recommendation to report the sum-only baseline is advice about method, not a result that could be wrong. Trivial.

It is true that there is no subsetting script and versions are not pinned. But the README documents how the subset was built, and the key says re-running the package reproduces results.json byte for byte. This is a minor reproducibility gap.

grade_b.detection_reason: The key marks B3100 as the clean version (error: null), so there is no documented error to detect. No finding claims that the split-half halves are dependent or that the ceiling has a load-bearing error. F4 explicitly says the ceiling is stable and treats the problem as one of interpretation. It also raises the point that Spearman-Brown is applied to the mean split-half r, which the key lists as a valid minor issue. None of the findings triggers the key's false-alarm rule for the ceiling.

findings.reason: This is the feature-target noise coupling that the key lists under other_real_issues as valid. The review's split-half numbers (0.433 when features and target share cells, 0.220 when they come from independent halves) match the key's build check (0.425 vs 0.227). It correctly argues that part of the 0.370 score and of the 'shrinkage' reading comes from regression to the mean. It challenges the headline claim that the model works.

This is not in the key, but it holds up. Sum-only explains 18.4% of pooled variance against a reliability of 0.566, and 0.370/0.752 squared is about 24%, so 'mostly shrinkage' and 'not pair-specific' are unsupported. They also contradict the SUMMARY's own claim 4 that most reliable signal is unexplained. I checked with independent halves after removing a noise-free shrinkage slope (-0.17). The residual's split-half r stays at 0.380, almost the same as I's 0.389. Residuals also correlate more with pairs that share a single perturbation (0.237) than with pairs that share none (0.135). The review's own 'pairs sharing a single' evidence is partly confounded by generic shrinkage, but the conclusion stands.

I reproduced the numbers. Under plain leave-one-pair-out the per-gene offset adds +0.024. When training pairs that share a single with the test pair are excluded, it adds +0.002. The key lists 'group CV by perturbed gene' as a possible false alarm, but this finding names a different mechanism: the shared single's estimation noise. My direct check under the pair-level split confirms that mechanism. When training-pair I (and so the offset) comes from the same single/control cells as the test target, the offset adds +0.017 to +0.019 (2 seeds). When it comes from the other half of the cells, it changes the score by -0.014 to -0.015. So the '+0.029 per-gene offset' and '54% of ceiling' headline gains are an extension of the noise coupling the key accepts as valid, not a true per-gene effect. The proposed fix (grouped CV) is what the key calls a stricter variant, but the problem itself is real.

It does not claim the ceiling halves are dependent; it says the ceiling is stable (0.747 ± 0.002) and that the problem is interpretation. Claim 4 reads a correlation ratio (0.539) as the share of reliable signal ('46% unexplained'). In variance terms about 29% is explained and about 71% is unexplained, so that headline number is misstated. Its point that comparing to the ceiling mixes in fitted shared noise follows from the valid F1. Its point about applying Spearman-Brown to the mean r is the key's listed minor real issue.

The title and claim 2 assert a ceiling/floor (saturation) mechanism that the analysis never tests. The key confirms that part of the shrinkage reading is regression to the mean, so an untested alternative exists. I confirmed the review's numbers: 8 entries below the floor, and slopes of 0.62 vs 0.85. Its claim that stronger shrinkage for down-regulated entries argues against a floor is weak, since compression near zero would also predict that. The core criticism, that the mechanism is asserted without a test, is still correct.

The key lists the pair-level bootstrap ignoring shared singles as a valid, minor issue. I reproduced the result: the naive interval is [0.298, 0.439] and the perturbation-level weighted interval is [0.187, 0.528]. It undermines the 'tight interval' wording, but the interval still excludes 0, so it does not by itself overturn a headline claim.

It is true that model-to-model increments have no paired CIs. But the SUMMARY already treats +0.007 as negligible, and the finding's conclusion (saturation adds nothing detectable) agrees with the SUMMARY. Missing paired uncertainty is a reporting gap of little consequence.

This is a generalisation and sensitivity point about a single dataset, alpha, seed and threshold. The key calls the untuned alpha not load-bearing and says the subsetting is documented. Asking for a sum-only baseline is reasonable advice in any case, so this is a scope/style comment.

It is true that the subset-building script and pinned versions are missing. The README documents how the subset was built, and the key confirms the package reproduces results.json byte for byte. This is a trivial reproducibility point.

review.summary:
I reproduced results.json exactly (sum-only 0.370, saturation 0.377, saturation+gene 0.406, ceiling 0.752), but the headline numbers and the main interpretation do not hold up.

The main problem is shared noise. The features (dA, dB) and the target (I = dAB − dA − dB) are built from the same estimated single and control means, so the sampling error enters both with opposite signs. That alone produces regression to the mean that looks like "shrinkage". I simulated perfectly additive data (true I = 0) with sampling noise matched to the data, and the pipeline still scores sum-only corr ≈ 0.18 and saturation+gene ≈ 0.26, against the claimed baseline of 0. When the test target is built from cells independent of the features, at matched sample size sum-only drops from 0.43 to about 0.22, the saturation features add nothing, and the per-gene offset adds about 0.01. 22 of 115 pairs score above their own reliability ceiling.

Even on the reported numbers, the claims of "mostly shrinkage", "not pair-specific" and "does not depend on which genes were perturbed" fail:
- The best model explains (0.406/0.752)² = 29% of the reliable interaction variance, so about 71% is unexplained, not the stated 46%.
- The shrinkage slope differs widely between pairs and replicates across independent halves (r = 0.92); about a quarter of pairs have positive slopes.
- Shrinkage is at least as strong when the two singles move a gene in opposite directions, which a ceiling/floor (saturation) account would not predict.

The bootstrap CI treats pairs as independent, but the 115 pairs share only 66 singles and one control mean. A jackknife over singles gives a standard error about 2.4 times larger, and none of the model differences are tested.

Checklist verdicts:
- P1 present and unaddressed: no noise or chance null.
- P2 partly addressed (sum-only baseline included), but the baseline itself is inflated by the noise.
- P3 present: the ceiling/floor mechanism is inferred without a test.
- P4 present: pseudoreplication, and clustered dependence ignored in the CI.
- P5 present: shared-noise "double use" of dA and dB, plus leakage through the per-gene offset.
- P6 present: no negative or positive control.
- P7 present: one dataset, one seed.
- P8 partial: there is a CI, but it is wrong and there are no sweeps.
- P9 present: "This is a ceiling/floor effect", "does not depend on which genes", "most of the interaction is not pair-specific".
- P10 minor: no script to build the data subset, no pinned versions.

Excluding the 7 CRISPRa target genes that are among the measured genes, or using Spearman instead of Pearson, leaves the numbers essentially unchanged (0.372, 0.388), so those are not issues.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 86-87, 119-120 (features dA,dB and target I built from the same single/control means); SUMMARY.md lines 7-17 (headline table and claim 1)
findings.description: Shared-noise (regression to the mean) artifact. I = dAB − dA − dB and the feature s = dA + dB use the same estimated single means and control mean. Their sampling errors therefore enter feature and target with opposite signs, which makes the sum-only coefficient negative and the per-pair correlation positive even when the double is exactly additive. A large part of the reported 0.370 / 0.377 / 0.406 is this artifact, not biological interaction. The ceiling (lines 88-95) uses independent halves and so excludes exactly the noise the models exploit, which makes 'share of ceiling' (49-54%) invalid.
findings.evidence:
Reproduced the run exactly.

Additive-null simulation: true I = 0 and sampling noise equal to the observed per-gene var/n for doubles, singles and control. The unchanged pipeline gives sum-only corr 0.180 and saturation+gene 0.257, against the claimed additive baseline of 0.000.

Half-split test, 3 seeds, singles and control split in half, features from half 1:
- Test target sharing the noise: sum-only 0.422-0.429, saturation 0.434-0.442, +gene 0.451-0.459.
- Test target built from the independent half 2: sum-only 0.215-0.225, saturation 0.209-0.223, +gene 0.225-0.233.

Analytic noise covariance (var_A/n_A + var_B/n_B + 2 var_c/n_c) accounts for about 0.136 of the mean per-pair correlation of 0.370.

22 of 115 pairs have sum-only correlation above their own per-pair reliability ceiling sqrt(SB(r_half)), which is impossible for a predictor of the true I.
findings.recommended_action: Rebuild the evaluation so the noise in features and test target is independent. For example, compute dA and dB (and the control mean used in the features) from one half of the single and control cells, and the test-pair I from the other half and the double cells. Alternatively, cross-fit, or subtract a noise-only null. Run the pipeline on a simulated additive null (negative control) and report every correlation as observed vs null mean ± SD. Recompute the ceiling on the same independent-split basis. Then restate the headline numbers, which drop to about 0.22, with no gain from the saturation features.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 19-26 (claims 2 and 3: 'The interaction term is mostly shrinkage', 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed', 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity')
findings.description: The central interpretive claims contradict the analysis's own numbers and are refuted by direct checks. A generic model explaining most of the interaction would need r²/reliability > 0.5. Instead the best model explains 29% of the reliable variance (less once F1 is corrected), and the shrinkage relation itself is strongly pair-specific and reproducible.
findings.evidence:
From the reported numbers: (0.4056/0.7522)² = 0.291 and (0.3700/0.7522)² = 0.242 of the reliable variance explained, so about 71-76% of the reliable interaction is not captured.

Per-pair shrinkage slope of I on dA+dB, with features and target from independent halves:
- Mean −0.10, SD across pairs 0.22.
- 5th to 95th percentile −0.46 to +0.26; about a quarter of pairs have positive slopes, i.e. amplification rather than shrinkage.
- Agreement between two independent replicate estimates: r = 0.92.

Per-pair sum-only correlations range from −0.51 to 0.95 (10th percentile −0.15).
findings.recommended_action: Delete or reverse claims 2-3. State that generic sum or saturation features capture a minority (≤ about 25-30%) of the reliable interaction variance before noise correction, and less after it. Report the heterogeneity of per-pair shrinkage across pairs as a finding, and test pair dependence explicitly (e.g. a per-pair random slope, or replicate agreement of per-pair coefficients).

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 21-23 ('This is a ceiling/floor effect. It needs no regulatory network'); code docstring lines 13-17
findings.description: The mechanism (saturation at a ceiling or floor) is asserted but never tested, and the available evidence goes against it. Saturation predicts shrinkage mainly when both singles push a gene the same way. Here the explicit saturation features (product, min, max, sign agreement) add +0.007 with shared noise and nothing with independent noise. Shrinkage is as strong or stronger for genes where the two singles act in opposite directions. The measured genes are the 1,000 most highly expressed, far from any floor. Plausible alternatives are untested: regression to the mean (F1), a uniformly weaker per-target CRISPRa dose in double-guide cells, and pair-specific biology.
findings.evidence:
Pooled slope of I (independent-half target) on dA+dB:
- All genes: −0.158.
- Same-sign genes: −0.152.
- Opposite-sign genes: −0.202.
- Top-10% |s|, same sign: −0.161; opposite sign: −0.209.

With the shared-noise target the slopes are identical across sign classes (about −0.26).

Saturation − sum-only = +0.0067 in results.json, and −0.006 to −0.002 with an independent target.
findings.recommended_action: Replace 'is a ceiling/floor effect' and 'needs no regulatory network' with 'is consistent with a uniform damping of the summed single response'. Test saturation directly (shrinkage vs sign agreement and vs baseline expression level), and check target-gene knock-up levels in doubles vs singles to rule out a guide-dosage explanation.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 28-30 (claim 4: 'just under half of the reliable interaction signal (46%) is unexplained')
findings.description: A ratio of correlations (0.406/0.752 = 54%) is presented as the share of the reliable signal explained. The share of reliable variance explained is the squared ratio, 29%, so about 71% is unexplained, not 46%. Corrected for F1, the unexplained share is larger still.
findings.evidence: (0.4056/0.7522)² = 0.291. results.json: frac_of_ceiling = corr/ceiling, a correlation ratio, not a variance share.
findings.recommended_action: Report the share of explainable variance as (r/ceiling)², i.e. about 29% explained and 71% unexplained before the noise correction, and recompute after fixing F1. Drop the 'just under half' wording.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 121-125 (per-gene offset goff = I[tr].mean(0)); SUMMARY.md lines 3-5 and 20-21 ('Per-gene offsets add another +0.029'; 'the double of an evaluation pair is never seen in training')
findings.description: Holding out whole pairs does not make the folds independent. Every pair's I contains the same control-mean estimation error (+e_c per gene), and singles recur across training and test pairs. The per-gene offset, which averages I over the training pairs, carries those shared errors into the test predictions. The observed +0.029 gain is smaller than the gain this leakage produces under a purely additive null.
findings.evidence:
Additive-null simulation: saturation+gene minus sum-only = +0.077 (0.257 vs 0.180), compared with the observed +0.029.

With an independent-noise test target the per-gene gain is +0.008 to +0.011.

The 115 kept pairs use only 66 distinct singles (PTPN12 in 12 pairs, KLF1 in 11, UBASH3B and CEBPE in 10, ...).
findings.recommended_action: Estimate the per-gene offset from control and single cells disjoint from those used to build the test-pair I, or use a split control (separate control halves for training and test). Group the CV so test pairs share no single with training pairs (GroupKFold by single), and report the per-gene gain against the null.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 128-134 (bootstrap over per-pair correlations); SUMMARY.md lines 12-17 ('with a tight interval') and 20-21 (model differences)
findings.description: The 95% intervals resample pairs as if they were independent, but pairs share singles (66 singles across 115 pairs) and all share one control mean. The intervals are therefore too narrow by a factor of about 2.4. No interval or paired test is given for the model differences (+0.007, +0.029) that claims 2-3 interpret. The '115,000 training examples' framing also overstates the effective sample size: the inference unit is pairs or singles, not (pair, gene) rows.
findings.evidence: Sum-only per-pair correlations: naive SE over pairs = 0.036, delete-one-single jackknife SE = 0.087, giving roughly [0.20, 0.54] instead of [0.303, 0.438]. The intervals for the three models overlap almost completely, and no paired bootstrap is run.
findings.recommended_action: Use a cluster or two-way bootstrap (resampling singles, or pairs with shared-single blocks), report paired-difference CIs between models, and state n as 115 pairs from 66 singles.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 115-118 and 128-135; outputs/results.json 'additive' entry (n = 0); SUMMARY.md line 11 and line 16
findings.description: The additive baseline's correlation of '0.000 [+0.0000, +0.0000]' is not measured: a constant prediction has undefined correlation, no pair is scored (n = 0), and the CI comes from a hard-coded bs = [0.0]. Separately, for sum-only the per-pair correlation equals ±corr(dA+dB, I) whatever the fit, since the fit learns only a sign. 'A trained model works' therefore overstates what training contributes.
findings.evidence: results.json additive: n = 0, lo = hi = 0.0. Sum-only coefficient is about −0.22 in every fold, so the per-pair correlation equals corr(−(dA+dB), I).
findings.recommended_action: Report the additive row as 'not defined' for correlation (0% variance explained only). Use the noise-only null from F1 as the chance anchor for the correlation metric, and describe sum-only as a one-parameter damping fit rather than as evidence that 'something can be trained'.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 93-95 (ceiling = sqrt(SB(mean per-pair r_half))) vs line 135 (mean of per-pair correlations)
findings.description: The ceiling is aggregated differently from the score it is compared with. The score is a mean of per-pair correlations, but the ceiling applies Spearman-Brown and the square root to the mean split-half r. By Jensen's inequality this overstates the attainable mean per-pair correlation. 3 pairs have negative split-half r. The ceiling also comes from a single random split.
findings.evidence: sqrt(SB(mean r_half)) = 0.752 vs mean over pairs of sqrt(SB(r_half_i)) = 0.710; 3 of 115 pairs have r_half < 0.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the ceiling per pair and average it the same way as the scores, average over many random splits, and report its uncertainty.

findings.description: Generality and stability are not established, and there is little reproducibility scaffolding. The analysis uses one dataset (K562 CRISPRa, Norman 2019), one random split/fold seed, one ridge alpha, one double-size threshold and only the 1,000 most highly expressed genes. The generalised recommendation ('Any method ... must report the sum-only baseline') rests on this single setting. There is no script to build data/norman2019_subset.npz from the scPerturb file, no pinned package versions and no data checksum. The README's '105 single perturbations' differs from the 66 singles that actually enter the analysis.
findings.evidence: The code has SEED fixed, Ridge(alpha=1.0) and min_double = 120 hard-coded as defaults, with no sweeps. The subset-generation code is absent from the folder. 66 distinct singles are used in the kept pairs.
findings.recommended_action: Add the subset-building script with versions and a checksum. Sweep seeds, alpha, the min-double threshold and gene-set size (including lower-expressed genes, which is relevant to any floor-effect claim). Test on a second perturbation dataset before generalising, and report the number of singles actually used.

grade_a.detection_reason: The key for B3100 marks the package as clean ("error": null). The ceiling splits the double, both singles and the controls into disjoint halves (lines 72-97). No finding claims those halves are not independent or that the ceiling is computed wrongly. F1 says the opposite: the ceiling correctly uses independent halves, and the model scores are inflated by noise that the ceiling excludes. That is the valid feature-target coupling issue, not a ceiling error. So there is no documented error to detect, and none of the findings is a false alarm under the detection rule.

findings.reason: This is the key's first other_real_issue (feature-target noise coupling), which the key marks as valid. I re-ran the split with features from half 1. Sum-only, saturation and +gene scored 0.418-0.428, 0.431-0.440 and 0.454-0.460 when the target shared the same single and control cells. They scored 0.218-0.232, 0.215-0.228 and 0.228-0.245 when the target used the other half. The key's own check gave 0.425 vs 0.227. In an additive-null simulation the unchanged pipeline gave sum-only 0.180 and saturation+gene 0.263, against a claimed baseline of 0. 22 of 115 pairs exceed their own per-pair ceiling. The ceiling remark does not say the halves are dependent; it says scores inflated by shared noise are being compared with a noise-free ceiling, which is correct. The finding is load-bearing because it says the headline 0.370/0.406 and the 49-54% shares are inflated.

Confirmed. Even on the reported numbers, (0.406/0.752)^2 = 0.29 and (0.370/0.752)^2 = 0.24, so a generic model captures a minority of the reliable variance, not 'most'. Per-pair slopes of I on dA+dB, with features and target from independent halves, had mean -0.100, SD 0.225 and 5th-95th percentiles -0.45 to +0.23, and 31% were positive. Two fully disjoint replicates (different quarters of singles and control, different double halves) agreed at r = 0.90 (0.92 with the reviewer's crossed design). So the shrinkage is clearly pair-specific, which refutes 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed' and 'not pair-specific'. Per-pair sum-only correlations range from -0.51 to 0.95. The key does not address this interpretive claim, but it is a real problem.

Confirmed. The saturation mechanism is asserted (in the title and in claim 2's 'ceiling/floor effect, needs no regulatory network') but never tested. With an independent target, the pooled slope was -0.161 for same-sign genes and -0.191 for opposite-sign genes. Saturation predicts the reverse. With the shared-noise target the sign classes were identical (about -0.257). The saturation features add +0.007 with the shared target and nothing, or a slight loss, with an independent target (0.223 vs 0.225). Exact values differ slightly with the random split, but the pattern matches the review. This undercuts the headline interpretation.

The arithmetic is right. A correlation ratio of 0.54 to the ceiling means about 29% of the reliable variance is explained, so 'just under half of the reliable interaction signal (46%) is unexplained' misstates the share; about 71% is unexplained. The key accepts share of ceiling as a correlation ratio, and the problem here is only the reading of it as a share of the signal. Not load-bearing: claim 4's point that real headroom remains is strengthened, not overturned.

The key states that the offset uses training pairs only and does not leak test targets, and the finding does not dispute that. Its mechanism is different: every pair's I shares the same control-mean error, singles recur, and the offset averaged over training I carries that shared estimation noise into test predictions. I confirmed this. In my additive-null run saturation+gene minus sum-only = +0.083 (0.263 vs 0.180). With features from independent halves, the offset gained only +0.01 when it carried noise independent of the test target, but +0.10 (0.225 to 0.32) when it was built from the same control and single halves as the test target. This extends the valid coupling issue. One recommendation (GroupKFold by single) matches a key false-alarm item, but the core claim, that the +0.029 per-gene gain is mostly an artifact, holds. Not load-bearing for the main sum-only headline.

This is the key's other_real_issue about bootstrapping pairs that share singles, which the key calls valid but minor. Confirmed: naive SE 0.036 vs delete-one-single jackknife SE 0.087. A bootstrap that resamples singles gives CI [0.19, 0.53] instead of [0.303, 0.438]. 115 pairs use 66 singles (PTPN12 in 12 pairs, KLF1 in 11). The model differences have no paired test. Sum-only stays clearly above 0, so the headline is not overturned.

True but presentational. The key says the additive model's n = 0 and corr = 0 are by design, and the finding does not call it a bug; it asks for the row to be labelled 'not defined'. It is also true that a one-feature ridge's per-pair correlation equals ±corr(dA+dB, I); the fold coefficients were -0.196 to -0.233. Trivial for the conclusions beyond what F1 already covers.

This is the key's minor other_real_issue, which is valid. Confirmed: the mean of per-pair ceilings is 0.710 vs 0.752, and 3 pairs have a negative split-half r. The share moves only from 54% to 57%. The single-split point is also minor, because the key reports the ceiling is stable over seeds (0.740-0.752).

Mostly true but minor. There is one dataset, fixed hyperparameters and no script to build the subset. But the key lists untuned alpha as not load-bearing and reports seed stability.
