The split-A ranks of the reported winners (171, 24, 53) also match what the finding says.

It does not say the formula 2ap/(a+p) is wrong, which the key lists as a false alarm. It says a single-predictor baseline is the wrong chance level for a statistic that is the maximum over 5,035 features and is affected by protein clustering. I reproduced its within-protein circular-shift null, taking the max over features (5 replicates): REPEAT 0.600 vs observed 0.626, VARIANT 0.356 vs 0.358, MUTAGEN 0.314 vs 0.309, HELIX 0.225 vs 0.229, TRANSIT 0.256 vs 0.257, COILED 0.368, ZN_FING 0.316±0.076, DNA_BIND 0.265, SIGNAL 0.21, DISULFID 0.11. So the 'mean margin +0.342' and '19 of 21' statements are not meaningful. The cause largely overlaps with the documented selection inflation, but it is framed as a problem with how the null and gate are calibrated, not as selection on the reported split.

Every factual claim checks out. VARIANT has margin 0.3545 and its F1 beats 13 of the 20 other concepts. All 145 split-B true positives of feature 3889 are in SMAD6_HUMAN, which holds 483 of the 494 split-B VARIANT positives (98%). With seed 2, the reported procedure gives VARIANT F1 0.663 and it passes. The null reproduces 0.356. The SUMMARY presents the control as a success, which is misleading, because the control fails only the F1 cutoff and not the margin. The inflation itself mostly comes from the documented error (key: VARIANT is 0.000 under honest selection), but the misreported negative control is a genuine extra problem with the write-up.

Confirmed. Proteins with positives in split A/B: REPEAT 3/7, COILED 8/6, DNA_BIND 8/6, ZN_FING 9/6, VARIANT 12/7. The ZN_FING true positives come from 2 proteins (124 from ADN1A_DANRE). REPEAT, COILED and DNA_BIND each have true positives in 5 proteins, MUTAGEN in 1. My protein-bootstrap CIs on split B match: ZN_FING [0.00, 0.67] with 54% of draws below 0.5, DNA_BIND 46%, COILED 41%, REPEAT 20%, DISULFID 12%, SIGNAL 0%. The key agrees that rare concepts sit in few proteins and are noisy. The caveat states precision in residue counts, which understates the uncertainty.

Every pass set matches my reruns. Swapped: DISULFID, REPEAT, SIGNAL, TRANSIT, ZN_FING. Seed 0: DISULFID, DNA_BIND, PROPEP, SIGNAL, TRANSIT. Seed 1: DISULFID, DNA_BIND, SIGNAL, TRANSIT, ZN_FING. Seed 2: DISULFID, PROPEP, REPEAT, SIGNAL, VARIANT. Seed 3: DISULFID, DNA_BIND, PROPEP, SIGNAL, TRANSIT. With honest selection, 2 to 5 concepts pass; only SIGNAL and DISULFID pass every time, and TRANSIT passes 3 times. The headline comes from one split and is unstable.

Calling the features 'monosemantic' is an overclaim from an F1 match against one label. The figures check out: DNA_BIND feature 3159 has precision 0.44 and fires in 25 split-B proteins, with true positives in only 5. ZN_FING fires in 13 proteins with true positives in 2, REPEAT in 32 with 5, COILED in 16 with 5. It is also true that four of the six do not survive split-A selection. This is a genuine problem with the interpretation claim.

The 'F1 is a lower bound' caveat is wrong. Selection on split B pushes the reported F1 upward (REPEAT 0.626 vs 0.003 under honest selection). Incomplete annotation also does not guarantee that true F1 is higher, because recall on unannotated true positives is unknown. This corrects a misleading caveat. It does not on its own overturn a headline.

The facts are true: the split is by protein, not by homology cluster, and 47 entry-name prefixes appear in both splits (ribosomal proteins, ATPB, LEXA, H2B and others). But the finding does not show that this inflates any reported F1. Its MOTIF example does not show leakage across splits: SYR_LARHH and SYR_SALHS are both split-B proteins and SYR is not a prefix shared between splits. This is a fair design limitation with no demonstrated effect.

No trivial, raw-neuron or residue-identity baseline is a scope limitation. The key says not to count it as an error unless the finding claims it makes the reported F1 values wrong, and this finding does not. Its statement that sequences are absent from the package is accurate.

True: package versions are not pinned and the SAE weights, label extraction and activation code are absent. The finding only says the SAE claims cannot be checked, not that they are false; the key confirms they are true. It correctly notes that the scoring step reproduces exactly. This is a reproducibility and documentation point.

review.summary:
I reran the analysis in memory without writing any files and got exactly the same outputs. The headline result has a fatal flaw. The script tunes each feature's threshold on split A, but it then picks the "best feature" for each concept as the one with the highest F1 on split B, the test split (code/score_concepts.py line 140). So the reported F1 is the maximum over about 5,035 features on held-out data. It is not a held-out estimate, and SUMMARY.md's statement that it "comes from proteins that were not used to tune it" is false.

When the feature is chosen on split A and then scored on split B, only SIGNAL (0.833) and DISULFID (0.721) pass. The other four headline concepts collapse: REPEAT 0.003, COILED 0.002, DNA_BIND 0.000, ZN_FING 0.245. Mean best F1 drops from 0.360 to 0.162, and the median from 0.300 to 0.031.

The random-rate baseline is far too weak for a statistic that is a maximum over features. In a null where labels are shifted within each protein:
- REPEAT reaches 0.60 ± 0.02 (observed 0.626).
- VARIANT reaches 0.345 (observed 0.358).
- MUTAGEN reaches 0.323 (observed 0.310).

The negative control (VARIANT) clears the 0.1 margin by +0.354 and is counted among the "19 of 21" concepts above random. Its F1 comes entirely from one protein, and with split seed 2 it passes the full gate (F1 0.663).

The residue is treated as the unit of analysis, but each passing concept appears in only 6–7 split-B proteins, and the true positives come from 2–5 proteins. Protein-level bootstrap 95% CIs for the borderline concepts include values well below 0.5.

The set of passing concepts changes with the split seed. Across seeds 1, 2, 3, 7 and 123, only SIGNAL and DISULFID pass every time.

The interpretation also overreaches: it calls the features "monosemantic" and claims "F1 is a lower bound". There is no simple baseline (amino-acid identity, residue position, raw ESM neurons), and pinned package versions and the upstream inputs are missing.

Verdict on each checklist pattern:
- P1: present and unaddressed.
- P2: present and unaddressed.
- P3/P9: present and unaddressed.
- P4: present and unaddressed.
- P5: present and unaddressed (critical).
- P6: the negative control is present but misread; no positive control was run.
- P7: present but acknowledged (one model, one layer, one SAE).
- P8: present and unaddressed.
- P10: minor gaps.

findings.description: For each concept, the best feature is chosen by its F1 on split B, the test split, and that same split-B F1 is then reported. Only the threshold is tuned on split A. The reported F1 is therefore the maximum of about 5,035 test-set scores (winner's curse / double-dipping), not a held-out estimate. SUMMARY.md says the reported F1 'comes from proteins that were not used to tune it', which is false.
findings.evidence: I reran score_all in memory. Choosing the feature by split-A F1 and scoring it on split B gives: SIGNAL 0.833 and DISULFID 0.721 (the same features), but REPEAT 0.003, COILED 0.002, DNA_BIND 0.000 and ZN_FING 0.245. Only 2 of 21 concepts pass, not 6. Mean held-out best F1 is 0.162 (median 0.031), against the reported 0.360 (0.300). The outputs show the same thing in their f1_a column: the split-A F1 of the reported features is REPEAT 0.046, ZN_FING 0.114, DNA_BIND 0.146, COILED 0.290, VARIANT 0.000, MUTAGEN 0.000 and HELIX 0.000, far below their split-B F1. When the concept is scored with the feature that is best on A, the split-B rank of the reported feature's concept score is 980 for REPEAT, 1218 for COILED and 1094 for DNA_BIND.
findings.recommended_action: Choose both the feature and the threshold on split A only, then report split-B F1 for that one feature. Or use nested selection, or a third held-out split. Rewrite the main result, the table, the mean and median, and the setup sentence: on this split only SIGNAL and DISULFID meet the gate. Drop REPEAT, COILED, DNA_BIND and ZN_FING from the list of discovered features and from the causal-test candidates.

findings.description: The only null is the expected F1 of a single random predictor at the same firing rate (about min(a, p), so 0.001–0.2). It ignores two things: the reported value is a maximum over 5,035 features × 20 thresholds, and labels come in long contiguous spans inside a few proteins. The 'margin over random' and the '19 of 21 concepts at least 0.1 above random' claim therefore cannot tell real concepts from noise.
findings.evidence: I built a null by shifting labels circularly within each protein, with a random offset per protein (8 repeats). This keeps per-protein label counts and span structure but breaks residue alignment. I then reran the pipeline's own selection (maximum split-B F1). Null mean ± SD against observed: REPEAT 0.601 ± 0.020 vs 0.626 (null at or above 0.5 in 8/8 repeats); VARIANT 0.345 vs 0.358; MUTAGEN 0.323 vs 0.310 (null always higher); TRANSIT 0.281 vs 0.257; HELIX 0.227 vs 0.229; TOPO_DOM 0.248 vs 0.261; COILED 0.383; ZN_FING 0.309; DNA_BIND 0.266. In every null repeat at least one concept reaches F1 ≥ 0.5. The VARIANT negative control has a margin of +0.354 and is one of the '19 of 21'.
findings.recommended_action: Anchor each best-feature F1 to a null that also takes the maximum over features. For example, use within-protein label shifts or protein-level label permutations, and report null mean ± SD and p95. Make the gate depend on exceeding that null, not the single-predictor random F1. Remove or rewrite the '19/21 above random' and 'mean margin +0.342' claims.

findings.description: The summary uses the negative control as reassurance, but it actually shows the method is biased. VARIANT's best feature reaches F1 0.358 by detecting one protein. It clears the margin criterion by a wide margin and misses only the arbitrary 0.5 F1 cut. With another split seed it passes the full gate.
findings.evidence: In split B, protein 526 holds 483 of the 494 VARIANT positives, and all 145 true positives of feature 3889 come from that protein. The same feature has 0 true positives on split A (f1_a = 0.000). The margin is +0.3545, larger than for 15 of the 20 real concepts. With split seed 2, VARIANT passes the gate with F1 0.663.
findings.recommended_action: Report the negative control as a failure of specificity. Show its margin and its value under a protein-aware null. Add a positive control (for example a planted residue-level label) and a protein-identity control so the gate is shown to reject protein-specific features.

findings.description: F1 is computed over pooled residues, which ignores the protein-level clustering of labels (pseudoreplication). The passing concepts occur in very few proteins, and their true positives come from even fewer. No confidence interval is reported. The caveat describes precision by residue counts (66–1,275), which overstates the effective sample size.
findings.evidence: Number of split-B proteins with positives: COILED 6, DNA_BIND 6, ZN_FING 6, REPEAT 7, VARIANT 7, DISULFID 18, SIGNAL 20. Proteins contributing true positives for the reported feature: ZN_FING 2 (124 of 155 from protein 14), REPEAT 5, COILED 5, DNA_BIND 5. For DISULFID, 57 of 102 true positives come from protein 75. Protein-level bootstrap 95% CIs on split B, with feature and threshold held fixed: SIGNAL [0.686, 0.931], DISULFID [0.367, 0.849], REPEAT [0.149, 0.812], COILED [0.149, 0.694], DNA_BIND [0.171, 0.725], ZN_FING [0.000, 0.665]. P(F1 < 0.5) is 0.41, 0.46 and 0.53 for COILED, DNA_BIND and ZN_FING.
findings.recommended_action: Report the number of proteins (and annotated spans) per concept and split, alongside residue counts. Bootstrap by protein to get CIs. Apply the gate to the lower CI bound, or require a minimum number of positive proteins per split.

findings.description: The headline pass set comes from one random protein split (seed 42), with fixed hyperparameters and no sensitivity analysis. The set of passing concepts is unstable across split seeds.
findings.evidence: With the pipeline's own selection, the passing concepts by seed are: seed 1 = DISULFID, DNA_BIND, SIGNAL, TRANSIT, ZN_FING; seed 2 = DISULFID, PROPEP, REPEAT, SIGNAL, VARIANT; seed 3 = DISULFID, DNA_BIND, PROPEP, SIGNAL, TRANSIT; seed 7 = DISULFID, DNA_BIND, SIGNAL, TRANSIT; seed 123 = DISULFID, DNA_BIND, SIGNAL, TRANSIT, ZN_FING. COILED never passes in these five seeds, and REPEAT passes only at seed 2. Only SIGNAL and DISULFID pass at every seed, including when the feature is chosen on split A.
findings.recommended_action: Repeat over many protein splits, or use cross-fitting with the A/B roles swapped. Report how often each concept passes and the mean ± SD of held-out F1. Restrict headline claims to concepts that are stable across splits. Sweep MIN_NONZERO and the threshold grid as well.

findings.description: The interpretation goes beyond the evidence. It calls the features 'monosemantic' on the basis of one residue-level F1 against one annotation key. It never checks what else the features fire on, and several have low precision. It lists six features as validated causal-test candidates, although four of them do not replicate. It also says the features pick out 'a small, specific set of residues, not a broad region', but the REPEAT, COILED, DNA_BIND and ZN_FING hits are contiguous spans in 2–5 proteins.
findings.evidence: DNA_BIND precision is 0.44, so 56% of the feature's firings fall outside the concept. Off-concept firings were not characterised for any feature. In split A, the REPEAT feature 4672 predicts 124 residues across 24 proteins, of which 27 are true positives (recall 0.025). The ZN_FING feature 624 has 25 true positives out of 371 split-A positives. These are protein-specific detections, not concept detectors (see F1 and F4).
findings.recommended_action: Replace 'monosemantic features' with something like 'single features whose activations align with UniProt annotations for SIGNAL and DISULFID (held-out F1 0.83 and 0.72)'. Back any specificity claim by showing which concepts and proteins each feature fires on. Limit the causal-test candidates to features that replicate on held-out data.

findings.description: The caveat 'F1 is a lower bound' is wrong. If annotation is incomplete, adding the missing positives can raise precision but lower recall, so the observed F1 bounds the true F1 in neither direction. Choosing the feature on the test split (F1) also biases the reported F1 upward, the opposite of a lower bound.
findings.evidence: Recall = TP/(true positives). If unlabelled true positives exist and the feature misses them, recall falls. The gap between split-A and split-B F1 (F1) shows an upward selection bias.
findings.recommended_action: Rewrite the caveat: incomplete annotation makes F1 uncertain in both directions, and the selection procedure (unless fixed) inflates it.

findings.description: There is no trivial or input-level baseline. Nothing shows that an SAE feature does better than a residue-identity predictor (cysteine for DISULFID), a position or hydrophobicity predictor for N-terminal SIGNAL, or the best single raw ESM-2 layer-16 neuron (the comparison InterPLM makes). The package has no sequences or raw activations, so this cannot be checked.
findings.evidence: The only comparator in the code is expected_random_f1 (lines 48-51). proteins.tsv has accessions and lengths but no sequences, and the README says the SAE weights and activations are not included.
findings.recommended_action: Add best-single-neuron F1 and amino-acid-identity / position baselines, and report the difference in F1 over those baselines for SIGNAL and DISULFID.

findings.description: Reproducibility gaps. Package versions are not pinned (only 'numpy and scipy'). The SAE weights, the ESM activations, and the list of SAE training proteins are missing, so two upstream claims cannot be checked from the package: 'none of the 600 proteins were used to train the SAE' and '74.6% variance explained'.
findings.evidence: README says 'The SAE weights are not included' and lists no environment file or training-set accession list.
findings.recommended_action: Add pinned versions, the list of SAE training accessions (or a hash of it), and the SAE checkpoint or a DOI, so the held-out status and the code generation can be checked.

It frames this as a null-calibration problem, and its '× 20 thresholds' is slightly wrong because thresholds are tuned on split A. It still meets the rule's 'maximum of the very F1 being reported' wording.

findings.reason: This is exactly the key's error: the feature is chosen by split-B F1 at line 140 and that split-B F1 is reported. I reran it in memory. With the split-A-ranked rule, SIGNAL 0.833 and DISULFID 0.721 are unchanged, REPEAT is 0.003, COILED 0.002, DNA_BIND 0.000 and ZN_FING 0.245. Only 2 of 21 concepts pass, with mean 0.162 and median 0.031, all matching the key. The f1_a values quoted match the CSV. The SUMMARY 'not used to tune it' statement is literally about thresholds, but the review correctly notes it misleads about feature choice.

Its core point is the same mechanism: the reported value is the maximum over about 5,035 features of the reported split-B F1, so the single-predictor random baseline and the margin gate cannot separate signal from selection. It does not claim the 2ap/(a+p) formula is wrong. I reran 3 within-protein circular-shift nulls and got roughly the reported values (REPEAT about 0.58-0.59, VARIANT about 0.34-0.36, MUTAGEN 0.31, COILED about 0.34-0.40, DNA_BIND about 0.28-0.30), and REPEAT is at or above 0.5 in every repeat. VARIANT's +0.354 margin is indeed counted in the 19 of 21. Two caveats: '× 20 thresholds' is inaccurate because thresholds are tuned on A, and the circular-shift null partly keeps the REPEAT labels, since REPEAT covers much of its few proteins.

Confirmed. In split B, protein 526 holds 483 of the 494 VARIANT positives, and all 145 true positives of feature 3889 come from it. f1_a is 0.000. With split seed 2 the leaky rule passes VARIANT at F1 0.663. SUMMARY presents the negative control as reassurance even though it clears the margin by far. One detail is wrong: the +0.3545 margin is larger than 13 of the 20 real concepts' margins, not 15. Under rule (c) this finding alone would not count as detection, because it does not name selection on split B as the cause.

Confirmed. Split-B proteins with positives are COILED 6, DNA_BIND 6, ZN_FING 6, REPEAT 7, VARIANT 7, DISULFID 18 and SIGNAL 20. ZN_FING's true positives come from 2 proteins (124 of 155 from protein 14), and 57 of DISULFID's 102 true positives come from protein 75. My protein bootstrap gave about the reported CIs, for example ZN_FING [0, 0.67] and P(F1<0.5) of about 0.42, 0.50 and 0.53 for COILED, DNA_BIND and ZN_FING. The pass status of several headline concepts is not robust, and the caveat quotes only residue counts. This fits the key's fact that rare concepts sit in few proteins, but the uncertainty point is not the documented error itself.

Verified exactly. Under the leaky rule, seed 1 passes DISULFID, DNA_BIND, SIGNAL, TRANSIT, ZN_FING. Seed 2 passes DISULFID, PROPEP, REPEAT, SIGNAL, VARIANT. Seed 3 passes DISULFID, DNA_BIND, PROPEP, SIGNAL, TRANSIT. Seed 7 passes DISULFID, DNA_BIND, SIGNAL, TRANSIT. Seed 123 passes DISULFID, DNA_BIND, SIGNAL, TRANSIT, ZN_FING. COILED never passes, and only SIGNAL and DISULFID pass at every seed under either rule. The headline pass set depends on a single split. This is partly driven by the documented error but is also a separate robustness gap.

The 'monosemantic' and causal-candidate claims go beyond the evidence. DNA_BIND precision is 0.44. Off-concept firing was never characterised. In split A, the REPEAT feature 4672 predicts 124 residues across 24 proteins with 27 true positives, and the ZN_FING feature 624 has 25 true positives, both verified. Four of the six candidates do not replicate when the feature is chosen on split A. This is partly a consequence of the documented error, but the interpretive overclaim is a genuine separate problem.

Correct: with incomplete annotation, observed F1 can be biased in either direction, not only downward, so 'lower bound' is wrong, and the leaky selection biases F1 upward. It concerns a caveat sentence only and changes no reported number.

The missing raw-neuron and residue-identity/position baselines are a fair scope limitation. The key lists missing raw-neuron baselines as a scope limitation that is not an error. The finding does not claim the reported F1 values are wrong, so it is not a false alarm.

True: versions are unpinned, and the SAE weights and training-protein list are absent. This is a reproducibility nicety. It does not claim the SAE was trained on these proteins, which the key confirms it was not.

review.summary:
I reviewed the analysis against all ten checklist patterns. I re-ran the pipeline in memory, without writing any files, and it reproduces outputs/ exactly. The headline does not hold up. In code/score_concepts.py:140 the best feature for each concept is the argmax of its split-B (test) F1 over 5,035 features, and that same split-B F1 is then reported. Only the threshold is tuned on split A. So the SUMMARY's statement that the reported F1 comes from proteins not used to tune it is false.

If the feature is picked by split-A F1 and then scored on split B, only 2 of 21 concepts pass (SIGNAL and DISULFID), not 6. Mean best F1 drops from 0.360 to 0.162, median from 0.300 to 0.031, and concepts with margin >= 0.1 drop from 19 to 8. For REPEAT, COILED, DNA_BIND and ZN_FING, the feature that is best on split A gets F1 between 0.000 and 0.245 on split B.

The random-firing baseline 2ap/(a+p) is far too weak for a best-of-5,035 statistic on labels that cluster within proteins. A null that circularly shifts the split-B labels gives a best F1 of 0.21-0.44 for COILED, DNA_BIND, ZN_FING, REPEAT, MUTAGEN and VARIANT. The negative control VARIANT gets margin +0.354, counts toward "19 of 21", and passes the full gate (F1 0.663) under split seed 2.

The real unit of inference is the protein. The positives for the questioned concepts sit in 6-7 split-B proteins, and the true positives come from only 1-5 of them. With a protein-level bootstrap, the 95% CIs for COILED, DNA_BIND and ZN_FING all span 0.5, with lower bounds near 0.17, 0.14 and 0.00. Which concepts pass changes with the split seed and with swapping the A/B roles. Only SIGNAL and DISULFID pass in all 10 split configurations.

The REPEAT feature fires essentially only on WD40/beta-propeller repeat proteins and catches 27 of 1,061 split-A repeat residues, so calling it monosemantic for a range of concepts is an overreach.

Verdict for each pattern:
- P1 (null too weak): present, not addressed.
- P2 (no trivial baseline): present, not addressed. There is no residue-identity, position or raw-ESM-neuron comparator. A position-only predictor for SIGNAL gets F1 0.113, so SIGNAL beats it.
- P3 (endpoint–object mismatch): present, not addressed. A single-label F1 is used as evidence of monosemanticity, and labels are heterogeneous within a concept.
- P4 (wrong unit of inference): present, not addressed. Inference is at residue level when the unit is the protein.
- P5 (double-dipping): present, not addressed. Features are selected on the test split.
- P6 (positive/negative control): the negative control is present but misread. It actually shows the pipeline gives high F1 from protein identity.
- P7 (single condition): present but acknowledged (one layer, one SAE, one split).
- P8 (stability): present, not addressed. There are no CIs and no split-seed sweep.
- P9 (overreach): present, not addressed ("monosemantic", "F1 is a lower bound").
- P10 (reproducibility): minor. Versions are not pinned and the SAE weights are absent, but the outputs reproduce from the code.

findings.location: code/score_concepts.py:140 (best = np.nanargmax(s['f1'][:, ci]), where s['f1'] is split-B F1); SUMMARY.md:8-14,16-27; README.md:64
findings.description: The best feature for each concept is chosen by its split-B (held-out) F1 over 5,035 candidate features, and that same split-B F1 is reported. Only the threshold is tuned on split A, so the reported F1 is a maximum over thousands of test-set evaluations and is biased upward. SUMMARY line 9-10 says the reported F1 'comes from proteins that were not used to tune it', which is false. The README (step 7) does not say the selection uses split B. The '6 of 21 concepts pass' headline, the six-feature table, the mean/median best F1, the mean margin and the 19/21 count all inherit this bias.
findings.evidence: Re-run in memory, selecting each concept's feature by split-A F1 (the f1_a array) and scoring it on split B: only 2/21 pass (SIGNAL 0.833, DISULFID 0.721). Mean best F1 is 0.162 (reported 0.360), median 0.031 (reported 0.300), mean margin 0.143 (reported 0.342), and 8 concepts have margin >= 0.1 (reported 19). The split-A-selected features for REPEAT, COILED, DNA_BIND and ZN_FING get split-B F1 of 0.003, 0.002, 0.000 and 0.245. The reported winners have poor split-A F1: REPEAT 0.046 (ranked 171st on A), COILED 0.290, DNA_BIND 0.146, ZN_FING 0.114 (ranked 53rd). HELIX, MUTAGEN, VARIANT and STRAND winners have f1_a = 0.000. For those, argmax on line 103 over an all-zero grid returns index 0, so the 'A-tuned' threshold is arbitrary.
findings.recommended_action: Choose the feature and the threshold on split A only (or with nested cross-validation inside A), then score that one pre-registered feature on split B. Report this as the headline: 2/21 passing (SIGNAL, DISULFID) for seed 42. Remove the claim that the reported F1 comes from untouched proteins, and describe the selection rule accurately in the README.

findings.description: The only null is a random predictor firing at the same rate, F1 = 2ap/(a+p). It ignores two things: the reported value is the maximum over 5,035 features, and concept labels come in contiguous spans concentrated in a few proteins. So any feature that fires on one protein's span can beat this baseline by a wide margin. The claims 'mean margin over random is +0.342' and '19 of 21 concepts at least 0.1 above random' therefore do not show encoding beyond chance, and 3 of the 6 'passing' F1s (0.501-0.519) are not well separated from a proper null.
findings.evidence: Null computed in memory: split-B labels circularly shifted by a random offset (10 shifts), which keeps span structure but breaks alignment with features, then the same best-on-B selection. Null best F1, mean ± SD (max): VARIANT 0.436±0.111 (0.636), MUTAGEN 0.314±0.080 (0.474), DNA_BIND 0.254±0.063 (0.339), COILED 0.244±0.036 (0.295), REPEAT 0.229±0.037 (0.286), ZN_FING 0.214±0.032 (0.270), TRANSIT 0.207±0.061, PROPEP 0.196±0.058. The random_f1 values in the output are 0.0005-0.03. The observed MUTAGEN (0.310) and VARIANT (0.358) sit at or below the null mean, yet both count toward '19 of 21 above random'. One concept passed the full gate in 3 of the 10 null shifts.
findings.recommended_action: Replace or supplement the random-rate baseline with a max-over-features null that keeps protein and span structure (circular label shifts or protein-label permutation, rerunning the full selection). Report each best F1 as 'F1 (null mean ± SD; p95)'. Drop or restate the 19/21 and mean-margin claims against that null.

findings.description: The negative control does not validate the gate. VARIANT's best feature clears the margin criterion (+0.354) and fails only the F1 >= 0.5 cut. Its F1 of 0.358 comes entirely from one protein (SMAD6_HUMAN). With a different random protein split, VARIANT passes the full gate. This shows the pipeline produces high F1 for a label that reflects protein identity, not residue properties. That undermines the reading of the borderline passes (ZN_FING 0.501, DNA_BIND 0.517, COILED 0.519) as concept-specific features.
findings.evidence: VARIANT positives: 466/492 in split A are in CWC27_HUMAN, and 483/494 in split B are in SMAD6_HUMAN. Feature 3889 gets all 145 split-B true positives from SMAD6_HUMAN and 0 true positives in split A (f1_a 0.000). Rerunning the unchanged pipeline with split seed 2 gives VARIANT passing with F1 0.663 (margin well above 0.1).
findings.recommended_action: Report that the negative control can pass the gate depending on the split. Use protein-structure-preserving nulls (F2) and train-only selection (F1), and show that VARIANT then fails across many splits before using it as reassurance. Consider a negative control that is not concentrated in a single protein.

findings.description: The analysis treats residues as the unit of inference, but the evidence lies at the protein level. For the questioned concepts, split-B positives sit in 6-7 proteins and the winning features' true positives come from 1-5 proteins. The caveat cites only residue counts (66 to 1,275), which hides how small n is. There are no confidence intervals, and a protein-level bootstrap shows that 3 of the 6 'passing' concepts are about as likely to fall below 0.5 as above it.
findings.evidence: Split-B proteins with positives: COILED 6, DNA_BIND 6, ZN_FING 6, REPEAT 7, TRANSIT 4, PROPEP 6, VARIANT 7. True positives of the winning feature come from: ZN_FING 2 proteins (124/155 from ADN1A_DANRE), REPEAT 5 (mostly BUB31, CIAO1, SC132), COILED 5, DNA_BIND 5, DISULFID 11 (57/102 from one protein). Protein-resampled bootstrap with feature and threshold fixed (2,000 resamples): ZN_FING 95% CI [0.000, 0.669], P(F1<0.5) = 0.54; DNA_BIND [0.139, 0.717], 0.46; COILED [0.168, 0.691], 0.41; REPEAT [0.156, 0.822], 0.20; DISULFID [0.360, 0.855], 0.12; SIGNAL [0.696, 0.935], 0.00.
findings.recommended_action: Report for each concept the number of proteins with positives in each split and the number contributing true positives. Require a minimum number of proteins (not residues) per split. Add protein-level bootstrap CIs, ideally including the feature-selection step, and limit claims to concepts whose CI stays above the gate.

findings.description: The list of passing concepts depends on a single random protein split. With other seeds, or with the A/B roles swapped, the set changes: COILED passes only in the reported configuration, and TRANSIT and PROPEP pass in others. Only SIGNAL and DISULFID pass consistently. ZN_FING at 0.501 sits right on the threshold.
findings.evidence: Pipeline run unchanged for seeds 42, 0, 1, 2, 3 in both directions (10 configurations). Concepts passing with test-selected features: COILED 1/10, REPEAT 5/10, DNA_BIND 5/10, ZN_FING 6/10, TRANSIT 7/10, PROPEP 4/10, VARIANT 1/10, SIGNAL 10/10, DISULFID 10/10. With train-selected features: SIGNAL and DISULFID 10/10, TRANSIT 7/10, ZN_FING 2/10, DNA_BIND 1/10, REPEAT and COILED 0/10.
findings.recommended_action: Repeat over many protein splits (or use cross-validation by protein) and report how often each concept passes, with mean ± SD F1. Only headline concepts that are stable across splits (on current evidence, SIGNAL and DISULFID).

findings.description: The SUMMARY says 'the layer-16 SAE has monosemantic features for a range of residue concepts', including repeats, coiled coils, DNA-binding regions and zinc fingers. A single F1 against one label does not test monosemanticity: what else the feature fires on is never examined, and precision is often low. Several winners detect one protein family inside a mixed UniProt key, not the key itself. The phrase 'not a broad region' also misdescribes span labels that come from a few proteins.
findings.evidence: The REPEAT feature 4672 gets its split-B true positives from WD40 (beta-propeller) repeat proteins, mostly BUB31_ARATH, CIAO1_NEMVE and SC132_CANGA, plus some from ADO1_ARATH. It recovers only 27 of 1,061 split-A REPEAT residues, which belong to other repeat proteins (RLP26_ARATH, RTN4R_RAT and NANM_ECOHS). DNA_BIND feature 3159 has precision 0.44 and recovers 30/290 split-A positives. ZN_FING feature 624 recovers 25/371 split-A positives. COILED feature 904 fires on 152 residues of RN168_DANRE and 137 of IQD4_ARATH in split A with no true positives.
findings.recommended_action: Replace 'monosemantic' with something like 'single features that align with the annotation in the held-out proteins'. Name the actual family-level specificity (e.g., a WD40-repeat feature). Check precision and top activations across proteins before calling a feature monosemantic. State the claim level as decoding/association, and note that causal tests have not been done.

findings.description: The caveat that incomplete Swiss-Prot annotation makes 'F1 a lower bound' does not hold. Missing annotations lower measured precision, but recall measured on labelled positives can be biased either way. More importantly, picking the feature on the test split (F1) and single-split noise (F4, F5) inflate the reported F1, so the number is if anything an optimistic estimate.
findings.evidence: See F1: train-selected split-B F1 is much lower than the reported F1 for 4 of the 6 passing concepts (e.g., REPEAT 0.003 vs 0.626).
findings.recommended_action: Remove the 'lower bound' wording. State that annotation incompleteness affects precision and recall in different directions and that the current estimates carry a selection bias.

findings.description: The analysis has no simple comparator to show that the SAE features add anything beyond simple residue statistics. Examples: cysteine identity for DISULFID, N-terminal position for SIGNAL/TRANSIT, residue composition for COMPBIAS, or the best single raw ESM-2 layer-16 neuron or a linear probe. Without these, the claim that the SAE contains concept features cannot be separated from these residues being easy to tell apart in the input or the raw activations.
findings.evidence: Position-only baseline (predict position < L, L tuned on A): SIGNAL F1 0.113 on B, so SIGNAL clearly beats it. TRANSIT 0.025, PROPEP 0.012. The package has no sequences, so a cysteine-identity baseline for DISULFID cannot be computed. No raw-neuron or dense-probe comparison is reported.
findings.recommended_action: Add a trivial-baseline line for each concept (residue identity, position, best raw ESM neuron, linear probe on layer-16) and report the SAE result as a difference over that baseline.

findings.description: Reproducibility scaffolding is incomplete. Package versions (numpy, scipy, Python) are not pinned. The SAE weights and the code that produced sae_codes.npz and residue_labels.npz (Swiss-Prot release, FT parsing) are not included, so the inputs cannot be regenerated or checked. The scoring step itself does reproduce: an in-memory re-run matches outputs/ exactly.
findings.evidence: There is no requirements or environment file. The README says 'The SAE weights are not included'. The Swiss-Prot release used for the labels is not stated.
findings.recommended_action: Add pinned versions, the Swiss-Prot release, and the label-extraction and SAE-encoding scripts or weights (or a DOI).

It names line 140 and s['f1'] as split-B, says the reported F1 is the maximum over 5,035 test-set evaluations and is biased upward, and gives the key's fix: rank by f1_a and report split B. F2 also meets the rule. It says the reported value is the maximum over 5,035 features, and its null keeps the same best-on-B selection. From that it concludes that the margin claims (19/21, +0.342) are inflated.

With the original test-set selection, these counts match: COILED 1/10, REPEAT 5/10, DNA_BIND 5/10, ZN_FING 6/10, VARIANT 1/10, SIGNAL and DISULFID 10/10. Two counts are off by one: I get TRANSIT 8/10 (stated 7) and PROPEP 5/10 (stated 4). With split-A selection, SIGNAL and DISULFID pass 10/10, ZN_FING 2/10, DNA_BIND 1/10, REPEAT and COILED 0/10, all as stated; TRANSIT is 6/10 (stated 7). These small count errors do not change the conclusion that only SIGNAL and DISULFID pass reliably.

The evidence checks out. Feature 4672 gets its split-B true positives from WD40-type proteins (CIAO1, SC132, BUB31, plus ADO1). In split A it recovers 27/1,061 REPEAT residues, all from NANM_ECOHS. DNA_BIND feature 3159 has precision 0.44 and recovers 30/290 split-A positives. ZN_FING feature 624 recovers 25/371. COILED feature 904 fires on 152 residues of RN168_DANRE and 137 of IQD4_ARATH in split A with no true positives. The 'monosemantic' interpretation in the SUMMARY is therefore not supported.
Correct: with selection on the reporting split, the reported F1 is optimistic, not a lower bound. But this is a single caveat sentence and a consequence of F1, so it is minor.

The key lists missing raw-neuron or trivial baselines as a fair scope limitation, not an error, and the finding does not claim the F1 values are wrong. The position-only baseline numbers check out (SIGNAL 0.113, TRANSIT 0.025, PROPEP 0.012).

These are reproducibility points: no pinned versions, no SAE weights, no label-extraction code. They are true but minor. The finding correctly says the scoring step reproduces the outputs, which agrees with the key.

review.summary: I re-ran the analysis in memory without writing files, and it reproduces every number in results.json, head_ap.csv, run_log.txt and SUMMARY.md exactly. The selftest passes. The data checks out: per protein, the candidate pairs are exactly all C(n_cys, 2) cysteine pairs, every listed position is a cysteine, bond counts match proteins.tsv, no cysteine sits in two bonds, every protein has at least one bond, select and test do not overlap, and row 660 equals the mean of the 660 head rows. The headline result stands. L32H13 is chosen on select and scores test AP 0.718. Its own within-protein permutation null is about 0.066. Its per-protein AP is 0.81 against about 0.25 by chance, and its P@1 is 0.80 against 0.15 by chance. No problem found is critical. The main weaknesses are in how results are framed. (1) The pooled-AP metric with 'no-skill = base rate' mixes differences between proteins with the within-protein discrimination the study asks about. A score that is the same for every pair in a protein (the number of candidate pairs) gets AP 0.146, which beats both baselines in the summary table. (2) A 40-cysteine cutoff with no stated reason removes only two test proteins. These would have added roughly 2,800 pairs, about 28% of the enlarged test set. (3) The null 'expected best of 661' is slightly underestimated. (4) The per-protein metrics and the CI have smaller presentation and robustness gaps.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 12-13, 42, 211, 228-233; README.md line 12; SUMMARY.md lines 16, 20-25, 30, 35-36
findings.description: AP is computed over all test pairs pooled across proteins, and its 'no-skill' value is taken to be the base rate (0.049). The study asks whether heads tell bonded pairs apart from the other cysteine pairs of the same protein. Pooled AP also rewards ranking whole proteins: proteins with few cysteines have a high fraction of bonded pairs. A score with no within-protein information therefore beats the base rate by a lot. The 'x base rate' column, the 'no skill' row, the 2x-base-rate count (192) and the baseline comparisons all use the wrong reference.
findings.evidence: Checks run on the test split. (a) A score that is the same for every pair in a protein, -(number of candidate pairs), gets pooled AP 0.146. This beats both summary baselines: sequence separation 0.113 and the mean of all heads 0.141. (b) An oracle per-protein base rate as the score gets 0.170. (c) The analysis's own within-protein permutation null gives a different AP for each head, with null means up to 0.096. L32H13's null mean is 0.066, not 0.049. The -separation null is 0.070, so its true lift is about 1.6x, not 2.3x. (d) 192 candidates reach 2x the base rate, but only 139 heads reach 2x their own null mean. (e) If L32H13 scores are replaced by within-protein ranks, pooled AP falls from 0.718 to 0.613, while -separation rises to 0.138. The pooled number therefore depends partly on how scores are scaled across proteins.
findings.recommended_action: Make the primary metric a within-protein one, such as mean per-protein AP or P@1, each with its chance level. Alternatively, report pooled AP next to each scorer's own within-protein permutation null instead of the base rate. Add a protein-level-only baseline (for example, the number of cysteines) to show how much pooled AP can come from between-protein differences. Rephrase the 'x base rate' column and the 192-candidate claim accordingly.

findings.location: README.md lines 26-28 (inclusion rule 'at most 40 cysteines'); SUMMARY.md Data table and lines 20-25
findings.description: The 40-cysteine cap has no stated reason; the only technical limit is the 1,022-residue ESM-2 input, which excluded no protein. The cap removes exactly two proteins, both from the test split (41 and 64 cysteines); the 41-cysteine protein is just above the threshold. Excluding test data with an unexplained rule that only affects the held-out split looks like post-hoc curation. Those two proteins would have contributed C(64,2)+C(41,2) = 2,016+820 = 2,836 candidate pairs. That is about 28% of an enlarged test set (7,463 → 10,299 pairs). Including them would change the pooled test AP, the base rate and every 'x base rate' figure.
findings.evidence: Every kept protein has at most 39 cysteines and at most 987 residues, so the length rule never applies. The largest remaining test protein (G1XAA9, 39 cysteines, 741 pairs, 3 bonds) alone holds 10% of the test pairs. This shows how much a few cysteine-rich proteins weigh in the pooled metric.
findings.recommended_action: State whether the cap was set before the test split was looked at, and why it is needed. Re-run with the two proteins included (scores can be extracted per protein) and report the test AP and per-protein metrics with and without them. Otherwise drop the rule.

findings.description: The 'expected highest test AP of 661 candidates under the null' is estimated from a single label permutation and only 256 sampled candidates. It then takes the maximum of 661 draws with replacement from those 256 values. This is close to the maximum of 256 values, not of 661, and it ignores variation between permutations. The reported null maximum is therefore biased low.
findings.evidence: The reported value is 0.087. Evaluating all 661 candidates under six independent within-protein permutations gives maxima of 0.093, 0.096, 0.088, 0.092, 0.085 and 0.093 (mean 0.091). This does not affect the headline, since 0.745 is far above it.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the null AP for all 661 candidates under many permutations (it is cheap). Report the distribution of the maximum (mean and 95th percentile), not a resampled point estimate.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 20-25 (P@1 column, 'no skill' row shows '-') and line 35 ('puts a bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins')
findings.description: The per-protein metrics are given without their chance levels, and the no-skill row leaves P@1 blank. Five test proteins have only one candidate pair, which is bonded, so any scorer gets P@1 = 1 on them. Without a chance reference, readers cannot judge the 0.207 and 0.317 baseline values. Sequence separation's P@1 of 0.207 is only slightly above chance.
findings.evidence: Chance mean P@1 on test (mean of bonds/pairs per protein) is 0.152. Chance mean per-protein AP from within-protein permutations is about 0.255. Five of the 123 test proteins have exactly one candidate pair. Without them, L32H13's P@1 is about 0.797.
findings.recommended_action: Add chance P@1 (0.152) and chance per-protein AP (about 0.25) to the no-skill row. Either drop single-pair proteins from the per-protein metrics or flag them.

findings.description: The bootstrap uses only 200 resamples, which makes the percentile CI ends noisy. It assumes proteins are independent, yet some select and test proteins are near-homologs (the split was by protein, not by family). The CI also does not reflect which head was selected.
findings.evidence: There are 4 cross-split pairs with 5-mer overlap above 0.5, for example Q47450/A0A0H2VAQ6 at 0.89 and B1JDQ5/A5VYT2 at 0.89. The bootstrap mean (0.722) differs from the point estimate (0.718).
findings.recommended_action: Use 2,000 or more resamples. Consider clustering proteins by homology for the split and for cluster-level resampling. Note that the interval is conditional on the selected head.

findings.description: The README says the scores were made on an Apple-silicon GPU. The extraction script defaults to --device cpu, and its documented command does not pass a device. bfloat16 attention can differ between backends, so running the documented command may not reproduce the shipped scores exactly.
findings.evidence: extract_attention.py has `ap.add_argument("--device", default="cpu")`, and its usage line has no --device flag.
findings.recommended_action: Document the exact command used (for example --device mps) and the library versions, or ship a checksum or tolerance for the rebuilt scores.

findings.description: The log line says 'heads with test AP >= 2x base rate: 192 of 661 candidates'. The 192 includes the mean_all_heads candidate, so only 191 are heads; the per-layer counts add up to 191.
findings.evidence: The per-layer n_heads_test_ap_at_least_2x_base_rate values in results.json sum to 191. mean_all_heads (test AP 0.141, above 0.098) is the 192nd.
findings.recommended_action: Count heads only (exclude row 660) in the 'heads' statement, or label the 192 as candidates throughout.

L32H13's test AP of 0.718 is far above chance under any reference used here (base rate 0.049; its own within-protein permutation null, which I measured at about 0.066). review.summary:
I re-ran the analysis inline without writing any files. Every number in results.json, run_log.txt, head_ap.csv and SUMMARY.md reproduces exactly: AP matches sklearn, L32H13 test AP is 0.7179 (bootstrap CI 0.664-0.782), P@1 is 0.805, the null max is 0.087, and 192 of 661 candidates reach 2x the base rate. The data are internally consistent:
- Each protein's candidate pairs are exactly all C(n_cys, 2) cysteine pairs from proteins.tsv.
- Bond counts match the TSV.
- No cysteine is in more than one bond.
- Row 660 equals the mean of the 660 head rows.
- Select and test accessions do not overlap.
- The metric helpers pass the selftest.

The headline result holds up under extra checks:
- Under a within-protein label-permutation null, L32H13's AP is 0.065 (observed 0.718).
- Restricted to pairs where both cysteines are bonded (the true pairing problem, base rate 0.128), L32H13 still reaches AP 0.847, and per-protein P@1 is 0.95.

No critical problem was found. The remaining problems are:
- Major: an undisclosed exclusion rule (at most 40 cysteines) that removed only test proteins.
- Minor: an understated chance level for pooled AP, an approximate null maximum, a split by accession rather than by homology, a weak 2x-base-rate threshold, a select-vs-test comparison that ignores composition, uncontextualised P@1, and possibly incomplete labels.

findings.location: README.md:26-28 (filter rule); SUMMARY.md:3-5 (Purpose: 'Every cysteine pair in 236 Swiss-Prot proteins')
findings.description: A rule of at most 40 cysteines removed exactly two proteins, and both are in the test split (64 and 41 cysteines). No select protein was affected. Unlike the 1,022-residue length cap, this rule is not justified by any ESM-2 limit. The cap sits just below one excluded protein (41), which suggests it was set after looking at the test data. SUMMARY.md does not mention the exclusion. It describes the data as every cysteine pair in proteins with at least one annotated bond.
findings.evidence: README line 27: 'at most 40 cysteines. Two test proteins were left out by the last rule (64 and 41 cysteines). No other protein was left out by the length or cysteine-count rules.' In proteins.tsv the maximum is 24 cysteines in select and 39 in test. The two dropped proteins would add C(64,2)+C(41,2) = 2,016+820 = 2,836 candidate pairs, about 38% more than the 7,463 test pairs. Pooled AP is weighted toward proteins with many pairs: the 9 test proteins with more than 20 cysteines already hold 41% of test pairs. Within the current data, pooled AP of L32H13 moves from 0.718 (all) to 0.724 (<=20 cys) to 0.789 (<=10 cys), so the exclusion probably does not overturn the result. Its effect cannot be checked from the shipped data.
findings.recommended_action: Give a rationale for the 40-cysteine cap that does not depend on the test data, or drop it. Score the two excluded test proteins (both are under 1,022 residues) and report test AP, the CI and P@1 with them included. Disclose the exclusion in SUMMARY.md.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:16, 20-25, 35 ('x base rate', 'AP 14.6 times the base rate'); README.md:12; code/disulfide_attention.py:211, 232
findings.description: The pooled base rate is presented as the no-skill AP. For pooled AP, the right chance level is the within-protein permutation null, which is the null the analysis itself uses. That null is higher than the base rate, because a pooled ranking can gain from differences in bond rate and score scale between proteins. The 'x base rate' ratios therefore overstate skill, most of all for the sequence-separation baseline.
findings.evidence: Over 200 within-protein label permutations, mean null AP is 0.065 for L32H13 (97.5th percentile 0.073), 0.070 for 'shorter first' separation and 0.0525 for the mean of all heads. The base rate is 0.049. Measured against this null, sequence separation is about 1.6x chance (reported 2.3x) and L32H13 about 11x (reported 14.6x).
findings.recommended_action: Report the within-protein null mean AP for each scorer as the chance level, or express lift relative to it. Alternatively, report the per-protein metrics next to their random baselines (see F7).

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py:220-224, 108-113; SUMMARY.md:27-28 ('expected highest of 661 candidates under the within-protein null is 0.087')
findings.description: The 'expected highest of 661 candidates' null is approximated, not computed. It uses a single label permutation and only 256 of the 661 candidates, then resamples those 256 values with replacement 661 times. That mostly returns the maximum of the 256 values, so the null maximum over 661 candidates is somewhat underestimated, and with a single permutation its variability is not shown.
findings.evidence: Scoring all 661 candidates under one fresh within-protein permutation gave a null maximum of 0.093, compared with the reported 0.087. The gap is negligible next to the observed 0.745, so the conclusion is unaffected.
findings.recommended_action: Compute null APs for all 661 candidates over many permutations (for example 100). Report the mean and an upper quantile of the per-permutation maximum.

findings.location: README.md:19-20 (split by protein); SUMMARY.md:36-37 ('it held from select to test proteins (0.742 -> 0.718)'); data/proteins.tsv
findings.description: Select and test were split by accession, not by sequence homology. Several test proteins are close homologs of select proteins, and the test split contains near-duplicates. This weakens the claim that the head 'held' on independent proteins, and the protein-level bootstrap CI is too narrow because the resampled proteins are not independent. In addition, all these Swiss-Prot sequences were very likely in ESM-2's UniRef pre-training data, so 'test' proteins are not unseen by the model.
findings.evidence: Approximate identity (difflib matched residues / shorter length): A0A0H2VAQ6 (select) vs Q47450 (test) 0.98; A5VYT2 vs B1JDQ5 0.97; Q1R984 vs B4TQB8 0.90; P00596 vs P60045 0.90; P83345 vs P60311 0.83; C0JB14 vs C0JAT5 0.70. About 24 cross-split pairs are above 0.45. Within test, B7MQZ4 vs B7M6V6 is 0.99. Only one of 661 heads is chosen on select and the margin over the null is very large, so the headline is not threatened.
findings.recommended_action: Cluster sequences by identity (for example MMseqs2 at 30-40%) and either split by cluster or show that results hold after removing cross-split homologs. Bootstrap over clusters instead of proteins. State that the evaluation proteins are probably in ESM-2's training data.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:30 ('192 of the 661 candidates reach at least 2x the base rate'); code/disulfide_attention.py:42, 228
findings.description: The 2x-base-rate threshold (AP >= 0.098) says little about which heads carry the bonding signal. It is below the trivial sequence-separation baseline (0.113) and close to the null maximum (0.087-0.093). A 'detector' at this threshold may be no better than sequence separation, so the count of 192 heads (and 'in 33 of 33 layers' in the run log) should not be read as evidence that the signal is broad.
findings.evidence: 2 x 0.049 = 0.098, which is less than the separation baseline's test AP of 0.113 and the mean head's 0.141. Only about 10 heads have test AP above 0.37 (head_ap.csv).
findings.recommended_action: Use a threshold tied to the separation baseline or to an upper quantile of the null maximum, or drop the count. Base the 'group of heads' statement on the top heads only, as conclusion 2 already does.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:36-37 ('it held from select to test proteins (0.742 -> 0.718)')
findings.description: Pooled AP is compared between splits as if the two were comparable. The splits differ in base rate (0.071 vs 0.049) and in composition: proteins with many cysteines dominate the test pool. A small drop in AP is therefore not a like-for-like replication measure. Relative to its base rate, the head did better on test (10.5x vs 14.6x).
findings.evidence: Proteins with more than 20 cysteines hold 11% of select pairs but 41% of test pairs. Test AP for L32H13 is 0.789 when restricted to proteins with at most 10 cysteines, against 0.718 overall.
findings.recommended_action: Compare splits with metrics that are not driven by composition (mean per-protein AP or P@1 against their random baselines), or match the splits on cysteine count.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:20-25, 34-35 ('puts a bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins'); code/disulfide_attention.py:134-153
findings.description: Per-protein P@1 and mean per-protein AP are reported without a chance level. Some proteins are trivially solved: 5 test proteins have a single candidate pair, which is always bonded, so P@1 = 1 for any scorer.
findings.evidence: The random P@1 per protein (mean of n_bonds/n_pairs) is 0.152 on test. 10 test proteins have 3 or fewer cysteines, and on these every scorer has mean per-protein AP of at least 0.90 (separation 0.90, L32H13 1.00). The headline is unaffected: on pairs where both cysteines are bonded, L32H13's per-protein P@1 is 0.95.
findings.recommended_action: Report the random-ranking baseline for P@1 and per-protein AP. Optionally exclude proteins with only one candidate pair from the per-protein summaries.

findings.location: README.md:22-24 (labels: 'A pair without a record is labelled not bonded'); data/proteins.tsv
findings.description: Some proteins have many cysteines but very few annotated bonds, which suggests incomplete Swiss-Prot annotation. Unannotated bonds are counted as negatives, which adds label noise. This most likely lowers the measured AP rather than raising it, but it affects per-protein metrics for these proteins. These proteins are concentrated in the test split.
findings.evidence: G1XAA9 (test): 39 cysteines, 3 annotated bonds. Q6NSJ5 (test): 21 cysteines, 1 bond. Q8BKG4 (test): 27 cysteines, 5 bonds. Q8NH81 (test): 16 cysteines, 1 bond. The mean number of cysteines not covered by an annotated bond is 3.7 in test and 2.8 in select (maximum 33 in test vs 13 in select).
findings.recommended_action: Run a sensitivity analysis restricted to proteins whose annotated bonds cover all or nearly all cysteines, or whose bonds are experimentally supported (for example, a PDB structure exists).

grade_a.detection_reason: The key marks B4174 as clean (error: null), so there is no documented error to detect. I re-ran the checks with the package's own code and data. Verified: over 200 within-protein permutations, mean null AP is 0.065 for L32H13 (97.5th percentile about 0.076), 0.070 for 'shorter first' separation and 0.052 for the mean head, against a base rate of 0.049. That gives about 11x for L32H13 and about 1.6x for separation. This is a fair framing nuance about the 'x base rate' ratios. The base rate is still the correct expected AP for an uninformative scorer, and no conclusion changes.

The description of the code is accurate: one permutation, 256 sampled candidates, then best-of-661 resampling with replacement. Scoring all 661 candidates under 5 fresh permutations gives a null maximum of about 0.091-0.098 (mean 0.095), and the key notes the source run gave 0.093.
