review.summary:
I reviewed B4174 (ESM-2 650M attention heads ranking disulfide-bonded cysteine pairs) against all ten checklist patterns. The data checks out: every candidate set equals all C(n_cys,2) cysteine pairs, bonded counts match proteins.tsv, no cysteine sits in two bonds, lengths are consistent, and score row 660 equals the mean of the 660 head rows. The metric selftest passes. Re-running the analysis in memory reproduces every number in the summary: L32H13 select 0.742 / test 0.718, CI 0.664-0.782, null max 0.087, 192 candidates at 2x base rate, the top-5 heads, and P@1 values of 0.805, 0.317 and 0.207.

The headline holds up. L32H13's test AP is far above every null and trivial baseline I could build, and its per-protein metrics confirm real within-protein discrimination. Excluding the select-homologous test proteins or the single-pair proteins barely changes it (0.715 and P@1 0.797).

The main problem (P1/P2) is how the results are anchored. The pooled AP rewards ranking whole proteins against each other, so the base rate (0.049) is not the no-skill level for the stated within-protein question. A scorer that knows only each protein's cysteine count, and nothing about which pair is bonded, gets test AP 0.146. That beats both reported baselines (sequence separation 0.113, mean of heads 0.141), so the "x base rate" column and the baseline comparisons are mis-anchored. The headline still stands.

The other issues are minor:
- P@1 and per-protein AP are reported without their chance levels (0.152 and 0.25).
- The expected-max null is slightly too low.
- The bootstrap uses only 200 resamples.
- A few test proteins have close homologs in the select set, and ESM-2 likely saw these sequences in pre-training.
- Labels are incomplete: a pair with no UniProt record is counted as not bonded.
- The cysteine cap that removed two test proteins is not mentioned in the summary.
- There is a single bf16 extraction run, and no pinned environment.

Verdicts by pattern:
- P1: present, unaddressed for the base-rate anchor; partly addressed by the within-protein null max.
- P2: present (a protein-level trivial baseline beats the reported baselines).
- P3: contact-vs-bond is present but acknowledged in Conclusion 3.
- P4: mostly clean (protein-level bootstrap); minor homology/independence issue.
- P5: minor (inclusion filter; label incompleteness).
- P6: not applicable (not a null finding).
- P7: single model and run, but claims are scoped to it; pre-training overlap not mentioned.
- P8: minor (200 resamples, no processing-choice sweep).
- P9: clean; the language is appropriately hedged.
- P10: minor (no version pins, extraction device/environment not recorded).

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 16 and 20-25 (base rate row, 'no skill' row and 'x base rate' column), lines 34-37 (Conclusion 1: '14.6 times the base rate', 'far above sequence separation (0.113) and the mean head (0.141)'); README.md lines 12-13; code/disulfide_attention.py lines 211 and 231-232 (test_ap_over_base_rate = chosen_ap / prev)
findings.description: The stated question is whether a head separates bonded pairs from the other cysteine pairs of the same protein. But the metric is AP pooled across proteins, so a scorer can earn a lot of AP just by ranking whole proteins (proteins with few cysteines have a high bonded fraction). The global base rate (0.049) is therefore not the no-skill level for this question. The reported baselines are weaker than a trivial scorer that has no within-protein information at all, and the 'x base rate' multipliers (2.3x, 2.9x, 14.6x) are anchored to the wrong reference.
findings.evidence: Recomputed with the package's own average_precision. A score of -log(number of candidate pairs in the protein) is constant within each protein and uses only the cysteine count, which is known from sequence. It gets pooled test AP 0.146 with ties grouped (0.161 with random tie-breaking); select AP is 0.162. An oracle protein-level bond fraction gets 0.180 on test. All of these exceed sequence separation (0.113) and the mean of all heads (0.141), and they reach 3.0-3.7x the stated 'no-skill' 0.049. A trivial protein-level score combined with shorter separation within each protein reaches 0.183. The correct within-protein null means are 0.065 for L32H13, 0.052 for the mean head and 0.070 for separation (10-50 within-protein label permutations). L32H13 at 0.718 remains far above all of these, so the headline survives, but the anchor and the baseline comparisons as stated do not hold.
findings.recommended_action: Anchor every pooled AP to the within-protein permutation null (mean ± SD) rather than the global base rate, or switch the primary metric to per-protein AP / P@1 with per-protein chance. Add the protein-level trivial scorer (cysteine count, optionally combined with separation) as an explicit baseline and report ΔAP over it. Restate the 'x base rate' column and Conclusion 1 accordingly.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md line 25 (P@1 per protein column) and lines 34-35 ('puts a bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins'); code/disulfide_attention.py lines 134-153 (per_protein_metrics)
findings.description: The per-protein P@1 values (0.805, 0.317, 0.207) and the per-protein AP are reported with no chance level next to them. The 80% figure also counts 5 test proteins that have only one candidate pair, where P@1 = 1 by construction.
findings.evidence: Mean per-protein chance P@1 on test = mean(n_bonds/n_pairs) = 0.152. Mean per-protein AP of a random scorer is about 0.25 (200 random scorings per protein). 5 test proteins have exactly one pair, all bonded. Excluding them, L32H13 P@1 = 0.797 and per-protein AP = 0.804, so the claim survives, but the chance anchor is missing.
findings.recommended_action: Report per-protein chance P@1 (0.152) and chance per-protein AP (~0.25) next to the observed values. Either exclude single-pair proteins from the per-protein metrics or flag them.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 108-113 and 220-224; SUMMARY.md line 27 ('expected highest of 661 candidates under the within-protein null is 0.087')
findings.description: The expected best-of-661 null is estimated from a single label permutation. It uses only 256 sampled candidates, which are then resampled with replacement up to 661, so the estimate can never exceed the largest of those 256 null APs. It is therefore biased low and has no variance across permutations.
findings.evidence: Across 10 independent within-protein permutations of all 661 candidates, the largest null AP reached 0.0985, versus the reported expectation of 0.087. Per-head null means range from 0.037 to 0.094. This does not threaten the conclusion: 190 candidates exceed 0.0985, and the test max is 0.745.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the null over all 661 candidates and several permutations (e.g. 100), taking the maximum within each permutation. Report the mean, SD and p95 of the null maximum.

findings.description: The 95% bootstrap intervals use only 200 protein-level resamples, which makes the 2.5/97.5 percentiles imprecise. There is also no paired bootstrap for the difference between the chosen head and the baselines.
findings.evidence: With 2000 resamples (three seeds), the L32H13 test-AP CI is 0.647-0.788, 0.648-0.787 and 0.651-0.788. The reported interval is 0.664-0.782, so the lower bound is about 0.015 too high. The gap to the baselines is large enough that the comparison still holds.
findings.recommended_action: Use at least 1000-2000 protein-level resamples, and add a paired protein-level bootstrap CI for (head AP - baseline AP).

findings.location: README.md lines 19-20 (split by protein); SUMMARY.md lines 4-6 and 34-37 (generalisation from select to test)
findings.description: The select/test split is by protein, not by sequence family. Several test proteins have close homologs in the select set, and one pair of test proteins are near-duplicates, so the test proteins are not fully independent of the selection set or of each other. ESM-2 UR50D was also pre-trained on UniRef, which very likely contains these Swiss-Prot sequences. Generalisation to sequences the model has not seen is untested and not mentioned.
findings.evidence: 3-mer Jaccard similarity between test and select proteins: Q47450~A0A0H2VAQ6 0.90, B1JDQ5~A5VYT2 0.87, B4TQB8~Q1R984 0.67, P60045~P00596 0.55, P60311~P83345 0.47. Within test: B7MQZ4~B7M6V6 0.93. Excluding the 5 homologous test proteins, L32H13 test AP is 0.715 (vs 0.718), so the impact is negligible here.
findings.recommended_action: Split, or at least run a sensitivity check, by sequence-identity clusters (e.g. MMseqs2 at 30-40%). Collapse near-duplicates in the bootstrap. State in the summary that the proteins are probably in ESM-2's pre-training data.

findings.location: README.md lines 22-24 ('A pair without a record is labelled not bonded'); SUMMARY.md lines 4-6
findings.description: Labels come only from UniProt DISULFID records, with no filter on evidence level ('By similarity'/'Potential' entries are included), and every unrecorded pair is treated as a true negative. Many proteins have several cysteines that are not in any annotated intrachain bond, so some 'non-bonded' labels may be missed bonds. The summary does not mention the annotation's evidence level or how complete it is.
findings.evidence: In proteins.tsv, 103 of 236 proteins have 3 or more cysteines outside any annotated intrachain bond; one has 33. Free cysteines, interchain bonds and missing annotations cannot be told apart from the data provided.
findings.recommended_action: Record the evidence code of each DISULFID record and run a sensitivity analysis restricted to experimentally supported or structure-backed bonds. Note in the summary that negatives are 'not annotated' rather than 'verified free'.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 4-5 ('Every cysteine pair in 236 Swiss-Prot proteins with at least one annotated intrachain bond'); README.md lines 26-28
findings.description: The summary leaves out the inclusion cap (at most 40 cysteines, at most 1022 residues). That cap removed the two test proteins with the most cysteines (64 and 41), which are the hardest ranking cases. Performance falls as cysteine count rises, so the reported numbers are likely slightly optimistic for the full population.
findings.evidence: L32H13 per-protein P@1 by test-protein cysteine count: 0.86 (2-4 Cys, n=22), 0.85 (5-8, n=46), 0.78 (9-12, n=27), 0.71 (13-40, n=28). The README discloses the exclusion; SUMMARY.md does not.
findings.recommended_action: State the cysteine and length caps, and the two excluded test proteins, in the summary. Optionally report results stratified by cysteine count.

findings.description: The attention scores come from a single extraction run with one configuration: bfloat16, symmetrisation + APC, one model size, Apple-silicon GPU. There is no check against fp32 or other processing choices (e.g. no APC), so the selected head and its AP rest on one unswept processing choice. Reproducibility support is thin. No numpy/torch/transformers versions are pinned. The device used is not recorded in the output (the README says Apple GPU; the code defaults to CPU). The from_pretrained(dtype=...) argument needs a recent transformers release. The npz has no accession index, so pair-to-column alignment cannot be checked independently.
findings.evidence: Row 660 equals the mean of rows 0-659 (max abs diff 9e-9), so the file is internally consistent. But no fp32 or alternative-processing scores are provided, and no environment file exists in the folder.
findings.recommended_action: Add an environment file with pinned versions, record the device and precision in the npz, and store the accession/position arrays alongside the scores. Re-extract at least the top heads in fp32 (and without APC) to confirm the head ranking.

grade_a.detection_reason: The key marks B4174 as clean (error: null), so there is no documented error to detect and error_detected is null. No finding claims that a headline result is wrong. F1 says outright that the headline survives. I re-ran its computations and they reproduce: test AP 0.146 for the -log(n_pairs) scorer with ties grouped, about 0.160 with random tie-breaking, and within-protein null means of 0.064 for L32H13, 0.052 for the mean head and 0.070 for separation. The other findings are minor caveats, or they repeat false alarms that the key lists in advance (homology or pretraining leakage).

findings.reason: Confirmed with the package's own code. A scorer that is constant within each protein (-log of the protein's number of candidate pairs) gets pooled test AP 0.146 with ties grouped and ~0.160 with random tie-breaking. That is above the separation baseline (0.113) and level with the mean head (0.141). The within-protein permutation null means are 0.064 for L32H13, 0.052 for the mean head and 0.070 for separation. So pooled AP rewards ranking whole proteins, and the global base rate of 0.049 is not the right 'no-skill' floor for the within-protein question. The 2.3x and 2.9x baseline multiples partly reflect that between-protein ranking. This is a genuine point about the choice of reference. It is not the same as the key's false alarm about attention scores being on different scales. The finding itself says L32H13 (0.718) stays far above every reference, so no headline claim is overturned.

Reproduced: chance P@1 is 0.152, chance per-protein AP is ~0.25, and 5 single-pair test proteins are all bonded. Excluding them gives P@1 0.797 and per-protein AP 0.804. This is a true but trivial reporting gap (no chance level shown); the 80% claim holds.

Technically true: resampling from 256 sampled null APs cannot exceed their maximum, and the null comes from a single permutation. Across 10 full permutations of all 661 candidates I found null maxima of 0.087-0.0985 (mean 0.094), close to the source's 0.093. That has no bearing on a test maximum of 0.745. The key treats the null code as standard.

Reproduced: with 2000 resamples the CI is about 0.647-0.788 versus the reported 0.664-0.782. This is a small precision nit with no effect on any conclusion, and the key treats the bootstrap as standard.

The similarity numbers are accurate (for example, a 5-mer Jaccard above 0.5 for 3 test proteins, as the key states). But the key lists homology leakage between splits and ESM-2 pretraining contamination as false alarms: only one parameter (which head) is selected, the selection cost is 0.027, and no labels entered pretraining. The finding itself shows a negligible effect (0.715 vs 0.718).

Reproduced: 103 of 236 proteins have 3 or more cysteines outside any annotated bond, with a maximum of 33. The finding frames this as an unstated limitation of the labels and does not claim the result is invalid. The key notes that missing bonds would lower AP for every scorer. This is a minor disclosure point.

Reproduced the stratified P@1 (0.86, 0.85, 0.78, 0.71 by cysteine count). The caps and the two excluded proteins are stated in the README, and the key says the cap does not bias the result. Leaving them out of SUMMARY.md is a trivial disclosure gap.

Partly true reproducibility nits: no pinned package versions, and the code's default device is CPU while the README says Apple GPU. The key confirms the scores match the source cache and that a CPU re-run gives correlation 0.9996, so the bfloat16 and single-configuration worry does not affect the result. No headline claim is challenged.

grade_b.detection_reason: The key's status is 'clean' with error = null, so there is no documented error to detect. None of the findings is load-bearing: each one, including the 'major' F1, says the headline (L32H13 test AP 0.718, far above the baselines) survives. I re-ran checks with the package's own code and data. They confirm the numbers behind F1-F7: the trivial -log(n_pairs) scorer gets test AP 0.146 (0.160 with random tie-breaks); within-protein null means are 0.065 / 0.052 / 0.069; chance P@1 is 0.152 with 5 single-pair proteins; a 2000-resample bootstrap CI is about 0.648-0.787; the true best-of-661 null max is about 0.098 versus the reported 0.087; 103 of 236 proteins have 3 or more unbonded Cys; P@1 by Cys stratum is 0.86/0.85/0.78/0.71; the 3-mer Jaccard pairs are as stated. None of these overturns a reported conclusion.

findings.reason: Confirmed by running the package's average_precision. A protein-level-only scorer, -log(number of pairs), gets test AP 0.146 (0.160 with random ties). That beats both the separation baseline (0.113) and the mean head (0.141). Within-protein permutation null means are 0.065 for L32H13, 0.052 for the mean head and 0.069 for separation, so pooled AP partly rewards ranking between proteins, and the global base rate overstates within-protein skill (about 11x rather than 14.6x). This is a genuine weakness of the metric and baseline design that the package does not discuss. The key's per-protein facts (P@1 0.805/0.317/0.207) show the conclusion stands, and F1 itself says the headline survives. The finding goes too far in saying the baseline comparisons 'do not hold': L32H13 is still far above all of them.

Verified: chance P@1 is 0.152 and 5 test proteins have a single pair, all bonded. Without them, P@1 is 0.797 and per-protein AP is 0.804. Adding a chance level is a reporting improvement. The claim is unaffected.

Technically true. Resampling 256 null APs with replacement up to 661 cannot go above the largest sampled value, and one permutation gives no variance. Five full permutations over all 661 candidates give a mean null maximum of about 0.098, versus the reported 0.087. This is irrelevant next to the test max of 0.745. The key treats the null as standard, and this cosmetic number does not affect any conclusion.
Verified: 2000 resamples give CI of about 0.647-0.651 to 0.785-0.788, against the reported 0.664-0.782. A slightly wider interval is a precision nitpick with no effect on the comparison.

The similarity numbers reproduce (3-mer Jaccard). But the key lists homology leakage between splits and ESM-2 pretraining contamination as false alarms. Only one parameter (the head) is chosen, the selection cost is 0.027, and no disulfide labels entered pretraining. The finding itself reports a negligible effect (0.715 vs 0.718).

The count is true: 103 of 236 proteins have 3 or more cysteines outside annotated bonds. The key says unannotated true bonds are a limitation that would lower AP for every scorer, not raise it. The finding only asks for disclosure and an evidence-level sensitivity check.

True that SUMMARY.md leaves out the caps, which README states. P@1 by cysteine count is confirmed (0.86/0.85/0.78/0.71). The key considers the caps a stated design choice that applies to every scorer. Only 2 test proteins were dropped, so the effect on the headline is trivial. This is a disclosure point.

The reproducibility nitpicks are true: the code's default device is CPU while README says Apple GPU, versions are not pinned, and the dtype= kwarg needs a recent transformers release. The worry that bf16 or the processing choice is unverified is a listed false-alarm theme: the key says a CPU re-run reproduces the scores with correlation 0.9996. The finding does not claim the ranking is wrong.

review.summary:
I reviewed B4174 (ESM-2 650M attention heads used to rank disulfide-bonded cysteine pairs) against all ten checklist patterns. I traced each summary claim to results.json, run_log.txt and head_ap.csv, then to code/disulfide_attention.py. Every number in SUMMARY.md matches the outputs. I recomputed the following in memory (no files written) and they match: per-head select and test AP (max diff 5e-7 against head_ap.csv; sklearn gives identical AP), the bootstrap CI (a naive protein-resampling bootstrap gives 0.653-0.782), and P@1 (0.805, with no ties at the top). The selftest passes. The data checks also pass: every labelled end is a cysteine, every cysteine pair is enumerated, no cysteine is in two bonds, and row 660 is exactly the mean of the 660 head rows. Head selection is honest: it is made on select only, select and test head APs correlate with Spearman 0.95, and L32H13 is chosen in 79/100 bootstrap resamples of the select proteins (L29H18 in the other 21). The headline holds up against the checks I ran: test AP 0.718 against a within-protein null mean of 0.065 (SD 0.005, p95 0.074); 0.715 after dropping the test proteins that look homologous to select proteins; 0.722 without the largest test protein; and P@1 0.805 against a chance level of 0.15. No finding is critical.

Verdicts by pattern:
- P1, present and unaddressed: the 'no-skill = base rate' anchor is wrong for AP pooled across proteins, and the P@1 and null-maximum figures are anchored incompletely.
- P2, present but acknowledged: the baselines are weak and there is no contact-map baseline.
- P3, present but acknowledged: the endpoint is essentially cysteine-cysteine contact. Label provenance is not tracked.
- P4, essentially clean: the bootstrap resamples proteins and redundancy within each split is negligible. The only gap is that the select/test split does not control for homology.
- P5, minor: a test-only cap of 40 cysteines.
- P6: not applicable, because no null finding is claimed.
- P7, minor: one model, and the proteins were probably in ESM-2's pretraining data.
- P8, minor: only 200 bootstrap resamples, no sensitivity analysis on preprocessing, and the headline value depends on pooling.
- P9, mostly clean: conclusion 3 explicitly disclaims mechanistic claims.
- P10, minor: no pinned environment, and the device and dtype used for extraction are ambiguous.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 16, 22-25 and 34-35; README.md line 12; code/disulfide_attention.py lines 12-13 and 211/232 (test_ap_over_base_rate = chosen_ap / prev)
findings.description: The analysis treats the pooled base rate (0.049) as the no-skill AP and reports every scorer as 'x base rate' (14.6, 2.9, 2.3). The AP is pooled over all pairs of 123 proteins whose base rates range from about 0.004 to 1. A score with no within-protein information can still rank whole proteins against each other (short proteins with few cysteines have high bond rates), so the true no-skill level for the stated question (which pair within a protein is bonded) is well above 0.049. The summary's 'no skill' row and multipliers therefore overstate lift over chance, especially for the baselines. The headline value also depends on cross-protein calibration of raw APC values.
findings.evidence: Recomputed in memory. A score that is constant within each protein (1/number of pairs) reaches pooled test AP 0.146 (3.0x base rate). That is above the mean-of-heads baseline (0.141) and the separation baseline (0.113), with zero within-protein skill. An oracle protein-level base rate reaches 0.164, and -length reaches 0.101. Means of the within-protein label-permutation null (200 permutations): separation 0.070 (SD 0.004), mean head 0.052, L32H13 0.065 (SD 0.005, p95 0.074). Lift over the proper null is therefore about 11x for L32H13 (not 14.6x), 1.6x for separation (not 2.3x) and 2.7x for the mean head (not 2.9x). Converting L32H13 scores to within-protein rank fractions gives pooled AP 0.59 instead of 0.718. Mean per-protein AP is 0.81 against a chance per-protein AP of 0.25.
findings.recommended_action: Replace the 'no skill = base rate' row with the within-protein-permutation null for each scorer (mean ± SD and p95), and restate the multipliers against it. Report the protein-only score (1/n pairs) as the floor that pooled AP can reach without within-protein information. Make the per-protein metrics (mean per-protein AP, P@1, P@n bonds, each with its chance value) the primary endpoint, or report pooled AP on within-protein-normalised scores next to the raw pooled AP.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 34-35 ("puts a bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins") and line 20 (P@1 column)
findings.description: Per-protein P@1 (0.805, 0.317, 0.207) is reported with no chance value. Chance P@1 is not trivially small: 5 test proteins have only one candidate pair (P@1 = 1 automatically), and 22 have 2-4 cysteines.
findings.evidence: Mean over test proteins of n_bonds/n_pairs is 0.152, and random scores give P@1 0.151, P@n 0.149 and per-protein AP 0.250. The sequence-separation baseline's P@1 (0.207) is therefore only about 0.06 above chance. L32H13's 0.805 is far above chance, so the headline survives.
findings.recommended_action: Add the chance values (P@1 ≈ 0.15, per-protein AP ≈ 0.25) to the table and the conclusion text. Optionally report P@1 restricted to proteins with at least 3 cysteines.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py lines 108-113 and 220-224; SUMMARY.md line 28 ("expected highest ... under the within-protein null is 0.087")
findings.description: The expected maximum under the null comes from one label permutation and null APs for only 256 of the 661 candidates. It is then resampled with replacement to n=661, which caps the maximum at the largest of those 256 values and ignores variation between permutations. The null maximum is therefore biased low.
findings.evidence: Scoring all 661 candidates under 5 independent within-protein permutations gives null maxima of 0.091, 0.097, 0.093, 0.093 and 0.099, against the reported 0.087. In one of the five, a head reached the 2x-base-rate threshold (0.098) under the null. This does not affect the headline (0.745 against about 0.095).
findings.recommended_action: Compute null APs for all 661 candidates over at least 100 permutations, take the maximum within each permutation, and report its mean and 95th percentile. Use that p95, not '2x base rate', as the detection threshold for the '192 of 661 heads' count.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 3, 6-7, 34-37 (baselines and framing) vs lines 42-44 (acknowledged limitation)
findings.description: The question is framed as whether ESM-2 can tell bonded cysteine pairs apart, but the comparators (sequence separation and the unselected mean of all 660 heads) are weak. Bonded cysteines are by definition in spatial contact, and ESM-2 attention is known to track contacts generally. Without a contact-prediction baseline (e.g., ESM-2's own contact head, or the same heads scored on non-cysteine contacts), the result cannot be attributed to disulfide-specific information rather than contact recovery. The summary acknowledges this in conclusion 3, but conclusion 1 still presents the beat over the two weak baselines as the main comparison.
findings.evidence: Conclusion 3: 'We did not test whether these heads prefer bonded pairs over other close pairs.' Bonded pairs are much closer in sequence (median separation 23 vs 101 for non-bonded). Within-protein null lift for separation is only about 1.6x.
findings.recommended_action: Add a contact baseline. For example, score cysteine pairs with ESM-2's contact-regression output, or with structure-derived Cβ distance where structures exist. Report ΔAP of L32H13 over it. Until then, state in conclusion 1 that the endpoint is consistent with generic contact recovery among cysteine pairs.

findings.description: The 40-cysteine cap has no stated rationale (unlike the 1,022-residue ESM-2 limit). It removed only test proteins: exactly two, with 64 and 41 cysteines (about 2,016 + 820 = 2,836 candidate pairs, about 38% of the current test pair count). The largest select protein has 24 cysteines, so the rule never affects select. Excluding the most cysteine-rich test proteins could change the pooled test AP and CI.
findings.evidence: Max cysteines per protein: select 24, test 39 (after the cap). Performance in the 21-40 cysteine bin (pooled AP 0.76, P@1 0.89) suggests the headline would probably survive. The direction and size of the effect cannot be checked, because the excluded proteins are not in the package.
findings.recommended_action: Justify the cap or remove it. Rerun with the two proteins included (both are under 1,022 residues if they passed the length rule) and report the headline with and without them.

findings.location: README.md lines 19-20 (split 'by protein'); SUMMARY.md lines 36-37 ('it held from select to test proteins')
findings.description: The select/test split is by accession, not by homology cluster. Both splits are reviewed Swiss-Prot entries, which are almost certainly in ESM-2's UniRef pretraining data. So 'held from select to test' shows that head selection transfers, not generalisation to sequences the model has not seen. Results are for a single model (ESM-2 650M) and a single bfloat16 extraction.
findings.evidence: 5-mer containment: 4-5 test proteins share 48-89% of 5-mers with a select protein (Q47450/A0A0H2VAQ6 0.89, B1JDQ5/A5VYT2 0.89, B4TQB8/Q1R984 0.71, P60045/P00596 0.62, P60311/P83345 0.48). Dropping them changes test AP from 0.718 to 0.715, so the impact is negligible. Redundancy within splits is negligible.
findings.recommended_action: State that the test proteins are held out from head selection only, not from pretraining. Optionally use a homology-clustered split, and check one other model size or family (e.g., ESM-2 150M/3B or a different pLM) before making general claims.

findings.location: README.md lines 22-24 (labels from UniProt FT DISULFID; unrecorded pairs labelled not bonded)
findings.description: The provenance of the ground truth is not tracked. UniProt DISULFID records mix experimentally determined bonds with 'By similarity' and other inferred annotations, some propagated from homologues by sequence. Pairs with no record are treated as true negatives, although annotation may be incomplete. Cysteines involved in interchain bonds stay in the candidate set as negatives. The sample is restricted to proteins with at least one annotated intrachain bond, so the claim is conditional on that.
findings.evidence: No evidence-code field in proteins.tsv or the pairs files. The README excludes single-position (interchain) records but keeps those cysteines as candidates.
findings.recommended_action: Record ECO evidence codes, report the headline on the experimentally supported subset, and state the conditioning (proteins known to have intrachain disulfides) in the Purpose.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py line 40 (N_BOOT = 200); README.md lines 44-48 (single APC/symmetrised, bfloat16 extraction)
findings.description: The headline CI uses only 200 protein-level bootstrap resamples. No sensitivity analysis is reported for the load-bearing preprocessing choices (APC vs raw attention, symmetrisation, bfloat16 vs float32) or for the pooling choice. There is no paired test for the head-vs-baseline differences, although the CIs do not overlap.
findings.evidence: Pooled AP for L32H13 falls from 0.718 to 0.59 under within-protein rank normalisation (see F1). The extraction was run once in bfloat16. Independent naive bootstrap (300 resamples): 0.653-0.782, against the reported 0.664-0.782.
findings.recommended_action: Use ≥1000 bootstrap resamples. Add a small sweep (raw vs APC, symmetric vs not, fp32 vs bf16) for the chosen head and report the worst case. Add a paired protein-level bootstrap for ΔAP between L32H13 and each baseline.

findings.description: Reproducibility gaps. There is no requirements or environment file and no pinned numpy/torch/transformers/sklearn versions. The README says extraction ran on an Apple-silicon GPU, but the script defaults to --device cpu and the device actually used is not recorded. EsmModel.from_pretrained(..., dtype=dtype) uses a keyword that only recent transformers versions accept (older ones use torch_dtype), so the stated bfloat16 precision depends on an unrecorded version. The scores could not be regenerated inside the package.
findings.evidence: No requirements.txt or environment.yml in the folder. The script argument default is '--device cpu'. Wall time and memory are given only for the analysis step, not for the extraction.
findings.recommended_action: Add a pinned environment file, record the exact extraction command (device, dtype, library versions) and its wall time, and optionally store a checksum of attention_scores.npz.

grade_a.detection_reason: The key's status is 'clean' (error: null), so no documented error exists and detection does not apply. I re-ran checks on the package. No finding shows that a headline number or claim is wrong: test AP 0.718, the CI, P@1 0.805, the baselines and the test maximum all stand. The one finding marked major (F1) has numbers that reproduce exactly, but it is a point about which reference level to use. Its own figures leave the headline intact (11x the within-protein null; per-protein AP 0.81 against a chance level of about 0.25).

findings.reason: Every number reproduces in memory. A protein-only score (1/n pairs) gets pooled test AP 0.1464, which is 2.99x the base rate and above both the mean-head (0.141) and separation (0.113) baselines. An oracle protein base rate gets 0.164 and -length gets 0.101. Within-protein permutation null means (200 perms): L32H13 0.065 (SD 0.0045, p95 0.073), separation 0.070, mean head 0.052. That puts lift at 11.0x, 1.6x and 2.7x. Rank-fraction-normalised pooled AP is 0.591. So the README's line 'The no-skill AP is the base rate' understates the no-skill level for the within-protein question it poses, and the baselines' multipliers mostly reflect between-protein structure. This is genuine and not in the key. It is not load-bearing: '14.6 times the base rate' is literally correct, the per-protein view keeps the same order (key: 0.812/0.383/0.331), and the headline 'far above chance' survives at 11x. Its side remark about cross-protein APC calibration matches the key's listed false alarm, but that is not the core of the finding.

True. P@1 is reported with no chance value. Mean n_bonds/n_pairs over test proteins is 0.152, 5 proteins have a single candidate pair, and random scores give P@1 of about 0.16 and per-protein AP of about 0.255. Separation's P@1 of 0.207 is close to chance, but L32H13's 0.805 is not. This is a presentation gap; the headline is unaffected, as the finding itself says.

The mechanism is real. Resampling 661 values with replacement from 256 null APs of a single permutation caps the estimate at the max of those 256. Recomputing all 661 candidates under 5 independent within-protein permutations gives null maxima 0.091, 0.097, 0.093, 0.093 and 0.098, all above the reported 0.087. One permutation had a single head at or above 2x the base rate. This agrees with the key's note that the source draws gave 0.093. The bias is small (about 0.007) and does not affect 0.745 vs the null or the 192-of-661 count (about 0-1 under the null), so it is trivial in impact.

There is in fact no contact baseline, and the comparators are weak, but SUMMARY conclusion 3 already says this. It states that attention follows contacts in general, that bonded cysteines are in contact, and that specificity versus other close pairs was not tested. Conclusion 1 claims only 'far above chance' and above the two stated baselines, which is accurate. Per the key, overreach-type criticism of this summary is not valid. What remains is an already-disclosed limitation plus a framing suggestion.

The key lists 'the <=40-cysteine rule ... biases the result' as a possible false alarm: the rule is stated in the README (two test proteins with 64 and 41 cysteines dropped) and applies to every scorer. The finding's counts are right (select max 24, test max 39 after the cap), but the bias it suggests is speculative, and the finding admits the headline would probably survive.

The key lists homology leakage and pretraining contamination as false alarms. ESM-2 was trained by masked-token prediction with no disulfide labels, and only one parameter (which head) is selected. The summary's 'held from select to test' only claims that head selection transferred, never generalisation to unseen sequences. The finding's own evidence (AP 0.718 to 0.715 after dropping similar proteins) shows no effect.

Partly true and trivial. No ECO evidence codes are kept, and unannotated pairs are labelled negative. The key notes this limitation would lower AP for every scorer rather than inflate it. The conditioning on proteins with at least one intrachain bond is already stated in SUMMARY's Purpose and the README. The finding does not claim the result is invalid.

True. N_BOOT is 200, with no paired delta test and no precision/APC sensitivity sweep. The CIs do not overlap by a wide margin, and the key reports a CPU re-run correlation of 0.9996, so bfloat16 is not a concern. Its rank-normalisation figure (0.59) reproduces as 0.591. These are robustness suggestions; nothing in the results changes.

The gaps are real but trivial. There is no environment file, the script defaults to --device cpu while the README says an Apple-silicon GPU was used, and the dtype= keyword depends on the transformers version. The key says the shipped scores are bit-identical to the source cache and the code reproduces them on a spot check, so the scores can be checked. The analysis step re-runs byte-identically.

grade_b.detection_reason: The key's status is "clean" (error: null), so there is no documented error to detect and error_detected is null. None of the findings shows that a headline result is wrong. Running the package code confirms the headline numbers (L32H13 test AP 0.718, per-protein AP 0.812, P@1 0.805). The only substantive confirmed issue is F1, which concerns how lift is framed rather than an error in the result: L32H13 still has about 11x lift over the within-protein null.

findings.reason: I reproduced the numbers by running the package code inline. A protein-only score (1/n pairs) reaches pooled test AP 0.146, which is above the mean head (0.141). An oracle protein base rate reaches 0.164 and -length reaches 0.101. Under within-protein permutation (200 draws), the null AP means are 0.070 for separation, 0.052 for the mean head and 0.065 for L32H13. Rank-normalised AP for L32H13 is 0.591. So labelling the base rate as the 'no-skill' level, and the resulting 'x base rate' multipliers, overstate within-protein lift, especially for the baselines (separation is about 1.6x, not 2.3x). This is a genuine interpretation and reporting issue that the key does not list. It is not quite the key's false alarm that 'pooled AP is invalid because of scale differences'. It is not load-bearing: the headline (L32H13 far above chance, beating both baselines) survives with about 11x lift over the proper null, and the per-protein metrics agree (0.812 vs chance about 0.25).

Confirmed. The mean n_bonds/n_pairs per protein is 0.152. Random scores give P@1 of about 0.159, P@n of about 0.155 and per-protein AP of about 0.255, and 5 test proteins have only one candidate pair. Adding chance values to the P@1 column is a reasonable reporting improvement. L32H13's 0.805 is far above chance, so the headline is unaffected.

The finding is roughly right. Scoring all 661 candidates under 5 independent within-protein permutations gave null maxima of 0.092, 0.100, 0.092, 0.099 and 0.090, against the reported 0.087, and in two draws the null maximum exceeded the 2x-base-rate threshold of 0.098. The key notes that the source's draws gave 0.093, so the value depends on the draws and is slightly low. The difference is trivial next to the test maximum of 0.745. The code is standard per the key and nothing depends on this estimate.

It is true that there is no contact baseline; the key's known facts say so. However, SUMMARY.md conclusion 3 already states that specificity versus general contacts was not tested and names this as a next step, and the summary never claims the signal is disulfide-specific. The key says overreach findings against this summary are false alarms. What remains is a wording suggestion for conclusion 1, which is trivial.

The facts are verified: the maximum cysteine count is 24 in select and 39 in test, and the README states that two test proteins (64 and 41 cysteines) were dropped. The key lists 'the <=40-cysteine rule biases the result' as a possible false alarm, because the rule is stated and applies to every scorer. This finding is hedged ('could change', 'headline would probably survive') and does not show any bias, so it is at most a trivial disclosure point.

The key lists homology leakage between splits and ESM-2 pretraining 'contamination' as possible false alarms. The finding itself concedes the homology impact is negligible (0.718 -> 0.715). The remaining pretraining point argues against a claim the summary does not make: 'held from select to test' refers to head-selection transfer, and no labels entered pretraining.

These are true but routine limitations. UniProt DISULFID evidence codes are not tracked, and unannotated pairs and interchain-bonded cysteines are kept as negatives. The key says unannotated true bonds would lower AP for every scorer rather than invalidate the result, and the scope (proteins with at least one intrachain bond) is stated in the README and Purpose.

200 bootstrap resamples is on the low side, but a 1000-resample protein bootstrap gives 0.653-0.788, against the reported 0.664-0.782, which is a trivial difference. The key rules out bfloat16 sensitivity (CPU re-run correlation 0.9996) and confirms the bootstrap is standard. Requests for a sensitivity sweep and a paired test are nice-to-haves; the CIs do not overlap.

The reproducibility gaps are real but minor: there is no pinned environment file, --device defaults to cpu, and the transformers 'dtype' keyword depends on the library version. The key confirms that the shipped scores are bit-identical to the source cache and that a CPU spot check reproduces them, and the analysis step re-runs byte-identically. So the implication that the scores cannot be checked is close to a key-listed false alarm, but the documentation gaps themselves are true and trivial.

review.summary:
I re-ran the analysis in memory (python -B, no files written) and every number in SUMMARY.md and outputs/ reproduced exactly: L32H13 select AP 0.742 and test AP 0.718 (CI 0.664-0.782); sequence separation 0.113; mean of all heads 0.141; null maximum 0.087; 192 of 661 heads at 2x base rate or more; P@1 0.805. The metric selftest passes, and the AP, permutation and cluster-bootstrap code is correct. The pairs files match proteins.tsv: every cysteine pair is listed, bond counts agree, and no cysteine is in two bonds. The row-660 mean matches the mean of the 660 head rows. The headline holds up under every stress test I ran. The chosen head's null AP when labels are shuffled within each protein is 0.065 ± 0.0045 (p95 0.074). The protein-level bootstrap with 2000 resamples gives 0.647-0.787. Even a worst-case refill of the two excluded cysteine-rich test proteins with no skill only lowers pooled AP to about 0.59-0.65. All 192 heads above 2x the base rate also beat their own 20-shuffle null maximum. The core claim (attention ranks bonded cysteine pairs far above chance and far above the sequence-separation and mean-head baselines) survives, and no finding is critical. The problems are about how exact the numbers are, how they are anchored, how the data were selected, and how the endpoint is read.

Verdicts per pattern:
- P1 (null/anchoring): present, unaddressed, minor. The fold-over-chance figures use the plain base rate, not the within-protein null. P@1 has no chance level. The null maximum is underestimated.
- P2 (trivial baseline): mostly clean. Sequence separation and the mean of all heads are given; a contact-prediction comparator is missing (covered under P3).
- P3 (endpoint): present but acknowledged. The endpoint is close to cysteine-cysteine contact, which conclusion 3 admits. Label evidence is mixed and probably incomplete.
- P4 (unit of inference): mostly clean. The bootstrap is by protein, but homologous families are ignored and only 200 resamples were used.
- P5 (selection): present and unaddressed. An unexplained cap of 40 cysteines removed only two test proteins.
- P6 (positive control): not applicable, because no null finding is claimed.
- P7 (generalization): present and partly acknowledged. One model, one bf16 run, one annotation source.
- P8 (stability): minor. Few bootstrap resamples, a one-shuffle null, and no sensitivity check on the scoring choices (APC, symmetrising).
- P9 (language): clean. Conclusion 3 hedges properly.
- P10 (reproducibility): minor gaps. No environment file, no data-building code, and a device mismatch between the README and the extraction script.

findings.location: README.md:26-28 (filter rule); SUMMARY.md:3-4 (data description); outputs/results.json arms.attention_esm2.test_ap
findings.description: Two test proteins (64 and 41 cysteines) were removed by a 'max 40 cysteines' rule. The rule has no stated reason; unlike the 1,022-residue limit, it is not an ESM-2 constraint. It removed proteins only from the test split, and the cutoff sits just below 41. SUMMARY.md does not mention it and says every cysteine pair in the 236 proteins was scored. The headline pooled test AP (0.718, 14.6x base rate) and its CI therefore hold only for this unexplained exclusion of the hardest cases. The code that applied the filters and built the labels is not in the folder, so the step cannot be audited.
findings.evidence: The two proteins would add C(64,2)+C(41,2) = 2016+820 = 2,836 candidate pairs, about 38% of the 7,463 retained test pairs. Pooled AP weights each protein by its number of pairs. L32H13 gets worse as cysteine count rises: mean per-protein AP is 1.00 for 2-3 cysteines (n=10), 0.86 for 4-7 (n=41), 0.77 for 8-15 (n=55) and 0.71 for 16-39 (n=17). In my simulation I appended 2,836 pairs with 20-52 bonds and gave those pairs no skill (scores drawn from the test negatives). Pooled test AP fell from 0.718 to about 0.59-0.63, or about 0.64-0.65 with half skill. The select split's largest protein has 24 cysteines, so the cap only affected test.
findings.recommended_action: Give a reason for the 40-cysteine cap or drop it. Score the two proteins (both are within the ESM length limit unless shown otherwise) and report test AP, CI and P@1 with and without them. State the exclusion and its effect in SUMMARY.md, and fix the 'every cysteine pair in 236 proteins' wording. Ship the label-extraction and filtering code and the UniProt release used.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:25, 34-36 (x14.6 base rate; 'bonded pair at the top in 80% of test proteins'); code/disulfide_attention.py:229-233
findings.description: The fold-over-chance figure is measured against the pooled base rate, not against the right null. Pooled AP already gets a lift from differences between proteins, so the null AP of a score that ignores which pair is bonded within each protein sits well above 0.049. The per-protein P@1 of 0.805 is given with no chance level. Some proteins make P@1 trivial: five test proteins have a single candidate pair, so P@1 = 1 there.
findings.evidence: With labels shuffled within each test protein (200 shuffles), L32H13's null AP is 0.065 (SD 0.0045, p95 0.074), not 0.049. Chance P@1 per protein is 0.144, and chance per-protein AP is 0.25 (mean per-protein base rate 0.152). Five test proteins have one candidate pair and ten have three or fewer.
findings.recommended_action: Report each headline as a value next to its null, for example 'AP 0.718 vs within-protein null 0.065 ± 0.005 (p95 0.074)' and 'P@1 0.805 vs chance 0.145'. Do the same for the baseline rows of the table.

findings.location: code/disulfide_attention.py:220-224 (null maximum from one shuffle and 256 sampled candidates); SUMMARY.md:27-28 ('expected highest of 661 candidates under the within-protein null is 0.087'); README.md:62-64
findings.description: The expected best-of-661 null maximum comes from one label shuffle and 256 sampled candidates, redrawn with replacement. This mostly returns the maximum of those 256 values and ignores the variation between shuffles, so the null maximum is understated. The 2x-base-rate cutoff (0.098) used for the '192 heads' count falls inside the true null-maximum range.
findings.evidence: Scoring all 661 candidates under 10 independent within-protein shuffles gives a null maximum of 0.095 ± 0.005 (largest 0.104), against the reported 0.087. The cutoff 2 x 0.049 = 0.098 is inside that range. The 192 count still holds: every one of the 192 heads beats its own maximum over 20 shuffles, and 159 heads beat the overall null maximum of 0.105.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the null over all candidates and several shuffles (for example 20-100), and report mean, SD and p95 of the maximum. Tie the 'detector' count to each head's own null p95 or the overall null maximum rather than to a fixed 2x base rate. Also report how many heads beat the sequence-separation baseline: 127 do.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md:3 (Purpose: 'Can ESM-2 tell which cysteine pairs ... are disulfide-bonded?'), SUMMARY.md:33-36 (Conclusion 1), SUMMARY.md:41-44 (Conclusion 3)
findings.description: Endpoint mismatch, acknowledged. Among cysteine pairs, the bonded pairs are almost exactly the cysteine pairs in close contact, so the test mostly measures whether APC-corrected attention tracks cysteine-cysteine proximity, which ESM-2 attention is known to do. There is no contact-matched comparator, such as ESM-2's own contact-prediction head or structure-derived contacts. Without one, 'tell which pairs are bonded' cannot be separated from general contact prediction. Conclusion 3 says this openly, but the Purpose line and Conclusion 1 still frame the result as recognising bonds.
findings.evidence: No contact baseline appears in the code or outputs. Conclusion 3 says the authors 'did not test whether these heads prefer bonded pairs over other close pairs.'
findings.recommended_action: Add a contact baseline: the ESM-2 contact-head probability for the same cysteine pairs, or Cβ distance from PDB/AlphaFold structures. Report the AP gain of L32H13 over it, or AP among cysteine pairs within a fixed distance. Until then, state Conclusion 1 as 'consistent with contact-tracking attention' at the claim level the evidence supports.

findings.location: README.md:22-24 (labels from UniProt FT DISULFID; 'a pair without a record is labelled not bonded'); data/proteins.tsv
findings.description: The labels mix evidence types. UniProt DISULFID features include experimental, 'by similarity' and predicted annotations, and no evidence filter was applied. Unannotated pairs are treated as true negatives even though many proteins have cysteines with no annotated bond, so annotation may be incomplete. 'By similarity' labels are copied from homologs, which partly overlaps with the evolutionary signal ESM-2 learns. The UniProt release is not stated.
findings.evidence: 72 of 123 test proteins and 62 of 113 select proteins have two or more cysteines in no annotated intrachain bond. For example, Q5RF57 has 9 cysteines and 2 annotated bonds. No evidence-code field exists in the data files.
findings.recommended_action: Keep the UniProt evidence codes and report AP separately for experimentally supported bonds (ECO:0000269, or PDB-derived) and for inferred ones. Record the UniProt release. Consider restricting the test set to fully annotated proteins with structures.

findings.location: README.md:19-20 (split 'by protein'); code/disulfide_attention.py:116-131 (protein-level bootstrap); README.md:65 (200 resamples)
findings.description: Proteins are treated as independent units, but the split was made by protein, not by sequence cluster. Homologous families inside and across splits make the protein-level bootstrap CI too narrow and slightly blur the select/test separation. The CI also rests on only 200 percentile-bootstrap resamples.
findings.evidence: By 5-mer overlap, test/select near-homologs include Q47450~A0A0H2VAQ6 (0.89), B1JDQ5~A5VYT2 (0.89), B4TQB8~Q1R984 (0.71) and P60045~P00596 (0.62). With 2000 resamples, the L32H13 CI is 0.647-0.787, against the reported 0.664-0.782 from 200.
findings.recommended_action: Cluster proteins by sequence identity (for example MMseqs2 at 30-50%). Bootstrap by cluster, and check the result with a split made by cluster. Use at least 1000-2000 resamples.

findings.description: Everything rests on one condition. One model (ESM-2 650M) was run once in bfloat16, with one annotation source and one fixed scoring recipe (symmetrise plus APC). The Purpose generalises to 'ESM-2', and Conclusion 2 says the signal is 'spread over a group of heads', but neither was checked on other ESM-2 sizes, another protein language model, a float32 run, or without APC.
findings.evidence: extract_attention.py has a single model and revision. Nothing checks sensitivity to the scoring choices. Head selection is near-tied on select (L32H13 0.742 vs L29H18 0.721), though both score high on test, so this particular choice is stable.
findings.recommended_action: Limit the claims explicitly to ESM-2 650M, or repeat the analysis on at least one other ESM-2 size and one model from a different family. Report results with raw symmetrised attention and with float32 attention as a sensitivity check.

findings.description: Reproducibility gaps. There is no requirements or environment file and torch/transformers versions are not pinned. The README says the scores came from an Apple-silicon GPU, but the extraction script defaults to CPU and its documented command passes no device flag. The code that built the dataset (parsing UniProt, the filters, the split of 18,176 entries) is not included. No wall time or memory figures are given for the extraction step.
findings.evidence: The folder has only code/disulfide_attention.py and code/extract_attention.py, with no environment specification. extract_attention.py uses '--device' default 'cpu', and its docstring command omits --device mps.
findings.recommended_action: Add pinned versions (requirements.txt or environment.yml), the data-construction script, the UniProt release, and the exact extraction command with its device. Report the extraction runtime and hardware.

review.summary: I reran the decodability numbers (scGPT 0.892/0.807, Geneformer 0.844/0.663, expression 0.929/0.858, shared cells 0.896/0.844/0.935). They match the outputs exactly and barely change with the CV seed (SD at most 0.002). I also rebuilt the stored null draw for expression, seed 100, and it matches bit for bit. The decodability results stand. The flat-circle part does not. (1) The expression null is wrongly calibrated: the noise search stops at a cap of 20, so its null loops are less noisy than the real data (circ-R2 0.952 vs 0.929). The reported null (17.9 +- 1.4) and p = 0.571 are therefore wrong. (2) The test has little power: it does not detect a clearly non-flat loop whose direction leaves the plane by about 31 degrees. Both real models also come out flatter than their own null (p 0.90 and 0.76). Conclusion 3 ('the loop fits a flat circle') is therefore not supported. (3) The phase label is, by definition, an angle inside one linear 2-plane of marker-gene expression. That pushes every representation, and above all expression, towards looking flat. (4) Expression's lead over the models comes entirely from the 87 marker genes that define the label. Without them expression scores 0.895, the same as scGPT's 0.892. Smaller issues: the kNN reasoning, a mismatch between the p-value and the rejection rule, and a README normalisation statement.

findings.description: The headline 'The loop fits a flat circle' is not supported. The flat-circle test has little power, and its null does not fit the real data. Real loops come out flatter than the matched flat-circle null, so failing to reject says almost nothing about whether the loop is flat.
findings.evidence: Power check at scGPT's settings: same phi, d = 512, noise tuned by the script's own binary search to linear circ-R2 0.892, compared with the stored scGPT null (95th percentile 29.2 deg). I added a second-harmonic term a*(cos 2phi, sin 2phi)@B in a second random plane. With a = 0.3 the true loop direction leaves the plane by about atan(0.6) = 31 deg everywhere, yet the out-of-plane angles were 26.2 and 29.2 deg: not rejected in 2/2 runs. Only a = 0.5 (about 45 deg) was rejected. The statistic depends far more on noise level than on geometry: for a flat null at d = 6546 it goes from 17 to 26 deg as circ-R2 falls from 0.95 to 0.905. Matching only on linear circ-R2 also counts any non-linearity in the real loop as extra null noise. Real values sit at or below the null centre: scGPT 22.7 vs 25.6 +- 2.3 (p 0.905), Geneformer 34.2 vs 35.7 (p 0.762). With a correctly calibrated null, expression is below every null draw (see F2). p-values bunched near 1 suggest the isotropic-noise null does not represent the real data.
findings.recommended_action: Drop or rephrase the claim to 'no evidence against flatness, but the test cannot detect out-of-plane angles of about 30 deg'. Add a power analysis with known non-flat loops. Use a better-matched null (e.g. noise structure taken from real residuals, more draws) and a more direct statistic, e.g. the variance of the phase-conditional mean explained beyond the best 2-plane.

verdicts.reason:
I checked this by running code on the package. The main claim holds and it weakens SUMMARY conclusion 3 ('The loop fits a flat circle'). One piece of the finding's evidence is wrong.

(1) The analytic point is correct. phase_angle (cc_common.py:63-79) takes phi = atan2(P2, P1) from a fixed 2-component PCA of the 87 z-scored markers. Its gradient therefore always lies in the plane of those two marker PCs.

(2) Expression's 20 whitened PCs encode marker P1 and P2 almost linearly (R2 0.980 and 0.932). The real sector tangents are on average 19.4 deg from this label plane and 17.9 deg from their own best-fit plane. The best-fit plane is only 5.3 and 11.6 deg (principal angles) from the label plane. So the tangent plane essentially is the label plane.

(3) The finding's numbers reproduce exactly. PC3 sector means of the marker PCA run from -0.63 to +0.71 (max SE 0.20). PC5 sector means run from -0.66 to +1.38, with R2 = 0.152 on harmonics 1-3 of phi.

(4) The tangent test cannot see this. With marker genes alone as the representation, the tangent out-of-plane angle is 12.6 deg against a null of 13.7+-0.8 (looks flat). Yet the 12 phase-binned mean positions put 24.2% of their energy outside their best 2-plane, against 3.75+-0.4% (max 4.6%) under the package's own flat_null.

(5) The direct measure the finding recommends rejects flatness in all three representations:
- expression: 0.305 vs null 0.038 (4 draws)
- scGPT: 0.297 vs null 0.047+-0.006
- Geneformer: 0.226 vs null 0.072+-0.007
In the same runs the tangent test reproduces the package's 'not rejected' (17.9 vs 18.3; 22.7 vs 25.9; 34.2 vs 35.5).

(6) Simulation supports the mechanism. I used a strongly non-planar loop (cos 2theta and sin 3theta components) with unit noise, labelled by atan2 of a linear 2-D projection. Tangent out-of-plane was 4.7 deg vs null 4.3, so the test missed it. 'Guaranteed' is too strong, though. At low noise the same setup gives 11.0 vs 2.8. And with the true phase as label the tangent test also has little power (27.5 vs 26.6). So the flat result comes from the label plane plus the test's general low power; 'largely by construction' is fair.

One sub-claim is wrong. The 'correctly calibrated null draws at 19.3-22.3 deg' do not match the package: its expression null draws span 15.5-21.0 (mean 17.9), my 4 recomputed draws give 18.3+-0.4, and the answer key says the null is calibrated correctly. This does not change the main point.

The answer key lists the package as clean and does not anticipate this issue. Still, the run results show that conclusion 3 is not supported: the loop's shape is clearly non-planar on a direct measure, and the tangent-of-label test for expression mostly reflects how phi is defined.

review.summary:
I checked the data, code and outputs against each other and re-ran the key steps in memory, without writing any files. The data are aligned. The phase labels match the expression file exactly (checked with phase_check). The decodability numbers reproduce, and so does a stored null draw (scGPT seed 100). So the reported numbers are what the code produces. The problems are in what the code measures and what the summary concludes from it.

1. Conclusion 3, "the loop fits a flat circle", cannot stand. Its test statistic measures the direction of the phase readout in each sector, not the shape of the loop. A simulation shows the test almost never detects loops that are clearly not flat. A direct check on the data also contradicts the claim: in all three representations the loop of sector mean positions leaves its best-fit 2-plane far more than the matched flat-circle null does.
2. For expression, the null's noise search hits its upper limit of 20. The null is therefore under-noised (circ-R2 about 0.95 against 0.929), and the reported null of 17.9 +- 1.4 deg is too low; matched draws give about 22-23 deg.
3. Conclusion 2 (expression beats both models; the models "do not add" to the phase signal) comes mostly from circularity. With the 87 genes that define the label removed, expression scores 0.895, the same as scGPT (0.892).
4. Geneformer's lower score is largely an effect of keeping only 20 principal components: it rises from 0.844 to 0.88-0.89 at 30-50 components.
5. "kNN is worse, so a linear readout is enough" does not follow from the evidence given.

findings.description: The out-of-plane test has almost no power and does not measure the shape of the loop. In each sector, the 'tangent' is the coefficient vector of a multivariate ridge regression of phase. That is the gradient of the best linear phase readout. Directions in which the loop bends but that add no extra phase information get near-zero weight. For expression the gradient lies in the marker-gene plane by construction. In addition, the statistic is dominated by estimation noise (about 26 deg for a perfectly flat null in scGPT). Because the null's noise is matched on linear circ-R2, adding curvature lowers the noise in the matched null, which cancels the effect. The 'not rejected' results (and the summary's framing of this as only a 20-draw limitation) therefore carry little information. The real values also fall below the null in scGPT and Geneformer, and well below the correctly matched expression null (see F3). Loop (cos phi, sin phi, cos 3phi, sin 3phi): 25.5, 24.7 and 20.6 deg, none rejected; the strongly non-planar loop scores below the flat null. Build a null that keeps the real noise covariance (e.g. replace the real phase-dependent signal by its 2-plane projection while keeping the real residuals). Present 'not rejected' with its estimated power.

review.summary:
I re-ran the core computations. The stored circ-R2 values, turning statistics and null draws reproduce exactly: scGPT 0.892/0.807, Geneformer 0.844/0.663, shared cells 0.935/0.896/0.844, and the seed-100 null draws for all three models. The phase-label check also reproduces. The problems are in the design and the claims, not in the arithmetic.

(1) The flat-circle test cannot tell planar loops from non-planar ones, so "the loop fits a flat circle" (Conclusion 3) is not supported. A clearly non-planar 4-D loop gives the same out-of-plane statistic as the flat null and is rejected in only 1 of 5 simulations. All three real values also fall below a flat-circle null.

(2) For expression the null is not noise-matched: the noise search hits its upper bound, so the null's circ-R2 is 0.952 against 0.929 real. The reported null (17.9 +- 1.4) and p = 0.571 are therefore wrong. A matched null gives about 22 deg.

(3) The expression flat-circle result is circular. phi is the atan2 of two linear marker projections, and those projections are linearly recoverable from the 20 whitened PCs (CV R2 0.98 and 0.91).

(4) "kNN does worse, so linear is enough" is an artefact of using 20 whitened PCs. With 5 PCs, kNN beats linear for all three representations.

(5) The 20-PC bottleneck lowers the models' scores, Geneformer's most. This inflates the expression-vs-model gaps. With a tuned linear readout on 300 in-fold PCs: scGPT 0.916, Geneformer 0.899, expression 0.925.

There are also minor issues: the rejection rule does not match the p-value, and the README's normalization description is inaccurate.

findings.description: The test behind 'The loop fits a flat circle' has little power, and its null is not calibrated. The out-of-plane angle measures the planarity of 12 noisy per-sector ridge directions in whitened PC space, and tangent-estimation noise and whitening drive it far more than the loop's geometry. Not rejecting the null therefore says almost nothing about flatness, and the heading 'The loop fits a flat circle' cannot stand.
findings.evidence: Power simulation at scGPT settings (n=3000, d=512, scGPT phi, noise matched by the same binary search to linear circ-R2 0.892). A clearly non-planar loop (cos phi, sin phi, cos 2phi, sin 2phi) gave out-of-plane angles of 25.2, 29.6, 29.0, 28.9 and 27.5 deg. Only 1 of 5 exceeds the stored null 95th percentile of 29.2. A near-noise-free version of the same 4-D loop gives an out-of-plane angle of 25.9 deg and planarity 0.805, essentially the same as scGPT's flat-null mean (25.6 deg, 0.799). Whitening equalizes the harmonics, so the tangent field is dominated by the 2nd-harmonic plane and looks 'planar'. The test does reject other shapes: a saddle in 4/5 runs and a 4-D loop with half-amplitude 2nd harmonic in 5/5. So detection depends on the shape and is not monotone in non-planarity. In all three representations the real value is at or below a flat-circle null, i.e. 'flatter than a flat circle'. With a second null built by permuting the real residuals around the fitted planar signal: scGPT 22.7 vs 26.0+-1.8, Geneformer 34.2 vs 35.1+-2.4, expression 17.9 vs 22.2+-1.3. The statistic does not measure geometry in a calibrated way.
findings.recommended_action: Run and report a power analysis against non-planar alternatives at matched noise. Use a geometry statistic that does not depend on whitening, e.g. the energy of phase-binned centroids outside their best 2-plane compared with a split-half or bootstrap noise floor. Use more null draws. Rephrase Conclusion 3 as 'the test could not detect departure from planarity; it has low power', not 'the loop fits a flat circle'.

findings.location: code/cc_geometry.py line 110 (lo, hi = 0.0, 20.0); outputs/cc_geometry_expr.json/.log; SUMMARY.md line 17; README.md line 55
findings.description: For expression (d = 6,546) the noise binary search cannot reach the real circ-R2: even the maximum noise s = 20 leaves the null more decodable than the data. Every expression null draw therefore uses the capped noise level and is less noisy than the real data. This contradicts the README's statement that noise is set so that circ-R2 matches. The reported expression null (17.9 +- 1.4 deg) and p = 0.571 are wrong; the exact match between real and null is an artefact.
findings.evidence: At s = 20 the expression null's linear circ-R2 is 0.952, against 0.929 for the real data. Re-running flat_null for seed 100 reproduces the stored draw exactly (out-of-plane 18.88 deg) and gives a final circ-R2 of 0.952. With the bound widened to 60, the search matches at s = 23.05 (R2 0.920) and the same draw's out-of-plane angle rises to 22.1 deg. The residual-permutation flat null gives 22.2 +- 1.3 deg. Against a matched null, the real 17.9 deg falls below every draw, so p is about 1.
findings.recommended_action: Widen or adapt the search bound (e.g. scale it with sqrt(d)). Assert convergence and store the achieved null circ-R2 for every draw. Re-run the expression nulls and correct the table and the p-value.

findings.location: code/cc_common.py lines 63-79 (phase_angle); SUMMARY.md lines 30-31 (Conclusion 3, expression row)
findings.description: phi is defined as atan2 of the first two PCs of z-scored marker genes, i.e. the angle in one linear 2-plane of expression. In the expression representation the phase gradient therefore lies, up to noise, in a single 2-plane by construction. The 'flat circle in expression' result is tautological, not an empirical finding. For the models, the test mostly asks whether they linearly encode that same marker plane. The summary presents 'in all three representations the loop does not leave its best-fit 2-plane' as evidence about loop geometry.
findings.evidence: With 5-fold CV linear regression from the 20 whitened expression PCs, the two marker-PC coordinates that define phi are recovered with R2 0.976 and 0.910 (scGPT: 0.907 and 0.771). So phi is almost exactly atan2 of two linear functions of the inputs to the tangent regression.
findings.recommended_action: State that the label definition imposes planarity in expression and drop expression as evidence for flatness. To test loop geometry, use a phase label not defined as a linear 2-D angle (e.g. a nonlinear or principal-curve ordering, or held-out marker sets), or examine the geometry of phase-binned centroids directly.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 24-25 (Conclusion 1); code/cc_common.py lines 95-101 (prep whitening); code/cc_geometry.py line 53
findings.description: The claim 'kNN does worse in all three representations, so a linear readout is enough' depends on the setup. Whitening scales the 18 mostly non-phase PCs to the same variance as the phase PCs, which degrades distance-based kNN, and kNN's deficit grows with dimension. Logically too, kNN underperforming one specific linear model does not show that a linear readout is 'enough'.
findings.evidence: Shared 2,000 cells, whitened PCs (linear vs kNN circ-R2). At 5 PCs kNN beats linear in all three: scGPT 0.490 vs 0.592, Geneformer 0.322 vs 0.366, expression 0.638 vs 0.711. At 10 PCs they are near parity (scGPT 0.883 vs 0.854; expression 0.925 vs 0.894). At 20 PCs kNN loses, and at 200 PCs it collapses (scGPT 0.919 vs 0.378). Without whitening at 20 PCs, scGPT's kNN rises from 0.807 to 0.836.
findings.recommended_action: Tune k and the dimensionality by nested CV, and use unwhitened or cosine-distance space for kNN. Report the comparison across settings. Remove the inference that linear is 'enough', or support it with a properly tuned nonlinear readout.

findings.location: code/cc_common.py line 19 (DIM = 20) and lines 95-101; SUMMARY.md lines 15-19, 23-29 (Conclusions 1-2)
findings.description: All decodability numbers are taken after a fixed 20-PC bottleneck. This understates the models' linear phase decodability, Geneformer's especially, and inflates the 'expression does better than both models' gap. The headline values 0.892 and 0.844 are specific to this setup, not estimates of how well phase can be read linearly from the embeddings. 'They do not add to it' cannot be tested at all, because the label is derived from expression.
findings.evidence: Shared cells, linear circ-R2 by number of whitened PCs. Geneformer: 0.581 (10), 0.844 (20), 0.892 (50), 0.902 (200). scGPT: 0.896 (20), 0.913 (50), 0.919 (200). Expression: 0.935 (20), 0.920 (200). With in-fold PCA to 300 plus RidgeCV: scGPT 0.916, Geneformer 0.899, expression 0.925. The expression-Geneformer gap shrinks from 0.091 to 0.026 and the expression-scGPT gap from 0.039 to 0.009 (at 200 PCs scGPT 0.919 vs expression 0.920). CV-seed spread is about 0.002, so the dimension effect is real.
findings.recommended_action: Choose the dimensionality and ridge alpha by nested CV, and report decodability as a function of dimension. Restate Conclusion 2's gap sizes accordingly, and drop or qualify 'they do not add to it'.

findings.description: The rejection rule (real > np.percentile(null, 95), with linear interpolation) does not match the stated one-sided p = (#null >= real + 1)/21. With 20 draws it can reject while p = 2/21 = 0.095, i.e. when one null draw is at or above the real value. Current conclusions are unaffected.
findings.evidence: With 20 draws, np.percentile(.., 95) interpolates between the 19th and 20th order statistics. A real value between them is 'rejected' while p = 0.095 > 0.05.
findings.recommended_action: Base rejection on p <= alpha. Use more draws (e.g. 200 or more) so that p can resolve the 0.05 level.

findings.description: The README says the expression matrix is log(1 + counts per 10,000) of all 6,546 genes. But expm1 of the stored values sums to 7,447-9,573 per cell, not 10,000. The normalization was evidently done over a larger gene set, or differently, so the documented data provenance is inaccurate. The effect on the per-gene z-scored labels is negligible.
findings.evidence: np.expm1(emb).sum(1) quantiles (min, median, max) = 7447, 9137, 9573.
findings.recommended_action: Correct the README to describe the actual normalization (e.g. 'CP10k computed on the full source gene set, then subset to 6,546 genes').
