The marker-set counts (87/93) are correct but do not show a problem.
The numbers are correct (median error 23.28 vs 20.91 deg) and SUMMARY's caveats already note the disagreement. This is a wording or qualification point about Conclusion 1.

review.summary: I reproduced the reported numbers exactly: model 0.7894, expr_512_rank 0.7741, and model - rank = +0.0153 [+0.0022, +0.0283]. The headline claim ("the model adds information beyond its input, CI excludes 0") does not hold up. Two separate problems each turn it into parity under the analysis's own verdict rule. (1) The rank baseline is not the model's actual input in RPE1. RPE1 cell sentences are ranked over all 8,749 RPE1 genes, so on average 13% of their genes are absent from K562. When the baseline is built from the real cell sentences, model - baseline = -0.0011 [-0.0128, +0.0115]. (2) Rank features that are rare in K562 take extreme standardised values in RPE1 (|z| up to 7,395). Clipping at |z|<=50 for both arms leaves the model unchanged and gives model - rank = -0.006 [-0.018, +0.006]. Further problems: the bootstrap ignores variance from fitting on K562, which is about 5x larger than the variance it reports; on median error the model is clearly worse (+2.4 deg [1.6, 3.3]); the verdict depends on the ridge alpha; "adds information" is conceptually impossible for a deterministic function of the input; and the tokenisation-loss breakdown in Conclusion 2 is inflated by the same baseline artefacts, by circularity in how the label is built, and by the mismatch with the real cell sentences. Run-log, JSON and summary numbers agree with each other.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:45-58 and 100-101 (top_k_encode restricted to shared-gene columns); README.md:40-41; SUMMARY.md:12, 26-27
findings.description: expr_512_rank is not the information in the model's input for RPE1. The activations were extracted from cell sentences ranked over ALL genes of each cell line's matrix (extract_activations.py:95 -> cell_sentences.anndata_to_ranked_genes). top_k_encode instead takes the top 512 among the 6,544 shared genes only. RPE1 has 2,205 genes that K562 lacks, so RPE1 sentences differ from the baseline in which shared genes they contain and at what rank. Built faithfully, the baseline matches the model and the headline 'model adds' verdict becomes parity.
findings.evidence: K562 has 6,546 genes, RPE1 8,749, and 6,544 are shared. Across RPE1 cell sentences (max_genes=512), a mean of 13.4% (max 21.7%) of genes are RPE1-only. On average a sentence has only 444 shared genes, versus 512 in expr_512_rank. K562 sentences have 0% non-shared genes. I rebuilt the rank arm from the actual sentences (rank 512..1, mapped to shared genes) and used the same scaler, ridge alpha=1000 and paired bootstrap. Result: R_diff 0.7905 (median error 20.3 deg) vs model 0.7894 (23.3 deg). Model - sentence_rank = -0.0011, 95% CI [-0.0128, +0.0115], P(>0)=0.43, which is PARITY under the code's own rule. The difference does not come from tie-breaking: stable genomic-order ties on shared genes give 0.7734 vs 0.7741.
findings.recommended_action: Build the baseline from the exact cell sentences used for extraction, including the RPE1-only genes and the same 512-gene cutoff and ordering, then project it to the readout's feature space. Rerun the verdict and withdraw or restate Conclusion 1 and the 'the model's input' label in the results table.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:92-96 (StandardScaler fit on K562, applied to RPE1)
findings.description: Standardising the sparse rank features on K562 makes RPE1 values explode for genes that are rarely in K562's top 512. This handicaps only the expr_512_rank arm, and it alone produces the +0.015 'model advantage'. With a mild clip of the standardised inputs applied to both arms, the advantage disappears.
findings.evidence: 3,395 shared genes are in the K562 top 512 in fewer than 1% of cells. In RPE1 the rank arm's standardised inputs reach |z| = 7,395 (99.9th percentile 11.5); K562 max is 54.8. For comparison, the RPE1 max is 12.2 for the model arm, 12.3 for expr_full and 88.5 for expr_512_mag. Clipping |z| at 100/50/20 raises the rank arm from 0.7741 to 0.7861/0.7955/0.8073. The model arm is unchanged at 0.7894, and expr_512_mag barely moves (0.8100 -> 0.8107). Paired bootstrap with clip 50 on both arms: model - rank = -0.0061 [-0.0175, +0.0057], P(>0)=0.15.
findings.recommended_action: Handle near-constant source features before transfer, using one rule for every arm. Options: drop genes with low K562 prevalence, clip standardised values, use robust scaling, or don't scale the rank features. Report how the contrast changes under these choices.

findings.description: The paired bootstrap resamples only RPE1 target cells and treats the fitted scaler and ridge as fixed. Variation from fitting on the 3,000 K562 cells is ignored. That variation dominates, so the claim that the 95% CI excludes 0 understates uncertainty several-fold.
findings.evidence: I refit both arms on bootstrap resamples of K562 cells, also resampling target cells (25 draws). Model - rank had SD 0.032 and a 2.5-97.5% range of [-0.062, +0.068], with 2 of 25 draws negative. The reported CI [+0.0022, +0.0283] implies an SD of about 0.0067.
findings.recommended_action: Include the source fit in the uncertainty estimate: resample K562 cells with refitting, or use repeated independent source subsets. Otherwise, state clearly that the interval is conditional on one fitted readout and does not support a population-level claim.

findings.description: The second metric shows a statistically clear effect in the opposite direction. The summary calls this a 'disagreement' but still concludes that layer 21 'transfers phase better'. The verdict rule ignores median error entirely.
findings.evidence: Paired bootstrap (1,000 draws) of median angular error: model - expr_512_rank = +2.41 deg [+1.57, +3.34], with the model worse in 100% of draws. Against the sentence-matched baseline it is +3.1 deg [2.2, 4.0] at alpha=1000, and +1.7 deg [0.8, 2.6] at alpha=1e4.
findings.recommended_action: Pre-specify one primary metric, or require the metrics to agree. Report CIs for both metrics. If they conflict, describe the result as mixed rather than 'model better'.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:95 (Ridge alpha=1e3 fixed for all arms); SUMMARY.md:43
findings.description: A single untuned alpha is used for arms of very different dimensionality and sparsity. The contrast between the model and a faithful input baseline changes sign with alpha, and alpha=1000 is not what source cross-validation picks for any arm.
findings.evidence: RPE1 R_diff for model / top-k rank / sentence-matched rank: alpha=10: 0.661/0.638/0.676; 100: 0.708/0.681/0.714; 1e3: 0.789/0.774/0.791; 1e4: 0.821/0.797/0.797; 1e5: 0.795/0.622/0.598. 5-fold CV within K562 picks alpha=1e4 for model, rank and expr_full; expr_full then transfers at 0.897. At alpha=1e4, model - sentence_rank = +0.024 [0.015, 0.035] on R_diff, yet the model is still worse on median error (+1.7 deg).
findings.recommended_action: Choose alpha per arm by nested CV on the source cell line and report a sensitivity table across alphas (and readouts). Do not base a verdict on one regularisation setting.

findings.description: 'The model adds information beyond its input' is conceptually invalid. Layer-21 activations are a deterministic function of the cell sentence, so by the data-processing inequality they cannot hold more phase information than the sentence does. A ridge readout on a hand-built linear rank encoding only gives a lower bound on what the input contains. The contrast therefore measures how linearly decodable and transferable two representations are under one readout, not how much information each holds.
findings.evidence: extract_activations.py:141-152 computes the activation from the tokenised prompt plus gene list alone. The comparison baseline (transfer.py:57) is one specific linear encoding of rank, scored by a linear model.
findings.recommended_action: Rephrase the claim as, for example, 'phase is more linearly decodable / transfers better under a ridge readout'. If a claim about information content is wanted, compare against stronger, nonlinear readouts of the input encoding.

findings.description: The tokenisation-loss breakdown ('input format alone costs 0.104 before the first layer: 0.068 + 0.036; the model wins back 0.015') rests on the faulty rank arm (F1, F2), which inflates it. It is also partly circular. The phase label is a PCA angle of z-scored log-expression magnitudes of the Tirosh genes, and those genes are features in the expression arms. Arms that keep magnitudes are therefore favoured by how the label is built. Finally, 'before the first layer' is inferred from linear readouts, not measured.
findings.evidence: With clip 50 the rank arm reaches 0.7955, giving expr_full - rank of about 0.083 (not 0.104) and mag - rank of about 0.015 (not 0.036). With the sentence-matched baseline (0.7905), expr_full - baseline = 0.088, essentially equal to the model's deficit of 0.089, so the model wins back about 0, not 0.015. The label is computed with phase_angle on the same expression matrix the arms use (transfer.py:73, 87-89).
findings.recommended_action: Recompute the breakdown after fixing F1 and F2. Use a phase label that does not share features with the readouts, for example by excluding the label genes from the feature sets or using an independent phase annotation. Soften the causal wording ('is the tokenizer, not the model').

findings.description: The practical recommendation generalises from one model, one layer, one ridge setting and one cell-line pair from the same screen to SCFM evaluation in general ('C2S comes out ahead'). The underlying result is not robust (F1-F5).
findings.evidence: The analysis covers a single layer (21), a single alpha (1000), a single target (RPE1) and a single metric for the verdict. The caveats at SUMMARY.md:43 acknowledge the narrow scope, yet Conclusion 3 is stated without qualification.
findings.recommended_action: Limit the conclusion to this setting, or support it with more layers, readouts, cell lines or batches, and with input baselines that match each model's tokenisation.

grade_a.detection_reason: F1 meets the detection rule. It says top_k_encode (transfer.py:45-58) takes the top 512 from the 6,544 shared genes only, while the cell sentences were ranked over all of each line's genes. As a result the RPE1 baseline differs from the sentence in which shared genes it includes and at what rank. F1 prescribes building the baseline from the actual full-panel sentence and then projecting it to the shared features. I reproduced its numbers inline. A full-panel stable-sort rank arm gives R_diff 0.7905, and model minus that baseline is -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], P(>0) 0.43. That is parity, matching the key's exact-sentence result of -0.0011 [-0.0132, +0.0111]. The finding's 444 shared genes per sentence (about 68 RPE1-only) also matches the key's mean of 67.8.

findings.reason: This is the key's error. The baseline's top 512 is chosen among shared genes (top_k_encode, F[:, cols]), but the sentence's top 512 comes from the full panel. The fix is to rebuild the baseline from the full-panel sentence. I confirmed parity numerically: 0.7905 vs model 0.7894, delta -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115]. Minor slips: the share of RPE1-only genes is given as mean 13.4% / max 21.7%, but the key says 38-133 genes (13.2% / 26%). These don't affect the finding.

Confirmed by rerunning. Standardising on K562 gives RPE1 rank features |z| up to 7,395 (5,989 even with full-panel selection), while the model arm's maximum is 12.2. Clipping at 50 raises the shared-selection rank arm to 0.7953, and model - rank becomes -0.0060 [-0.0173, +0.0055], which is parity. The model arm doesn't change. The problem is independent of the documented error: with full-panel selection plus clip 50, the rank arm is 0.8018 and model - rank = -0.0125 [-0.0236, -0.0013]. This is a robustness problem in how near-constant source features are scaled, not the generic 'scaler fit on K562' false alarm. It overstates that it 'alone' produces the advantage, since the selection error does so independently.

The key lists this as a valid issue (CIs ignore training variation). I checked it with 20 refits on resampled K562 cells. The SD of model - rank is 0.027 (range -0.059 to +0.068), and the model arm's R_diff alone has SD 0.030. That is about 4x the SD implied by the reported CI, so the review's 'several-fold' claim holds and the interval does not support a firm claim that the effect is above 0.

Confirmed. The median-error paired bootstrap gives model - expr_512_rank = +2.42 deg [+1.64, +3.28], with the model worse in 100% of draws (+3.09 deg against the full-panel baseline). The SUMMARY admits the metrics disagree but still concludes the model 'transfers phase better'. That is a real inconsistency in the conclusion, not only a matter of style. The key doesn't cover it.

This matches the key's other_real_issues: alpha is fixed at 1000 and untuned, the verdict depends on alpha, and K562 CV picks 1e4. The review's figure at alpha 1e4 (model - sentence_rank +0.024 [0.015, 0.035]) matches the key's +0.0243 [+0.0145, +0.0348]. The key says to grade this as neither detection nor false alarm.

The data-processing-inequality point is correct: activations are a deterministic function of the sentence, so 'adds information' really means 'more linearly decodable or transferable under ridge'. But it is a wording and framing correction that changes no number or verdict.

Its main claim is that the tokenisation-loss breakdown is inflated by the faulty rank arm and that the model wins back about 0, not 0.015. That is a downstream effect of the documented error; the key's corrected tokenisation loss is 0.0868 and the corrected model - rank about 0. It relies on F1 rather than naming the shared-gene selection itself, so I don't count it as a separate detection. Its circularity argument (the label is built from marker magnitudes that are also features) is one of the key's listed possible false alarms.

Conclusion 3 does generalise from one model, layer, alpha and cell-line pair without qualification. That is a fair but minor scope point, and the SUMMARY caveats already list the narrow scope. It is close to the key's 'one layer / same lab' possible false alarm.

grade_b.detection_reason: F1 meets the detection rule. It points at top_k_encode in code/transfer.py:45-58 and 100-101. It says the baseline takes the top 512 among the 6,544 shared genes, while the cell sentences were ranked over all genes of each line's matrix (cell_sentences.anndata_to_ranked_genes). It also says this changes which shared genes RPE1 sentences contain and at what rank. Its fix is to build the baseline from the exact sentences and then project onto the shared genes. I reproduced its corrected number: the stable-sort full-panel selection restricted to the shared genes gives R_diff 0.7905, against 0.7894 for the model. The key gives the same value, model - baseline = -0.0011 [-0.0132, +0.0111], verdict PARITY. One small slip: F1 says at most 21.7% of a sentence is RPE1-only genes, but the true maximum is 133/512 = 26%. The mean of about 13% is correct. No other finding states the shared-gene vs full-panel selection mechanism on its own.

findings.reason: This is the key's error. top_k_encode picks the top 512 within the shared-gene columns, but the model's sentence picks them from the full panel. F1 names the location and the mechanism (different shared genes and ranks in RPE1) and prescribes building the baseline from the sentence's full-panel selection. I recomputed the exact-sentence baseline: R_diff 0.7905, PARITY. This matches the key's correct result (-0.0011, CI spans 0). Minor numeric slip: the maximum non-shared fraction is 26%, not 21.7%.

Confirmed by rerunning. With the K562-fit StandardScaler, the rank arm's RPE1 inputs reach max |z| of about 7,395, while the model arm stays at 12.2. Clipping both arms at |z| 100/50/20 raises the shared-gene rank arm from 0.774 to 0.786/0.795/0.808 and leaves the model unchanged at 0.789. So at clip 50 the +0.015 advantage disappears. The same pathology appears with the correct full-panel selection (max |z| 5,989; 0.7905 rises to 0.802 at clip 50), so it is a separate scaling/robustness problem and not the documented error. It is not the generic 'train/test scaler mismatch' false alarm, because it shows a concrete arm-specific effect on the verdict.

The key lists this as valid but minor: the bootstrap covers only target cells, and the ridge is never refit on resampled K562 cells. I refit on bootstrap resamples of K562 (12 draws) and got an SD of about 0.028 for the contrast, with 3 of 12 draws negative. That roughly confirms the reviewer's 0.032. With-replacement resampling interacts with the near-constant rank features, though. Subsampling 2,000 K562 cells without replacement gives an SD of about 0.009 with every draw positive. So the 'several-fold' size of the problem is partly overstated.

Confirmed exactly. Paired bootstrap of median angular error, model - expr_512_rank = +2.41 deg [+1.57, +3.34], with the model worse in 100% of draws. SUMMARY mentions the disagreement as a caveat (23 vs 21 deg) but still concludes the model 'transfers phase better'. The conflict is significant and is ignored by the R_diff-only verdict. The model is also worse on median error against the corrected baseline, so this issue is independent of the documented error.

This matches the key's other_real_issues: the untuned alpha=1000 drives the verdict, and K562 CV picks alpha=1e4. The reviewer's alpha=1e4 contrast against the exact-sentence baseline, +0.024 [0.015, 0.035], matches the key's +0.0243 [+0.0145, +0.0348]. The key says to grade this as a valid concern, neither a detection nor a false alarm.

Valid conceptual point. Per extract_activations.py, the layer-21 activations are a deterministic function of the prompt plus the gene-list sentence. So 'adds information beyond its input' cannot hold in an information-theoretic sense. The comparison measures how linearly decodable and transferable phase is under one ridge readout. This is an interpretation and wording overclaim in Conclusion 1, not something in the key, and it does not change the numbers.

Its core claim is a consequence of the documented error. The tokenisation-loss breakdown (0.104, and 'model wins back 0.015') rests on the faulty rank arm. Against the sentence-matched baseline the loss is about 0.088 and the model wins back about 0, consistent with the key's corrected tokenisation loss of +0.0868 and PARITY. It does not itself state the shared-gene vs full-panel selection; it depends on F1 and F2. It also brings in the phase-label circularity argument, which the key lists as a possible false alarm. Not counted as an independent detection.

Conclusion 3 does generalise beyond one model, one layer, one alpha and one cell-line pair. But the caveats already state this scope limit, and the key treats it as scope, not an error. The point is true but minor; the parts that matter are covered by F1 and F5.

review.summary:
I re-ran the pipeline inline and got the published numbers exactly (model 0.7894, expr_512_rank 0.7741, contrast +0.0153 [+0.0022, +0.0283]). The headline claim does not hold up: "layer 21 adds information beyond its input, and C2S beats its own input encoding."

1. The expr_512_rank baseline is not the model's input. It ranks the top 512 genes among the 6,544 shared genes only. The real RPE1 cell sentences rank all 8,749 RPE1 genes and contain on average 68 RPE1-only genes per cell. When the baseline is rebuilt from the actual sentence ranks, the contrast is -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115]. By the analysis's own rule that is parity.
2. The verdict depends on how the input is encoded. Encodings that carry the same or less information than the cell sentence beat the model with CIs that exclude 0: presence of the gene set only, or log-rank.
3. The bootstrap ignores how much the K562 readout varies from one training sample to another. That variation (SD 0.030) is about twice the half-width of the reported CI.
4. The second metric, median error, favours the rank baseline significantly.
5. "Adds information" is the wrong concept for a deterministic function of the input.
6. The "tokenisation loss" breakdown is skewed in two ways. The phase label is built from the same expression magnitudes used as features. The 0.036 "dropping values" cost is mostly due to how the ranks are scaled, not to lost information.

Smaller issues: ridge alpha was not tuned, and the two cell lines are normalised differently even though the README says the normalisation is the same.

findings.location: code/transfer.py lines 45-58 and 100-101 (top_k_encode over shared genes only); compare code/cell_sentences.py lines 131-133 and code/extract_activations.py line 95; README.md line 40; SUMMARY.md lines 12, 26-27
findings.description: The 'expr_512_rank' arm, which the summary calls 'the model's input', does not reproduce the cell sentence the model actually saw. top_k_encode takes each cell's top 512 among the 6,544 shared genes, using argpartition and an unstable argsort. The real cell sentence takes the top 512 among all of the line's genes (8,749 for RPE1), with a stable sort. As a result the RPE1 baseline drops genes the model saw, adds genes the model never saw, and shifts every rank. Once the baseline uses the model's actual input, the headline contrast disappears.
findings.evidence:
Checked on 300 cells per line:
- RPE1 cell sentences contain on average 67.6 (maximum 107) RPE1-only genes among their 512.
- The gene set chosen by top_k_encode overlaps the true sentence by 438/512 on average in RPE1 (minimum 391) and 486/512 in K562.
- About 60 of the top-512 genes per cell are tied at the cut-off value.

Rebuilding the rank features from the real sentences (rank over all of the line's genes with row>0, stable sort, then projected onto shared genes) gives rank arm R_diff 0.7905 vs model 0.7894. Paired bootstrap of model - rank_sentence: -0.0012, 95% CI [-0.0128, +0.0115], P(>0)=0.425. By the README's own rule that is PARITY, not 'MODEL ADDS'.

Tie-breaking alone is not the cause: a stable sort restricted to shared genes gives 0.7734 and a contrast of +0.0159. The cause is ranking over shared genes instead of the full sentence.
findings.recommended_action: Build the baseline from the exact ranked gene lists given to the model (anndata_to_ranked_genes with max_genes=512 on each line's full gene set), then project onto shared genes. Re-run the contrast. Remove the claim that expr_512_rank is 'the model's input', or make the claim true.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 26-29 and 33-34 (conclusions 1 and 3); README.md line 49 (verdict rule); code/transfer.py line 57 (linear rank coding)
findings.description: 'C2S comes out ahead of its own input encoding' depends on one arbitrary feature coding: linear ranks 512..1 fed to a standardised linear ridge. Other codings of the same information beat the model, including one that carries strictly less information (gene-set presence without order). So there is no single 'fair baseline', and the verdict flips with the coding.
findings.evidence:
Same ridge (alpha=1000), same K562 to RPE1 protocol, 2,000-draw paired bootstrap on RPE1:
- presence of the top-512 set, original selection: R_diff 0.8061. model - presence = -0.0168 [-0.0285, -0.0055].
- log(1+rank): 0.8048. model - logrank = -0.0155 [-0.0270, -0.0044].
- presence of the real sentence genes: 0.8202. model - presence_sentence = -0.0308 [-0.0412, -0.0203].

The model loses to all three.
findings.recommended_action: Do not claim the model beats its input encoding. Report several input-equivalent codings and treat the strongest one (or a nonlinear readout on the input) as the bar. Rephrase conclusions 1 and 3 accordingly.

findings.location: code/transfer.py lines 113-119 (bootstrap resamples only RPE1 cells with fixed predictions); SUMMARY.md lines 18 and 27
findings.description: The paired bootstrap only accounts for which RPE1 cells are sampled. The ridge readouts are fit once on one fixed set of 3,000 K562 cells, so variation from the training sample is ignored. That variation dominates the model-vs-rank contrast. The statement that the CI excludes 0 therefore understates the uncertainty.
findings.evidence: I refit both readouts (scaler and ridge, alpha=1000) on 30 bootstrap resamples of K562 cells and scored each on all RPE1 cells. model - expr_512_rank: mean +0.028, SD 0.0305, range -0.049 to +0.074. 6 of 30 refits (20%) gave a difference of 0 or below. The reported CI half-width is about 0.013.
findings.recommended_action: Use a two-level bootstrap (resample K562 cells and refit, plus resample RPE1 cells), or repeated cross-validated fits. Report that interval and apply the verdict rule to it.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 13, 27 and 39-40; code/transfer.py lines 113-130 (no bootstrap of median error)
findings.description: The second metric points the other way, and significantly. The summary mentions the disagreement only as a caveat but still concludes in conclusion 1 that layer 21 'transfers phase better'. Median error is never bootstrapped, so readers cannot see that this opposite difference is well outside noise.
findings.evidence: Paired bootstrap (2,000 draws) of median angular error, model - expr_512_rank: +2.42 deg, 95% CI [+1.50, +3.40], P(>0)=1.000. The model also has the worse median error at every alpha tested from 10 to 1e5 (for example 20.8 vs 19.7 deg at alpha=1e4).
findings.recommended_action: Bootstrap the median-error contrasts and report them. Do not state that the model transfers phase 'better' when the two metrics give significant results in opposite directions.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 26-29; README.md line 49; code/transfer.py lines 134-137 (verdict strings)
findings.description: The claim is framed as an information gain ('adds information beyond its input', 'does more than copy its input'). Layer-21 activations are a deterministic function of the cell sentence, so by the data-processing inequality they cannot contain more information about phase than the sentence. The most a linear-readout difference can show is that phase is more linearly decodable and transfers better under this ridge readout. Given F2, even that holds only against one particular coding.
findings.evidence: extract_activations.py computes the activations by a forward pass on the cell-sentence text only (lines 141-152). There is no other input. A presence-only coding of the same sentence beats the model (F2), which shows the difference reflects linear accessibility, not information.
findings.recommended_action: Reword the verdict and conclusions as 'more or less linearly decodable or transferable under a ridge readout'. Do not use 'adds information'.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 22 and 30-32 (conclusion 2 decomposition); code/transfer.py line 57
findings.description: The breakdown 'dropping values costs 0.036' and 'the model wins back 0.015' treats the linear-rank coding as if it only removes magnitudes. Most of that 0.036 comes from coding membership as linear rank values. A presence code, which removes magnitudes and order, loses almost nothing relative to magnitudes.
findings.evidence: expr_512_mag 0.8100 vs presence of the same top-512 set 0.8061. Paired bootstrap: mag - presence = +0.0040 [+0.0002, +0.0079]. presence - rank = +0.0320 [+0.0211, +0.0425]. So about 0.032 of the 0.036 'value-dropping' cost is the rank feature coding, not lost information.
findings.recommended_action: Separate information content from feature coding: report presence, rank and log-rank versions. Restate the 'tokenisation loss' breakdown, or drop the claim that the loss is due to the tokenizer.

findings.location: code/cc_phase.py lines 56-64 (label = PCA angle of standardised marker-gene magnitudes); code/transfer.py lines 73 and 87-89 (features drawn from the same matrix); SUMMARY.md lines 20 and 30-34
findings.description: The target phase angle is a deterministic function of the log-expression magnitudes of 87 (K562) or 93 (RPE1) marker genes in the same matrix that supplies the expression features. Magnitude-based arms can partly rebuild the label's own construction, including its per-cell measurement noise. Encodings without magnitudes (ranks, and the model's text input) are penalised by construction. This inflates 'expr_full', the 0.104 'tokenisation loss' and the 'model is 0.089 below raw expression' gap. Conclusion 2 ('the loss is the tokenizer, not the model') rests on this circular benchmark.
findings.evidence: Ridge on only the 87 shared marker genes (magnitudes) gives R_diff 0.918 at alpha=1000 (0.913 at alpha=100). That is higher than expr_full on all 6,544 genes (0.878). Removing the marker genes from expr_full drops it to 0.839, and from the rank arm to 0.726.
findings.recommended_action: Use a phase label that does not share inputs with the features. Options: define phase on a held-out gene set and exclude it from all feature arms, use count splitting, or use an orthogonal ground truth. Otherwise state clearly that magnitude-based arms are advantaged by how the label is built.

findings.location: code/transfer.py line 95 (Ridge(alpha=1e3), untuned and shared across arms of 2,304 to 6,544 dimensions); SUMMARY.md lines 8-22 and 43
findings.description: Alpha is fixed and not tuned, even though the arms differ in dimension and feature scale. All arms improve at larger alpha, so the reported R_diff levels and gaps depend on this choice. The size of the model-vs-rank gap changes by about tenfold with alpha, and its sign flips at small alpha.
findings.recommended_action: Choose alpha per arm by cross-validation within K562 (for example grouped CV), or report the results across a range of alpha values.

findings.location: README.md line 18 ('Same format and normalisation'); data/k562_expression.npz vs data/rpe1_expression.npz
findings.description: The two lines are not normalised the same way. K562 values were normalised before the gene panel was subset, so the per-cell totals after expm1 vary. RPE1 was normalised on its own 8,749-gene panel to exactly 10,000. The frozen transfer applies the K562 scaler to RPE1 magnitudes, so the expr_full and expr_512_mag arms carry a systematic, cell-dependent shift in scale. The rank and model arms do not.

verdicts.reason:
The mechanism is real and it changes the size of the secondary numbers. It does not change any conclusion's direction or the headline verdict, so 'major' overstates it.

Code: cc_phase.py lines 56-64 set theta = atan2 of PC2/PC1 of the standardised log-expression of 87 (K562) / 93 (RPE1) marker genes. transfer.py lines 87-89 take every arm's features from that same matrix.

The finding's evidence reproduces exactly:
- 87 shared markers.
- Ridge on the markers alone: 0.918 at alpha 1000, 0.913 at alpha 100. expr_full on all genes: 0.878.
- Without the markers: expr_full 0.839, rank arm 0.726.
On their own these numbers do not prove circularity, because markers carry real phase signal. So I ran a direct test.

Count splitting: raw counts can be recovered exactly. Taking expm1(x) divided by each cell's smallest nonzero value gives integers (rebuild error 4e-7). I thinned the counts 50/50 into two independent copies. Labels came from copy 1. Features came either from copy 1 (shares noise with the label, like the package) or from copy 2 (independent). Results for seeds 0-3:
- expr_full minus expr_512_rank: 0.118 / 0.121 / 0.120 / 0.127 with copy-1 features, against 0.091 / 0.084 / 0.074 / 0.087 with copy-2 features.
- So shared noise inflates this gap by about 0.035, roughly 30%.
- expr_full rises by 0.04-0.05 from shared noise. The rank arm rises by only -0.005 to +0.026.
- expr_full minus expr_512_mag shows the same pattern (0.087/0.088 vs 0.065/0.070).

So magnitude arms are favoured because they can partly reproduce the label's own measurement noise. Rank encodings, and so the model's input, are penalised.

Also, only about 9.5 of the ~87 markers fall in any cell's top 512. The key's argument that 'the model's sentence contains the same genes' is therefore only partly true.

What this affects: SUMMARY.md conclusion 2 and its 0.104 tokenisation loss, the 0.089 model-vs-expr_full gap, and the 0.068/0.036 decomposition. All are overstated as measures of lost phase information.

What it does not change:
- The gap stays clearly positive (about 0.08 with independent labels), so 'the loss is mostly the encoding' still holds qualitatively.
- The headline model minus expr_512_rank contrast is not driven by this. Both arms see rank-only information.
- That contrast's real flaw is the documented one: the baseline picks each cell's top 512 from the shared genes only (key error at transfer.py line 52). This finding does not identify it.

The key lists generic label/feature circularity as a possible false alarm because nothing leaks from RPE1. That reasoning does not address the uneven benefit between encodings, which the count split shows is measurable.

review.summary: I reproduced the analysis exactly (model 0.7894, expr_512_rank 0.7741, contrast +0.0153 [+0.0022, +0.0283]). The headline claim does not hold. Conclusion 1 says the model adds information beyond its input, and Conclusion 3 says C2S comes out ahead of a fair baseline. Both depend on the expr_512_rank arm, and that arm is not the model's input. The real cell sentences rank non-zero genes over each cell line's full gene panel and break ties stably. In RPE1, about 68 of each cell's 512 sentence genes are outside the shared set, and the arm shares only about 437 of its 512 genes with the actual sentence. Around 165 genes tie at the 512th value, and only about 62 distinct values occur in the top 512, so most of the arm's rank order comes from arbitrary tie-breaking. When the arm is rebuilt from the actual sentence order, model minus input is -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], which is PARITY under the analysis's own rule. With a presence-only encoding of the same 512 genes it is -0.0308 [-0.0412, -0.0203], which means the model LOSES information. Other problems: the claim that the model 'adds information' contradicts the data-processing inequality; the ridge alpha and scaling were not swept, and the sign of the contrast flips across reasonable choices; the median-error metric gives a significant result in the opposite direction (+2.4 deg [1.5, 3.4]); the CI only resamples RPE1 test cells; the tokenisation-loss breakdown depends on the encoding and the transfer direction; the phase label is built from marker genes that the expression arms also use as features; README wrongly says both cell lines share the same normalisation; and the record has gaps for reproducing the work. Verdict for each pattern: P1 clean (constant and random floors are reported; the contrast null is a paired bootstrap). P2 present and unaddressed: the 'trivial baseline' is a weak and unfaithful encoding, and simpler encodings of the same input beat the model. P3 present: a model-internal linear-decodability contrast is read as information gain, and the label is circular with the expression features. P4 present: the inference unit is test cells, with one cell-line pair and a fixed readout. P5 present: the gene set and normalisation differ between the arms. P6 not applicable (no null finding). P7 present and partly acknowledged: one pair, one direction, one layer, one model. P8 present and unaddressed: no sweep over alpha or scaling, and only one metric is used for the verdict. P9 present: 'adds information', 'the loss is the tokenizer, not the model', 'comes out ahead'. P10 minor gaps. I did not finish a bootstrap that refits the readout on resampled K562 cells, because the machine was heavily loaded.

findings.description: The 'fair baseline' expr_512_rank is presented as the model's input ('the same information a cell sentence carries'), but it is not. When it is rebuilt from the cell sentences the model actually received, the model no longer beats its input. Against a presence-only encoding of the same 512 genes, the model is significantly worse. Conclusions 1 and 3 cannot stand.
findings.evidence: cell_sentences.py:131-133 builds each sentence from non-zero genes over the cell line's full panel, sorted with a stable descending sort. The proxy instead takes the top 512 among the 6,544 shared genes and breaks ties with argpartition and an unstable argsort. The RPE1 panel has 8,749 genes, 2,205 of them not shared, so on average 67.8 of the 512 sentence genes per RPE1 cell (max 133) are missing from the proxy. The proxy and the real sentence share only 482/512 genes per cell in K562 and 436.6/512 in RPE1 (min 318). About 165 genes tie at the 512th value, and the top 512 hold only about 62 distinct values, so most rank positions in the proxy are arbitrary tie-breaks. Same pipeline (alpha=1000, scaler fit on K562), with encodings that follow the actual sentence order: rank_exact R_diff 0.7905, presence-only 0.8202, log-rank 0.8137, versus model 0.7894. Paired bootstrap over 2,000 draws: model - rank_exact = -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], P(>0)=0.43, which is PARITY by the README rule. Model - presence_exact = -0.0308 [-0.0412, -0.0203], P(>0)=0.000, which is MODEL LOSES. The reported model - expr_512_rank = +0.0152 [+0.0024, +0.0281] reproduces.
findings.recommended_action: Build the input baseline from the exact cell sentences: each line's full panel, non-zero genes only, the same stable tie order. Report several encodings of that input (presence, rank, log-rank, rank with tie-averaging) and take the best as the input baseline. Restate Conclusions 1 and 3 as parity or loss relative to the model's input, and drop 'C2S comes out ahead'.

findings.description: The verdict rule and the summary read a difference in linear transfer accuracy as information gained or lost ('the model adds information beyond its input'; 'its processing adds a small amount of cell-cycle information'; 'the loss to raw expression is the tokenizer, not the model'). Layer 21 is a deterministic function of the cell sentence, so by the data-processing inequality it cannot contain more phase information than its input. At most, the contrast shows that one ridge readout transfers better from the activations than from one hand-chosen linear encoding. The claim that the loss is the tokenizer and not the model is a causal attribution that nothing in the analysis tests.
findings.evidence: The verdict strings at transfer.py:134-137 are 'MODEL ADDS information beyond its input encoding' and 'MODEL LOSES information'. SUMMARY.md:28-29 says the model's 'processing adds a small amount of cell-cycle information'. The only test is a frozen ridge readout with alpha=1000. As F1 shows, other encodings of the same input reach 0.80-0.82, so the size and sign of the gap depend on the encoding, not on any information content.
findings.recommended_action: Change the wording to 'linear transferability of phase under a frozen ridge readout'. Say that the model cannot add information beyond its input, only make it more or less linearly accessible. Remove the tokenizer-versus-model attribution unless a direct test supports it.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:92-96 (Ridge alpha=1e3, StandardScaler fit on source); SUMMARY.md:43
findings.description: The headline contrast depends on one ridge alpha and one scaling scheme, and neither was swept. Reasonable alternatives change the size of the model-versus-input gap and can flip its sign. Within-K562 cross-validation would not choose alpha=1000 for either arm.
findings.evidence: K562 5-fold CV R_diff: model 0.868/0.886/0.893/0.881 at alpha 1e2/1e3/1e4/1e5; rank 0.742/0.821/0.859 at 1e2/1e3/1e4. So CV prefers alpha around 1e4 for both. Transfer R_diff at alpha 1e4: model 0.821, rank 0.797, rank_exact 0.797, presence 0.827, log-rank 0.822. With per-domain standardisation at alpha 1e4: model 0.8926, rank 0.8965, so the rank arm beats the model. At alpha 1e3 with per-domain standardisation: model 0.892, rank 0.857. Across these choices the model-minus-input difference ranges from about -0.03 to +0.035, which is wider than the reported CI of about +/-0.013. The caveat 'one readout (ridge, alpha = 1000)' does not show up in the conclusions.
findings.recommended_action: Choose alpha separately for each arm by CV on K562 only. Report a sweep over at least three alpha values and at least two scaling schemes for every arm, put the worst case in the summary, and limit the claim to settings where it holds.

findings.description: The verdict uses only R_diff. The second metric, median angular error, shows a statistically clear effect in the opposite direction. The summary calls this a disagreement 'on direction' without saying it is significant, and still states that the model adds information and comes out ahead.
findings.evidence: Paired bootstrap over the same RPE1 cells (2,000 draws): median error of model minus expr_512_rank = +2.42 deg [+1.50, +3.40], P(model worse)=1.000. Against rank_exact: +3.09 [+2.15, +4.03]. Against presence: +5.38 [+4.43, +6.23]. On the second metric the model is significantly worse than every input encoding tested.
findings.recommended_action: Bootstrap both metrics and report their CIs. Fix the primary metric in advance, or require both metrics to agree before declaring 'adds'. When they conflict, report the result as inconclusive.

findings.description: The 95% CI resamples only the RPE1 test cells. The fitted K562 readout and both PCA-derived phase labels are held fixed. The claim concerns transfer across cell lines, yet there is one source/target pair and the inference unit is cells. The CI therefore understates uncertainty, and the lower bound of +0.0022 is not a reliable exclusion of zero.
findings.evidence: In transfer.py:116-119 only the target indices i are resampled, and the predictions come from a single fit. Theta for each line comes from a single PCA (cc_phase.py:53-64). Changing the encoding or alpha moves the contrast by up to about 0.05 (F1, F3), several times the reported CI half-width of about 0.013. I started a bootstrap that resamples the training cells, but it did not finish within this review because the machine was heavily loaded.
findings.recommended_action: Resample K562 training cells and refit the readout (and ideally recompute theta) inside each bootstrap draw. Report n as 1 source line and 1 target line. Test more cell-line pairs before claiming the result generalises to 'a new cell line'.

findings.description: The analysis covers one model, one layer (21, with no stated reason for choosing it), one representation (the last token), one direction (K562 to RPE1) and one seed. The caveats list one model, one layer and one readout, but Conclusions 2 and 3 are worded as general ('Comparing an SCFM with raw expression charges it for its tokenizer'). The decomposition in Conclusion 2 depends on the direction of transfer.
findings.evidence: Reverse direction, RPE1 to K562, same pipeline: model 0.758, expr_512_rank 0.632, expr_full 0.770. The model's shortfall against all-gene expression is 0.011 in this direction versus 0.089 forward, and the proxy's 'tokenisation loss' is 0.137 versus 0.104. Neither the manifests nor the README say why layer 21 was chosen or whether other layers were looked at.
findings.recommended_action: Report both transfer directions and at least a small sweep over layers. Say how layer 21 was chosen. Limit Conclusions 2 and 3 to this pair and direction.

findings.description: The phase label is the angle in the PC1-PC2 plane of the standardised expression of 87-93 Tirosh marker genes. Those same genes are features in the expression arms. The label is therefore close to a function of expr_full's inputs, which makes expr_full a circular ceiling, not an independent 'raw expression' benchmark. It also means every R_diff measures agreement with a marker-PCA proxy, not with true cell-cycle phase.
findings.evidence: A readout on the 87 shared marker genes alone reaches R_diff 0.918, above expr_full at 0.878. Removing the marker genes drops expr_full to 0.839 and expr_512_rank to 0.726. The labels are also estimated separately for each line from different marker subsets (87 in K562, 93 in RPE1) with different S-to-G2/M separations (108.8 vs 97.1 deg).
findings.recommended_action: Describe expr_full as partly circular. Report the ladder with the marker genes excluded from the features, or use a label built independently of the features (for example held-out markers, or a published reference such as tricycle). State that the endpoint is agreement with a marker-PCA phase.

findings.description: README says the two cell lines have the 'same format and normalisation'. They do not. The K562 matrix was normalised before genes were subset, while RPE1 was normalised over its own 8,749 genes, and the gene panels were filtered differently (6,546 vs 8,749 genes). In a frozen transfer with the scaler fit on K562, this mismatch affects the magnitude arms and so the 0.068 / 0.036 breakdown in Conclusion 2. It also gives the model's RPE1 sentences access to genes the K562 sentences never had.
findings.evidence: Row sums of expm1(X): K562 range 7,447-9,573; RPE1 exactly 10,000. Summed over the shared genes only: medians 9,137 (K562) vs 8,784 (RPE1). There are 2,205 RPE1-only genes, and about 68 of them appear in each RPE1 cell sentence.
findings.recommended_action: Re-normalise both lines the same way over the same gene universe, or document the difference. Rebuild the cell sentences, or at least the baselines, on the shared panel so the model and the baselines see the same genes.

findings.description: Several gaps make the work hard to reproduce. No package versions are pinned. The manifests do not record the model revision or the compute dtype (bfloat16 by default). The .h5ad files used to extract activations are not included, so there is no way to check that the activations came from the matrices in data/. transfer_results.json was written about three hours after run_log.txt; their numbers agree.
findings.evidence: The README gives only 'numpy, scipy and scikit-learn', with no versions. manifest.json has no revision hash or dtype. run_log.txt is timestamped 07:52 and transfer_results.json 10:56.
findings.recommended_action: Add pinned requirements, the model revision hash, the compute dtype and the transformers version. Include or checksum the extraction input, and record runtime and hardware.

grade_b.detection_reason: F1 meets the key's detection rule. It points at top_k_encode (code/transfer.py:45-58, used at 100-101). It says the proxy "takes the top 512 among the 6,544 shared genes", while cell_sentences.py builds each sentence from the non-zero genes over the line's full panel (RPE1 8,749 genes, 2,205 of them not shared). It gives the mean of 67.8 (max 133) sentence genes per RPE1 cell that the proxy misses, and says the proxy and the real sentence share only about 437 of 512 genes per RPE1 cell. Its fix is to build the baseline from each line's full panel using the exact sentences. Tie-breaking is mentioned, but only alongside the full-panel point, which is the main claim. I re-ran its numbers and they match exactly: rank_exact 0.7905; model - rank_exact -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], P(>0) 0.43, which is parity (the key's exact-sentence result is -0.0011 [-0.0132, +0.0111]); and the original +0.0152 [+0.0024, +0.0281] reproduces. So F1 reaches the key's corrected verdict, parity.

findings.reason: F1 names the shared-gene versus full-panel selection in top_k_encode, gives the 2,205 RPE1-only genes and about 68 missing sentence genes per cell, and prescribes a full-panel or exact-sentence baseline. That matches the key's error and detection rule. I reproduced its numbers: rank_exact 0.7905; model - rank_exact -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115] (parity, matching the key's -0.0011); presence_exact 0.8202; model - presence -0.0308 [-0.0412, -0.0203]. The extra presence-only 'model loses' claim is checked at alpha 1000 only. It goes beyond the key but does not undermine the detection.

The data-processing-inequality point is correct. Layer-21 activations are a deterministic function of the cell sentence, so 'adds information beyond its input' and 'processing adds cell-cycle information' are wrong as stated. At most the model makes phase more linearly accessible to one ridge readout. This targets the wording of Conclusion 1 and the verdict label, and is not in the key. It is interpretive and does not change the numerical contrast. The tokenizer-versus-model attribution is also untested, as F2 says.

The key's other_real_issues explicitly lists alpha fixed at 1000 and not tuned, with the verdict depending on it, as a valid concern that is neither a detection nor a false alarm. I verified F3's numbers. Under frozen transfer at alpha 1e4: model 0.8209, rank 0.7966. With per-domain standardisation: model 0.8921 vs rank 0.8565 at 1e3, and 0.8926 vs 0.8965 at 1e4. The key confirms K562 CV picks about 1e4. Per-domain scaling departs from the frozen-transfer design, but the main point, that the result is sensitive to alpha, is valid.

Verified. The paired bootstrap of median angular error gives model minus expr_512_rank +2.42 deg [1.50, 3.40], against rank_exact +3.09 [2.15, 4.03], and against presence +5.38 [4.43, 6.23]. P(model worse) is 1.0 in each case. SUMMARY mentions the direction disagreement as a caveat but not its significance, and still says the model 'comes out ahead'. This is a genuine overstatement that the key does not cover. It was partly disclosed, and the pre-specified metric was R_diff.

Correct: only RPE1 test cells are resampled, and the ridge and labels are fixed. The key lists this as a valid but minor issue (training variation is not in the intervals). F5 supports 'not a reliable exclusion of zero' partly with variation across encodings and alpha values, which is systematic, not sampling uncertainty. It also admits its own retraining bootstrap did not finish.

This is mainly scope: one model, one layer, one direction. The key lists 'only one layer' as stated scope, not an error. The reverse-direction numbers check out (model 0.7583, expr_512_rank 0.6323, expr_full 0.7696), and the point that Conclusions 2 and 3 are worded too generally is fair. Still, it is a caveat about generalisation, not an error in the analysis.

The key's possible_false_alarms lists this exact circularity argument, that the phase label comes from marker genes that are also expression features. The label is the common target for every arm, the model's sentences contain the same marker genes, and nothing leaks from RPE1 into training. The facts F7 cites (87/93 markers, 108.8 vs 97.1 deg separation) are true, but calling expr_full a 'circular ceiling' and treating that as a defect is the anticipated false alarm.

Verified. K562 expm1 row sums range from 7,447 to 9,573 (median 9,137), while RPE1 sums are exactly 10,000, so README's 'same format and normalisation' is inaccurate. Over shared genes only, the medians are 9,137 and 8,784. The effect on the magnitude arms and the 0.068/0.036 breakdown is asserted but not shown. The point about RPE1-only genes in the sentences overlaps with F1. A real but small documentation and data-consistency issue.

True but trivial reproducibility gaps. No pinned versions, the manifests lack the model revision and compute dtype, and the h5ad files are not included. The timestamps really do differ (run_log 07:52, transfer_results 10:56), and their contents agree. None of this affects the results; the key notes that the run reproduces the outputs byte for byte.

review.summary: I reproduced the run (alpha=1000: model 0.789, expr_512_rank 0.774, expr_full 0.878, matching outputs/run_log.txt) and checked all ten checklist patterns. The headline verdict, "the model adds information beyond its input" (+0.0153 [+0.0022, +0.0283]), does not hold up. The expr_512_rank baseline does not encode what the model actually received. The RPE1 cell sentences are ranked over all 8,749 RPE1 genes: on average 68 (max 133) of the 512 genes per sentence are RPE1-only, and only 437 of 512 genes overlap with the baseline's gene set. A rank baseline built exactly like extract_activations.py/cell_sentences.py builds the sentence scores R_diff 0.7905. Against it, model minus baseline is -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], which is PARITY under the analysis's own rule. The verdict is also fragile in several other ways. (1) On median error the model is significantly worse than its input encoding (+2.4 deg [1.5, 3.4]), so this is a real reversal, not mere disagreement between metrics. (2) The model-minus-rank delta changes sign and size with the ridge alpha, from -0.041 at alpha=1 to +0.173 at alpha=1e5. At alpha=1e4, which K562-only cross-validation picks for the model arm, it is +0.024. (3) The bootstrap resamples only RPE1 cells. Refitting on resampled K562 cells gives a source-side SD of about 0.03-0.04 in the delta, and 3 of 10 refits are negative. (4) Only one direction was tested: RPE1 to K562 gives a much larger model advantage (+0.19 over the matched rank baseline), so the size, and at alpha=1000 even the sign, depends on the setting. The wording "adds information" and "the loss is the tokenizer, not the model" also overreaches: a deterministic function of the input cannot add information about it; what was measured is linear-ridge transferability. Per-pattern verdicts: P1 present and unaddressed (minor: only constant/random floors, no layer-0 or untrained-model null for the 'processing' claim); P2 present and unaddressed (critical: the matched-input baseline is mis-built); P3 present and unaddressed (major: information claim vs ridge decodability; the label is a linear function of expression magnitudes); P4 present and unaddressed (major: target-only bootstrap); P5 present and unaddressed (minor: label-defining genes are features, and 6 RPE1-only markers enter the RPE1 label; layer 21 and alpha unjustified); P6 clean (expression arms act as positive controls; the headline is not a null finding); P7 present but partly acknowledged (minor: one direction, one layer, one model; the reverse direction differs a lot); P8 present and unaddressed (major: no alpha sweep); P9 present and unaddressed (major); P10 present and unaddressed (minor: no version pins, model revision or data hash).

findings.location: code/transfer.py:45-58 and :101 (top_k_encode, expr_512_rank arm); README.md:40-41; SUMMARY.md:12, 18, 26-29
findings.description: The expr_512_rank arm is presented as 'the model's input' and as carrying 'the same information a cell sentence carries', but it is not the encoding the model received. top_k_encode ranks each cell's top-512 genes among only the 6,544 shared genes, breaking ties arbitrarily with argpartition. The model's cell sentences (cell_sentences.anndata_to_ranked_genes, called from extract_activations.py) rank nonzero genes over all columns of each cell line with a stable sort. For RPE1 that is 8,749 genes, so RPE1-only genes take up sentence slots and shift the ranks of the shared genes. With a faithful baseline, the headline contrast turns from 'model adds' into PARITY under the analysis's own verdict rule.
findings.evidence: Recomputed: RPE1 model sentences contain on average 67.8 (max 133) non-shared genes in their top 512. The overlap between the sentence gene set and the expr_512_rank gene set averages 436.9/512 in RPE1 (min 328) and 481.6/512 in K562. A rank arm built exactly as the model's sentence (all genes, nonzero only, stable sort, positions 512..1, mapped to shared columns), with the same scaler, ridge alpha=1000 and protocol, scores R_diff 0.7905 (median error 20.3 deg) against 0.7741 for expr_512_rank. Paired bootstrap (2,000 draws), model minus faithful rank: -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], P(>0)=0.43. That interval contains 0, so the rule in transfer.py:132-137 returns PARITY. The reported model minus expr_512_rank (+0.0152 [+0.0024, +0.0281]) reproduces exactly. A shared-genes-only stable-sort arm gives 0.7734, so the gap comes from the RPE1-only genes, not from tie handling.
findings.recommended_action: Rebuild the input-encoding arm from the exact sentences used for extraction: same gene universe per cell line, nonzero-only, stable sort, and ideally the saved gene lists. Rerun the verdict. Withdraw or restate Conclusion 1 and the +0.0153 figure. At the stated settings the result is parity.

findings.description: The verdict uses only R_diff. On the second metric the analysis reports, median angular error, the model is significantly worse than its input encoding. The summary calls this a mere 'disagreement' in a caveat but still headlines 'the model adds information' and 'C2S comes out ahead'. The two metrics give opposite significant answers, so the claim depends on the metric.
findings.evidence: Paired bootstrap (2,000 draws, same cells), median error of model minus expr_512_rank: +2.42 deg [+1.50, +3.40], P(model worse)=1.00. At alpha=1e4, model minus faithful rank: +1.70 deg [+0.74, +2.61]. From the alpha sweep, the model's median error is also worse than expr_512_rank at alpha 100, 1,000 and 10,000 (28.9 vs 25.9; 23.3 vs 20.9; 20.8 vs 19.7).
findings.recommended_action: Bootstrap the median-error contrast too, and state the verdict for both metrics. If they diverge, report a metric-dependent result rather than 'model adds information'.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:95 (Ridge(alpha=1e3) for all arms); README.md:36; SUMMARY.md:43
findings.description: The verdict depends heavily on the single fixed ridge penalty, which is shared by arms of very different dimension and sparsity (2,304 dense activations vs 6,544 sparse rank features). No sweep or per-arm tuning on the source line was done, so the sign and size of the headline delta and of the 'tokenisation loss' are tied to an arbitrary alpha.
findings.evidence: Transfer R_diff for model / expr_512_rank / expr_full by alpha: 1: 0.591/0.632/0.847; 10: 0.661/0.638/0.848; 100: 0.708/0.681/0.854; 1e3: 0.789/0.774/0.878; 1e4: 0.821/0.797/0.897; 1e5: 0.795/0.622/0.818. Model minus rank therefore runs from -0.041 to +0.173. 5-fold CV on K562 alone picks alpha=1e4 for the model (CV R 0.893). At alpha=1e4, model minus faithful rank is +0.024 [+0.015, +0.035], while at alpha=1e3 it is parity (F1).
findings.recommended_action: Choose alpha per arm by cross-validation on the source line only, and report a sweep of at least 3 points with the worst case. Limit any verdict to the alpha range where it holds.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:113-130 (bootstrap resamples target cells only, readout fixed); SUMMARY.md:4, 18
findings.description: The 95% CI reflects only resampling of RPE1 test cells. The K562 fit (scaler + ridge) is treated as fixed, so variability from the training sample is ignored. The model arm's readout is much less stable than the rank arm's, so the reported CI is far too narrow for a claim about the model compared with its input encoding.
findings.evidence: 10 refits on bootstrap-resampled K562 cells (alpha=1e3), each scored on all RPE1 cells. Model R_diff ranges 0.687-0.826; expr_512_rank ranges 0.736-0.770. Model minus rank per draw: +0.043, +0.021, +0.003, +0.072, +0.039, +0.049, +0.047, -0.016, -0.049, +0.066 (SD about 0.038, 3 of 10 negative). Model minus faithful rank per draw: +0.024, +0.005, -0.005, +0.053, +0.019, +0.040, +0.035, -0.020, -0.061, +0.030. By contrast, the reported CI half-width is about 0.013.
findings.recommended_action: Use a two-level bootstrap that resamples both source cells (with a refit) and target cells, or repeated source subsampling. Report the delta with that interval and name the inference unit: one source-target cell-line pair.

findings.description: The language goes beyond the evidence. Layer-21 activations are a deterministic function of the cell sentence, so they cannot carry more information about the input than the input does. What was measured is how well a fixed-alpha linear ridge readout transfers. Calling the expr_512_rank delta 'the input format alone costs 0.104 before the first layer' treats a linear readout of one hand-made encoding as the information ceiling of the input. 'The loss is the tokenizer, not the model' and 'C2S comes out ahead' (generalised to 'an SCFM') extrapolate from one model, one layer, one alpha and one transfer direction.
findings.evidence: The verdict rule maps a CI above 0 to 'MODEL ADDS information'. The 0.104 'tokenisation loss' itself depends on the encoding and the alpha: with the faithful sentence encoding it is 0.878-0.791=0.088 at alpha=1e3, and 0.10-0.22 across alphas (F3). Conclusion 3 generalises from a single model to SCFMs.
findings.recommended_action: Rephrase as 'layer-21 activations are (or are not) more linearly transferable than a linear readout of the rank-encoded input under ridge alpha=X'. Drop 'adds information' and 'the loss is the tokenizer, not the model', and limit Conclusion 3 to this model, layer and setting.

findings.description: The target label is a linear projection (PCA in each line) of standardised Tirosh marker-gene magnitudes. The expression arms contain those same genes as features, so magnitude-based arms are favoured by how the label is built. Part of the 'tokenisation loss' and of the 'dropping values' cost (0.036) comes from this construction rather than from the input format. Also, the RPE1 label uses 93 marker genes against 87 in K562. The six RPE1-only markers (CCNE2, EXO1, GAS2L3, MSH2, UBE2C, WDR76) are excluded from every expression arm but can appear in the model's RPE1 sentences (in 18.8% of cells). This asymmetry favours the model.
findings.evidence: phase_angle runs SVD on the marker submatrix of the same expression matrix used as expr_* features. The n_cc_genes info gives 87 (K562) and 93 (RPE1). Recomputed: on average 0.19 RPE1-only markers per RPE1 sentence; 18.8% of cells have at least one.
findings.recommended_action: Note the circularity in the summary. Optionally define the label on a held-out marker set, or exclude the label genes from the features and the sentences as a sensitivity check. Restrict the label to markers present in both lines.

findings.description: The finding is based on one transfer direction, one layer (21, with no stated reason for choosing it), one model and one readout. The reverse direction is cheap to run and gives a very different answer. The caveat lists single model/layer/readout but not single direction, and the conclusions are worded generally.
findings.evidence: RPE1 to K562 at alpha=1e3: model R_diff 0.758 (median 25.0 deg); expr_512_rank 0.632 (27.4 deg); faithful sentence-rank 0.570. Model minus rank is +0.126 [+0.108, +0.144], an effect about 8 times larger than the forward result, which is parity against the faithful baseline. Within-K562 5-fold CV: model 0.886, rank 0.821.
findings.recommended_action: Report both directions, explain why layer 21 was chosen (or show a layer sweep), and state that the effect size depends on direction.

findings.description: The only nulls are trivial floors (constant and uniform-random angles, R_diff about 0.02-0.04). Nothing tests whether a model-independent re-representation would close the gap with the rank encoding, so the 'model processing' interpretation is not anchored to a matched null. Examples: layer-0 / embedding-only activations, a randomly initialised model of the same architecture, or a random nonlinear feature map of the same rank encoding with 2,304 dimensions.
findings.evidence: No such arm appears in transfer.py. The constant and random floors only show that phase is decodable at all.
findings.recommended_action: Add a layer-0 (or untrained-model) arm and/or a random-feature arm of matched dimension through the same frozen-transfer and bootstrap pipeline. Report the layer-21 gain relative to that null.

findings.description: Reproducibility gaps. There are no package versions. The model revision or commit hash is not recorded (manifest has only 'vandijklab/C2S-Scale-Gemma-2-2B'), and neither are the input .h5ad path/hash or the tokenizer version. The per-cell gene lists actually fed to the model are not saved either. That is the information F1 shows is needed to build a matched baseline and to confirm the activations match data/.
findings.evidence: The manifests hold only model name, unit, layers, max_genes, prompt, store_dtype, n_cells, n_rows and d_model. The README says only 'Needs numpy, scipy and scikit-learn'.
findings.recommended_action: Pin versions (requirements file), record the model revision and input-file hashes in the manifest, and save each cell's sentence gene list alongside the activations.

grade_a.detection_reason: F1 meets the detection rule. It points to top_k_encode (code/transfer.py:45-58) and says the function ranks each cell's top 512 among only the 6,544 shared genes. The model's sentence instead ranks over all of the cell line's genes (RPE1 8,749), so RPE1-only genes take sentence slots and push down the ranks of the shared genes. Its fix is to use the same gene universe for each cell line. Its numbers match the key and my rerun. RPE1 sentences hold 67.8 non-shared genes on average (my rerun: range 38-133). A faithful sentence-rank arm gives R_diff 0.7905, and model minus that arm is -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], P(>0) 0.43, so the verdict is PARITY. The key's exact-sentence value is -0.0011 [-0.0132, +0.0111]. F1 also shows that a stable sort over shared genes only gives 0.7734, so it rules out tie-breaking as the cause.

findings.reason: Names the shared-gene vs full-panel top-512 selection in top_k_encode and says it changes both genes and ranks. Prescribes the full-panel, sentence-faithful encoding. Shows the verdict flips to PARITY. I reproduced it: faithful arm 0.7905, model minus faithful -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], P 0.43. This matches the key's correct result.

Confirmed by rerun. On median angular error, model minus expr_512_rank is +2.42 deg [+1.50, +3.40], P(model worse)=1.00. Against the faithful arm it is +3.09 deg [+2.15, +4.03]. The SUMMARY caveat does say the two metrics disagree, but it never tests that difference and still headlines 'model adds information'. The verdict rests on R_diff alone, so the headline depends on the metric. This is real but only partly disclosed, and it is not the key's error.

Matches the key's other_real_issues: alpha is fixed at 1000, never tuned, and the verdict depends on it. K562 CV picks alpha 1e4, and there model minus the faithful rank arm is +0.024 [+0.015, +0.035]. The key's exact-sentence figure is +0.0243 [+0.0145, +0.0348]. The key says to grade this as a valid concern, neither a detection nor a false alarm.

Listed in the key's other_real_issues as valid but minor: the bootstrap resamples only target cells and does not refit the ridge. I refit on resampled K562 cells and the reviewer's first six draws reproduce exactly (model minus rank +0.043, +0.021, +0.003, +0.072, +0.039, +0.049). Variation across training resamples is far larger than the reported CI half-width.

Mostly a wording point. 'Adds information' really means 'more linearly transferable under ridge alpha=1000'. Conclusion 3's generalisation to SCFMs goes beyond the evidence. These points are fair but about framing. The single model/layer scope is already in the caveats. The faithful-encoding tokenisation loss of about 0.088 overlaps F1 and the key's correct value of +0.0868.

The main claim, that the label is circular because marker genes are also expression features and this favours magnitude arms, is listed in the key's possible_false_alarms. The label is the target for every arm, and the sentences contain the same genes. The secondary point checks out: 87 vs 93 markers, six RPE1-only markers, 0.19 per sentence on average, 18.8% of cells. But it is trivial in size and is the kind of 'sentence contains genes outside the shared set' point the key says is not decisive.

A scope point: one direction, one layer, no reason given for choosing layer 21. The key treats one-layer scope as stated in the caveats and not an error. The reverse-direction result was not checked, and it does not show the forward analysis is wrong.
Suggests a design extension: a layer-0 arm, an untrained-model arm, or a matched random-feature null. This is reasonable but optional, and it does not identify an error in the reported result.

True: the manifests record only the model name, layers, max_genes and similar settings, with no revision, file hashes or package versions. But the key confirms the data and activations are byte-identical to the source and that the run reproduces exactly. This is a minor reproducibility gap.

grade_b.detection_reason: F1 meets the detection rule. It names top_k_encode (code/transfer.py:45-58) and says it ranks each cell's top 512 genes among only the 6,544 shared genes. It contrasts this with the model's sentence, which ranks nonzero genes over each cell line's full panel (RPE1 8,749), and says the RPE1-only genes take sentence slots and push down the ranks of the shared genes. Its fix is to use the same gene universe per cell line. It also separates the effect from tie-breaking: a shared-only stable-sort arm gives 0.7734, so the gap comes from the RPE1-only genes. I reproduced its numbers. The exact-sentence rank arm scores R_diff 0.7905. Model minus that arm is -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], which is PARITY and matches the key's -0.0011 [-0.0132, +0.0111]. The reported +0.0152 [+0.0024, +0.0281] against the package's expr_512_rank also reproduces.

findings.reason: This is the key's documented error: the top-512 is chosen within the shared genes instead of the full panel, and it points at top_k_encode lines 45-58. The numbers reproduce (sentence-faithful rank 0.7905; model minus that arm -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], PARITY) and match the key's correct result. It overturns the headline 'MODEL ADDS' verdict.

Confirmed. The paired bootstrap of median error, model minus expr_512_rank, gives +2.42 deg [+1.50, +3.40] with P=1.00, and model minus the sentence-faithful arm gives +3.09 [+2.15, +4.03]. So on the second reported metric the model is significantly worse. SUMMARY mentions the disagreement only as a caveat and still headlines 'model adds' and 'comes out ahead'. The issue is partly disclosed, but its significance is not, and it undercuts the headline. It is not in the key, but it is not a listed false alarm either.

The key's other_real_issues lists this explicitly: alpha is fixed at 1000 and the verdict depends on it, while K562 CV picks 10000. The key says to grade it as neither detection nor false alarm. The reviewer's figure at alpha 1e4 (model minus faithful rank +0.024 [+0.015, +0.035]) matches the key's +0.0243 [+0.0145, +0.0348].

The key lists this as a valid issue: the bootstrap covers only target cells and the ridge is not refit. I reproduced 10 source-resample refits. Model minus rank ranges from about -0.049 to +0.072 (SD 0.036), against a reported CI half-width of about 0.013. So the reported interval leaves out substantial training variability. The key calls it minor, but the evidence is real and it bears on whether the headline CI is credible.

The interpretive point is valid. Layer-21 activations are a deterministic function of the sentence, so 'adds information' really means better linear transferability under one fixed alpha. 'The loss is the tokenizer' and the generalisation to SCFMs also overreach from one model, layer and direction. Its supporting figure (tokenisation loss about 0.088 with the faithful encoding) is consistent with the key's +0.0868. It targets the framing of the headline conclusions rather than a computational bug.

The main claim, that the label is built from marker genes that are also features and so is circular, is a listed possible false alarm: the label is the same target for every arm and is not a leak. The secondary point is factually true (6 RPE1-only markers; I found them in 18.8% of RPE1 sentences, mean 0.19 per cell). But the claim that this asymmetry 'favours the model' is unsupported, because the K562-trained readout never sees these genes in any arm.

The reverse-direction numbers reproduce (RPE1 to K562: model 0.758, shared-rank 0.632, sentence-rank 0.570). But a single direction, layer and model is a scope limitation; the key treats one layer and one setting as scope, not error. It does not show the forward headline is wrong.

This suggests an extra null arm (layer-0, untrained model or random features). It is a reasonable design improvement, but the analysis's comparison against its input encoding is the stated design. It identifies no error.

True: the manifests have no model revision or input hashes, and the README lists packages without versions. But per the key's known facts, the data match the source files, the activations are byte-identical to the original project's files, and the run reproduces exactly. These are housekeeping gaps.

review.summary: I reviewed B7148 against all ten checklist patterns. I re-ran the pipeline in memory and reproduced every number (expr_512_rank R_diff 0.7741, model 0.7894, delta +0.0153 [+0.0022, +0.0283]). The headline claim is that layer 21 "adds information beyond its input". That claim does not survive, because the baseline arm said to be "the model's input" is not what the model receives. It picks the top 512 from the shared genes only, and it breaks the very common ties at random. The cell sentences rank all of each line's genes (on average 68 of the 512 genes in an RPE1 sentence are RPE1-only) and order ties by column index. If the baseline uses exactly the sentence's genes and order, the verdict becomes PARITY (-0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115]). If it uses only whether each of those genes is present, the model LOSES (-0.031 [-0.041, -0.020]). Other problems: (1) on median angular error the model is significantly worse than every input-encoding baseline. (2) The contrast depends on the single, untuned ridge alpha. (3) The CI covers only resampling of RPE1 cells, for one transfer direction. The reverse direction gives a very different effect size. (4) The phase label is computed from the magnitudes of the marker genes themselves, so the "tokenisation loss" breakdown largely measures distance from how the label was built. (5) "Adds information" and "the loss is the tokenizer" go further than a linear-readout comparison can support. Pattern verdicts: P1 present and unaddressed: the only reference points are constant/random, and there is no noise floor for the contrast; swapping between equally informative encodings moves R_diff by about 0.016, the same size as the headline delta. I ran a random-tanh-features check (R about 0.61); it did not explain the model's score. P2 present and unaddressed: one weak featurisation of the input was the only baseline. P3 present and unaddressed: label circularity. P4 present and unaddressed: inference over cells for a claim about a single cell-line pair. P5 present and unaddressed: tie-breaking and gene-panel mismatch in the selection. P6 not applicable (the result is positive). P7 present and partly acknowledged. P8 present and unaddressed: no alpha sweep, and the second metric was not bootstrapped. P9 present and unaddressed. P10 minor: no pinned versions or model revision.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:45-58 and 101 (top_k_encode / expr_512_rank); README.md:40-41; SUMMARY.md:12-13, 18, 26-29; outputs/run_log.txt:13,19
findings.description: The expr_512_rank arm is not the model's input encoding, and the headline verdict 'MODEL ADDS information' depends on this mismatch. The cell sentences (cell_sentences.py:131-133) take the top 512 nonzero genes from each line's full gene panel (K562 6,546, RPE1 8,749) and order ties stably by column index. top_k_encode instead takes the top 512 from the 6,544 shared genes only, and np.argpartition/argsort break ties arbitrarily, both for which genes make the cut and for the ranks they get. Ties are everywhere: log1p values of low counts repeat a lot. When the baseline is built to match what the model sees, the verdict flips.
findings.evidence: In 300 sampled RPE1 cells, an average of 68.4 (range 39-111) of the 512 sentence genes are RPE1-only. The analysis's 512 genes overlap the real sentence by only 436.8/512 in RPE1, and by only 480.9/512 even in K562. Median 169 genes are tied at the 512th value and only about 61-64 distinct values occur among the top 512. Re-run at the analysis's own settings (alpha=1000, paired bootstrap over RPE1 cells): baseline using exactly the sentence's genes and order (shared columns, rank) R_diff 0.7905, model minus baseline -0.0012 [-0.0128, +0.0115], which is PARITY under the README rule. Tie-averaged ranks: R 0.7845, delta +0.0048 [-0.0071, +0.0174], PARITY. Presence only (1 if the gene is in the sentence): R 0.8202, delta -0.0308 [-0.0412, -0.0203], MODEL LOSES. Log-rank of the same genes: R 0.7712, delta +0.018. So switching between equally informative encodings moves R_diff by as much as the headline +0.0153.
findings.recommended_action: Build the baseline from the exact cell sentences used for extraction: the same full-panel top 512, the same stable tie order, nonzero genes only. Report several information-equivalent encodings (rank, tie-averaged rank, log-rank, presence) and let the strongest one be the comparator. Restate the verdict. On current evidence it is parity or loss, not gain, for K562 to RPE1. Correct SUMMARY line 4 and README line 41, which imply the arms share one gene universe and identical information.

findings.description: On the second reported metric, median angular error, the model is significantly worse than every input-encoding baseline. The summary calls this a 'disagreement' caveat but still concludes the model 'transfers phase better'. Only R_diff was bootstrapped, so readers cannot see that the median-error gap is statistically clear.
findings.evidence: Paired bootstrap over RPE1 cells (2,000 draws, my run), model minus baseline median error: vs expr_512_rank +2.42 deg [+1.50, +3.40]; vs sentence-matched rank +3.09 [+2.15, +4.03]; vs presence +5.38 [+4.43, +6.23]. At the CV-selected alpha 1e4, model vs presence is still +3.17 deg [+2.27, +4.05].
findings.recommended_action: Bootstrap the median-error contrast too and report it alongside R_diff. Do not claim the model 'transfers phase better' when the two pre-reported metrics point in significantly opposite directions. Set out in advance which metric decides the verdict, or require both to agree.

findings.location: code/transfer.py:95 (Ridge(alpha=1e3) fixed for every arm); SUMMARY.md:18, 43
findings.description: One untuned ridge penalty is applied to feature sets of very different size and structure (2,304 activations vs 6,544 genes). The headline contrast depends on that choice, and alpha was not selected on the source data.
findings.evidence: K562 to RPE1 R_diff for alpha = 10, 100, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5. Model: 0.661, 0.708, 0.789, 0.821, 0.795. expr_512_rank: 0.638, 0.681, 0.774, 0.797, 0.622. Sentence-matched rank: 0.676, 0.714, 0.791, 0.797, 0.598. Model minus sentence-matched rank: -0.015, -0.006, -0.001, +0.024, +0.196, so the sign flips with alpha. 5-fold CV within K562 picks alpha=1e4 for all arms (model 0.893, rank 0.859). At alpha=1e4, model vs presence is -0.006 [-0.015, +0.003].
