The key says rerunning the extractors reproduces the stored embeddings, so loading worked. Housekeeping only.

review.summary:
I reran code/learn_interaction.py in memory, without writing any files, and got exactly the published numbers. The ceiling is 0.629 / 0.772 / 0.879, and the models score sum-only 0.370, saturation 0.377 and saturation+gene 0.406. The numbers reproduce, but the design behind them has two serious flaws that undermine the main results.

First, the features and the target share measurement noise. The target is I = dAB - dA - dB, and the features are built from the same estimated dA, dB and control mean. So sampling noise in the singles shows up with opposite signs in the features and in the target, and that alone creates a negative correlation between dA+dB and I. When every group is drawn from control cells (so no perturbation has any effect), the sum-only score is 0.74 ± 0.03. With singles and controls split into independent halves (features from one half, target from the other), the sum-only score falls from 0.43 to 0.21. Removing the shared-noise covariance analytically at full data gives about 0.23 instead of the reported 0.370.

Second, the split-half ceiling splits only the double's cells; the singles and the control are the same in both halves. Their sampling noise is therefore counted as reliable signal. Splitting everything independently gives a split-half value of 0.385 instead of 0.629, a full-data reliability of 0.556 instead of 0.772, and a ceiling of about 0.75 instead of 0.879.

The per-gene offset also lets target noise cross the fold split, because every pair's I contains the same control-mean estimate. The summary's wording goes further than its own numbers. The generic models explain at most about 21% of the variance of I, so 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific' and 'mostly shrinkage' cannot stand. The claim that 54% of the signal is unexplained treats a ratio of correlations as a share of variance; in variance terms about 79% is unexplained. The ceiling/floor explanation was never tested, and 27 of the 115 pairs show the opposite (synergistic) direction. Some real sub-additivity does remain: the slope of the double's response on dA+dB is about 0.82 after correcting for noise. But the size of the effect, the share of the ceiling and the conclusions about headroom all need to be redone with a design where features and target are estimated from independent cells.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 61, 76-78, 107-108, 114 (features A_/B_ are the same DA estimates subtracted inside I); SUMMARY.md lines 12-17, 19-22
findings.description: The features and the target are mathematically coupled. I = mean(AB) - mean(A) - mean(B) + mean(ctrl), and the feature dA+dB = mean(A) + mean(B) - 2*mean(ctrl) uses the same estimates. Sampling noise in the singles and the control therefore enters the features with one sign and the target with the opposite sign. That alone gives a positive score to a model with a negative coefficient on dA+dB. The fitted sum-only coefficient is -0.215, and since prediction is a linear function of dA+dB, the per-pair score is simply corr(-(dA+dB), I). Holding out whole pairs does not help, because the noise is inside each test pair's own features. As a result the sum-only correlation (+0.370), the variance explained (18.4%), the claim that 'a trained model works' and the size of the 'shrinkage' are all substantially inflated.
findings.evidence: Null test: I drew all groups from control cells (A = 300, B = 300, AB = 200, control = the remaining 1,200), so the true I is 0. corr(-(dA+dB), I) was 0.744 (sd 0.029, 40 draws), which is higher than the real-data 0.370. Cross-fit test at matched sample size: I split singles and controls into independent halves and repeated the same 5-fold ridge. Coupled scores were sum-only 0.43-0.45 (R2 0.23-0.25), saturation 0.44-0.46 and saturation+gene 0.45-0.48. Independent scores (features from one half, target from the other) were 0.21-0.22 (R2 0.09-0.10) for all three models. At full data, subtracting the expected shared-noise covariance per pair (var(eA) + var(eB) + 2*var(ectrl)) lowers the mean per-pair corr(-s, I) from 0.370 to 0.234. Single and control sampling noise makes up about 24% of var(I) across genes.
findings.recommended_action: Estimate features and target from disjoint cells: cross-fit with split singles and controls, or use independent guides or replicates. Alternatively, model dAB directly with an errors-in-variables correction. Calibrate every model against a null in which the true I is 0. Then report the corrected correlations and variance explained, and rewrite claims 1-2 to match.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 74-83 (rel1/rel2 share `add`, which comes from the full single and control means); SUMMARY.md line 7 and the 'share of ceiling' column
findings.description: The split-half ceiling splits only the double's cells. Both halves subtract the same add = DA[x] + DA[y], which is built from the same single and control estimates. The sampling noise of the singles and the control is therefore perfectly shared between rel1 and rel2 and is counted as reliable interaction signal. This inflates the reliability, the ceiling and the 'share of ceiling' column. It also makes the 'reproducible residual' in claim 4 partly single-perturbation measurement noise.
findings.evidence: With independent halves of the double, the singles and the control, the split-half value is 0.385 (range 0.377-0.391 over 5 splits), against 0.629 with the shared singles the code uses. The corrected full-data reliability is 0.556 (vs 0.772) and the ceiling is 0.746 (vs 0.879). Analytically, single and control noise is about 24% of var(I) and double noise about 25%. The code's reliability of 0.772 is roughly 1 - 0.25, so it counts only the double's noise as noise.
findings.recommended_action: Compute reliability from fully independent halves: split the double, both singles and the control. Alternatively, derive it from the per-gene sampling variances of every term in I. Recompute the ceiling and the share of ceiling. Note that a model whose features carry the target's noise can beat a properly defined ceiling, so fix F1 first.

findings.description: The statements 'The interaction term is mostly shrinkage', 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity' and 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed' are contradicted by the analysis's own results. The '91%' compares sum-only with the best model; it is not a share of the interaction. The generic models leave most of the interaction variance unexplained, and claim 4 itself says more than half of the reliable signal is unexplained. The direction and strength of the effect also vary widely between pairs.
findings.evidence: Pooled variance of I explained is 18.4% for sum-only, 19.7% for saturation and 21.1% for saturation+gene. In variance terms, (0.377/0.879)^2 = 18% of the claimed reliable variance. Per-pair sum-only correlations range from -0.51 to 0.95 (median 0.44), and 27 of 115 pairs are negative (synergistic), e.g. FEV_CBFA2T3 -0.51, UBASH3B_CNN1 -0.46, FEV_ISL2 -0.43, CNN1_UBASH3A -0.41. These figures come from coupled estimates (F1); with noise-independent features the generic models explain only about 10% at half data.
findings.recommended_action: Withdraw or rephrase claims 2 and 3. At most: a linear sub-additive term explains a minority (around 10-20% before the F1/F2 corrections) of the interaction variance, and the large majority is unexplained by generic features. Report the spread across pairs and show which pairs depart from shrinkage.

findings.description: The headroom claim mixes up correlation and variance. A correlation ratio of 0.406/0.879 = 46% does not mean 46% of the reliable signal is explained, so '54% is unexplained' is wrong. The residual is also described as 'reproducible', but that rests on the inflated split-half reliability in F2, which counts single-perturbation sampling noise as reproducible. Both the explained fraction (F1) and the ceiling (F2) are biased, so the headroom figure cannot be read as stated.
findings.evidence: (0.4056/0.8786)^2 = 0.213, so about 79% of the reliable variance is unexplained even under the authors' own ceiling, not 54%. Pooled R2 0.211 / reliability 0.772 = 27% explained. With the corrected ceiling of about 0.75 and a corrected model correlation of about 0.23 for sum-only, the picture changes again.
findings.recommended_action: Express the explained share as (r/ceiling)^2 or as R2/reliability, with consistent definitions. Recompute it after fixing F1 and F2. Drop the claim that the residual is 'reproducible' unless it is shown with fully independent replicates.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 109-113 (goff = I[tr].mean(0)); SUMMARY.md lines 14 and 21
findings.description: The per-gene offset lets target noise leak across the fold split. Every pair's I contains the same control-mean estimate (+mean(ctrl)). Single perturbations also recur across pairs: PTPN12 is in 12 pairs, KLF1 in 11, CEBPE and UBASH3B in 10 each. So the mean of I over training pairs carries noise that also sits in the held-out pair's target. The +0.029 gain credited to 'per-gene offsets' is therefore partly leakage, not a genuine gene-level effect.
findings.evidence: In a half-data cross-fit (features from half 0, target from half 1), the saturation model without an offset scores 0.204. Adding an offset from fully independent halves gives 0.226. An offset sharing only the target's control half gives 0.310, one sharing only the target's singles gives 0.256, and one sharing both gives 0.346. At full data, the control-mean sampling variance (mean 9.6e-5) is about 18% of the across-gene variance of the per-gene mean I (5.2e-4). The offset coefficient is 0.56.
findings.recommended_action: Build the per-gene offset from I estimates that share neither control nor single cells with the test pair. For example, use a separate control split, and estimate singles from disjoint cells or leave out pairs that share a single with the test pair. Re-estimate the gain and its paired CI.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 1, 21-23 (title 'what it learns is saturation'; 'This is a ceiling/floor effect')
findings.description: The saturation (ceiling/floor) mechanism is asserted, not tested. The nonlinear 'saturation' features add almost nothing, and once the noise is made independent they add nothing at all. What remains is a near-linear, proportional sub-additivity that is partly regression dilution. The rest fits several mechanisms equally well, for example weaker per-guide activation in double-guide cells or technical differences between doubles and singles. The analysis does nothing to tell these apart from expression bounds.
findings.evidence: The paired gain of saturation over sum-only is +0.0067 (95% CI 0.0001-0.0139). In the independent cross-fit it is 0.216 → 0.212. The fitted relation is linear: dAB ≈ 0.78*(dA+dB), pooled slope 0.779. Because dA+dB has a reliability of 0.949, about 0.05 of the shrinkage is attenuation; the slope corrected for this is about 0.82. The shrinkage ratio changes only mildly with |dA+dB| (0.895 in the lowest bin, 0.784 in the top 1%). Median library size is 15,351 for control, 13,847 for singles and 12,753 for doubles, so the groups differ technically.
findings.recommended_action: Test saturation directly: check whether sub-additivity depends on baseline expression and on how close a gene is to its expression limits, compared with proportional shrinkage. Control for library size and guide or activation strength in the doubles. Rephrase the claim as 'sub-additivity of unknown mechanism' unless saturation is specifically supported.

findings.description: The additive baseline's correlation is undefined, because a constant predictor has zero variance. The code excludes every pair (n = 0) and fills in corr = 0, CI [0, 0]. 'Sum-only reaches +0.370 against an additive baseline of exactly 0' therefore compares against a placeholder, not a measured score. Under the per-pair correlation metric, any non-constant predictor, even one built from pure noise (F1), 'beats' additive.
findings.evidence: results.json shows additive n = 0 and lo = hi = 0. Under a no-effect null, the sum-only correlation is 0.74.
findings.recommended_action: Report the additive baseline as not applicable for the correlation metric. Compare models on a metric that is defined for it (e.g., MSE or R2 against 0), plus a null-calibrated benchmark.

findings.description: The uncertainty is understated. The bootstrap resamples pairs as if they were independent, but pairs share singles and the control. It also ignores variation from the single random fold assignment, and the folds are unbalanced (25/20/31/22/17). The differences between models get no paired test. The '115,000 training examples' are strongly dependent within pairs and recurring singles, and each fit actually uses about 92,000.
findings.evidence: PTPN12 appears in 12 kept pairs, KLF1 in 11 and CEBPE in 10. The paired bootstrap differences I computed are saturation − sum-only +0.0067 [0.0001, 0.0139] and +gene − saturation +0.0288 [0.0161, 0.0416]. The summary reports point differences only and calls the interval 'tight'.
findings.recommended_action: Use a cluster or block bootstrap that accounts for shared singles. Repeat the CV over several fold seeds. Report paired CIs for differences between models. Describe the sample size as 115 pairs rather than 115,000 independent examples.

findings.description: The ceiling comes from one random split, as Spearman-Brown applied to the mean of per-pair split-half correlations. It is then compared with the mean of per-pair model correlations. Averaging correlations before a nonlinear transform, across pairs whose reliability differs, does not give the mean per-pair ceiling. Doubles with an odd number of cells also drop one cell from the target I.
findings.evidence: 10 of 115 doubles have an odd cell count, giving a max |ΔI| of 0.015 against using all cells. The split-half value is computed only once (seeded) and has no reported uncertainty.
findings.recommended_action: Compute a per-pair ceiling, or disattenuate each pair's correlation, and average over many random splits. Use all cells to compute the target I.

grade_a.detection_reason: F2 meets the key's detection rule exactly. It targets the split-half ceiling at code/learn_interaction.py lines 74-83. It says only the double's cells are split, while both halves subtract the same add = DA[x] + DA[y], built from the full single and control means. That shared sampling noise counts as reproducible and inflates the split-half value, the reliability and the ceiling. F2 also prescribes splitting the double, both singles and the control. Its corrected numbers match the key's correct result: split-half 0.385, reliability 0.556, ceiling 0.746, against the key's 0.383-0.395 and 0.744-0.752. F4 refers back to this inflation but does not detect the error on its own.

findings.reason: This is the feature-target noise coupling listed in the key's other_real_issues, and the key says to grade it as a valid concern. The null-test figure of 0.744 matches the analytic value: cov = 2/300 + 2/1200, var(I) = 1/200 + 2/300 + 1/1200, var(s) = 2/300 + 4/1200, which gives 0.745. The cross-fit gap (about 0.43 coupled vs 0.22 independent) agrees with the key's build check (0.425 vs 0.227). It says the headline sum-only score, the variance explained and the size of the shrinkage are inflated.

It names the shared add term built from the single and control means, points at lines 74-83, and prescribes independent splits of the double, the singles and the control. Its corrected ceiling of 0.746 matches the key. It undermines the 0.879 ceiling, the share-of-ceiling column and claim 4.

Confirmed. The analysis's own pooled variance explained is only 18-21%, so 'mostly shrinkage' and 'most of the interaction is not pair-specific' overstate it. The '91%' is a ratio of correlations, not a share of the interaction. I reproduced the per-pair sum-only correlations: min -0.514, max 0.946, median 0.440, with 27 of 115 negative. Claims 2-3 are headline conclusions.

The arithmetic is correct: (0.406/0.879)^2 = 0.21, so a correlation ratio of 46% does not mean 54% of the reliable signal is unexplained in variance terms. The key itself uses the correlation-ratio framing, so this part is a defensible interpretive point, not a calculation error. Its second half, that the 'reproducible residual' rests on the inflated split-half, overlaps with the documented error (it defers to F2). Claim 4 cannot be read as stated.

The key's false alarm is about the offset using test targets, which it does not. F5 instead argues that the offset carries noise shared with the test target: the common control mean, plus recurring singles. I checked this directly with the control split in half. When the offset used the same control half as the target, the gain over no offset was +0.025 to +0.028. When it used the independent control half, the gain was only +0.006 to +0.009, and with independent-control features it was about +0.002 vs +0.045. So most of the claimed +0.029 offset gain is shared control noise. This is a real secondary issue; it does not overturn a main conclusion.

The title and claim 2 assert a ceiling/floor (saturation) mechanism, but the saturation features add only +0.007 over a linear term. The key's other_real_issues notes that part of the 'shrinkage' is regression to the mean from coupled noise. I confirmed the library-size differences: medians 15,351 control, 13,847 singles, about 12,800 doubles (12,860 for the kept doubles; F6 says 12,753, which is the median over all doubles, kept or not). I also confirmed the near-linear pooled slope of about 0.78-0.79. Saturation is asserted, not tested.

The key says the additive model's corr = 0 and n = 0 is by design, and F7 does not call it a bug. It makes a true presentational point: the 'exactly 0' baseline is a placeholder, not a measured score. SUMMARY claim 3 already concedes that beating additive shows nothing.

The key lists the pair-independence of the bootstrap as a minor valid issue. I confirmed the fold sizes (25/20/31/22/17) and the recurrence of singles (PTPN12 in 12 pairs, KLF1 in 11, UBASH3B and CEBPE in 10). These are refinements to the uncertainty estimates and do not change any conclusion.

The key lists applying Spearman-Brown to the mean r, rather than per pair, as a minor valid aggregation bias (0.872 vs 0.879). It also lists the dropped odd cell as negligible. Neither is the documented error.

grade_b.detection_reason: F2 meets the key's detection rule. It points at code/learn_interaction.py lines 74-83 and says that only the double's cells are split. It says both halves subtract the same add = DA[x] + DA[y], built from the full single and control estimates, so the single and control sampling noise is shared and gets counted as reliable signal. That inflates the split-half value, the reliability and the ceiling. Its fix is to split the double, both singles and the control. Its corrected numbers match the key's correct result: split-half 0.385, reliability 0.556, ceiling 0.746 (key: 0.3823 / 0.744 on the full-data rerun). My own rerun gives a double-only ceiling of 0.877-0.880 against 0.749-0.750 with every group split. F4 repeats the point by referring back to F2, but it does not make the argument on its own, so only F2 is listed.

findings.reason: This is the feature-target noise coupling listed in the key's other_real_issues: a valid concern that is not the documented error. The key's build check found sum-only at 0.425 with coupled single cells and 0.227 with independent ones. I reproduced the null test: with all groups drawn from control cells, corr(-(dA+dB), I) = 0.75. The finding says the headline sum-only 0.370, the 18.4% variance explained and claim 1 are inflated, so it is load-bearing.

This is the key's documented error: the split-half ceiling splits only the double, and both halves subtract the same add term (singles plus control), so shared noise inflates the split-half value, the reliability and the ceiling. The location, mechanism, fix and corrected numbers (0.385 / 0.556 / 0.746) all match the key and my rerun (0.389 / 0.560 / 0.749).

Claims 2 and 3 ('the interaction term is mostly shrinkage', 'most of the interaction is not pair-specific') go beyond the results. The generic models explain 18-21% of the variance of I, and the summary's own claim 4 says most of the reliable signal is unexplained. I confirmed the per-pair sum-only correlations: range -0.51 to 0.95, median 0.44, 27 of 115 negative, with the named pairs as the most negative. These are real interpretive overclaims that the key does not cover.

Mathematically, a correlation ratio r/ceiling is not a share of explained variance: (0.406/0.879)^2 = 0.21, so '54% unexplained' misstates the variance share. The finding also notes that 'reproducible residual' relies on the inflated ceiling, which overlaps the documented error by pointing back to F2. The key itself uses correlation-share language, so the variance point is a definitional disagreement, but it is correct. It targets the claim-4 numbers.

The key lists 'the per-gene offset leaks test information' as a false alarm because the offset uses training pairs only. F5 accepts that and argues a different mechanism: every I contains the same control-mean estimate, so its noise is shared between the training-pair offset and the test target. The data confirm this. In F5's half-data cross-fit I get 0.204 without the offset, 0.224 with an independent offset and 0.306 with a shared-control offset. With features and target from one control half, the offset's gain was +0.008 with the other control half against +0.025-0.032 with the same half. So most of the offset gain comes from shared control noise. This affects a secondary result (the +0.029 gain), not the headline.

The title and claim 2 say the effect is saturation (a ceiling/floor effect), but the nonlinear saturation features add only +0.007 and the fit is essentially linear proportional shrinkage. The key confirms that part of the shrinkage reading is regression to the mean. The mechanism is asserted rather than tested, which is a real interpretive problem. The library-size medians roughly check out: control 15,351 and singles 13,847 match; doubles 12,860 in my count against 12,753 in the finding.

The key says the additive model's n = 0 / corr = 0 is by design. F7 does not call it a bug. It objects to the summary's wording 'against an additive baseline of exactly 0', which compares against a placeholder. That is true but only a framing point.

The bootstrap treating pairs as independent is listed in the key's other_real_issues as minor but valid. Fold sizes 25/20/31/22/17 and the recurrence counts (PTPN12 12, KLF1 11, CEBPE/UBASH3B 10) check out. Missing paired tests and the dependence among the '115,000 examples' are minor points.

Applying Spearman-Brown and the square root to the mean r instead of per pair is a minor issue listed in the key's other_real_issues. The key calls dropping one cell from odd-sized doubles negligible. Neither point detects the documented error under the key's rule.

review.summary:
The code runs and reproduces outputs/results.json and run_log.txt exactly. The summary's arithmetic matches the outputs (91%, +0.007, +0.029, 42/43/46%). The data description checks out: 105 singles with 113-400 cells, 131 doubles, 115 kept, 2,000 controls. The headline conclusions do not hold, though.

(1) The target I = dAB - dA - dB is built from the same single-perturbation and control means used as features. Their sampling error therefore enters the features and the target with opposite signs, which produces a regression-to-the-mean artefact. About half of the "shrinkage" signal is this noise. When features and target come from independent cells, sum-only falls from 0.370 to about 0.22 and the best model from 0.406 to about 0.31.

(2) The split-half ceiling keeps the singles and the control mean fixed across the two halves. Their noise is therefore counted as reliable signal: split-half r is 0.629 against 0.389 with fully independent halves, and the ceiling is 0.879 against about 0.75.

(3) The claims that the interaction is "mostly" shrinkage and "not pair-specific" go against the analysis's own numbers. The best model explains only 21% of the variance. The shrinkage slope also varies strongly by pair (5-95% range -0.57 to +0.18), and a per-pair slope explains 44% of the variance against 19% for one global slope.

(4) The ceiling/floor (saturation) reading is not supported. Opposite-sign gene responses shrink as much as same-sign ones.

(5) "54% of the reliable signal unexplained" mixes up a ratio of correlations with a share of variance. In variance terms about 79% is unexplained.

Smaller issues: the bootstrap CIs treat pairs as independent although all of them share singles, the "additive = 0" correlation is undefined rather than zero, and the per-gene offset is fitted in-sample.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 61, 76-77, 107-108 (I built from the same DA[x], DA[y], cmean that are used as features); SUMMARY.md lines 12, 16-23
findings.description: The target I_h = dAB_h - dA_h - dB_h uses the same estimated single responses (and the same control mean) that are the model's features. Sampling error e in dA+dB appears as +e in the features and -e in the target, so I correlates negatively with dA+dB even when the true interaction is zero. This is regression to the mean, not biology. The sum-only result (+0.370, 18.4% of variance) and the 'interaction is mostly shrinkage' finding are substantially inflated by this artefact, and so are all the other models.
findings.evidence: At matched cell counts (singles and control split in half), corr(dA+dB, I) is -0.43 when features and target share the same half of the singles and control cells, but only -0.22 when the target comes from the independent half (3 seeds: -0.429/-0.215, -0.422/-0.225, -0.428/-0.218). An analytic estimate from per-gene sampling variances, Cov = -sum(varA/nA + varB/nB + 2 varc/nc), says about -0.136 of the observed -0.370 mean correlation comes from shared noise alone. Rerunning the code's exact CV with features from half 1 of the single/control cells and I from half 2: sum-only 0.215-0.225, saturation 0.205-0.221, saturation+gene 0.309-0.317, compared with the reported 0.370 / 0.377 / 0.406. The pooled slope of I on dA+dB is -0.221 with the same data and -0.175 with independent data.
findings.recommended_action: Estimate features and target from disjoint cells: split each single and the control cells, use one half for dA and dB and the other half to build I (or use cross-fitting and average). Alternatively, model the measurement error explicitly with an errors-in-variables / attenuation correction. Re-report all model correlations, variance explained and the shrinkage slope under this design, and remove or qualify the 'mostly shrinkage' claim.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 74-83 (rel1 = ab1 - add, rel2 = ab2 - add with the same add and cmean); SUMMARY.md line 7 and lines 28-31; results.json _ceiling
findings.description: The split-half reliability splits only the double's cells. Both halves subtract the same add = dA + dB (and the same control mean), so the noise in the singles and the control is shared between the halves and counted as reliable signal. The reported reliability (0.772) and ceiling (0.879) are therefore too high. The 'share of ceiling' figures (42/43/46%) and the headroom claim (0.406 vs 0.879) rest on this wrong denominator, and their numerators are also inflated (F1).
findings.evidence: With fully independent halves (double, both singles and control each split, so I1 and I2 share no cells), the mean per-pair split-half r of I is 0.389 (Spearman-Brown 0.56, ceiling about 0.75), against the code's 0.629 / 0.772 / 0.879. A variance decomposition agrees: per pair, singles+control sampling noise is about 24% and double sampling noise about 25% of var(I). The code's r_full of 0.772 matches excluding only the double noise (about 0.75), so true reliability is about 0.5.
findings.recommended_action: Compute reliability from fully independent halves, splitting the singles and control cells as well as the doubles. Make the ceiling and the model evaluation consistent: the target must be built from cells not used for the features (F1). Restate the ceiling, the share-of-ceiling column and claim 4.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 21-26 (claims 2 and 3: 'mostly shrinkage', 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed', 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity')
findings.description: These headline claims go against the analysis's own outputs. The best model explains only 21.1% of the variance of I (sum-only 18.4%), so a generic function of (dA, dB) does not account for 'most' of the interaction. The 'shrinkage' itself is strongly pair-specific: the size and even the sign of the relationship between I and dA+dB vary a lot across pairs. The 91% figure is only relative to the other weak models tested. It does not show that most of the interaction is generic.
findings.evidence: results.json: var_explained is 0.184 (sum-only) and 0.211 (best). On the code's own I, one global slope of I on dA+dB gives R2 = 0.19, while one slope per pair (one parameter per 1,000 genes) gives R2 = 0.44. Per-pair slopes have 5/25/50/75/95th percentiles of -0.574 / -0.315 / -0.193 / -0.020 / +0.179, so some pairs show synergy rather than shrinkage. Once the shared-noise artefact is removed (F1), sum-only falls to about 0.22 and per-gene offsets add about 0.09 rather than 0.029. Sum-only is then about 70% of the best model, not 91%.
findings.recommended_action: Remove or reword claims 2 and 3. State that a global function of (dA, dB) explains about one fifth of the variance of I (less after the noise correction). Report how much of I depends on pair identity, e.g. per-pair scaling factors or a random-slope model with out-of-sample checks, before making any claim about pair-specificity.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 1, 21-23 ('what it learns is saturation', 'This is a ceiling/floor effect'); code docstring lines 13-17
findings.description: The saturation / ceiling-floor reading was never tested, and the data contradict it. Saturation predicts sub-additivity mainly when both perturbations push a gene the same way. The 'saturation' features that encode this (product, sign agreement, min/max) add essentially nothing (+0.007, and -0.004 to -0.010 with independent noise). The learned shrinkage is a uniform scaling of dA+dB that is just as strong for genes pushed in opposite directions, where no ceiling or floor can apply. Measurement noise (F1) also gives exactly this linear pattern.
findings.evidence: With features from half 1 of the singles and the target from half 2 (independent noise), the slope of I on dA+dB is -0.172 for same-sign genes (both |d| > 0.05, n = 27,402) and -0.214 for opposite-sign genes (n = 8,617). Independent-noise CV: saturation 0.205-0.221 against sum-only 0.215-0.225.
findings.recommended_action: Drop the title claim and the 'ceiling/floor effect' interpretation, or test it directly, e.g. compare shrinkage for same- vs opposite-sign genes and its dependence on baseline expression near zero, using noise-independent estimates. Discuss other explanations such as a global sub-additive scaling of double responses or measurement error.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 17, 28-29 ('46% of the ceiling', 'more than half of the reliable interaction signal (54%) is unexplained'); code lines 125-127
findings.description: frac_of_ceiling is a ratio of correlations (r_model / r_ceiling), not a share of the reliable signal. Turning 46% into '54% of the reliable interaction signal unexplained' mixes up the two. In variance terms the share of reliable variance explained is the square of the ratio, so the unexplained share is far larger than 54%. This is separate from the ceiling's own bias (F2).
findings.evidence: (0.4056 / 0.8786)^2 = 0.213, so about 21% of the reliable variance is explained and about 79% is not, rather than 54%.
findings.recommended_action: Report the share of explainable variance as (r / ceiling)^2, or present the ratio clearly as a correlation ratio, and fix the '54%' statement. Recompute after fixing F1 and F2.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 120-122 (bootstrap over pairs); SUMMARY.md lines 12-17, 19-21 (CIs, 'tight interval', +0.007 and +0.029 increments)
findings.description: The 95% intervals resample pairs as if they were independent, but pairs share single perturbations, and therefore share the same dA estimates and their noise. The CIs are too narrow. The model-to-model gains (+0.007, +0.029) are reported with no paired uncertainty, although the marginal CIs overlap almost completely. Calling the data '115,000 training examples' also overstates the information content: about 92k per fold, strongly dependent within pair and through shared singles.
findings.evidence: The 115 kept pairs use only 66 distinct singles. All 115 pairs share a single with at least one other pair, and some singles recur up to 12 times (PTPN12 12, KLF1 11, CEBPE 10, UBASH3B 10, ETS2 9, MAPK1 8).
findings.recommended_action: Use a cluster- or two-way-aware bootstrap, resampling singles or using pair-graph-aware resampling. Report paired bootstrap intervals for the differences between models. Describe the sample size as 115 pairs and 66 singles rather than 115,000 examples.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 116-117 and 123; results.json 'additive' (n = 0); SUMMARY.md lines 11, 16, 26
findings.description: For the additive baseline the correlation between a constant prediction and I is undefined. The code drops every pair (n = 0) and reports corr = 0.000 with interval [0, 0]. The summary calls this 'an additive baseline of exactly 0', but any non-constant predictor 'beats' it by construction on this metric. Also, the sum-only per-pair correlation is just -corr(dA+dB, I) whenever the fitted slope is negative, so 'a trained model works' adds nothing beyond the sign of one coefficient.
findings.evidence: results.json: additive corr = 0.0, n = 0, lo = hi = 0.0.
findings.recommended_action: Report the additive baseline as undefined (n/a) for correlation and compare models on an error metric such as MSE / variance explained, where I = 0 is a real baseline. Reword claim 1 accordingly.

findings.description: The per-gene offset feature goff is the mean of I over the training pairs, and the same training pairs' I are then the regression target. The feature therefore contains each training target in-sample, and the pooled regression fits its coefficient at about 1 rather than the shrunken value that would be optimal out of sample. Part of what the offset captures is also control-mean sampling noise (+e_c,h), which is identical for every pair, so not all of the offset gain is gene biology.
findings.evidence: Regressing I on its own across-pair mean over the same pairs gives a slope of exactly 1 by construction. Control-mean noise is about 2-3% of var(I) (from per-gene control variance / 2,000 cells).
findings.recommended_action: Compute goff for each training pair leave-one-pair-out (or by nested CV within the training folds), and use a control half not used for the target, so the offset gain reflects genuine gene-specific non-additivity.

review.summary:
I reproduced the run exactly: same ceiling (0.629, 0.772, 0.879) and same model correlations (0.370, 0.377, 0.406). The data description in the README also checks out: 2,000 control cells, 105 singles with 113–400 cells, 131 doubles, and 115 kept doubles whose singles are all present. The arithmetic in SUMMARY.md matches results.json.

The main problem is in the design. The target I = dAB − dA − dB is built from the same noisy single-perturbation estimates dA and dB that the models use as features, and from the same control mean. So sampling noise alone creates a negative relationship between I and dA+dB (regression to the mean). I simulated a perfectly additive null with the observed sampling noise. With no interaction at all, the pipeline still gives about 0.18 for sum-only, 0.19 for saturation and 0.26 for saturation+gene, and its own ceiling gives a split-half of 0.33 and a "perfect model" of 0.70. When I estimated the features from cells separate from those used in the target, the sum-only correlation fell from 0.44 to 0.23.

The ceiling has the same flaw: the two split halves share the singles and the control. Splitting every group, not just the double, gives a split-half of 0.39 and a ceiling of 0.75. Under the code's method, about 40% of the "reliable" split-half signal is shared sampling noise.

A real sub-additivity does remain after correcting for noise. But it is a roughly uniform scaling, by about 0.7–0.9, of each single's effect in the double. It is the same for genes the two singles push in the same direction and in opposite directions, and the saturation-specific features add nothing significant. So the title and claims 1–4 overstate or misattribute the effect: "saturation / ceiling-floor", "most of the interaction is not pair-specific", the 54% headroom, and the per-gene offsets.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 55-56, 61, 76-77 (target I built from DA[x]+DA[y] and cmean), 107-108 (features are the same DA); SUMMARY.md lines 16-17, 19-23, 26
findings.description: The target I = dAB − dA − dB contains −(sampling error of dA + dB) plus the control-mean error. The features are the same noisy dA and dB. Regression to the mean therefore produces a negative coefficient on dA+dB and a positive held-out correlation even with zero true interaction. 'I = 0' is not a valid null baseline, and the size of the 'shrinkage' is substantially inflated.
findings.evidence: In a perfectly additive null (true double = exact sum of the singles' means, with Gaussian noise at the observed per-gene SEs for singles, doubles and control), the unmodified CV pipeline gave mean per-pair correlations of sum-only 0.172–0.193, saturation 0.175–0.197 and saturation+gene 0.253–0.263, over 3–5 replicates. Observed values are 0.370, 0.377 and 0.406. A cross-fitting check on real data split single and control cells in half. Features from half 1 with the target built from half 2 gave sum-only corr 0.225 and R² 0.106. Features and target from the same half 2 gave 0.438 and 0.226. Saturation behaved the same way: 0.219 vs 0.447. Sampling noise is about 46% of the per-pair variance of I.
findings.recommended_action: Estimate the features (dA, dB) and the singles subtracted in I from disjoint cell sets, with disjoint control cells too, or apply an errors-in-variables correction. Calibrate every model against a simulated or permuted additive null instead of I = 0. Restate claims 1–2 and the 'beating additive shows nothing / sum-only baseline' message only after this correction.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 74-83 (rel1 = ab1 - add, rel2 = ab2 - add share add and cmean); SUMMARY.md lines 7, 28-31; README ceiling description
findings.description: Only the double's cells are split. Both halves subtract the same add = dA + dB and the same control mean, so the split-half correlation counts the singles' and control's sampling noise as reproducible 'interaction signal'. The ceiling (0.879) and the 'share of ceiling' column therefore do not measure reliable interaction. Claim 4 says the 54% residual is 'reproducible' and 'the best-defined open target'. That is not supported, because part of what is called reproducible is just the shared noise.
findings.evidence: With singles, control and double all split into independent halves, the I-profile split-half is 0.389–0.391, giving Spearman-Brown 0.560 and a ceiling of 0.749 (3 seeds). The code's method on the same data gives 0.628–0.630, giving 0.879. In the zero-interaction null simulation, the code's ceiling procedure still reports split-half 0.323–0.327 and a 'perfect model reaches' 0.70.
findings.recommended_action: Compute reliability from fully independent replicates, splitting singles and control as well as the double. Express model performance relative to that ceiling, using noise-decoupled features (see F1). Remove or rewrite claim 4's assertion that the residual is reproducible interaction signal.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 1, 21-23 (title; 'This is a ceiling/floor effect. It needs no regulatory network and does not depend on which genes were perturbed')
findings.description: No analysis tests the saturation (ceiling/floor) mechanism, and the available evidence argues against it. The features meant to capture saturation (product, min/max, sign agreement, |dA|+|dB|) add nothing significant beyond sum-only. After correcting for noise, the dampening is a near-uniform proportional scaling of each single's effect. It is the same whether the singles push a gene in the same or in opposite directions. A floor/ceiling effect should act mainly on same-direction effects. Other explanations fit uniform dampening: reduced per-guide CRISPRa activation in double-guide cells, cell mixtures, or residual regression to the mean. 'Does not depend on which genes were perturbed' and 'needs no regulatory network' were also not tested.
findings.evidence: Sum-only coefficient is −0.22. Paired bootstrap of saturation minus sum-only per-pair correlation is +0.005, 95% CI [−0.002, +0.012]. Using independent-half features with an attenuation reference, dAB scales the single effects by about 0.74–0.91 for same-sign gene entries and about 0.73–0.82 for opposite-sign entries (|dA|, |dB| > 0.05 or 0.1).
findings.recommended_action: Drop the 'ceiling/floor' and 'saturation' attribution, including the title, or test it directly. For example, use noise-decoupled features and check whether shrinkage depends on sign agreement, on baseline expression near zero, or on high expression. Also check on-target activation in doubles vs singles to rule out reduced CRISPRa activity per guide.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 25-26 ('Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity.')
findings.description: The models' own numbers contradict this claim. The best generic model explains about 21% of the variance of I (pooled), and its per-pair r of 0.41 corresponds to r² of about 0.16. Even against the inflated ceiling, 0.46² ≈ 21% of the 'reliable' variance is explained. Most of the interaction variance is therefore not captured by the generic non-linearity, and part of what is captured is sampling noise (F1). The claim also conflicts with claim 4, which says most reliable signal is unexplained.
findings.evidence: results.json: var_explained 0.184 / 0.197 / 0.211, frac_of_ceiling 0.421–0.462. Null simulation: about half of the sum-only correlation is reachable with no interaction.
findings.recommended_action: Rephrase as: a generic dampening term captures a minority (at most about 20%) of the variance of I, much of it attributable to noise until corrected. Do not claim that most interaction is generic.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 28-29 ('more than half of the reliable interaction signal (54%) is unexplained')
findings.description: 54% is 1 − corr/ceiling, which is a correlation ratio, not a share of signal. In variance terms the unexplained share of the reliable variance under the code's own ceiling is 1 − 0.462² ≈ 79%. The statement therefore understates the unexplained part, and the ceiling itself is invalid (F2).
findings.recommended_action: Report headroom in variance units (r²/reliability), using a corrected ceiling, or describe it explicitly as a correlation ratio.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 109-113 (per-gene offset = I[tr].mean(0)); SUMMARY.md line 21 ('Per-gene offsets add another +0.029'); docstring line 23-24 ('some genes are simply always non-additive')
findings.description: Every pair's I contains +cmean, the same estimate from the same 2,000 control cells. The per-gene mean of I over training pairs therefore carries the control-mean sampling error that also appears in the test pairs. Singles recurring across pairs add more shared noise, for example MAPK1 is in 8 kept pairs. So the +0.029 gain cannot be read as genes being systematically non-additive. In the no-interaction null, adding the offset raises correlation by even more (about +0.06 to +0.08).
findings.evidence: Null simulation: saturation 0.175–0.197 rises to saturation+gene 0.253–0.263 with zero true interaction. Observed gain is +0.029; paired bootstrap 95% CI [+0.009, +0.046].
findings.recommended_action: Compute I for training and test pairs against independent control subsets, or compare the offset gain to a null-calibrated gain, before attributing it to gene-specific non-additivity.

findings.description: The bootstrap resamples pairs as if they were independent, but pairs share singles and all share the control cells. It also ignores variability from the single random fold assignment and double split. '115,000 training examples' and 'tight interval' overstate the effective sample size (about 115 non-independent pairs). The summary reports differences between models (+0.007, +0.029) without paired tests, and the per-model CIs overlap heavily.
findings.evidence: Pairs share singles, for example MAPK1 in 8 kept pairs and SET in 4. The paired bootstrap difference saturation − sum-only is +0.005 with CI [−0.002, +0.012], which is not significant.
findings.recommended_action: Use a cluster or block bootstrap that respects shared singles, and repeat over CV seeds. Report paired differences between models with CIs, and phrase increments that are not significant as such.

grade_a.detection_reason: F2 meets the detection rule. It says only the double's cells are split, and that both halves subtract the same add = dA + dB and the same control mean. It explains that the singles' and control's sampling noise is therefore counted as reproducible signal, which inflates the split-half value and the ceiling. It points at learn_interaction.py lines 74-83 and prescribes splitting the singles and controls as well. Its corrected numbers (split-half 0.389-0.391, ceiling 0.749) match the key's correct result (0.395 / 0.752; 0.740-0.752 over seeds). I reproduced them inline: 0.3893 / 0.7486, 0.3913 / 0.7500 and 0.3885 / 0.7481 for seeds 1-3. No other finding names the shared single terms in the ceiling computation. F5 only cross-references F2.

findings.reason: This is the key's listed other_real_issue: feature-target noise coupling. dA and dB are both the features and are subtracted inside the target I, so regression to the mean creates part of the 'shrinkage' and part of the score. The key's build check gave 0.425 (same cells) vs 0.227 (disjoint cells); F1 reports 0.438 vs 0.225, which is consistent. Per the key it is valid but is neither a detection nor a false alarm. It is load-bearing because it challenges claims 1-2, including that I = 0 is a valid baseline and how large the shrinkage is.

This is the documented error. Only the double's cells are split, and both halves subtract the same add = DA[x] + DA[y] and the same cmean. As a result the split-half 0.629, the reliability 0.772, the ceiling 0.879 and the 'share of ceiling' / '54% unexplained' claims are all inflated. Its corrected figures (split-half ~0.39, ceiling ~0.749) match the key and my own rerun.

The title and claim 2 attribute the shrinkage to a ceiling/floor (saturation) effect, but nothing tests this. The saturation features add only +0.007 over sum-only, as the summary itself reports. I checked inline with noise-decoupled features: independent single halves and control halves, with an attenuation reference. Dampening factors were about 0.70-0.92 for same-sign entries and 0.76-0.85 for opposite-sign entries. Uniform dampening like this is not specific to same-direction effects, which supports F3. The summary's statements that it 'needs no regulatory network' and 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed' were also never tested. This is a genuine overinterpretation of the headline mechanism.

Claim 3 says most of the interaction is a generic, non-pair-specific non-linearity. The package's own numbers say otherwise. The generic models explain 18-21% of the pooled variance of I. Even against the inflated ceiling, (0.406/0.879)^2 ≈ 21% of the reliable variance is explained, and against the corrected ceiling it is about 29%. Claim 3 also conflicts with claim 4, which says most reliable signal is unexplained. The claim is overstated, and that is a substantive interpretive error.

The arithmetic is right: 54% is 1 - corr/ceiling, a correlation ratio, and in variance units the unexplained share would be about 79%. But this is a choice of units and framing. The key itself states the corrected result as a correlation ratio (54% of the ceiling, 46% unexplained). Reframing makes the 'more than half unexplained' wording stronger, not wrong, so it does not overturn a headline conclusion. Its point that the ceiling is invalid only refers back to F2.

This is not the key's false alarm about test leakage. F6 accepts that the offset uses training pairs only. Its point is that every pair's I contains the same +cmean, so the per-gene offset picks up shared control-mean noise. I confirmed this inline using half-control estimates and 5-fold CV over 3 seeds. With the same control half for training and test, the offset gain is +0.028 to +0.033. With independent control halves for training and test pairs, the gain falls to about 0 (-0.001 to +0.002). So the +0.029 gain is essentially a measurement artifact, not gene-specific non-additivity. It is a genuine problem but affects a secondary increment, not the main headline.

The key lists this as a minor, valid issue: the pair bootstrap ignores that pairs share singles and the control, so intervals may be somewhat narrow. The remark that the +0.007 saturation increment is not significant is also true, but the summary already calls it small. It is trivial relative to the headline claims.

grade_b.detection_reason: F2 meets the key's detection rule. It points at learn_interaction.py lines 74-83 and says that only the double's cells are split, while both halves subtract the same add = dA + dB and the same control mean. It names the shared single-perturbation terms explicitly, as the rule requires: the noise in the singles and the control is counted as reproducible interaction signal. It also prescribes splitting the singles and the control as well as the double. Its corrected numbers (split-half 0.389-0.391, Spearman-Brown 0.560, ceiling 0.749) match the key's correct result (0.395 / 0.566 / 0.752; ceilings 0.740-0.752 across seeds). It also rejects claim 4's 'reproducible residual' wording, which rests on the inflated ceiling.

findings.reason: This is the key's other_real_issue on feature-target noise coupling: dA and dB are both features and part of the target. The key says to grade it as valid, not as a detection and not as a false alarm. The finding's cross-fit numbers (0.225 vs 0.438) match the key's build check (0.227 vs 0.425). It challenges the size of the shrinkage and the use of I=0 as the null in claims 1-2, so it is load-bearing. It does not detect the ceiling error, because it is about the model score.

This is exactly the documented error. Only the double is split, and both halves subtract the same add = DA[x]+DA[y] and control mean. That inflates the split-half (0.629), the reliability (0.772) and the ceiling (0.879). The finding's corrected ceiling of about 0.749 matches the key's 0.740-0.752, and its fix (split singles and control too) matches the key's fix. It overturns the 'share of ceiling' figures and claim 4.

I checked this by building the features and the target from independent halves of the singles and the control. Relative to an attenuation reference, the double scales the summed singles by about 0.80-0.81 for same-sign entries and about 0.80-0.84 for opposite-sign entries (thresholds 0.05 and 0.1). So the dampening is near-uniform and does not depend on sign agreement, and a floor/ceiling effect should act mainly on same-sign entries. The saturation features add only +0.007 over sum-only. The title and claim 2 ('what it learns is saturation', 'This is a ceiling/floor effect') are asserted without being tested, and the data argue against them.

Claim 3 ('Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity') does not fit the reported numbers. The generic models explain only 18-21% of the pooled variance of I. Even against the corrected reliability (about 0.57), the explained share of the reliable variance stays well under half, and part of it comes from noise coupling (F1). Claim 3 also conflicts with claim 4, which says most of the reliable signal is unexplained. This is a genuine overstatement of a headline claim.

It is true that 54% is 1 - corr/ceiling, a correlation ratio, and that in variance units the unexplained share would be larger (about 79%). However, 'more than half unexplained' holds in either unit, and the key itself uses the correlation-ratio convention for both the flawed and the corrected result (54% vs 46% unexplained). This is a reporting or units issue. The ceiling problem it mentions is F2's error, which this finding does not establish on its own.

I confirmed this with a check. Every pair's I contains +cmean from the same 2,000 control cells. When I rebuilt the training pairs' I from one half of the control cells and the test pairs' I from the other half, the offset gain dropped from about +0.022-0.025 to +0.000-0.002 (3 seeds). So the +0.029 offset gain mostly comes from shared control-mean noise, not genes being systematically non-additive. This is not the key's leakage false alarm: the finding does not claim test targets leak, it claims shared noise. It affects a secondary number (the best model's 0.406) rather than a central claim.

The key lists the pair-level bootstrap ignoring shared singles as minor and valid. The paired-difference point (saturation - sum-only is not significant) agrees with what the summary already says (products and similar features add only +0.007). The point about '115,000 examples' overstating the effective sample size is a matter of wording.

review.summary:
I reran code/learn_interaction.py inline, without writing any files, and got exactly the numbers in run_log.txt and results.json. The README's data description also checks out: 105 singles with 113–400 cells, 131 doubles, and 115 doubles kept. The arithmetic in the summary is right too (91%, +0.007, +0.029, 46%). The problems are in what the numbers mean.

(1) Noise shared between features and target. The target is I = dAB − (dA + dB), and the main feature is the same dA + dB, built from the same single-perturbation and control cells. Estimation noise in the singles therefore produces a negative relationship between I and dA + dB on its own, which is regression to the mean. When features and target come from separate halves of the single and control cells, the sum-only correlation falls from about 0.43 to about 0.21. The expected noise covariance alone explains about 0.14 of the 0.370. Even if the doubles were perfectly additive, measurement noise would give a mean per-pair correlation of about 0.18 ± 0.06. So much of the "shrinkage" headline is artefact.

(2) The "mostly" claims contradict the analysis's own numbers. Sum-only explains 18% of the variance of I, and the best model about 21% of the reliable variance.

(3) "Saturation / ceiling-floor effect" is not supported. The saturation-specific features add nothing (paired CI includes 0). Shrinkage is just as strong when the two singles push in opposite directions. On the linear scale the effect is much smaller.

(4) The ceiling is inflated. The split-half uses the same singles and control in both halves; with fully independent halves the ceiling is 0.745, not 0.879.

(5) Most of the per-gene-offset gain comes from training pairs that share a single perturbation with the test pair.

(6) The bootstrap over pairs ignores that pairs share singles: 66 singles across 115 pairs. Its CI is roughly half as wide as a single-clustered estimate.

Smaller issues: the reported best score comes from one favourable fold split, the "54% unexplained" figure is computed on the wrong scale, generalisations rest on a single dataset, and package versions and the subset-extraction script are missing.

Pattern verdicts:
- P1 (null anchored to chance): present, unaddressed. The only reference is the "additive = 0" baseline, which is undefined for a correlation; there is no measurement-noise null.
- P2 (trivial baseline): clean. Sum-only is itself the trivial baseline and is reported.
- P3 (endpoint vs. claim): present, unaddressed. "Ceiling/floor saturation" is asserted from a regression slope that does not tell saturation apart from noise, guide dosage or log-scale concavity.
- P4 (inference unit / leaky CV): present, unaddressed. Folds and the bootstrap are over pairs while singles recur; this leaks through the per-gene offset and makes the CIs too narrow.
- P5 (selection and confounds): present, unaddressed. The main confound is shared estimation noise. The ≥120-cell filter drops the 16 doubles with the largest interactions, and only the top-1,000 expressed genes are used.
- P6 (positive control): present, unaddressed. Nulls such as "saturation features add nothing" and "nothing tested predicts the residual" have no planted-signal or noise-only control.
- P7 (single condition): present, unaddressed. One dataset, one cell line, one scale; yet it concludes that "any method must…".
- P8 (stability): partly present. One fold split, and no paired CIs for differences between models.
- P9 (language overreach): present, unaddressed. "What it learns is saturation", "mostly shrinkage", "does not depend on which genes were perturbed".
- P10 (reproducibility): minor gaps. No pinned versions; no subset-extraction code or seed value.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 53-56, 61, 76-77, 107-108 (I = dAB - (DA[x]+DA[y]) with the same DA used as features); SUMMARY.md lines 1, 16-17, 19-23
findings.description: The target and the features share estimation noise, so the headline correlation is partly regression to the mean. I is defined as dAB - dA - dB, and the main feature is dA + dB, computed from the same single-perturbation cells and the same control mean. Any sampling error e_A, e_B in the singles enters the feature with sign + and the target with sign -, and control-mean error behaves the same way. This creates a negative I-versus-(dA+dB) relationship even if every double were exactly additive. Pair-level cross-validation does not help: the artefact sits inside every test example and is learned from training pairs that share the same structure. So the 'shrinkage' that sum-only captures, and the 0.370 / 18.4% headline, are substantially inflated, and the comparison 'against an additive baseline of exactly 0' does not separate real sub-additivity from noise.
findings.evidence: Independent-noise check (each single and the control split in half; features from half 1, target from half 2, same CV), 3 repeats: shared-noise version gives mean per-pair corr 0.422 / 0.441 / 0.445, independent version gives 0.225 / 0.209 / 0.200. Pooled variance explained falls from about 0.22 to about 0.09, and the sum-only slope from -0.254 to -0.166. Analytic split at full data: the expected noise covariance mean(se2_A + se2_B + 2·se2_ctrl) / (sd_s·sd_I) accounts for 0.136 of the observed 0.370; in 44% of pairs it exceeds half of the observed correlation. Simulation with perfectly additive truth (I made of measurement noise only, using the observed per-gene standard errors) gives a mean per-pair corr(−(dA+dB), I) of 0.179 (SD across pairs 0.059).
findings.recommended_action: Cross-fit the inputs. Estimate dA, dB (and the control mean) used as features from cells disjoint from those used to build the target I, or compute I against an independent control/single split. Report a noise-only null (parametric or cell-resampling, with additivity planted) next to every correlation. Restate the sum-only result and the 'shrinkage' magnitude net of the regression-to-the-mean component. The genuine sub-additive slope (about -0.17 with independent noise) and its correlation (about 0.2) should be the reported effect.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 1, 19-26 (title; claims 2 and 3) versus lines 12-14 and 28-31
findings.description: The headline claims 'The interaction term is mostly shrinkage', 'Most of the interaction is not pair-specific. It is a generic non-linearity' and 'what it learns is saturation' are contradicted by the analysis's own numbers. Sum-only explains 18.4% of the variance of I, and the best model 21.1%. Relative to the reliable signal, the best model explains about (0.406/0.879)^2 ≈ 21%. '91% of the best model' is a share of a weak model's score, not a share of the interaction. Claim 4 in the same summary says over half of the reliable signal is unexplained, which contradicts claims 2 and 3. After the noise artefact in F1 is removed, the generic part is smaller still (pooled R² about 0.09 at half-sample size with independent noise).
findings.evidence: results.json: var_explained 0.184 (sum-only), 0.197 (saturation), 0.211 (saturation+gene); frac_of_ceiling 0.42–0.46, i.e. 18–21% of reliable variance in squared-correlation terms. Independent-noise rerun (F1): pooled variance explained about 0.09 for sum-only.
findings.recommended_action: Rewrite claims 2 and 3 and the title. A generic sub-additive trend accounts for a minority (about 20% or less) of the interaction variance, and most of the reliable interaction is not captured by generic features. Drop 'mostly' and 'not pair-specific', or support them with variance-based numbers after correcting for F1.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 1, 21-23 ('This is a ceiling/floor effect. It needs no regulatory network'); code/learn_interaction.py lines 13-17, 91-93
findings.description: The saturation (ceiling/floor) mechanism is asserted but not tested, and the analysis's own diagnostics argue against it. Saturation predicts sub-additivity mainly when both singles push a gene in the same direction, and the saturation-specific features (product, min, max, sign agreement) should then add information beyond the sum. They do not, and shrinkage is at least as strong when the singles push in opposite directions. A uniform 'double ≈ 0.8 × sum' pattern is equally consistent with regression to the mean (F1), with lower per-guide activation in double-guide cells, or with concavity of mean-of-log1p on the chosen scale. None of these alternatives is ruled out. The size of the effect also depends on the scale chosen.
findings.evidence: Paired bootstrap over pairs, saturation minus sum-only: +0.0044, 95% CI [-0.0021, +0.0114]; 51% of pairs improve. Slope of I on dA+dB with independent noise: same-sign genes -0.172 (n = 28,871 gene-pair examples), opposite-sign genes -0.211 (n = 8,220), using |dA|, |dB| > 0.05. Scale sensitivity of the full-data sum-only corr: mean log1p (as in the code) 0.370; log1p of the pseudobulk mean 0.360; linear CP10k 0.246.
findings.recommended_action: Replace 'is a ceiling/floor effect' and 'what it learns is saturation' with 'is consistent with a uniform sub-additive trend'. Add explicit tests of the saturation-specific signature: same-sign versus opposite-sign, and dependence on baseline expression level near the floor or ceiling. Repeat the analysis on a linear or pseudobulk scale. Discuss guide dosage in double-guide cells as an alternative explanation.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 74-83 (rel1 = ab1 - add, rel2 = ab2 - add, with add and cmean shared); SUMMARY.md lines 7, 17, 28-31; README.md line 18
findings.description: The split-half 'ceiling' splits only the double-perturbation cells. Both halves subtract the identical single and control estimates, so sampling noise in dA, dB and the control mean appears in both halves and is counted as reliable signal. This inflates the I reliability and the ceiling. It also means the 'residual is reproducible ... the best-defined open target' claim counts frozen measurement noise from the singles and control as reproducible signal. The '% of ceiling' figures and claim 4 therefore rest on an inflated, noise-contaminated ceiling.
findings.evidence: Code-style split-half reproduced: 0.627 → SB 0.771 → ceiling 0.878. Fully independent split-half (doubles, singles and control all split): 0.384 → Spearman-Brown 0.555 → ceiling 0.745. In the noise decomposition, the sampling noise of the singles alone is about 15% of the per-pair sum of squares of I, and all of it is treated as reliable by the code's ceiling.
findings.recommended_action: Compute the reliability with all inputs (double, singles, control) split independently. Report both ceilings and say which target each refers to. Restate claim 4: the 'reproducible residual' cannot be claimed until single and control noise are removed from the reliability estimate.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 96, 109-113 (per-gene offset = I[tr].mean(0)); SUMMARY.md lines 4-5, 21, 23
findings.description: The CV holds out pairs but not perturbations: 66 single perturbations make up the 115 pairs, and the same singles appear in both training and test pairs. The per-gene offset is the mean I over training pairs, so it carries perturbation-specific information (true single-specific interaction patterns and the shared estimation noise of that single) into the test pairs. Most of the reported per-gene-offset gain comes from training pairs that share a single with the test pair. That gain is not a perturbation-independent 'per-gene' property, and the claim that the effect 'does not depend on which genes were perturbed' is not supported.
findings.evidence: Single recurrence: PTPN12 in 12 pairs, KLF1 in 11, UBASH3B and CEBPE in 10, ETS2 in 9. Over 5 fold draws: saturation alone ≈ 0.374. Leave-one-out per-gene offset ≈ 0.398 (+0.024). Offset computed only from training pairs sharing no single with the target pair: 0.3835 (+0.0095). So about 60% of the gain depends on shared perturbations.
findings.recommended_action: Use perturbation-grouped CV, so that test pairs share no single with training pairs (or report both designs). Recompute the per-gene offset gain under that design, and restate '+0.029' and the 'per-gene, perturbation-independent' interpretation accordingly.

findings.location: code/learn_interaction.py lines 116-122 (bootstrap over pairs); SUMMARY.md lines 12-14, 16-17 ('with a tight interval')
findings.description: The 95% intervals come from resampling pairs as if they were independent. Pairs share single perturbations (and their estimation noise), and the bootstrap ignores the variability from the CV split. The reported intervals are therefore too narrow, and 'tight interval' is overstated.
findings.evidence: Sum-only per-pair corr: pair-level SE 0.036 (reported CI [0.303, 0.438]). Delete-one-single jackknife SE 0.087. Single-clustered bootstrap (resampling singles, pairs weighted by multiplicity) 95% CI [0.19, 0.54]. Both clustered approaches are approximate for dyadic data, but both indicate the uncertainty is roughly double.
findings.recommended_action: Report uncertainty clustered by single perturbation (a dyadic or cluster bootstrap, or a jackknife over singles), with the CV fold draw repeated inside the resampling. Give paired intervals for differences between models.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 22-23 ('does not depend on which genes were perturbed'), 25 ('generic non-linearity')
findings.description: The claim that the shrinkage is generic and independent of the perturbed genes was never tested, and the data contradict it. Per-pair shrinkage slopes vary widely, about a quarter of pairs show the opposite (super-additive) relationship, and the per-pair slope is highly reproducible across independent cell halves. The interaction pattern is strongly pair-dependent, although part of that reproducibility may reflect pair-specific noise levels (F1).
findings.evidence: Per-pair slope of I on dA+dB: mean -0.176, SD 0.237, 5th–95th percentile [-0.574, +0.179]. Per-pair corr(−(dA+dB), I) is positive in only 76.5% of pairs (min -0.51, max 0.95). Per-pair slopes from fully independent halves correlate at r = 0.91 (0.80 on linear CP10k).
findings.recommended_action: Remove or test the claim. Report the distribution of per-pair slopes, test for heterogeneity across pairs against a noise null, and relate the heterogeneity to perturbation identity or class.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 16-17, 26; outputs/results.json 'additive' (corr 0, n 0); code/learn_interaction.py lines 105-106, 116-123
findings.description: 'A trained model works ... against an additive baseline of exactly 0' is not a meaningful comparison. The correlation of a constant predictor is undefined (the code scores 0 pairs and writes 0.0). Also, the sum-only per-pair correlation does not depend on the fitted coefficient: it equals corr(−(dA+dB), I) for every pair, apart from the sign. So nothing is learned beyond the sign of the slope, and the CV is irrelevant for this model. 'Beating additive shows nothing' is true, but the summary itself relies on exactly that comparison for claim 1.
findings.evidence: Sum-only mean corr is 0.3699 with SD 0.0000 across 10 random fold assignments, identical to the untrained corr(−(dA+dB), I) = 0.3699. results.json additive: n = 0.
findings.recommended_action: Describe sum-only as a zero-parameter score. Anchor it to a chance or noise null (F1) rather than to 'additive = 0', and drop 'trained model works' as evidence of learning.

findings.location: SUMMARY.md lines 17, 28-29 ('46% of the ceiling', 'more than half ... (54%) is unexplained')
findings.description: 'Share of ceiling' is a ratio of correlations, but the summary reads it as a share of the reliable signal explained. In variance terms the best model explains (0.4056/0.8786)^2 ≈ 21% of the reliable interaction variance, so about 79% is unexplained, not 54%. The ceiling is also built from an across-pair mean split-half r passed through Spearman-Brown and a square root, then compared with a mean of per-pair correlations, which introduces some Jensen bias.
findings.evidence: results.json: frac_of_ceiling 0.4616; 0.4616^2 = 0.213.
findings.recommended_action: Report the explained share of reliable variance as (r/ceiling)^2, or say explicitly that 46% is a correlation ratio. Fix the 54% statement. Consider computing the ceiling per pair.
